News.title: Woman ‘who killed 2 girls with poisoned berries in revenge plot’ fights extradition over brutal foreign jail conditions
News.content:
JAIL PLEA Woman ‘who killed 2 girls with poisoned berries in revenge plot’ fights extradition over brutal foreign jail conditions







Next

A WOMAN accused of killing two schoolgirls with poisoned berries in Colombia is fighting extradition over brutal jail conditions.

Ines de Bedout, 14, and her friend Emilia Forero, 13, died days after eating chocolate-covered raspberries laced with the highly toxic metal thallium, known as the “silent killer” in April last year.



The girls believed the berries were a free gift from a delivery company, a court heard.

The 21-year-old brother of one of the victims and another teenage girl also ate the laced berries and were raced to hospital.



Zulma Guzman Castro, 55, is wanted in Colombia on suspicion of murdering the two girls and is battling against extradition at Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

Ms Bedout was the daughter of Castro’s former lover, Juan de Bedout, and her friend was visiting for a sleepover when the deadly delivery arrived.

Castro – a mum-of-one who founded electric car sharing company Car B in 2015 – carried out the poisonings as an “act of vengeance” following a failed affair with Mr de Bedout, prosecutors claim.

A worldwide hunt was launched for the 55-year-old after she left Colombia last year.



She was later found on Battersea Bridge in London on December 16, where she was hauled from the water after jumping in and later arrested.

Rosemary Davidson, for the Colombian government, told the court a delivery driver attended the de Bedout address at 6.30pm on April 4 last year ‘”with a parcel the family initially refused to accept”.

“On hearing that the chocolate-covered raspberries were a free gift from the delivery app, the parcel was brought in and kept in the freezer,” she said.

“Later Ines ate eight raspberries, Emelia ate about five, and a third girl, referred to as GBC, ate three. All three were taken to hospital. Emelia died of multiple organ failure on 5 April.”

Ines also died, and GBC suffered serious illness – all three were found to have suffered acute thallium poisoning.



The colourless, odourless and tasteless metal is commonly used to make electronics and radiation detection equipment.

Guzman, who has been held on remand at HMP Bronzefield, appeared in court wearing a white shirt under a dark jacket, her blonde hair in a sweeping bob.

She refused an interpreter and made copious notes during the hearing.



Guzman has also received a summons from Colombia requiring her to attend a virtual hearing there in relation to two charges of murder and two attempted murder next Monday.

Ms Davidson said: “This is a case involving very serious allegations where the public interest in extradition is very high. The Colombian authorities have worked with us in a spirit of maximum cooperation.”

She dismissed concerns that temporary detention facilities provided for Ms Guzman while awaiting trial in Colombia would be inadequate.

“There would be a well-lit and ventilated cell and there is certainly plenty of space. Her article 3 rights would be respected.”

Joel Smith, KC, defending Guzman, took issue with the suggestion “that the Colombians have given every cooperation”.



He said: “We have been waiting two days for requested information.

“The issue of temporary detention has not been addressed. There is the history of detention in Colombia to consider …urinating into bottles, men and women together.”

Mr Smith described conditions in Colombian prisons as a “crisis” and recalled a case where a woman accused of killing a child was attacked by five inmates and her cell was set alight.

The court also heard a vet used by Guzman in Bogota had told Colombian police he accepted a payment of 12,000 Pesos from her as credit on a delivery app in lieu of cash after he vaccinated her cats.

A digital transaction for the same sum has been linked to the delivery of the poisoned raspberries, Ms Davidson said.



Colombian police geolocation expert Diana Hernandez tried to pin down the movements of Guzman on the day of the delivery by analysing a phone number thought to be hers.

“The phone number ending in 686 registered in Argentina can be shown to be at the delivery address at around the time of the pick up,” said Ms Davidson.

She added: “Deleted searches for ‘uses of thallium’ were made and deleted from an email address linked to the defendant.”

Earlier a tribute to Emilia Forero was shared on social media by her devastated father, saying: “Fourteen years ago, a life of hopes, joys and dreams began; a life that filled a family, a father and a mother.

“But it wasn’t just the joy of someone else’s life; it was the beginning of the life of an excellent human being who had dreams, hopes and goals.



“As a father, it is incomprehensible to think that someone was capable of taking this away. She did not just take away my opportunity to be a father-in-law, grandfather and everything else one can be as a parent.

“She took away my daughter’s opportunity to be a girlfriend, a professional, a wife, a mother and a daughter.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I am sorry I could not protect you from this broken world. Despite the pain, I am glad to have had you in my life. I hope to have one last hug from you, even if it is only in my dreams.”

The hearing continues.

News.title: Son, 33, ‘chopped dad’s body into 238 pieces & stuffed remains in freezer’ after beating him to death over ‘poison plot’
News.content:
GRISLY END Son, 33, ‘chopped dad’s body into 238 pieces & stuffed remains in freezer’ after beating him to death over ‘poison plot’







Next

A MAN accused of chopping up his father’s body into 238 pieces is set to appear in court in the Netherlands today.

Tijmen Visser, 33, was arrested in 2024 after police found 19 bin bags with body parts stuffed across two freezers in their home in Heerhugowaard.



His father, Albert, was reported missing in 2021 – with authorities initially believing that he had taken his own life or left the country.

It was not until 2023 that police issued a missing person‘s report after a friend of the victim raised the alarm.



The last sign of life was an entry into his notebook, where he tracked all his expenses.

A major search uncovered the frozen remains in the home where they had been hidden for almost four years.



At first, officers had started digging up the garden – but K-9 sniffer dogs eventually led them to the house.

Visser’s lawyer, Daniel Fontain, had previously told the court that his client had attacked his father in self-defence.

“His father offered him a cup of tea and he saw that his father wanted to poison him with rat poison,” he said, according to NH.

“After he confronted him about it, he attacked his son with a knife.”



During the struggle, Visser kicked and punched his father multiple times until he noticed that he was no longer breathing.

Panicked, he sawed the body into pieces and stored them in freezers, after which he psychologically repressed the event for years, according to the lawyer.

Fontain told the court that the pair had a “bad relationship” marked by a lot of violence.

He said: “My client experienced a difficult childhood with a lot of violence.

“His father had a sex, alcohol, and gambling addiction and was loathed by the neighbourhood.”



Neighbours told investigators that they often heard arguments from the house.

“Albert was known to have loud arguments with his son,” one person said. “But no one thought it would end like this.”

Visser’s 31-year-old ex-girlfriend has been named as a co-suspect, but her case will be heard later.

The case continues.

News.title: Man ‘drugged & raped unconscious wife for over 20 years before inviting strangers online to have sex with her’
News.content:
UK 'PELICOT' Man ‘drugged & raped unconscious wife for over 20 years before inviting strangers online to have sex with her’







Next

A MAN drugged and raped his unconscious wife for more than 20 years before inviting strangers online to have sex with her, a court heard.

In his 60s, the man is accused of indulging “barbaric fantasies” after coming up with a “blueprint” to drug and rape her with nine other men.



He held down a respectable job and was a trusted member of the community in Stockport, Greater Manchester.

But his marriage was torn apart when cops swooped on their home last October.



He was arrested in front of his shocked wife, who was told by cops they believed he had been raping and sexually abusing her for over 20 years.

Detectives also said he had been drugging her so other men could come round and abuse her, Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court heard.

They all led “double lives” and had hidden their depravity, which “knew no bounds” it is alleged.

A jury of nine men and three women were told the husband took a million photos and videos of his wife being abused.



Today, prosecutor Louise Oakley KC told how he was in contact with men online who shared an interest in sexually abusing “unaware” women.

Ms Oakley told jurors: “He did not hide the fact that his wife was and would be unaware of the third parties he communicated with.

“His profile specifically referred to her being ‘out of it’.



“At no point did he suggest, the Crown say, to any of these defendants that as a couple they engaged in sleepy roleplay or fantasy.

“She was quite clearly wasted, unconscious, out of it – however you want to describe it.

“The sad reality of this case is that there are many, many men out there whose fantasy is to have sex and abuse an unconscious and unresponsive woman.”



The court had already heard that the man admitted 62 charges including multiple rapes.

Among them was defendant David Graves, 60, who the man befriended in an online chat group in 2018 before the pair messaged directly on Skype.

Graves encouraged the husband to send him pictures of his wife in September 2018 when she was “unaware”.

In return Graves is alleged to have offered to supply “some tablets” to the husband to help render her unconscious.



In February 2020, Graves asked the husband “How’s my slut?” to which he responded “you don’t have something to knock her out properly?”.

A few days later the husband messaged saying “I want GHB or something soon”, lamenting that his wife drinking wine each night was “unreliable”.

Other messages revealed the husband and Graves arguing after tablets Graves said he had sent failed to arrive on three occasions.

The husband was so desperate for drugs to arrive he provided Graves with the home address of a recently deceased relative, the court heard.



In return, Graves asked to be sent some of the victim’s underwear, Ms Oakley added.

Graves also made derogatory comments about her appearance in pictures sent to him by the husband, saying that it was “embarrassing for you”.

When the tablets finally arrived, the husband complained they were hard to dissolve in liquid when crushed and made his wife’s wine “cloudy”.

Graves suggested hiding them in her food, with the husband later complaining that his wife said a curry they were eating tasted funny.

Earlier the jury heard how the first man to visit and abuse the wife was defendant Robert Stewart, 70, in 2016.



But after the wife “stirred” while in bed, he left with no sexual activity taking place.

Ms Oakley told the court this led the husband to start researching drugs which would knock his wife out rather than just relying on alcohol.

She said: “His perversity did not wane. He wanted to share her but recognised that alcohol alone was not going to be enough.

“So desperate was he, he would share imagery of his wife with complete strangers.

“He would then discuss how they would supply him with drugs in order that she be raped, and sharing their home address.”



The court heard the husband carried out online research including news articles and charity websites.

He is alleged to have search information about sleeping pills, side-effects and use of date rape drugs including GHB.

In early 2019, the husband purchased Zolpidem sleeping tablets online, Ms Oakley said.

Opening the trial on Monday, Ms Oakley told jurors Stewart sent a message to the husband after he visited the house.

It urged him to “delete all images” and said “remember what happened to the guy in France”, which she said was referencing Dominique Pelicot.



Mr Pelicot was jailed for 20 years after being found guilty of raping his ex-wife Gisele along with 47 other men.

Stewart, 70, denies rape, conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to administer a substance with intent, Graves, 60, denies conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent and Philip Wild, 59, denies sexual assault, attempted rape, assault by penetration and conspiracy to rape.

Daniel Rayner, 42, denies conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent, Mohammed Sabir, 28, denies rape and conspiracy to rape and Jordan Wallace, 31, denies rape and attempted rape.

Alan Keelan, 42, denies attempted rape and assault by penetration, Richard Townsend, 38, denies assault by penetration and Jonathan Kirk, 43, denies rape and conspiracy to rape.

The offences are said to have taken place on various dates between 2015 and 2025.



In September, the woman’s husband of 40 years admitted 62 charges including multiple rapes, jurors were told.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Four other men – Karl Lindsay, 56, of Taunton, Somerset, Graham Brougham, 74, of Northwich, Cheshire, Keith Fotheringham, 59, of Dundee, and Sean Peers, 38, of Stockport – have pleaded guilty to various sexual offences at earlier hearings.

The trial continues.

News.title: Teen ‘monster’ strangled girlfriend, 14, to death and dumped body in river after being told she may be pregnant
News.content:
Next

A “MONSTER” teen strangled his 14-year-old girlfriend to death and dumped her body in a river after she revealed she might be pregnant.

Raymond Wright Jr, now 18, was found guilty of the second-degree murder of Samantha Humphrey after a jury deliberated for just five hours.



The couple were both aged 14 when schoolgirl Samantha vanished into thin air after a late-night walk in New York state in November 2022.

Her tied-up remains were pulled from the freezing Mohawk River three months later.



But it took until May 2025 for a medical examiner to confirm the teen had been strangled to death.

Wright took the stand and confessed to having a physical scrap with Samantha, but claimed he left her alone by the riverbank.

His defence team even suggested the youngster had taken her own life after battling with mental health issues.

But prosecutors tore his story to shreds, pinpointing a suspicious 90-minute black hole in his movements on the night she died.

Christina Tremante-Pelham, Schenectady County’s deputy chief assistant district attorney, told jurors: “He was never able to account for an hour-and-a-half gap in his account.

“And that’s of course because he was killing her and disposing of her body.”



In court, it emerged Samantha’s phone history showed searches for early pregnancy symptoms – though it was never confirmed whether she was expecting at the time of her death.

Meanwhile, Wright’s sick search history chillingly included queries on how human bodies decompose in water.

Samantha’s devastated loved ones wept as the guilty verdict was read out, while Wright’s mother launched a foul-mouthed tirade before storming out of the courtroom.



The victim’s father, Jeffrey Humphrey, raced to catch the verdict but arrived just as the vile killer was being escorted out.

He told Times Union: “So I didn’t get to see the look on that monster’s face.

“But I got to see the look on the face of the monster that made the monster.”

Speaking outside court, Jeffrey warned: “Hopefully, the danger that he poses won’t be ignored in his parole hearings.

“As it unfortunately was when we went to certain local agencies and told them about the danger he posed more than a year before he killed Sam.”



He said he hoped the verdict means the monster teen won’t hurt anyone else.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wright was 14 when he killed Samantha, so was convicted as a juvenile.

When sentenced in January, he faces up to 15 years to life in prison.

News.title: ‘Anticyclonic gloom’ grips UK ahead of Bonfire Night as Met Office reveals how long fog, drizzle & grey skies will last
News.content:
Next

AN ‘anticyclonic gloom’ is covering the UK in fog, grey skies and drizzle this week, according to the Met Office.

However, weather conditions should remain largely dry.

The phenomenon occurs when high-pressure settles over the country in the winter, creating a still atmosphere that suppresses the movement of air.



This traps moisture and low-level cloud, and prevents fog from dispersing, which cannot lift and clear due to very light winds and weak sunshine at this time of year.



As a result, Met Office spokesperson Grahame Madge confirmed to The Sun that the anticyclonic gloom has returned to the UK this week, as Brits should expect to see more fog, drizzle and light winds.

Explaining that anticyclone is a meteorological term for an area of high pressure, he added: “It is a circumstance you get with high pressure in the winter – where mist, fog and clouds can be trapped under the high pressure causing murkiness and an absence of sunshine.

“When you combine this with still conditions, it means that the mist, fog and air that builds up doesn’t have a chance to be blown away”.



A return to westerly conditions – winds coming in from the Atlantic- can quickly remove high pressure in favour of fresher air.

However, Madge reassured that anticyclonic glooms are common throughout the autumn months, adding “the good news is that the high pressure will change shape and move around over the UK”.

“That means, for example, along the South, strong easterly winds should blow some of the high pressure and move the misty conditions out the way.

“Those in the centre of the UK may continue to experience these weather conditions for a few days”.



As for the weather forecast, in London and the South East, high pressure will continue throughout the week with a brisk breeze which will make the temperature appear cooler than forecast.

Meanwhile, the more northern parts of England can expect to see similar weather conditions and temperatures, with patches of fog in the morning.

The Met Office also forecast that while high pressure is likely to remain influential into the start of the weekend, there should be dry weather for many.

News.title: Horror moment huge road roller reverses over man in wheelchair and crushes him to death
News.content:
Next

THIS is the harrowing moment a man riding an electric wheelchair is crushed to death by a reversing road roller in China.

Horror footage shows the heavy engineering vehicle driving on a patch of road freshly coated with asphalt before the driver begins to reverse directly towards the victim.



The fatal incident happened on Jiefang South Road in Qiaotou Town, in Qinghai Province, on October 28.

Identified by authorities only as Li, the victim had entered the roadworks area through a gap in the barriers.



Emergency medical workers rushed to the scene and desperately tried to save Li, but to no avail.

The municipal maintenance department had been carrying out routine road maintenance work at the time.



Authorities are now investigating whether the construction site was properly sealed off and whether the on-site safety officer had fulfilled their responsibilities.

A statement said: “An investigation team has been established to investigate the closure of the construction site and the performance of duties by the on-site safety officer.”

The official announcement did not disclose further details about Li’s age or the identity of the road roller operator.

A similar incident was reported in the village of Tandalija, in the Indian state of Gujarat, in August.



A 19-year-old woman was killed after she came under a road roller when her scooter skidded on a wet road.

Two young women who were travelling with her managed to escape with minor injuries.

All three fell on the road and the victim was run over by the vehicle that was passing alongside them.

She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Similarly, the incident was captured on a CCTV camera near the junction.

News.content:

TORTURED TO DEATH Parents of girl, 4, found dead on motorway with iron burns & bite marks 39 YEARS ago face trial after shock DNA clue







Next

THE parents of a girl who was found dead in a roadside ditch with iron burns and bite marks have been charged 40 years after she was found.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, and her ex-husband Ahmed Touloub, 74, have been accused of torturing their four-year-old daughter in France in the 1980s.



The mum has been charged with torture that led to death, while her former partner has been accused of failing to report the abuse.

El Bakhti, the main defendant, appeared in court on Monday trying to cover her face with a scarf.



Touloub struggled to make his way up the courtroom steps as he arrived using a cane, wearing a black hat, a face mask and dark glasses.

Little Inass Touloub was found in a ditch next to a French motorway in 1987.

Her remains showed signs of violence, including iron burns and human bites from a woman, according to forensic documents.

When the body was found, no children in the nearby area had been reported missing.



So police launched a plea for help across 30 countries – sparking an urgent operation to identify the girl.

Her image was plastered in tens of thousands of French school and town halls.

But the case went dark as it was never resolved.



Decades later, a DNA sample from a suspect in a separate violent case triggered a match with genetic traces from Inass’ clothes.

The DNA belonged to the girl’s brother – with the development leading to the case’s reopening.

Their parents were arrested shortly after in 2018.

The couple had seven children in total, including Inass.

Neither parent admitted to allegations they were behind their daughter’s death.



Instead, they accused each other of domestic abuse.

Additional health experts have requested to assess the two suspects.

The mum has severe kidney pain while her elderly former partner claims he suffers from memory problems.

The defence’s request was accepted for Touloub but the mum has been refused a test.

News.title: The 8 unexpected joys of working on Christmas Day include a peaceful drive & giving back to the community, poll finds
News.content:
FESTIVE FUN The 8 unexpected joys of working on Christmas Day include a peaceful drive & giving back to the community, poll finds







Next

THE EIGHT unexpected joys of working on Christmas Day have been revealed and they are not all about the money.

A poll of 1,000 adults who have worked a shift on December 25 saw a lack of pressure to have a “perfect” day and avoiding long distance travel to see relatives ranked high on the list.



Meanwhile, 27 per cent of festive workers value not having to worry about cooking Christmas Dinner, while 19 per cent love escaping the mountain of washing up afterwards.

Others cherish the peace and quiet of traffic-free roads on their morning commute (37 per cent) and having a space from tricky family dynamics (15 per cent).



For 37 per cent, the biggest draw is making Christmas special for someone else, while a quarter enjoy giving back to their local community.

Among healthcare staff, 45 per cent said they cherish helping making the day meaningful for patients who cannot be with their families.



The research was commissioned by pub chain Greene King, whose Big Christmas Shift scheme is offering 30,000 free meals to Christmas Day workers between December 2 and December 5.

Carried out by OnePoll, the study found the typical festive worker is now on their fourth Christmas shift in a row, with 21 per cent having worked 10 or more during their career.



Official data from the Office for National Statistics showed 1.2million worked on Christmas Day last year, up from 1.1million in 2018.

Key moments for medical and care staff included comforting someone struggling and helping those who would otherwise spend the day alone.

Others have helped people take part in the festive tradition (16 per cent) or connect with loved ones (20 per cent).



Among all workers polled, 30 per cent said their highlight was watching someone’s mood improve because of their help, while 27 per cent loved receiving an unexpected thank you.

Many have even received a card, a gift or festive treats on the day.

To make their shifts work, 79 per cent tweak their own traditions, with some moving their family celebrations before (25 per cent) or after (8 per cent) December 25.

Others simply move key moments to different times; including their roast dinner (45 per cent), seeing extended family (37 per cent), opening presents (31 per cent) or taking a festive walk (18 per cent).

Andrew Gallagher, from Greene King, said: “Behind so many special moments that the rest of us enjoy, there are people giving up time with their loved ones to make Christmas special for somebody else.



“Offering 30,000 free meals is our way of saying thank you to every person behind the scenes and giving them a chance to enjoy some well-earned festive cheer of their own.”

News.title: Learjet faced 'perfect storm' and pulling up 'wasn't possible' before Florida crash
News.content:
Learjet faced 'perfect storm' and pulling up 'wasn't possible' before Florida crash

Nine people were killed on a Learjet 60 when it crashed in Greenacres, Florida, en route from Austin to the Bahamas, having met an unusual storm system

Learjet plane may have received warning months prior

A private jet crashed in a "perfect storm", killing all nine on board in Florida after an attempt to ascend failed - and may not even have been possible, according to experts.

‌



‌



The plane burst into flames when it crashed in Greenacres, about seven miles southwest of West Palm Beach, with thick black smoke engulfing the crash site.

‌



Victims included the 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, who made the final radio transmissions, as well as technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children.

‌



The plane, a Learjet 60, had departed Austin, Texas and was en route to the Bahamas when it crashed on Sunday having encountered an unusual convective storm system.

View 3 Images Nathalia Gadelha, 20, was the co-pilot (Image: itsnatfilg/Threads)

Questions over Learjet black box which could explain final moments before horror Florida crash READ MORE :

Horror Florida Learjet crash theory emerges as investigators issue major update READ MORE :

The plane appears to have attempted to climb above the storm, having requested and received clearance at 35,000ft to ascend to 37,000ft after reporting freezing temperatures and ice forming on the jet’s hull. Ice can be dangerous as it affects the air flows around the wings and makes it harder for the plane to remain aloft.

‌



“This was kind of the perfect storm of trouble,” aviation lawyer Zachary S. Gorwitz told the New York Post. When there is ice on wings it is harder to achieve lift - and the angle where a plane can stall is lower than would normally be the case. And so it possible that an attempt to climb with ice on the wings led to the plane stalling.

View 3 Images Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children Emma and Charlie, all died in the crash (Image: Family Handout)

‌



The aircraft likely started breaking apart before it slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball, a federal investigator has said. The jet did a steep nosedive, leaving behind a crater and a wide debris field as rain pounded the area.

“At that point, I’m sure the pilot was trying to pull back on the controls and get the nose up, but I’m sure at that speed and that angle, it just wasn’t possible,” Mr Gorwitz said.

‌



Authorities said weather will be a key initial focus of the investigation, and that the National Transportation Safety Board will also examine the actions of the crew and look for any mechanical problems with the plane.

View 3 Images The plane crashed in Greenacres (Image: @X)

‌



The plane was heading east when the pilot started to report problems. According to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net, Ms Filgueiras said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700ft.

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the co-pilot told controllers in a professional tone. The situation rapidly deteriorated and within a few transmissions panic set in as the crew realised their fate.

‌



The co-pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000ft and then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.

“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000ft per minute,” she radioed. “We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute.”

Article continues below

Moments later, she added: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”

News.title: Cooking now a go-to way to unwind on weekends as 6 in 10 Brits ditch nights out
News.content:
Cooking now a go-to way to unwind on weekends as 6 in 10 Brits ditch nights out

Three quarters of adults now look forward to spending their weekends at home, and many are using cooking as their main form of relaxation.

View 3 Images Cooking has become a popular way to relax on weekends (Image: Getty Images)

Six in 10 adults have ditched nights out at bars and clubs in favour of evenings spent at home cooking. Research involving 2,000 adults revealed 73% now look forward to spending their weekends at home, with 56% doing so more frequently than they once did. However, it's not purely about cutting costs; four in ten of those choosing to remain home feel happier as a result.

‌



‌



While at home, 32% opt to spend their weekends cooking. Four in ten will utilise the additional time to experiment with new or more elaborate recipes, with 34% feeling they have greater energy to dedicate to cooking.

‌



View 3 Images People use the extra time to try out new recipes (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The slower pace can turn cooking into valuable downtime, with 22% claiming it helps them slow down and be more present, while 18% feel it allows them to switch off from screens and digital distractions.

The study was commissioned by Hotpoint, which has partnered with Fuschia Sirois, professor of social and health psychology at Durham University, to explore how our weekends have shifted towards resting and recharging at home.

Prof. Sirois said: "A night out can feel like the best way to unwind after a long week, but, psychologically, it often isn't.

‌



"Studies on how we recover from work look at switching off, relaxing, learning something new and feeling in control of our time. A night in cooking can cover all of those, which a night out rarely does.

"At home we get to choose how we use our time and who we share it with. People talk about the joy of missing out, and I think that's exactly what we're seeing."

‌



Find out which kind of weekender you are with this quiz

The research also revealed that preparing meals has become a social activity, with one in four people cooking for friends and family at weekends. Nearly half (47%) make spending time with loved ones a weekend priority, while 14% described cooking for others as their love language.

‌



For many, however, time spent in the kitchen has evolved into a form of self-care, with 33% relishing the opportunity to treat themselves – and others – to quality food.

Meanwhile, 22% derive a genuine sense of accomplishment from their culinary creations, with 19% embracing the idea of having a 'special' weekend routine.

‌



View 3 Images Cooking can be very sociable (Image: Getty Images)

Yet despite having more time to try new things, those surveyed, via OnePoll, are largely sticking to tried-and-tested favourites on Saturdays, with Spaghetti Bolognese leading the weekend menu, followed by curry and stir-fry.

‌



Adam Norris, senior product manager at Hotpoint, said: "As autumn sets in, the weekend gives people permission to slow the pace, spend more time at home and enjoy cooking without the pressure of the working week.

"What's interesting is how cooking transforms from a midweek chore into a weekend pleasure.

‌



"For those trying a new recipe, it can be daunting, but with the right appliances on hand and the time to enjoy the process, cooking can be a great way to build confidence, switch off from digital distractions, and share the feeling of home."

News.title: Black Friday shoppers plan to spend £304 on themselves this year
News.content:
Black Friday shoppers plan to spend £304 on themselves this year

The average Black Friday shopper will spend £304 treating themselves this year — £170 more than last year — with fashion, beauty and tech among the top buys

View 3 Images People are more likely to treat themselves when Black Friday comes around (Image: Getty Images)

Shoppers are set to spend an average of just over £304 on themselves this Black Friday, new research has revealed. A survey of 2,000 adults who participate in the November sales event found 35% intend to purchase items for themselves rather than hunt for Christmas presents for loved ones.

‌



‌



The typical Black Friday shopper will part with £170.33 more than they did last year, with 32% believing they deserve a treat. Over four in 10 (41%) have held off until the one-day event to snap up something they genuinely want, while 29% have been contemplating their purchase for the past three months.

‌



Fashion items (25%), beauty products (20%) and small household appliances (16%) featured amongst the most popular planned purchases.

‌



View 3 Images One in four plan to buy clothes in the sale (Image: Getty Images)

The research, commissioned by Samsung ahead of its Black Friday offers launching on 4th November, revealed Millennials are the generation set to spend the most on treating themselves (£386.34) on Friday 27th November.

Zeena Hill, a spokesperson for the brand, said: "The smartest shoppers aren't chasing the lowest price tag, they're hunting for long-term value.

‌



"We're seeing a clear trend where households are making calculated adjustments in their everyday spending so they can invest in home upgrades that will last."

View 3 Images Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy big expensive items (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The research found 21% of Black Friday shoppers plan a major purchase up to three months beforehand, reducing spending on takeaways or dining out (25%), coffees and snacks (20%) and nights out (19%) to save for it. Among those major purchases, 23% are planning to invest in technology such as phones, tablets, laptops and TVs.

Regarding tech purchases, the study found that long-term value mattered significantly, with half of respondents believing a more expensive product justifies the additional cost if it's built to last.

‌



But while 43% point to better features or performance, the same amount also said buying from a brand they trust makes the additional spend worthwhile.

The study, conducted through OnePoll.com, also revealed that 14% have postponed upgrading their mobile phones in anticipation of securing a Black Friday discount.

Article continues below

More than a fifth (24%) delayed their purchase to secure the best deal, while 22% wanted better value for money, with 42% satisfied they held off on their purchase.

Zeena Hill, from Samsung, added: "Finding a good deal provides the tipping point, but the real motivation is buying better - whether that's larger, cinematic displays, smarter, energy-saving appliances that help save you money, or a flagship phone upgrade to unlock the latest AI features."

News.title: 8 perks of working Christmas Day as 1.2 million Brits took on festive shift last year
News.content:
8 perks of working Christmas Day as 1.2 million Brits took on festive shift last year

While many people dread working on Christmas Day, a new survey has highlighted several unexpected perks of taking on the festive shift

Santa confesses all in Greene King Christmas advert

The eight surprising benefits of working on Christmas Day have been revealed. Based on Office for National Statistics data, approximately 1.2 million people worked on Christmas Day in 2025, a slight increase from 1.1 million in 2018. However, it's not entirely gloomy - a recent survey of 1,000 adults who have worked on 25th December reveals several positive elements of taking on the festive shift.

‌



‌



In the recent survey, 27% of those working on Christmas Day appreciate avoiding the stress of cooking or tidying up afterwards and the expectation to have a flawless day. Meanwhile, others relish not having to make lengthy journeys to visit relatives - and enjoy the space away from family, and potential squabbles.

‌



View 3 Images More than a million people worked on Christmas Day last year (Image: PinPep)

‌



Yet for 37%, the primary appeal is the opportunity to make Christmas memorable for someone else, while 25% appreciate contributing to their community. For instance, amongst healthcare workers, 45% treasure helping to make the day feel significant for those unable to celebrate it with their loved ones.

Conducted through OnePoll, the survey discovered the average festive worker is now on their fourth consecutive Christmas, with 21% having completed 10 or more shifts throughout their career.

The research was commissioned by Greene King, whose second annual Big Christmas Shift offers Christmas Day workers a free meal from 2nd to 5th December - they have until 16th November to sign up or to be nominated by loved ones.

‌



View 3 Images Greene Santa and two reindeer arrive at The George in Southwark, London, to launch The Big Christmas Shift, (Image: PinPep)

View 3 Images The brewing company is offering a free festive meal to the 1.2 million Britons expected to work on Christmas Day (Image: PinPep)

‌



Amongst all workers surveyed, 30% highlighted how meaningful it was to witness someone's spirits lift as a direct result of their actions, while 27% cherished receiving an unexpected expression of gratitude.

Many have even been given a card (28%), a gift (25%) or a tasty token of appreciation (33%) on 25th December.

‌



Those on shift on Christmas Day find ways to adapt their own festivities. Some choose to reschedule the entire day so they can spend it fully with their loved ones.

Others opt to set aside a handful of cherished traditions, such as sitting down for Christmas dinner (45%), visiting extended family (37%), unwrapping presents (31%), or heading out for a festive stroll (18%).

‌



Andrew Gallagher from Greene King, said: "Behind so many special moments that the rest of us enjoy, there are people giving up time with their loved ones to make Christmas special for somebody else.

"So, this year, we are giving Santa a little less of the credit and putting the spotlight on Britain's real Christmas shift workers.

Article continues below

"Offering 30,000 free meals is our way of saying thank you to every person behind the scenes and giving them a chance to enjoy some well-earned festive cheer of their own."

News.title: BBC doctor issues warning to anyone who gets health information online
News.content:
BBC doctor issues warning to anyone who gets health information online

"If I'm honest, we should be very concerned." Dr Ranj reveals the alarming truth behind those viral health videos you've probably scrolled past

View 3 Images BBC Morning Live experts have urged people to be wary when it comes to health claims (Image: BBC Morning Live)

A doctor has said he is deeply worried about the health content spreading online. Speaking on BBC Morning Live, Dr Ranj Singh said images and videos using his likeness have been shared to promote health claims.

‌



‌



He said the clips were created with AI and have fooled large numbers of people. Hosts Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton asked Doctor Ranj whether he was worried about AI-generated health content - and if the public should be concerned. He replied: "If I'm honest, we should be very concerned."

‌



Sadly, he shared that "AI-generated imagery of Morning Live" is being used to sell false health claims, and some of it can "mislead people." Showing a photo of Jones with a so-called expert on the BBC show, the host stressed that it was fake and not actually him.

‌



The doctor then said that it "genuinely misled a lot of people." He added: "I’ve had AI videos of myself out there that are completely fake - and there’s virtually no regulation in the space at the moment."

View 3 Images BBC Morning Live said this picture is fake (Image: BBC Morning Live)

AI can be good, says Dr Ranj Singh

The doctor said he isn’t completely opposed to artificial intelligence, pointing out it can be helpful in many areas, including healthcare. He said he’s working with the NHS on a project to speed up sepsis diagnosis in children, and added that AI can be a valuable tool when it’s properly regulated and used for that kind of purpose.

‌



While AI can be useful, it also has drawbacks. It can invent facts, generate realistic-looking videos and photos, and create deepfakes that make false claims seem credible. It can also give a misleading sense of authority. Because of this, he urged people to check sources, verify any claims, and not rely on AI alone for health advice.

Energy drinks may be behind heart attack surge among young adults, new study suggests READ MORE :

Ask these five questions

The doctor urges people to ask these five questions when looking at information about health or any other topic.

‌



What’s the evidence? Is it backed by genuine scientific research and high-quality studies? Is the research new, up-to-date and current, or is it old information that has been rehashed Is the person presenting trying to sell you something? If yes, it does not mean they are not credible, but the doctor warns there needs to be "transparency" Go back to official sources like NICE, NHS and relevant charities and fact-check claims Who is it that’s presenting the information? Are they qualified? Are they relevant? Are they registered? Are they an expert?

He added: "Popularity is not proof. Don’t share unverified claims unless you are absolutely sure it’s true and if it sounds too good to be true, then it probably is."

‌



Misleading online health claims

In the same segment, the BBC expert said the public "have to be cautious and wary" of information that circulates online - even if it's not AI-generated. He said the key thing to watch for with health claims online is that they often start with a kernel of truth grounded in real science, before being twisted into something inaccurate, untrue and misleading.

View 3 Images BBC Morning Live hosts Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton (Image: BBC Morning Live)

‌



In a "classic example" of something he experienced recently, he said that there are misleading claims about alkaline water. He explained: "When we’re sick, our bodies can be more acidic and that’s not a particularly good thing. The claim is that alkaline water reduces the acidity in our blood and in our bodies."

Setting the facts straight, he said: "Drinking alkaline water doesn’t do anything to your blood acidity because your body is already very good at doing that. And actually if you drink water that's too alkaline, you end up in serious trouble because it’s not very good for you."

‌



Publication does not equal truth

Dr Ranj said some tactics insist there’s evidence or scientific studies to back a claim, but not all medical research is the same. Some studies are rigorous and high-quality, while others are poorly designed - and being published doesn’t automatically make a claim true

He also stressed that a study in five mice is "not the same" as a large randomised controlled trial involving many people. Finally, he warned about confusing correlation with causation: just because two things happen around the same time doesn’t mean one caused the other - they may be unrelated.

‌



What key words could suggest fake information?

Dr Ranj urged people to look out for keywords such as miracle, detox, and guaranteed results. In fact, one phrase is "what doctors don’t tell you - that’s a big red flag for me", he said.

These fake health claims often promise a quick fix, target a worry or problem, and then try to sell you a “solution,” the expert said. He added that health is complicated for many people, and warned that this kind of content often uses misleading or emotionally charged language.

Article continues below

Concluding his advice, he warned that seeing the same person online again and again can create a misleading sense of trust. He added that what helps one person may not help another, and urged people not to change their health routine based solely on something they’ve seen online. If you are concerned about your health, seek help from your doctor.

News.title: NASA issues incredible spacewalk photos showing astronaut hanging upside down
News.content:
NASA issues incredible spacewalk photos showing astronaut hanging upside down

Astronauts taking part in the critical mission to install new infrastructure designed to augment power to the International Space Station celebrated a major milestone

View 5 Images Anand Menon took one of the most daring photos from the expedition (Image: ISS/NASA / SWNS)

NASA has released a series of incredible photographs to mark the 100th US spacewalk carried out from the International Space Station (ISS).

‌



‌



New photos released by the agency show the latest spacewalk from the orbital station, which was undertaken by two astronauts, NASA's own Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency's (CSA) Joshua Kutryk. The pair were deployed outside the ISS' airlock to install and deploy an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, which was attached to the station's 2A electrical power channel.

‌



The series of daring shots captured the ISS, the Earth and the astronauts themselves, who were decked out in high-tech gear to carry out the new array.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

SpaceX crew 13 launch led by first black female commander sets US speed record READ MORE :

View 5 Images Menon also took a stunning picture of the Earth (Image: ISS/NASA / SWNS)

It was NASA's Menon who took most of the spectacular photos, appearing to hang upside-down at one point and capturing both his spacesuit and part of the space station in his visor while the Earth loomed large behind him.

‌



Kutryk was seen during the spacewalk hanging off the side of the station's exterior as the pair spent seven hours and 11 minutes working outside the orbiting laboratory.

View 5 Images Kutryk is pictured during a spacewalk (Image: ISS/NASA / SWNS)

‌



During that time, the pair attached the array to the exterior before releasing a series of tension bolts, which allowed it to unfurl on its own in around 10 minutes.

Menon was seen riding the Canadarm2 robotic arm as he carried the rolled-up solar array to its installation site, while Kutryk made his way along the station's truss structure, tethered to the ISS.

‌



View 5 Images Joshua Kutryk was pictured hanging off a truss structure (Image: CSA / SWNS)

The new array is the seventh roll-out solar array installed on the station and is designed to boost its power-generating capacity as NASA prepares for the ISS's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.

‌



The advanced, sail-like structure is designed to augment aging legacy solar panels which have been generating power for the ISS since they were rolled out between 2000 and 2009.

View 5 Images The engineers unfurled the new solar array (Image: ISS/NASA / SWNS)

Article continues below

On top of being critical for the ISS' infrastructure upgrades, the spacewalk also marked an important milestone for the station, being the 100th carried out since the first astronauts set foot there in 2000. Menon commemorated the achievement on a post on X, formerly Twitter, on October 30, revealing it is "always sunny in space".

He said: "Can confirm. It's always sunny in space. Yesterday, we completed USOS EVA 100 and installed a new solar array on space station. Over 25 years operating in the harshest environment and using the sun's energy to do it!"

News.content:
After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.

According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.

In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.

Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in (which you can follow later on our results page) and what it could mean for the country.

News.title: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
News.content:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.

He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.

There has been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also at the summit, has previously said he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but that financial reparations were "not the right answer".

While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.

He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures â the good they did as well as the wrongs."

The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.

The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.

The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.

The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

News.title: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
News.content:
The case raises highly unusual legal issues concerning whether a court should stop publication when an individual claims that a media investigation would lead to them inflicting harm on themselves.

The celebrity first asked the court in the summer to stop the publication of the investigation after journalists contacted him with allegations about this sexual activities with a large number of young women.

ITN and the Guardian said their investigation had uncovered how the celebrity had allegedly abused his "power and status".

During last week's application for a permanent injunction, Mansoori said making the allegations public would have a "potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court that the man had tried to kill himself after he had been contacted by the media organisations and was later detained in hospital for his own protection - but later absconded and tried a second time to end his life.

Those incidents of self-harm had not been because of the allegations themselves but the result of "long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media", she argued.

"The only reason [suicide attempts] would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life," she said.

Lawyers for the media groups argued that there was a strong public interest in allowing their investigation to be publicised because of the serious nature of the allegations.

In his judgment, Nicklin wrote: "The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the conduct of a prominent person and the alleged use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls.

"The subject matter includes alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons.

"Those are matters capable of making a significant contribution to public debate."

The celebrity argued that publishing the allegations would breach his protections under the European Convention on Human Rights, including articles that guarantee the right to life and protection from inhuman or degrading treatment.

However, the judge rejected the claim that publication would violate the man's right to life, writing: "No prior case establishes that the Court's knowledge of a suicide risk, together with its power to prohibit the event expected to increase that risk, is by itself enough to require the Court to act."

The judge accepted that publishing would cause the man "acute and potentially prolonged mental suffering" â but said "established law did not impose a positive obligation upon the Court to prevent that suffering by restraining publication".

The man also cited the right to private and family life.

While the judge acknowledged that publication "would interfere exceptionally seriously with the Claimant's private and family life", he also rejected that claim, saying a permanent injunction "would have been an exceptionally serious restriction upon freedom of expression".

The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

News.title: Jewellery sold as sterling silver on Amazon and Temu found to contain toxic chemicals
News.content:
Jewellery advertised as sterling silver on Amazon, eBay, Temu, Etsy and OnBuy was found to contain toxic chemicals, following a BBC investigation.

Some 25 items were examined by experts for BBC Watchdog on The One Show. Laboratory analysis found eight contained illegal levels of cadmium - a chemical that can cause cancer. Only two items could be classified as sterling silver.

Amazon, eBay, Temu and OnBuy said misleading listings were prohibited and that it had removed the jewellery identified by Watchdog. Etsy did not respond.

Meranda, 34, bought a necklace advertised on Etsy as handmade sterling silver but says after a few days of wearing it her "neck started getting really irritated".

"I remember looking at it as I took it off and thinking the colour on this doesn't look right."

Meranda's necklace and the 25 other pieces purchased by Watchdog were analysed by the Sheffield Assay Office.

According to preliminary testing, Meranda's necklace was found to contain nickel - another toxic chemical that can cause skin irritation. There are strict legal limits on how much nickel jewellery can contain.

News.title: Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault
News.content:
In total, Madgwick, who is from the the Anchorage Park area of Portsmouth, has been charged with 12 counts of rape, two counts of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault.

Madgwick has also been charged with two counts of making indecent images of children, two of controlling or coercive behaviour and eight of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

He faces one charge each of causing or inciting sexual exploitation of a child, distributing an indecent image of a child, stalking, making threats to kill, false imprisonment, theft and criminal damage.

A spokesperson for the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings."

The 37-year-old councillor represents North East Havant on Hampshire County Council and Paulsgrove on Portsmouth City Council.

Madgwick was elected to his position on the county council by a large margin in May - just months after he was first arrested by police.

In a statement, the local authority said it was aware of the "extremely serious allegations" and that "as criminal proceedings are now under way, it would not be appropriate" to comment further.

It added that being charged with a criminal offence did not disqualify a councillor, such as Madgwick, from office.

Last month, he featured in the the ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform - after which he accused the broadcaster of "electoral interference".

In the programme, he was shown voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group.

He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.

News.title: Third teen arrested after Halloween party stabbings
News.content:
A third teenage boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.

Police said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.

One 17-year-old boy remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.

A 16-year-old from Bristol has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. He remains in custody, as do two boys arrested on Monday.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

News.title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
News.content:
The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save Â£10bn.

But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.

While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.

In March, the Home Office said, external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at Â£10bn under existing rules.

Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.

She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "Â£10bn drain on our public finances".

Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least Â£25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.

Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.

Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

News.title: A simple guide to the midterms
News.content:
Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.

A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.

The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.

News.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
News.content:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see Â£5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for Â£200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for Â£25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

News.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
News.content:
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

News.title: UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
News.content:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

News.title: Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
News.content:
The jury has begun considering the verdicts in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial.

The media personality, 51, has been on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London for three weeks, facing three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Giving evidence, he told the court he had been "obsessed" with sex in the past, but insisted it was always consensual.

The charges relate to allegations from six women spanning a decade between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors said the complainants described him as someone who "didn't listen" when they said no, and "didn't care".

On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury of eight men and four women he can only accept a verdict they all agree on.

Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.

At the trial, he admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access", which he now said was wrong, but denied ever doing anything criminal.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

He also said none of the women reported the alleged incidents to police at the time, and that allegations in a 2023 TV and newspaper investigation had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting women to come forward afterwards.

Meanwhile, prosecutors depicted Brand as someone who saw women as a "disposable commodity" who "didn't matter to him" and were simply a "means to an end".

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that the women said his personality changed "from charming to frightening to nasty" during the alleged attacks.

She said the women, who do not know each other, had been "haunted for years" by their experiences.

One woman accuses Brand of raping her after they had met at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

She claimed he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.

When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he told the court: "No."

Another woman claims that the entertainer grabbed her breasts at a bar in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet, where he allegedly orally raped her.

Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with the woman but did not drag or force her there, or force her to perform oral sex.

A third woman had a consensual sexual encounter with Brand and another fan in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009.

She accuses the star of later raping her after he invited her to his house in Hampstead.

She said she had agreed to vaginal sex but did not consent to anal sex. After he texted her six months later, she said she told him he had "treated me like an animal".

Brand told the court they had consensual sex, and denied committing anal rape.

The other allegations come from a woman who says she was pinned against a wall and groped; another who claims he put his head into her lap when she had been forced to give him a massage; and a complainant who says he tried to drag her into a toilet. Brand also denies these charges.

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence in his defence at the trial, describing him as "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first made in a Channel 4 documentary and a Times and Sunday Times investigation in 2023.

He denied those allegations, which related to different women than those involved in the criminal trial.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years Brand has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

News.title: Cambridge scientist killed in Spain train crash was 'a light for all of us'
News.content:
The aunt of a University of Cambridge scientist killed in the Spanish rail disaster has paid an emotional tribute, describing her niece as "a light for all of us".

Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to collect a prize for scientific excellence in Andalusia on 28 October, when her train crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.

MarÃ­a JosÃ© Alonso told the BBC a funeral had been held in Madrid on Monday for the mother of two.

"Hundreds of friends came from all over the world... because Marta was an amazing lab mate and amazing friend," she said. "She was the friendliest person you can imagine, with lots of energy. She was a light for all of us."

Shahbazi, 41, had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development.

She was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.

Alonso said her niece had originally intended to travel to the ceremony by car with her family, but decided to take the train.

"Her family was here in Madrid, and they could have gone together by car - but she said 'no, stay here'," she said.

News.title: Speeding driver jailed for fatal Lamborghini crash
News.content:
A driver who caused the death of her friend when she lost control of a rented Lamborghini and crashed into a motorway barrier has been jailed for 10 years.

Mohammed Shaan Hussain, 20, died when Humaira Batool crashed the Â£200,000 supercar on the M62, near Ripponden, in West Yorkshire, in December 2022, causing it to flip over and burst into flames.

During her trial, jurors heard Batool, 26, from Bradford, had been driving at speeds of up to 140mph (230km/h) in wet conditions shortly before the crash.

Passing sentence, Judge Ray Singh said Hussain died as a result of Batool's decision to drive the "powerful performance vehicle" at "eye-watering extreme speeds on a damp motorway in darkness".

The judge said: "This was not a momentary lapse of concentration. It was a conscious decision to drive at extraordinary speed in conditions that made such driving especially dangerous.

"You deliberately exposed your passenger, yourself and other road users to an obvious and grave risk of death or serious injury. Tragically, that risk materialised."

During the trial, the court heard Hussain, also from Bradford, had rented the vehicle and was driving to HMP Leeds with Batool to collect a friend.

The pair switched places en route and the car crashed off the carriageway within eight seconds of Batool taking the wheel.

In court, Batool tried to blame Hussain, saying he had "reached over" while she was driving and touched something, causing the car to surge, but this was rejected by the jury.

The judge said: "During the trial, various alternative explanations were advanced on your behalf, all of which were rejected â the possibility of mechanical failure, aquaplaning and your suggestion that, just prior to the collision, the controls of that vehicle had been tampered with by Shaan.

"The jury rejected those explanations. I do likewise.

"The sole cause of this collision was the manner of your driving."

Hussain died as a result of the injuries he sustained in the crash, while Batool suffered serious injuries, including burns to around 10% of her body and a shattered tibia.

Batool was found guilty of causing death by dangerous driving in September.

News.title: The Crown star Josh O'Connor reacts to Bond rumours
News.content:
BAFTA-nominated actor, Josh O'Connor, who portrayed Prince Charles in Netflix's The Crown says he is "very honoured" by the speculation he could be the next James Bond.

The 36-year-old who grew up in Cheltenham, Gloucestershire and trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School - has been reported to be in the running for the role alongside Callum Turner and Jack Lowden.

The chosen actor will replace Daniel Craig, who took over the role of Bond with Casino Royale in 2006 and bowed out after his fifth film, No Time To Die, in 2021.

Opening the Everyman Theatre's new education and community centre in his hometown, O'Connor said: "To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary".

News.title: Teen admits bank holiday stabbing on beach that left 17-year-old with amputated leg
News.content:
A teenager has admitted stabbing a 17-year-old boy in an "unprovoked" attack which led to him having his leg amputated.

Newport Crown Court heard the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was visiting the beach with a group of friends in May 2026, when the incident happened during a bank holiday trip to Barry Island.

Idris Ahmed, from Riverside in Cardiff, previously denied grievous bodily harm with intent and possessing a knife - but changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.

Ahmed, 19, attacked the teenager "without warning" after the victim acted "as a peacemaker" between the group Ahmed was socialising with and those in his own party. Ahmed is expected to be sentenced on 27 November.

The 17-year-old victim previously told the jury he had bled heavily, and fallen in and out of consciousness immediately after the stabbing.

He was airlifted to hospital where he underwent four surgeries, but despite several transfusions, oxygen was not flowing properly to the leg.

The jury heard it was determined the teenager needed a through-knee amputation, removing the lower half of his leg.

News.title: Man United latest: Michael Carrick urged to drop ‘selfish’ star ahead of Roma clash in Champions League
News.content:

Michael Carrick is clinging onto his job by a thread as he takes charge of Manchester United’s meeting with Roma in the Champions League, desperate for a change of fortunes to save his skin.

United lost again on the weekend as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea, leaving them 17th in the Premier League, hovering above the relegation zone on goal difference.

After surviving initial club crisis talks at Carrington last week, every game now feels like it could be Carrick’s last unless he can manage to turn the tide, with United winless in nine for the first time in 40 years.
