Sports.title: Tenerife footballer Jesús de Miguel dies aged 30 after on-pitch collision
Sports.content:
Spanish football was in shock on Tuesday after the Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in the second division. The homicide division of the national police has opened judicial proceedings into a possible involuntary manslaughter, a routine procedure after any death not by natural causes. The chief public prosecutor in Santa Cruz de Tenerife told the state news agency EFE that it was “very difficult” for a case to come to court.

Tenerife announced that De Miguel had died at 8am on Tuesday after he had been taken into intensive care on Monday afternoon. He did not regain consciousness after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

The collision occurred in added time at the end of Andorra’s visit to Tenerife, a game put back 24 hours because of the risk of torrential rain. With the score 2-2, in the 96th minute, a long ball was played away from the Tenerife area and up the pitch. De Miguel chased it into space and Owono came a long way out of his goal, jumping forward, with his right knee up, and crashing into the attacking player inside the centre circle.

Quick Guide How do I 

Owono was sent off, walking straight to the touchline. De Miguel was left unconscious, with players from both sides appealing for medical assistance. The match was abandoned by the referee, Manuel Ángel Pérez Hernández, having run into the 108th minute.

Medics restored De Miguel’s pulse in the ambulance and transferred him to the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz. Tenerife said he was able to breathe unassisted and was stable but that he remained unconscious and in a critical condition. At 5am the club announced De Miguel’s condition had worsened neurologically.

“CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesús de Miguel Alameda on Tuesday 3 November 2026 at 8:00am,” said a statement released at 9.31am. The statement described the club as “broken by pain, with a lump in the throat and unable to believe that this is true”, and accompanying the forward’s “devastated family, loved ones and everyone associated with Tenerife who mourns this cruel end … there are no words of consolation”.

View image in fullscreen Tributes to Jesús de Miguel at Tenerife’s stadium. Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters

The former Barcelona defender Gerard Piqué, who is Andorra’s majority shareholder and attended the game, wrote on social media: “I am so deeply sorry, to my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús.” The club’s president, Ferran Vilaseca, told reporters: “This has had a huge emotional impact on our players, coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. Our sincerest condolence arriving on the Spanish mainland after midnight, still unaware of the outcome.”

The chief public prosecutor in Santa Cruz de Tenerife, José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui, told EFE it was “very difficult” for a legal case to be taken up given that the impact happened in the course of the game. A formal legal complaint could still be brought. Sentences for involuntary homicide range from three months to four years of imprisonment. There is no precedent of a footballer facing legal proceedings as a result of a challenge in the course of a game.

According to federation protocols Owono could face a 12-game ban, with the disciplinary committee due to decide.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal players hold a minute’s silence in memory of Jesús de Miguel. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

The report from the referee said: “In minute 90+6, player no 25 Ferrer Owono, Jesus Lazaro, was sent off for the following reason: for impacting sharply upon an opponent with his leg high and excessive force in dispute of the ball. The player was treated on the field of play, which he then abandoned on a stretcher. At the close of this report, no medical certificate had been presented.”

Tenerife have asked to postpone their next two games, against Granada on Saturday and Badajoz in the cup the following week. Andorra have requested that their meeting with Mallorca at the weekend be postponed. The Spanish football federation announced the postponement of all games due to be held on Tuesday in the Copa del Rey and the Copa de la Reina.

Clubs across Europe, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, paid tribute to De Miguel. “Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times,” Barcelona said. Real Madrid said they sent “condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones”.

De Miguel had played most of his career in Spain’s third tier, at Leganés B, Inter Madrid, Fuenlabrada, Navalcarnero, Unionistas de Salamanca and Castellón. He was Castellón’s top scorer when they were promoted to the second division in 2024 and joined Tenerife in 2025.

Sports.title: Football Daily | West Ham want promotion – so it’s time to call in an understated club legend
Sports.content:
HAMMER TIME

While Football Daily hasn’t actually seen much of West Ham this season, we’ve noted enough of their results to presume they were doing OK in their attempt to bounce back to the Premier League after relegation. Less than a third of the way through the Championship season under Nuno Espírito Santo, they’d already spanked six without reply past both Wrexham and Lincoln, while scoring three or more in wins over Wolves, Derby and Bolton. However, it turns out that of the 13 matches they’ve played in a league that is famously difficult to get out of (unless you were Sheffield Wednesday last season), they have actually lost three times and currently sit in eighth place, a whopping six points off leaders Middlesbrough. Given the context of such an unbridgeable chasm, it is small wonder West Ham fans woke up to news that Nuno had been unceremoniously bounced out of the London Stadium with a P45 in hand.

Coming on the back of consecutive home defeats by Southampton and West Brom, Tuesday’s news won’t have come as a huge surprise to Hammers fans, treated to the sight of a sad Nuno on the London Stadium touchline on Saturday, eyes glazed and grey beard glistening in the early evening mist as he stared blankly in the direction of several celebrating Baggies. “West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team head coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect,” droned a club statement. “Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.”

Determined to secure one of the two automatic promotion places up for grabs, West Ham have decided to nip any prospective long-term slump in the bud by approaching Scott Parker. An understated club legend of sorts, the 46-year-old is best known for wearing expensive Thom Browne four-bar ripstop blouson jackets in his technical area while masterminding immediate promotion to the Premier League for the only three English clubs he has managed thus far.

Indeed, it is a testament to the breezy optimism of certain West Ham fans on several Social Media Disgraces that they are already discussing how dismal Parker’s Premier League record is, while arguing over who should replace him when he becomes the first top-flight gaffer to get sacked in 12 months’ time. With their team having scored 33 goals in their opening 13 games this season, West Ham fans can now presumably look forward to seeing them bag the same number in their remaining fixtures as they clock up 33 consecutive, risk-averse 1-0 wins. It may not be the fabled West Ham way but it will do until the next guy comes along.

JESÚS DE MIGUEL (1996-2026)

“Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8am, of Jesús de Miguel Alameda. There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today. The family of Jesús de Miguel is grateful for each and every expression of support received, and also requests, from the bottom of their hearts, the utmost respect for their privacy during these terrible times” – Tenerife have announced the death of striker Jesús de Miguel, who died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in Spain’s second division. De Miguel suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest and did not regain consciousness.

View image in fullscreen RIP Jesús de Miguel. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA

double quotation mark While my heart aches for Jesús de Miguel, who has died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, I shudder to think the trauma that shall haunt Owono for the rest of his life. I do hope and pray the wider community understands and extends their support in his recuperation” – Krishna Moorthy.

double quotation mark As an upgrade to Steve Plever’s suggestion of paper thin shirts [Monday’s letters]: how about Velcro shirts? If the bit comes off, it is a shirt pull and the offender has the honour of putting it back in place before being awarded a yellow card” – Mike Harold.

double quotation mark To dive or not to dive seems to be biggest dilemma in the Premier League right now. It’s not. The problem with today’s highly paid professionals is that they simply have no panache at all when they go down. I recall watching Francis Lee pick up the ball on the halfway line at a mud soaked Maine Road in the late 1960s, he put his head down and headed for goal, he was determined, he was single minded. He was 30 yards from goal, he was in full flow. He was tackled from behind and then he really took off, he grew wings, he soared. I swear he landed in the penalty area over 10 yards away. He dragged himself to his feet and without a semblance of a smile smashed the well-deserved penalty, with a very heavy leather ball straight at the centre of the goal at over 70 mph. The goalkeeper, obviously no fool, simply dived out of the way. The press christened him “Lee Won Pen” He was my hero. That man had panache, he had style” – Myles Flynn.

double quotation mark I am interested to read that Aston Villa considered the words of Jamie Carragher “unacceptable insults”. It would obviously help matters if they could publish examples of acceptable insults” – Rupert Jeffery.

Send your letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day goes to … Mike Harold, who wins a copy of Programmes! by Richard Crooks. It’s out now and available to buy on the Pitch Publishing website. Terms and conditions for our competitions are here.

Sports.title: ‘An absolute afterthought’: the story of the Nigeria women’s team’s fall from grace
Sports.content:
It was a historic result in Casablanca – but not in a good way. Nigeria’s 2-1 defeat against South Africa in a playoff in August meant that the Super Falcons are missing out on the World Cup for the first time. It is a crushing blow for the most decorated national side in Africa across both men and women, one that has won no fewer than 10 Wafcon titles.

The journalist and lecturer Dr Victor Ademola was in Morocco the day of the defeat. “It was a very difficult evening,” he says. “Some players were visibly emotional while others appeared to be processing what had just happened. I saw players crying as they got on to the team bus while some sat alone or remained on their phones, looking very sad.”

The blow of missing out on the World Cup in Brazil next year came only a few days after they were eliminated from Wafcon at the quarter-final stage by Cameroon – only the semi-finalists qualified for the World Cup automatically, hence Nigeria ending up in that ill-fated playoff.

“What struck me most was the weight of what the result represented,” Ademola says. “These players knew the history of the Super Falcons and understood that this was not simply another defeat. There was a sense of disappointment, disbelief and heartbreak.”

The loss is not only historical but consequential. Nigeria will miss out on developmental funding with next year’s prize fund expected to rise from the previous tournament four years ago. In 2023 the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pledged to equal the men’s and women’s tournaments prize funds by 2027. The figure for the men’s World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico was $727m (roughly £539m). Recent news suggest Fifa will miss out on its target but it is nevertheless a blow for Nigeria not to be involved.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino has said the next Women’s World Cup will have increased prize money, but Nigeria will not be there to benefit from it. Photograph: Luisa González/Reuters

Janine Anthony, the African women’s football journalist, says the stakes for the Super Falcons were especially high as “women’s football does not have the luxury of not being at a World Cup”. Anthony adds: “A spot at the World Cup is the ultimate window and it’s a dream to be able to represent your country at any stage, whether it’s in music or football. For women’s football, the World Cup is such a commercially marketable vehicle. The Super Falcons team were one of only seven teams that had been to every World Cup, [and] the only African team. Now that’s gone.”

Anthony says that despite the Super Falcons’ success they are treated as an “absolute afterthought” in terms of the domestic leagues, management and preparation. The lack of preparation games proved problematic in Morocco, she suggests, manifesting itself in a lack of cohesiveness in most games. The then coach, Justine Madugu, frequently changed the starting XI throughout the tournament.

Before the tournament the team played two games against Senegal, who have never qualified for the World Cup, whereas before the 2025 edition they had three friendlies, against France, Cameroon and Portugal. “Imagine if they had more games to prepare,” Anthony says. “Then they could have probably done all the tweaking from a tactical perspective. The Nigerian Football Federation absolutely failed to capitalise on the Wafcon being moved to July.”

The landscape of African women’s football is changing, and Morocco are the only country from the continent who played in the 2023 World Cup who are guaranteed to be at next year’s tournament. South Africa are going into the inter-continental playoffs which start this month, and Nigeria and Zambia are out.

At the Wafcon, Malawi and Cameroon emerged as the standouts. It was Malawi’s debut at the tourmanent and the team gave a stellar performance with the attacking skill of the Chawinga sisters, Tabitha and Temwa, standing out. They will play at their first World Cup. The winners, Cameroon, were unexpected competitors at Wafcon, only qualifying after the Confederation of African Football expanded the tournament from 12 to 16 teams.

The Super Falcons’ absence from the World Cup next year is just the latest setback in a long line of disappointments. The men’s team have failed to qualify for two World Cups in a row while the under-17 men’s team have not reached the World Cup since 2019 or even Afcon since 2023. There have been signs of progress for the the under-20 women, who beat England 3-0 to reach the quarter-finals at their World Cup in September, but they then promptly lost against Colombia 1-0.

View image in fullscreen The Nigeria men’s team have missed out on the past two World Cup tournaments. Photograph: Themba Hadebe/AP

Players and coaches have long spoken out and protested against unpaid allowances and bonuses by the Nigerian Football Federation. The Super Falcons have staged numerous sit-ins and training boycotts to protest against the conditions, including at the Wafcons in 2004, 2016 and 2022 as well as the 2019 World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The NFF is under investigation by the country’s department of state services for an alleged misuse of a 17bn naira (£9.5m) fund issued by the government in 2024 to address outstanding payments owed to players and staff of the national teams, according to local media. The NFF did not comment when contacted by the Guardian regarding the accusations.

Nigeria’s president, Bola Tinubu, is unhappy about the situation. “Nigerian football must undergo far-reaching changes to strengthen governance, administration, stakeholder representation, player development, domestic competitions and accountability,” he said in August.

That came shortly after Ibrahim Gusau resigned as NFF president along with several other board members. The NFF was scheduled to hold elections in September but they were suspended. They are now expected to take place following reforms made in consultation with Fifa and Caf.

What does the future hold for the Super Falcons? Anthony hopes for more investment, accountability and a bridge between veteran players and the current team on an administration level. “We can only hope that there is the understanding that the Nigerian fans are really disappointed and sad that their national teams aren’t bringing the joy that Nigerians are used to as a football loving nation,” she says. “We can only hope that the Super Falcons can finally be given the respect they’ve always deserved.”

Sports.title: AFC postpones Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia to late 2027 due to conflict in Middle East
Sports.content:
The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed as a result of the conflict in the Middle East.

After a month of speculation following the airport attack on Riyadh’s international airport, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) confirmed on Tuesday that the tournament had been pushed back 11 months.

The rescheduled tournament is expected to kick off in the 2027 Christmas break with a 23 December start date leading up to a 21 January 2028 final.

“The organising committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions,” the AFC said in a statement.

“Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.”

The proposed new dates – which fall in one of the busiest periods in European club football – must be approved by Fifa.

Saudi Arabia’s suitability to host the tournament has been a hot topic since the Riyadh airport attack by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Other nations, who were scheduled to travel to Saudi Arabia in the November international window, have been forced to relocate their friendlies.

There was little appetite for another host nation to step in at such short notice – the tournament was slated to start on 7 January 2027 – but going ahead as planned in the current climate was fraught with risks.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In Australia, the delayed tournament could have ramifications for coach Tony Popovic, who signed a short-term extension on the eve of the World Cup.

Popovic’s contract is due to expire after the previously scheduled January tournament, where Australia were due to face Tajikistan, Singapore and Iraq, who are coached by ex-Socceroos boss Graham Arnold.

Arnold was handed a job reprieve by the Iraqi FA last month after a form slump following the country’s first World Cup qualification in 40 years.

Sports.title: Fifa to share documents on World Cup sell-off plans with council members
Sports.content:
Fifa will grant its council members access to documents regarding the doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme but has not responded directly to more than 50 questions from Uefa about its governance and recent scandals.

In a letter sent to the Fifa Council by Mattias Grafström, the governing body’s secretary general, members were told material relating to FFE will be released for them to view in person at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich. They will be allowed only to view the documents, of which the exact nature and scope are unclear, under strict confidentiality protocols. A deadline of 16 November has been set to apply for such visits; eyebrows may be raised in some quarters about the fact this is two days before candidates for the Fifa election next year are required to declare their hand.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Uefa had written to Grafström on 19 October giving Fifa a fortnight to answer a series of questions about FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair, the Fifa peace prize, the organisation’s relations with Donald Trump and other major decisions that have caused controversy in the past 12 months. It had asked for all documents regarding FFE to be made accessible, saying refusal to comply with any of its demands should be “justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon”.

The deadline imposed by Uefa expired on Monday night, although Fifa Council members are understood to have been told a response is being worked upon and will be shared with them. Fifa’s stance is that Uefa’s questions, posed after Gianni Infantino told delegates at the Fifa Council meeting last month to submit questions in writing before they next convened in December, were too substantial in number for the two-week turnaround.

It remains to be seen whether those Fifa Council members who travel for the document inspection will depart with the answers they require. In August Uefa made an application to four courts in the US for the release of documents pertaining to FFE, with a view to lodging a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement. Preliminary rulings are yet to be handed down and the amount of information available to view may be affected. Fifa has accused Uefa of “harassment” and “misinformation” and denied wrongdoing by Infantino.

As reported last week Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate who could stand against Infantino in March, with movement possible early this month.

Sports.title: Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache
Sports.content:
Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.

Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against opponents who ended with 10 men after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.

And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.

Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”

Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”

Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”

Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.

Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.

View image in fullscreen Matthias Jaissle struggles to get his message across to his Newcastle players. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.

Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.

Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.

Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Jacob Ramsey sees red in stoppage time after coming on as a substitute for Newcastle. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.

Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.

Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.

The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.

“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

Sports.title: Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family
Sports.content:
Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Exciting, right?

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

View image in fullscreen Fans of Boca cheer from beneath their umbrellas. Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

View image in fullscreen River Plate fans clash with riot police outside the Monumental prior the final of the Copa Libertadores against Boca Juniors in 2018. The match was rescheduled after the bus carrying Boca players was attacked, injuring several players. Photograph: Sebastian Pani/AP

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

View image in fullscreen Leonel Flores of Boca celebrates with teammates following the team’s victory in the Superclásico. Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

View image in fullscreen River Plate’s Gonzalo Montiel leaves the pitch under police protection against Boca. Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

Sports.title: Don’t call it a remontada: Emery’s Camp Nou comeback focuses European blur
Sports.content:
“One more match. Just one more match.” Sure, Unai. Sure. Just like all the other matches that generated a local tremor measured at 1 on the Richter scale when that seventh and final goal went in at the Camp Nou in March 2017.

It was inevitable that Unai Emery would be asked about the Remontada game on the eve of Aston Villa’s Champions League engagement with Barcelona, his own first trip back to the Camp Nou in this competition since one of the most visceral and traumatic experiences of his managerial career.

Emery was Paris Saint-Germain’s manager the night the Neymar-Messi-Suárez triple-godhead reversed a 4-0 first-leg quarter-final deficit in this stadium.

For all the talk of lasting trauma Emery stayed in Paris for another season, won a domestic treble, and three clubs later has two more European trophies to his name. Plus, of course a trip back here now, with only the lurking shadow of being asked to do the Manchester United job hanging over an otherwise cloudless period in his elite coaching career.

“What happened in that match we know. I started coaching in 2004, 22 years in a row. I’ve played in Europe 16 years in a row. And I’ve learnt in all the competitions and matches. And in that match I learnt so, so much.”

View image in fullscreen On the night his PSG threw away a 4-0 aggregate lead and lost 6-1 to Barcelona, Unai Emery said: “There’s no explanation for what happened.” Photograph: Alejandro García/EPA

European football has done a pretty good job in the last two seasons of turning its autumn fixture blizzard into a hopeless and baggy blur. What serious sport actually has a 36-team mega table? And a deeply predictable 36-team mega-table at that, one where you pretty much know who’s going to be up there at the end of it. If the intention was to create a series of exhibition-style TV-product events, thereby heading off the Super League’s desire to do exactly the same, then mission semi-accomplished.

There are still exceptions in the period of drift, one-off events that speak to the colour and cultural weight of this competition. Tuesday night is one of them, for Villa’s fans a genuine staging point in the progress of this ever-evolving team, with a chance, dependent on results elsewhere, to actually top the Champions League mega-table at this early stage.

Mainly this feels like a deeply Emery occasion. Not so much a homecoming; the Basque coastal town where he grew up is 350 miles northwest of here. As a player Emery never made it on to the pitch against Barça. But as a manager this has been an endlessly gruelling two-hander: 30 games across Almería, Valencia, Spartak Moscow, Sevilla, PSG and Villarreal, and an ongoing tale of sorrow, with 21 defeats and just three wins.

Not that you’d know it. Emery has always come here with teams that are punching up. He spoke on the eve of his latest return with a genuine conviction about learning from each of those occasions, focused as ever on the possibilities in front of him.

“These games gave me experience to learn, to get better, to intensify for the next matches I face. With the players we talked about our experiences together. We had our experience in Europe, two years ago, last year. This year we have won three matches and done fantastic work. Tomorrow we are facing one of the favourites to win the competition so we are going to face a huge challenge.”

The Camp Nou is still in a state of furious full-body renovation, surrounded by hoardings and railings and rubble-strewn strips of land, but inside the fixings are taking shape. The current team is also a high-functioning work in progress. La Masia continues to produce omni-talented high-technique teenagers. There is a slight, and understandable, sense of a soft centre at times. But also of fluent and dreamy possession football.

View image in fullscreen Aston Villa have won all three of their Champions League games and only trail the leaders, PSG, on goals scored. Photograph: Manjit Narotra/ProSports/Shutterstock

Villa will be aggressive, hard-pressing, geared to assert their physical advantages. Their captain, John McGinn, was sat next to his manager in the pop-up press conference room and revealed that he had been here only once before, as an eight-year-old on holiday the same day Ricardo Quaresma signed for Barcelona and had his unveiling at the stadium.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McGinn talked about his own journey alongside the Villa fans from the Championship to this elite stage. He praised Barcelona’s humility and work ethic. He also said Villa had the players to hurt them.

It is at last a fitting palate cleanser, a chance to move on from the dominant piece of Aston Villa news this so far week, which isn’t actually news or even really anything to do with Aston Villa.

There was a great deal of digital heat over the weekend at Jamie Carragher’s assertion there is “a food chain” in English football, that Aston Villa would naturally remain below Manchester United in this hierarchy, and as such Emery would always feel the need to climb to that higher level.

The only part of this statement that seems unarguably true is that Jamie Carragher doesn’t know how food chains work. In reality a food chain is mutable. This is not a fixed order. Dynamic population. Habitat shifts. Mutable omnivore status. The food chain is constantly rotating, overlapping, redefining itself.

A more accurate analogy would be that the Premier League is unlike a food chain, but is instead a place where money has created genuine stratification. On the other hand, is the thing Jamie Carragher thought he was saying even true?

Villa are pushing hard at the envelope. They’re in Barcelona. They have a proper manager, not Lee Hendrie or similar bringing the emergency DNA. Manchester United is an idea, beloved of legacy consumers, its footprint still vast, but a footprint in sands that are shifting and have shifted and will shift even faster and further.

For Barcelona, Dani Olmo, Andreas Christensen, Eric García and Xavi Espart are expected to miss the game, opening up a little potential defensive frailty. Nicolas Jackson is expected to be fit to start for Villa after playing 90 minutes at the weekend.

Sports.title: Arsenal given solution to Ezri Konsa vs William Saliba problem as injured star returns to training
Sports.content:
Arsenal given solution to Ezri Konsa vs William Saliba problem as injured star returns to training

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta will soon have a selection headache now that star defender William Saliba has returned to training.

The France international has been sidelined since July, having undergone surgery on a long-term back problem.



2 Saliba is back on the grass in a huge boost for Arsenal - but what does it mean for Konsa? Credit: Getty

The France centre-back has not played since the World Cup semi-finals and his absence led to the Gunners' £55million move for Ezri Konsa.

Signed from Aston Villa, the England star has made an immediate impact, most recently helping Arsenal keep three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League.

However, Saliba is widely considered one of the top-flight's best defenders, and he is now closing in on a return.



But could there be room for both Konsa and Saliba in the same starting XI?

Manchester United legend Rio Ferdinand has suggested Konsa could move to right back once Saliba is back full-time.



Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ferdinand said: "I think Saliba is one of those guys that you have to find room for in the team. He's that good, he's top.

"I said to my son yesterday, 'watch Ezri Konsa', because everything he does is efficient. That's a great problem for Arteta to have.



"I wouldn't be surprised if Konsa goes back to right-back once Saliba comes back. I wouldn't be surprised because Konsa is top."

Beyond his Arsenal form, Konsa has established himself as a first-choice option for England, starting seven of their eight games at the World Cup.

However, Saliba and Gabriel were a huge reason for the Gunners' Premier League title last season after a 22-year wait.

2 Konsa has slotted in for Saliba superbly - ensuring Arsenal remain the Premier League's most fearsome defence Credit: AFP



They only conceded 27 league goals across the entirety of last term and Saliba was named in the PFA team of the year for the fourth consecutive time.

Konsa at right-back?

Usually, Ben White or Jurrien Timber start in the right-back position for the Gunners.

But Konsa has shown the versatility to play there throughout his career.

At Villa, he deputised for Matty Cash at right-back on numerous occasions under manager Unai Emery.



Meanwhile, both Gareth Southgate and Thomas Tuchel have deployed Konsa as a right-back for England when necessary.

Most recently, the Arsenal defender came to the rescue for England in the 2026 World Cup quarter-final against Norway when Jarrell Quansah was suspended and Reece James was not fit to start.

Sports.title: Ballon d’Or winner could quit managerial role after key tournament postponed
Sports.content:
Fabio Cannavaro is reportedly considering quitting his job as Uzbekistan manager after the 2027 Asian Cup was postponed.

The tournament was set to take place from January 7 through to February 5, but it has now been pushed back by 11 months.

2 Cannavaro has been Uzbekistan manager for just over a year and led them into the World Cup - but he could now leave his role Credit: Getty

It was announced on Tuesday that due to attacks on host country Saudi Arabia, it will take place at the end of 2027 instead.

The decision has been a positive for some, with multiple Premier League clubs now having key players available at the turn of the year as they won't be called up for international duty.

However, for Cannavaro, he could potentially step down from his job after the postponement of the tournament.

According to journalist Fabrizio Romano, the 2006 Ballon d'Or winner could now decide to quit as Uzbekistan manager.

The Italian icon was only appointed in October 2025, but his tenure may end up being just a short one.

He has only taken charge of 14 games for the nation, winning seven and losing seven of his side's outings altogether.

Cannavaro led Uzbekistan into the 2026 World Cup this summer, but they were beaten in every group game.

They lost 3-1 to Colombia in their opener in the USA, also being beaten 5-0 by Portugal and 3-1 by DR Congo.

If he does leave, the 53-year-old manager's final match in charge would have been a 2-0 defeat to South Korea on October 6.

Specific reasoning behind a potential resignation from Cannavaro has not been revealed, but the rescheduling of the Asian Cup is said to have had an impact on his future.

2 Cannavaro is reportedly considering stepping down as boss after the Asian Cup was postponed due to recent conflict in Saudi Arabia Credit: Getty

Why has the Asian Cup been postponed?

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) revealed that the Asian Cup had been postponed until December 2027 on Tuesday.

They confirmed that "following extensive discussions and close consultation with the Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the AFC Asian Cup Saudi Arabia 2027 and the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF)", the tournament had been moved.

Recent conflict in Saudi Arabia, including a missile attack in October, led to the tough decision.

Part of their statement read: "The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions.

"The new dates of the tournament will be presented to FIFA for approval.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.

"The AFC commends SAFF and the LOC for their commitment to delivering a world-class tournament for the Continent’s players and fans.

"The AFC will continue to work closely with the LOC, Participating Member Associations and its valued sponsors and broadcast and commercial partners and all stakeholders to stage a showpiece befitting the stature and operational excellence synonymous with Asia’s most prestigious men’s national team competition, while minimising the impact of the postponement."

Sports.title: Jermain Defoe could become assistant manager at EFL club four months after leaving Woking
Sports.content:
Jermain Defoe could become assistant manager at EFL club four months after leaving Woking

Karl Robinson has emerged as a candidate for the Bromley job, with Jermain Defoe being discussed as a potential assistant.

According to the Daily Mail, ex-Premier League striker Defoe has been sounded out for a role with the League One side if former Salford boss Robinson is chosen to fill the vacant manager's role.

2 Defoe spent just six matches in charge of National League side Woking earlier this year Credit: Getty

The Ravens are currently without a manager after Andy Woodman was dismissed on October 22 following a five-and-a-half year tenure.

Bromley currently sit bottom of League One, but could be in line for a bold appointment if they turn to Defoe for their assistant role.

The former Tottenham star left his last job as Woking manager after less than four months in July following a breakdown in his relationship with the club's director of football.

His departure came in dramatic circumstances having failed to turn up for training on the eve of the new season before calling the club to say he would not be returning.

Meanwhile, Robinson has been without a club since he was axed by Salford City in June after their League Two play-off final defeat.

He has also previously had spells in the EFL with Charlton, MK Dons and Oxford.

The experienced boss has previously sought out Defoe as a player, having tried to sign him on a free transfer whilst in charge of Oxford United after the forward left Rangers in 2022.

Defoe enjoyed a stellar Premier League career, featuring 496 times for six different clubs and scoring 163 top-flight goals.

He is Tottenham's seventh-highest all-time goalscorer and ranks 10th on the Premier League's all-time scoring list.

And it now remains to be seen whether Robinson could offer him a route back into coaching, with Woking his first managerial role.

2 Karl Robinson has previously managed four clubs in the EFL Credit: Getty

Bromley search continues

Bromley have been considering several candidates as their search for a new manager enters its second week.

talkSPORT previously revealed that Chelsea and England legend Ashley Cole was interviewed by the south London outfit last week.

The 45-year-old had an eight-game spell in charge of Serie B Cesana last season.

Meanwhile, the Mail report that former Oxford boss Matt Bloomfield is also in the frame, following his sacking in June.

This is a developing story and is being updated.

Stay tuned for further developments as this story continues to break.

Sports.title: Football news LIVE: Scott Parker set to succeed Nuno Espirito Santo at West Ham, Saliba boost for Arsenal, Man United in Champions League
Sports.content:
Confusion

Simon Jordan has questioned what Aston Villa were threatening to take legal action against Jamie Carragher for.

Villa released a statement on Friday night after Carragher spoke on their head coach Unai Emery possibly going to Manchester United.

The Liverpool legend claimed Villa would never be bigger than United and said: "Shut the f*** up Villa fans!"

Carragher issued an apology, and Villa have reportedly dropped their threat of legal action.

"First of all, I'd be fascinated to see what was actionable about what he said," Jordan said on talkSPORT.

"There's one thing suing somebody for defamation, where they have deliberately besmirched your football club, and been misrepresentative and inaccurate in their observations.

"I don't really know what Jamie said that was inaccurate. You might not like it, but that's called freedom of speech and freedom of expression.

"It's called having an opinion, that's what he's paid to do. You might not like the language... you regularly see STFU (shut the f*** up) on people's digital footprints and how they respond to someone saying something.

"When I listened to it, I thought Jamie was just having banter with Aston Villa fans that were probably giving him a load of abuse for something else he said about Villa earlier on in the day, or earlier on in the week. I would assume that Jamie has been told to apologise.

"I would assume that he's been leant on by some organisation like Sky that run away from anything because they don't want to jeopardise their relationship with the football club and, all of a sudden, they might be told they're not going to get access.

"I'm surprised. I was saying the other day that Emery's got to leave Aston Villa and go to a bigger football club if he wants to achieve the things he wants to achieve, the governance is there.

"So, I'm assuming I'll be getting a bit soon because on that basis, what, you can't have an opinion?"

The former Crystal Palace owner added: "I have brought actions against newspapers as a football club owner on the basis of damages, and won damages for doing it.

"I cannot see, despite the fact you might not like what he had to say, what is actionable about that. So, if it's not really actionable, then what are you saying sorry for?

"Are you saying sorry because someone's told you to say sorry? Or you suddenly woke up in the morning and thought, 'That was a terrible thing that I said, and that language is so (out of character) of how I speak'."

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp told he must pick West Ham loanee for Germany – he’s playing at Kylian Mbappe level
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp told he must pick West Ham loanee for Germany – he’s playing at Kylian Mbappe level

Jurgen Klopp has been urged to hand Niclas Fullkrug a shock Germany recall amid his prolific goalscoring form.

The West Ham striker, who joined Werder Bremen on loan in August, is currently the top scorer in the Bundesliga this season.



3 Fullkrug has been tipped to receive his first Germany call-up in 14 months Credit: Getty

Following his return to the club, Fullkrug has scored nine goals in eight league appearances.

Those strikes include scoring in seven Bundesliga matches in a row as well as a further three goals in the DFB Pokal this term.

Fullkrug is the first player to do manage this for Bremen since Rudi Voller during the 1982/83 season.



His feat of scoring in eight successive competitive appearances is a first for the club since the Bundesliga was founded.

It follows a difficult spell with the Hammers for Fullkrug, who has just three goals in 29 appearances since joining the club in 2024.



Meanwhile, a brief loan stint at AC Milan last season saw him find the net just once for the Italian giants.

Fullkrug tipped for Germany recall

The 33-year-old's current run of form is enough to land him a place in Klopp's Germany squad on Thursday, though, says European football journalist Andy Brassell.



Fullkrug has not been included by the current national team boss, who was appointed on a four-year deal back in August.

Speaking exclusively to talkSPORT, Brassell explained: "It's like something that might happen in Black Mirror.

"Before he went to West Ham, he's scoring loads of goals for Dortmund. He's a starter for Dortmund.

3 Fullkrug scored just three goals in 29 appearances for the Hammers Credit: Getty



"He nearly scored in the Champions League final against Real Madrid. If that Fullkrug shot had gone in rather than hitting the post, maybe Dortmund go on and win the Champions League at Wembley in 2024.

"Then he goes to West Ham and sort of gets trapped in this London Stadium striker vortex that they have, where these guys, however good they are, get lost.

"If you look at West Ham's record with strikers and Fullkrug's injury history going all the way back, it was only really going to end one way.

"He goes back to Werder Bremen, where he had a great time in the first place. He's now scored in seven successive Bundesliga games after he got the opener at the weekend.



"The last Werder Bremen player to do that was Rudi Voller in 1982/83. That's the sort of company we're talking about. He's flying at a sort of Kylian Mbappe kind of level.

"Jurgen Klopp picks his Germany team on Thursday. He can't not pick Fullkrug. I know he wants to make them younger, but Germany haven't got a nailed on centre forward.

3 Fullkrug has scored in seven consecutive Bundesliga appearances Credit: Getty

"I know Kai Havertz divides opinion. Is he a centre forward? Is he not a centre forward? I would sort of veer towards no, to be honest, even though he plays there fairly regularly for Arsenal.



"If you're looking for a reference point centre forward. Fullkrug fits it."

Fullkrug's Germany career

Fullkrug has 14 goals in 24 senior caps for Germany having been handed his debut by Hansi Flick in November 2022.

Despite being a member of their 2022 World Cup and Euro 2024 squads, he has not been called up since September last year.

Meanwhile, his last cap for the four-time world champions came against France in June 2025.



Germany will conclude their Nations League campaign against Serbia and the Netherlands this month.

As well as leading the Bundesliga scoring charts, Fullkrug has scored more league goals than any other German in Europe this season.

Of those players included in Klopp's previous squad, his nearest challenger is Eintracht Frankfurt forward Younes Ebnoutalib, who has scored six Bundesliga goals this term.

Sports.title: Sacked EFL boss feels ‘misled’ after brutal firing despite two promotions in three seasons
Sports.content:
Sacked EFL boss feels ‘misled’ after brutal firing despite two promotions in three seasons

Andy Woodman has lifted the lid on his shock Bromley exit after being sacked by the League One club.

The promotion-winning manager was dismissed on October 22 after five-and-a-half years in charge of the Ravens.

3 Woodman has admitted he was 'upset' by the handling of his Bromley exit Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Woodman guided the club from the National League into the third-tier following his appointment in March 2021.

He also lifted the FA Trophy in 2022 prior to their play-off final victory at Wembley Stadium two years later.

However, he has admitted he was left 'upset' at the manner of his exit following a 4-0 defeat to Leicester City last month.

It came amid a run of just one win in 10 league matches since their opening weekend victory at Barnsley.

Those results had left Bromley 23rd in the table following their promotion as League Two champions last season.

Despite Woodman's historic success in charge, though, he was told his tenure was over in a meeting lasting less than four minutes.

Reflecting on his exit, the 55-year-old told the Inside the 72 podcast: "I think there's loads of ways of speaking to people and trying to sort of toe the line, but I think you've just got to speak honestly.

"The easiest way I can sum this up is that when I got the job at Bromley, my first game was Wealdstone and my last game in the league was Leicester.

"I was pretty disappointed and pretty upset. It felt like I'd been misled, in numerous ways.

"To give five-and-a-half years of your life to a club and a fanbase that I really loved and bought into, where I gave everything I had, to then be told in no more than three or four minutes 'thanks'. That was it really.

3 Woodman was sacked last month after five-and-a-half years as Bromley boss Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

"There's no other way of dressing it up. That's the truth. I'm disappointed, but that's football as we know it guys. Unfortunately it never, ever surprises us."

Prior to winning promotion under Woodman in 2024, Bromley had never played in the Football League during their 132-year history.

They are now into their maiden campaign in the third-tier of English football.

Meanwhile, Woodman improved on the previous season's league finish in his final four full campaigns as manager.

talkSPORT verdict

Former Premier League boss Alan Pardew was critical of Bromley's decision to sack Woodman following his departure.

The pair previously worked together at West Ham United, Charlton Athletic, Newcastle United and Crystal Palace.

3 Woodman guided Bromley into the EFL for the first time in their history Credit: Getty

Woodman had been the goalkeeping coach during Pardew's tenures in charge of each club.

Speaking to talkSPORT Breakfast on October 23, he was asked if he was disappointed to see Bromley part ways with Woodman.

Pardew admitted: "Yes, I am. I'm glad you brought it up actually because on my show, The Final Word, he will be our Clown of the Week, that chairman, Robin Stanton-Gleaves.

"Ridiculous. They're a non-league team, and Andy Woodman has taken them not just to an FA Trophy final, which they won by the way, they've never done it before.

"He takes them through the National League and then into the Football League; he takes them on a National League budget through League Two. They get to League One, they're still on a League Two budget, really.

"And after ten games, he dispenses with his services as if to say, 'Well, it was all about me and nothing to do with Andy Woodman'.

Bromley's league positions under Andy Woodman *Appointed midway through season 2020/21: Seventh in the National League* - Beaten in play-off quarter-final 2021/22: 10th in the National League - Won FA Trophy 2022/23: Seventh in the National League - Beaten in play-off semi-final 2023/24: Third in the National League - Promoted via the play-offs 2024/25: 11th in League Two 2025/26: 1st in League Two - Promoted as champions

"It's ridiculous, and I think that it's probably the injustice you see sometimes in the game. That hurts, and that hurt me yesterday."

Sports.title: What time is Fenerbahce vs Liverpool as clubs meet for first time in early kick-off
Sports.content:
What time is Fenerbahce vs Liverpool as clubs meet for first time in early kick-off

Liverpool head to Istanbul for a tough game after an inconsistent start to the season with new manager Andoni Iraola.

The Reds have done well in the Champions League so far despite only sitting fifth in the Premier League, recording three wins from their three opening matches in Europe.



3 Liverpool have been apart of high scoring games this season in the Champions League Credit: Getty

They stand in third place in the continental competitions league phase, only behind Paris Saint-Germain and Premier League rivals Aston Villa.

Liverpool beat Atletico Madrid 2-1 in their opening fixture and followed that up with an eventful 6-3 win at LASK last month.

Additionally, Iraola's side defeated Villarreal in a hard-fought 4-3 win at Anfield last time out in Europe.



The Reds now take on Fenerbahce and will be facing a familiar face as fan favourite Dirk Kuyt is in interim charge following Ismail Kartal's departure.

The Turkish giants drew 1-1 with AS Roma in their opener, then lost 6-0 to Aston Villa before securing another point in a 2-2 draw against Slavia Prague.



Where to watch Fenerbahce v Liverpool

The fixture will kick-off at 5:45pm on Wednesday, November 4.

It's being played at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium in Instanbul.

The Reds have a bad record in Turkey's biggest city.

Despite one of the club's greatest nights taking place there in the 2005 Champions League final against AC Milan, they have lost five visits to the city.

This includes being beaten twice last season by Galatasaray.

Fans can listen to the match on talkSPORT 2 with commentary from Alex Crook and former Chelsea defender Scott Minto.
