Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: These states could elect their first female governors
World.content:
This year’s midterm election is likely to change history as several gubernatorial candidates from the Midwest to the South are vying to become their states’ first female governors.

Georgia’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms is running to become not only the state’s first female governor, but the first Black female governor in the nation.

“I wake up as a Black woman every day, so it’s no surprise to me that I’m capable and I’m qualified and I’m able,” Bottoms told CNN. “But if it’s representation for other people who may not have thought that it was possible, then it’s all worth it.”

Bottoms is locked in a tight race with Republican Rick Jackson in a race that has taken center stage.

Minnesota is also set to elect its first woman governor, with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar in a strong position in her race with Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth. Tennessee is in the same spot, with Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn leading over Democrat Jerri Green.

Ohio could also join the list, if Democrat Amy Acton prevails over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. Although the state briefly had an interim female governor nearly 30 years ago, it has yet to elect a woman to the office.

World.title: If a blue wave is coming, here are the races where it will start
World.content:
Midterm elections are almost always bad for the president’s party. Sometimes they are very bad for the president’s party. And every so often they are historically bad.

The first outcome seems guaranteed on Tuesday. Republicans are increasingly wary of the second. And more Democrats are daring to dream of the third.

Late polling mostly provides Democrats reason for optimism. Attitudes toward the president have become the most important factor shaping midterm outcomes, and President Donald Trump’s approval rating today is much lower than in 2018 when Republicans lost over 40 House seats; it’s well below the levels of Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton before their parties suffered major midterm losses. Surveys in the campaign’s final days have found Democrats showing strength in states that Republicans have long dominated, including Texas, Ohio, and even Kansas and South Carolina.

But precisely because the electoral battlefield is concentrated so heavily in Republican-leaning terrain, most Democrats remain nervous about the outcome, especially in the Senate. In most of the states and House districts that both parties are fully contesting, Republican voters still outnumber Democrats; if the combination of Trump’s campaign blitz and the heavy GOP spending advantage can mobilize more of them than pollsters now expect, that would erase some of the narrow Democratic advantages in red places.

“The best news for our side is that the vaunted Republican surge at the end that many would have expected given all their money just hasn’t happened,” says Paul Maslin, a longtime Democratic pollster. “In these double-digit red states, it’s simply a case of are (our leads) baked in enough for us to pull through?”

What follows is an election night guide organized, in effect, by degree of difficulty. Moving from East to West, it’s my attempt to identify House, Senate and governor races that indicate whether Democrats are on track for a good night, a very good night, or a historic breakthrough comparable to the Republican landslides in 1994 and 2010, and the Democratic “thumpin’” in 2006.

Conversely, if Democrats on Tuesday lose more than a handful of the races in the “good” category, it will indicate the results could leave them disappointed, or worse.

The Northeast

The first big indications of the night’s direction will come primarily from races in the East, because polls close earliest in the region.

In Virginia, where polls close at 7 p.m. (all closing times are Eastern), a Democratic win in the VA-2 House race will be a sign the party is on track for a solid performance. In that race, former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria is pursuing a rematch against Republican Jen Kiggans, who beat her in 2022 in a district Trump carried by less than a point in 2024. Not winning this race would be an early sign that Democrats are underperforming.

If Democrats also win the VA-1 congressional seat, that will augur a larger wave. In that seat, Republican Rob Wittman is straining to hold off Democrat Shannon Taylor in a seat Trump carried by five points. If former Democratic Rep. Tom Perriello ousts Republican Rep. John McGuire, who is finishing his first term in VA-5 — a seat Trump carried by 12 points — it will signal the party is on track to win even more than the 235 seats they captured in 2018, predicts Kyle Kondik, managing editor of the Sabato’s Crystal Ball newsletter published by the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics.

Pennsylvania, where polls close at 8 p.m., offers a similar progression. Democrats will be on track for a solid performance if they beat Republican incumbents in Ryan Mackenzie in PA-7 and Scott Perry in PA-10, two heavily blue-collar districts that Trump won by five points or less. Republicans will grow even more nervous if Democrat Paige Cognetti ousts first-term GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in PA-8, another heavily blue-collar district in Northeast Pennsylvania that Trump won by over eight points.

On paper, PA-1 should offer Democrats their best chance of flipping a House seat in the commonwealth. It’s crowded with the well-educated, upper middle-class voters who have recoiled from the GOP in the Trump era. But GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who was first elected in 2016, has for years effectively walked the tightrope of distancing from Trump without fully breaking from him. If Democrat Bob Harvie beats Fitzpatrick, that will be another sign of a historic wave — and an indication that white-collar voters disenchanted with Trump are demanding more unconditional opposition to his agenda.

Democratic congressional candidate Bob Harvie greets attendees during an “Autumn Alive” community celebration in downtown Quakertown, Pennsylvania, on October 17. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images

“This is the kind of stuff that happens in a wave,” says Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst for Decision Desk HQ, a political website. “An incumbent has been strong; he’s been able to distinguish himself from his party enough to outperform (the district’s partisan lean). And then the environment gets bad enough and … suddenly it’s a lot harder to keep yourself separate from the party.”

In Maine, where polls also close at 8 p.m., a comfortable victory for Democrat Hannah Pingree in the Maine governor race will be a sign that the party is meeting its marks for a solid night. If progressive Democrat Matthew Dunlap beats former GOP Gov. Paul LePage to hold the heavily blue-collar and rural ME-2 Congressional District, that will signal an even better night for Democrats.

The Maine Senate contest between Republican incumbdent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson will be the most closely watched race in the state — and indeed the entire Northeast. Collins is the last Republican senator left in the 19 states that have voted against Trump in all three of his presidential races. And she was the only Republican Senate incumbent or challenger during Trump’s first term who won in a state where the exit polls showed more voters disapproved than approved of his job performance.

Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is seen through a window as he speaks during a “Retire Susan” press conference in Portland, Maine, on October 30. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Jackson has been a solid, though uneven, campaigner since Democrats tapped him as a replacement candidate when their primary winner Graham Platner was capsized by scandal. If Jackson wins, it will be another sign that Democrats are exceeding expectations — and that the Trump undertow (his disapproval hit 67% in the latest CNN Maine poll last week) is submerging even the most skillful and entrenched Republicans in swing or blue-tilting areas.

Elsewhere in the region, a win for Democrat Rebecca Bennett over Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in the NJ-7 House race, another well-educated district Trump won narrowly, would show the party on track for a good night. If Democrat Cait Conley beats GOP Rep. Mike Lawler, a more formidable opponent, in NY-17, yet another white-collar seat Trump narrowly carried, it would signal a stronger wave. And if Democrat Blake Gendebien flips NY-21, the preponderantly working-class White upstate New York seat being vacated by Rep. Elise Stefanik, the wave will be reaching historic heights.

The South

The first clues from the South will come from Georgia, where polls close at 7 p.m. A solid reelection victory for Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff, who has led Republican Mike Collins in polls for the Georgia Senate race all fall, would show the Democrats meeting expectations. An upset win for Keisha Lance Bottoms over Republican Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor race, despite the massive sums he has poured into his own campaign, would show the party exceeding them.

A voter enters a polling location on the first day of early voting for the midterm election, in Atlanta on October 13. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg/Getty Images

North Carolina, where polls close at 7:30 p.m., will also offer early markers. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper is strongly favored to flip the North Carolina Senate seat, but if he wins by at least 6 points, it will be a sign that the party is headed for a good night, says Michael Bitzer, professor of politics and history at Catawba College, and principal author of a blog on Carolina politics.

Other signs of a good Democratic performance will come if Rep. Donald Davis survives in the NC-1 seat, which state Republicans redistricted to produce one that Trump carried by over 11 points. As impressive will be if moderate Democrat Jamie Ager flips NC-11, a district vacated by scandal-tarred Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards that Trump carried by about 10 points. If Democrats capture any other GOP-held seats — including Rep. Gregory Murphy in NC-3, a district Trump won by 22 points, or the NC-9 seat now held by Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — that would signal historic breakthroughs for the party.

In Florida, where the last polls close at 8 p.m., the baseline tests for Democrats are whether they can hold two seats that Republicans redistricted to tilt more red. A win for Rep. Jared Moskowitz in FL-25 would show a positive trend for Democrats; reelection for Rep. Kathy Castor in FL-14 would measure an even stronger current, as would a win for Rep. Darren Soto in FL-9, another seat the GOP redrew to tilt right. Victories for Democrats in either FL-13, now held by Republican Anna Paulina Luna, or FL-7, a Republican open seat, would also mark a very good night for Florida Democrats. So would a victory by Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former Republican, over Byron Donalds in the Florida governor race.

President Donald Trump listens to Republican candidate for Florida governor Byron Donalds speak during a rally at Florida Gulf Coast University’s Alico Arena, in Fort Myers, Florida, on October 23. Umit Bektas/Reuters

The storm will reach historic proportions if Democrats oust veteran GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in heavily Hispanic FL-27, a seat Trump carried by 15 points; she has broken with Trump more openly over immigration enforcement than any other Congressional Republican. And the gale will reach Category 5 levels if progressive Democrat Angie Nixon beats Republican Ashley Moody in the Florida Senate race.

Likewise, an upset for Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham, in the South Carolina Senate race (where polls close at 7 p.m.), would mark a historic night for Democrats; the party hasn’t elected a senator there since Fritz Hollings in 1998. A victory for Democrat Scott Colom over Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race would be even more remarkable: No Democrat has won a Senate seat there since 1982.

In Texas, where the last polls close at 9 p.m., Democrats haven’t elected a US senator since 1988. A win for James Talarico over Ken Paxton, the scandal-tarred Republican nominee, in the Texas Senate contest despite massive Republican super PAC spending funded by Elon Musk and others, would show Democrats progressing toward a very good night, both in the state and nationally. If Democrat Gina Hinojosa beats Republican Greg Abbott in the Texas governor race, despite his massive spending advantage, that would represent an even more historic breakthrough for Democrats. Victories for either candidate, but especially Hinojosa, would constitute “a generational win” for Texas Democrats, says Bill Miller, a leading lobbyist who has run campaigns for candidates in both parties.

“The key down here is that environment is good for Democrats and the money is good for Republicans, and how that washes out will be: Who gets their vote out?” says Miller. “There are more Republicans than Democrats, and if Republicans do a better job, they will win a close election. If they don’t, they will lose a close election.”

Attendees cheer during a campaign event with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the University Of North Texas in Denton, Texas, on October 19. Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Texas House races will also offer a revealing gauge, especially for measuring how much of Trump’s Latino breakthrough in 2024 he has squandered since. Reelection wins for Democrats Henry Cuellar in TX-28 and Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 in South Texas seats Republicans redistricted to undercut the incumbents would show the party meeting expectations; if Tejano singing star Bobby Pulido beats Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in TX-15 (a seat Trump won by 18 points) and/or sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia holds TX-35 (an open seat Trump carried by almost 11 points), it would show Democrats overperforming among Hispanics. An upset win for Democrat Katy Padilla Stout over bomb-throwing Republican Brandon Herrera in the open TX-23 seat would capture a Democratic tide reaching tsunami levels.

The Midwest

After moving sharply toward Trump and the GOP over the past decade, the middle of the country is once again back in the center of American politics.

High prices for gas and diesel; the disruptive impact of Trump’s tariffs on the farm economy; and the president’s loosening grip on the White working-class voters plentiful across these states have all allowed Democrats to dream of recovery in places where they have declined for years. As Skelley notes, all these factors give Democrats reason for optimism that the Midwest may swing toward them even more than other regions.

The region’s initial soundings will come in two states where all polls close at 7 p.m. If Democrat Zach Dembo captures a Republican open seat in KY-6, a seat Trump carried by 15 points, or J.D. Ford defeats Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz in IN-5, where Trump won by nearly 17 points, either would put the party on track for a very good night.

The first comprehensive signal from the region will come in Ohio, where polls close at 7:30 p.m. After Republicans redrew the state’s congressional map, reelection victories for Democratic incumbents Greg Landsman in OH-1 and especially Marcy Kaptur in OH-9 would show the party on a solid path. So would a win for Democratic ironworker Brian Poindexter against embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller in OH-7, a seat Trump carried by 11 points.

Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton embrace during “Fighting for Toledo” rally in Toledo, Ohio, on October 29. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Wins for Democrats in the key statewide races would mark bigger breakthroughs. A victory for Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown over GOP incumbent Jon Husted in the Ohio Senate race would show Democrats recapturing at least some of the ground they have surrendered with blue-collar White voters in the Trump years. Although Democrats haven’t won an Ohio governor race since 2006, Amy Acton has emerged as a clear favorite over self-funding Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, especially after the searing bipartisan backlash over his recent ad featuring her estranged mother. “As long as turnout (for Democrats) doesn’t collapse, Brown’s on track, and she’s on track,” predicts Ohio-based Democratic consultant Jeff Rusnak.

More surprising would be Democratic upsets in either the OH-10 or OH-15 districts now held by GOP Reps. Mike Turner and Mike Carey, respectively. Trump won the former by eight points and the latter by 10. “The big tidal wave would be Turner and Carey,” says Rusnak.

The next big Midwestern signals will come from states where all polls close at 9 p.m. In Iowa, Democratic victories over Republicans Mariannette Miller-Meeks in IA-1 and Zach Nunn in IA-3, seats Trump won by eight and four points respectively, would show the party meeting expectations. So would a win in the Iowa governor race for Democrat Rob Sand, who has led in polls all year even though Democrats have not elected a governor there since 2006.

An upset win for Democrats in IA-2, the more reliably Republican seat being vacated by Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate nominee, would mark a bigger wave. So would a win for Democrat Josh Turek over Hinson in the heated Iowa Senate race; like Brown in Ohio, a Turek win would only be possible if Democrats recover at least some support among working-class Whites, including in rural areas hit hard by Trump’s tariffs and rising diesel costs.

Wisconsin presents a similar profile: A win for Democrat Rebecca Cooke over Republican Derrick Van Orden in the WI-3 House race would mark a good night for the party; a victory for Democrat Mitchell Berman over Republican Bryan Steil in WI-1, and for Democrat David Crowley in the open seat Wisconsin governor race, would signal something more.

Democratic congressional candidate Rebecca Cooke raises hands with Sen. Bernie Sanders during a rally in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, on October 25. Tom Baker/Getty Images

In Michigan, a comfortable win for Democrat Jocelyn Benson in the Michigan governor race is the baseline for a good Democratic night. Flipping Republican-held House seats in MI-4 and MI-7 would also show Democrats staying on track for a good night; the 7th is a more favorable district for Democrats, but their nominee, progressive William Lawrence, is a weaker candidate than state Sen. Sean McCann in the 4th, notes David Wasserman, senior elections analyst for the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter.

However these contests turn out, the verdict on Democrats’ performance will pivot on the bitter Michigan Senate race. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost a Senate bid in 2024, are locked in a close contest that recently has been dominated by Islamophobic remarks from Trump and other Republicans portraying El-Sayed, who is Muslim, as a “jihadist.”

Before this onslaught, an El-Sayed win that preserved this open Democratic seat might have only represented holding serve for his party. But if El-Sayed survives this firestorm, even amid conspicuous defections by some Jewish Democrats, it will be another indication the Trump undertow (his disapproval soared to 66% in the new CNN Michigan poll) is too strong for Republicans to overcome, even when other factors favor them.

Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Mike Rogers debate on at WXYZ Channel 7 in Southfield, Michigan, on October 21. Robin Buckson/Detroit News/Pool/AP

That message would be reinforced even more powerfully if Republican Roger Marshall beats Democrat Adam Hamilton in the Kansas Senate race (the state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932); if independent Dan Osborn topples Republican Pete Ricketts in the Nebraska Senate race; or if independent Brian Bengs upsets GOP Sen. Mike Rounds in the South Dakota Senate contest. Democratic wins in any of those races would propel the night squarely into tsunami territory.

The West

Both Colorado and Arizona, where polls close at 9 p.m. Eastern, present a clear progression of opportunity for Democrats.

A win in the CO-8 House race, where Republican Gabe Evans is trying to hold off former state Rep. Manny Rutinel, in a district north of Denver that Trump carried by less than two points, would track with a good Democratic performance. A win by Democratic Army veteran Jessica Killen over Republican Jeff Crank in CO-5, a district Trump won by nine points, would mark a very good night for the party. And if Democrats oust either Republican Reps. Jeff Hurd in CO-3 or, especially, Lauren Boebert in CO-4, a seat Trump won by more than 18 points, the flood will be mountain-high.

In Arizona, which has become a perennial swing state, a comfortable reelection for Democrat Katie Hobbs over hard-line Republican Andy Biggs, now seems the minimum for a good Democratic night. So does success in flipping AZ-1, the very well-educated and affluent seat in the northeast Phoenix suburbs, being vacated by Republican Rep. David Schweikert; Trump has taken a special interest in promoting the GOP nominee, Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker and longtime golfing buddy of the president, but he’s now the underdog against Democrat Amish Shah. More impressive will be if Democratic Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza defeats Rep. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican who has tried to position himself as a moderate, in AZ-6, a seat centered on the Tucson suburbs that Trump carried by less than a point.

In Alaska, where the last polls close at 1 a.m., Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, has established himself as such a strong favorite (even drawing an endorsement last week from Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski) in the Alaska governor race, that a win would show Democrats on a solid path in the state.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a campaign event in Juneau, Alaska, on October 29. Chloe Anderson/AP

More significant would be a victory in the Alaska Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US representative, over Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who has stressed his role in opening the state to greater oil and gas development, which most Alaskans view positively as an engine of prosperity. Alaska has elected only four Democratic senators since it entered the union in 1959 and just one since 1980. But Peltola, who would be the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate, has grounded herself in the state (her unique campaign slogan is “Fish, Family, and Freedom”) and has been boosted by pervasive discontent over soaring gas and diesel costs.

The Trump administration has preemptively sued to invalidate the results if Peltola wins because a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan made the final-four ballot in the state’s ranked choice voting system. Most legal observers give that litigation little chance of success. But the stunning New York Times reporting late last week showing that Democrats aligned with Peltola’s campaign worked to recruit the other Dan Sullivan into the race has prompted investigations from both Alaska’s Republican governor and the Justice Department. The controversy could hurt her electorally — even if many election law experts believe it is also unlikely to provide any legal basis for rejecting the outcome.

Elsewhere across the West, it will be a good result for Democrats if progressive Randy Villegas finally ousts Republican David Valadao, who has long survived in CA-22, a swing and heavily Hispanic district in California’s Central Valley. A reelection for center-right Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in WA-3, a Southwest Washington seat that Trump carried by three points, represents a similar level of difficulty for the party. Polls close at 11 p.m. in both states.

If Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek holds off Republican Christine Drazan in the Oregon governor race (where polls also close at 11 p.m.) despite drooping approval ratings and discontent over the economy and persistent homelessness in Portland, it will send a stronger signal that the backlash against Trump is virtually insurmountable for blue state Republicans. An upset for Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford over Republican Joe Lombardo in the Nevada governor race (where polls close at 10 p.m.) would likewise mark a stronger Democratic current. As would a win for Democratic smoke jumper Sam Forstag in MT-1, a seat Trump carried by nearly 12 points.

Democratic wins in two other House districts would mark an historic tide. One is AZ-2, a seat Trump won by 15 points, where Republican Rep. Eli Crane is facing former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez. The other is NV-2, an open seat in northern Nevada that gave Trump a 14-point margin two years ago.

A turnout surge from die-hard Trump supporters, which pollsters have missed before, could still blunt the Democratic gains. But a good night for Republicans this week might be anything that stops short of historically bad.

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Republican Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton are the candidates in the Kansas Senate race.

World.title: OpenAI says its AI is getting better at doing things humans do, like shopping and meal planning
World.content:
People already use OpenAI’s ChatGPT for things like helping with homework and creating presentations.

Now, the tech giant claims its AI models are getting better at everyday tasks largely left up to humans — like shopping and creating a budget.

OpenAI on Monday announced a new internal tool for assessing how AI handles tasks like these, along with research on how its own models performed. OpenAI claims its GPT-6 Astra model scored 93.1% at finding the right kindergarten after moving, a 98% score at managing community volunteers preparing for a flood and a 90.4% score at creating a meal plan for a parent recently diagnosed with diabetes.

The new benchmark comes at a time when OpenAI faces fierce competition from Meta, Anthropic and Google — all of which are racing to develop AI agents that can handle real-world tasks. OpenAI and its rivals are also grappling with AI safety concerns and pressure to turn a profit from their massive investments in the technology.

But first, OpenAI had to come up with a way to figure out whether ChatGPT is actually any good at errands like putting together a grocery cart and filling out online forms.

“Because so many people are using the app, we want to capture all the different use cases and the ways that they’re using it, and really understand like how we’re improving over time,” Jenny Yang, a researcher at OpenAI, told CNN ahead of the evaluation’s release. “What are the things that we’re not so good at yet? And how do we just like make this technology better for people?”

How OpenAI created the test

Standardized evaluations are critical in AI development because AI labs use them as guidance to train and optimize their models to improve in specific areas. Last year, OpenAI released a benchmark called GDPVal to measure how AI performs in work-related skills across industries like manufacturing, government work, finance and sales, among others.

The new benchmark could be critical in OpenAI’s push to stay ahead of the competition by turning ChatGPT from a tool for generating content to an assistant that can get things done on users’ behalf.

But measuring how AI performs in everyday life presents new challenges. The steps and skills required to adequately shop for groceries or pick out the right kindergarten for a child are broad and vague. And the results can be subjective.

Even figuring out what tests to come up with can be difficult because many people use AI differently, and an AI agent’s answers can vary depending on the information it’s given.

OpenAI started by looking at broad surveys breaking down how people spend most of their time, like the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ American Time Use survey and the United Kingdom’s Multinational Time Use Survey. The problem, however, was that some of the things that topped the list weren’t tasks that AI could help with, like sleeping or eating.

So OpenAI asked ChatGPT users: What kinds of things do you wish an AI assistant could help with?

The company surveyed around 4,000 people and had a smaller group of about 100 users write down tasks they wanted AI to do for them, and what personal context they would give the AI model to get the desired result. They also asked the users to come up with a rubric for evaluating whether the AI model successfully completed the task.

OpenAI also made sure ChatGPT users had a thorough understanding of the task they were proposing. For example, a person suggesting a test related to how AI handles financial planning should have experience working with a financial advisor for multiple years.

Yang said they had a strict list of requirements.

“You had to like have evidence that you were some kind of like expert or really understood what the right answer looked like for you,” she said.

The tasks that OpenAI is testing can vary widely — from apartment hunting to caring for a loved one. So, what exactly is OpenAI measuring?

It’s evaluating the types of skills the model would need to get the right answer, like how well it can navigate websites, apply context by looking at large troves of information in a user’s chat history and make conclusions that align with a user’s needs and expectations.

OpenAI’s testing indicates its GPT-6 Astra model, which was released in September, scored 80% on general performance related to prompts involving everyday tasks. Its GPT-5.2 model from December 2025 scored just 49.3%.

“There’s just so much information, and a better model would be able to sift through that quickly and really pull out the most relevant pieces,” said Yang.

The race to create personal AI agents

OpenAI wants ChatGPT to play a more prominent role in everyday life, but it’s facing an onslaught of competitive pressure — particularly from Meta.

Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in September, amassed 10 million downloads in the United States in its first 40 days, making it one of the few apps to achieve that milestone, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. OpenAI introduced its Dots agent, which it says can work on long-running tasks in the background while users go about their day, within the same month. And Anthropic announced its new AI agent app, Claude Duet, in October.

The race to develop personal AI agents also comes as the technology has raised safety concerns following a string of incidents in which AI models broke out of testing environments and breached companies’ systems. Those incidents occurred during testing, not with consumer products, but still raised questions about whether the technology is moving too fast.

There’s also the question of whether people will rely on AI too much, and how to draw boundaries when figuring out which tasks to outsource to AI. An anecdote former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer shared with The New York Times of how she used AI to summarize what makes her daughter special for a school project drew criticism online.

To Yang, the goal is to create AI models that can help people get more time back in their day by either cutting out time-consuming errands — like returning a package or helping them learn a new skill.

“I think there’s so many cases like this where being able to use AI just empowers you to do things that you wouldn’t have been able to do, or just makes your life easier overall,” said Yang. “And I think that’s like the main use case that we’re really excited about.”

World.title: At least 31 dead after Russia drops nine bombs on a Ukrainian school building
World.content:
Dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter.

At least 31 people have been confirmed dead and another 48 are still unaccounted for after the attack on the building in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, which was being used as a shelter and a humanitarian aid distribution center, local governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

They were in a newly-built, EU-funded reinforced basement designed to withstand most strikes, Semikin said, but the massive force of the bombs caused the concrete structure to collapse and a fire broke out.

The shelter was built last year in an effort to keep classes going during wartime, but many civilians have since left as the fighting got closer to the village, and it is not currently used as a school. Instead, local authorities are using it as an administrative center and humanitarian hub.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky described the strike as “utterly horrific.”

He said the shelter was attacked on Monday during the time when humanitarian aid was being distributed.

He said the attack came just before Russia launched another massive barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of powerful cruise and ballistic missiles targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure – despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for energy ceasefire.

“It is very telling that all of this is happening on the day of the US congressional elections. The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said on Tuesday morning.

“Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that,” Zelensky added.

Double-tap strike

The strike on Monday is among the deadliest since the start of the war, but the past few months have been exceptionally bloody for Ukrainian civilians.

Russia ramped up its aerial attacks on towns and cities across the country over the summer, striking at all times of the day.

At least 33 people were killed last month when Russia hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. And a mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage.

Rescuers carry the body of a person killed by the Russian airstrike in the frontline town of Komyshuvakha. State Emergency Service/Reuters

The assault against Komyshuvakha on Monday followed a familiar scenario in which Russian forces launch the first wave of strikes, wait for emergency services to arrive and then strike again.

At least two first responders, named locally as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksiy Sushchevsky, both 44, were killed after rushing to the scene of the first strike.

The Ukrainian Police said at least four of its officers have also been killed in the attack. They were named as Mykhailo Buzhenko and Mykola Balanda, both of who had more than two decades of police service under their belts, and Mykhailo Romanov and Dmytro Besedin, both of whom have been community police officers for more than a decade.

“(They) were helping local residents take shelter in an underground school. A treacherous follow-up strike trapped everyone who was trying to escape,” the police said in a statement.

Semikin told Ukraine’s national TV broadcast on Tuesday that Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs in the attack.

“To put this into perspective, this is a three-ton aerial bomb containing nearly 1.5 tons of explosive material; such weapons are primarily designed to destroy heavy concrete fortifications and bunkers,” he said.

World.title: Abdelrahman Younes wins three medals, breaks world record at weightlifting championships
World.content:
Egyptian Youth and Sports Minister Gohar Nabil on Monday, November 2, 2026, congratulated weightlifter Abdelrahman Younes after he won three medals and broke a world record at the 2026 World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo, China.

Younes claimed gold in the men’s 85kg total with a combined lift of 390kg, setting a new world record. He also won silver in the snatch with 177kg and bronze in the clean and jerk with 213kg.

The championships count towards qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games.

Nabil praised the achievement, saying it reflected sustained efforts and hard work that had led to the Egyptian athlete’s success on the world stage.

He also congratulated Younes’s coaching, medical and administrative teams, commending their role in his preparation and performance.

The minister extended his congratulations to the Egyptian Weightlifting Federation, headed by Mohamed Abdel Maqsoud.

“What Abdelrahman Younes, our world champion, has achieved is a source of pride and joy for all Egyptians,” Nabil said, wishing him further success in upcoming competitions.

World.title: Egypt, UAE probe cooperation to develop Omayed Natural Reserve
World.content:
Executive President of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA) Sherif Abdel Rahim discussed on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with Abdullah Al Jabri and Nasser Al Kaabi, members of the Board of Directors of the International Fund for Houbara Conservation in the UAE, mechanisms for joint cooperation to develop al Omayed Nature Reserve in Matrouh governorate.

The meeting discussed enhancing public access to the reserve in accordance with environmental regulations that ensure the protection of its natural resources, as well as supporting scientific research and specialized studies that contribute to preserving its biodiversity and strengthening its status as a biosphere reserve listed under UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere Program.

The meeting was held in line with directives from Minister of Local Development and Environment Manal Awad to strengthen efforts to develop Egypt’s nature reserves.

The meeting was attended by Head of the Nature Conservation Sector Khaled Abbas, Minister’s Assistant for Sustainability and Corporate Social Responsibility Saber Othman, and Head of the Central Administration for Nature Reserves Mohamed Youssef.

Abdel Rahim said the meeting discussed ways to develop the reserve’s management system, organize visitor reception, raise environmental awareness and regulate visitor movement within the reserve.

These measures aim to enable the public to explore the reserve’s natural richness and environmental value, while promoting awareness of the importance of biodiversity conservation and adhering to regulations that protect natural habitats and preserve ecological balance.

World.title: PM attends opening of AISU summit
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly attended on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, the opening of the 19th Arab Steel Summit and Exhibition.

The event is organized by the Arab Iron and Steel Union (AISU).

The event was attended by Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem, a number of ministers and senior state officials, heads of Arab iron and steel-producing companies, as well as international suppliers of steel technology.

The two-day conference aims to discuss the future of the Arab steel industry amid rapidly changing global developments, and to strengthen its competitiveness and sustainability.

World.title: Egypt, Indonesia seek closer religious cooperation to counter extremism
World.content:
Egypt’s Grand Mufti Nazir Mohamed Ayyad has called for stronger cooperation between religious institutions in Egypt and Indonesia to address contemporary intellectual and religious challenges and promote moderate Islamic teachings.

Speaking during a meeting with a delegation from Indonesia’s Ulema Council, led by Deputy Chairman General Khalil Nafis Hassanuddin, Ayyad highlighted Egypt’s experience in developing fatwa services, training religious scholars and using artificial intelligence in religious guidance.

He also outlined Dar al-Ifta’s efforts to counter extremism, hatred speech and Islamophobia, highlighting its international cooperation through the General Secretariat for Fatwa Authorities Worldwide, which comprises 111 members from 108 countries.

Hassanuddin said the Indonesian council relies on Egyptian fatwas, particularly those concerning Hajj, and expressed interest in expanding cooperation in research, training and digital transformation.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-NSA Official Gets 50 Years for Statutory Rape of 16-Year-Old Boy; Kidnapping Charge Returns to Court
World.content:
Judge Wesseh Upholds Rape Conviction, Acquits Jallah of Gang Rape; Defense Heads to Supreme Court

Monrovia – A former National Security Agency (NSA) official who once served within Liberia’s national security establishment has been sentenced to 50 years in prison for the statutory rape of a 16-year-old boy. This brings a dramatic new chapter to a criminal case that has tested the country’s justice system, raised questions about the protection of vulnerable children, and drawn intense public attention.

By: Willie N. Tokpah



Peter Bon Jallah, 63, was sentenced Tuesday, November 3, 2026, by Criminal Court “E” Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr., following his conviction for statutory rape. He is to serve his sentence at the Monrovia Central Prison.

The sentence comes after weeks of contentious legal proceedings, competing interpretations of medical and forensic evidence, and a defense challenge that has already signaled its intention to take the matter before the Supreme Court of Liberia.

But while the 50-year sentence marks a major development in the statutory rape proceedings, the case is not entirely over. The court has quashed its earlier guilty finding on kidnapping and ordered that the charge be pursued afresh before Criminal Court “A.” Jallah was also acquitted of gang rape after Judge Wesseh ruled that the prosecution failed to establish sufficient evidence to sustain that particular charge.

The distinction is legally important: Jallah stands convicted and sentenced for statutory rape, but the kidnapping allegation remains unresolved and subject to fresh proceedings.

A 50-Year Sentence, A Case Far From Over

In his sentencing decision, Judge Wesseh maintained that the prosecution had established the legal elements necessary to convict Jallah of statutory rape. However, the judge drew a clear line between the evidence supporting that conviction and the prosecution’s failure to prove gang rape.

The court determined that the state had not presented sufficient direct evidence to establish Jallah’s participation in gang rape, resulting in his acquittal on that charge. The statutory rape conviction, however, survived the defense’s attempt to have the entire verdict overturned.

The sentence follows Monday’s ruling, November 2, 2026, in which Judge Wesseh denied Jallah’s motion for a new trial but granted the prosecution’s request to set aside the kidnapping conviction and send that charge to Criminal Court “A” for fresh proceedings. The ruling effectively separated the three charges that had initially been determined in the October 23 verdict.

The court’s decision means that the prosecution cannot rely on the quashed kidnapping finding as an existing conviction. It must pursue that allegation through the appropriate fresh proceedings.

The Defense’s Last-Ditch Legal Challenge

Jallah’s sentencing followed a contentious hearing over his October 27 motion for a new trial. The defense argued that:

Verdict inconsistencies: The October 23 verdict contained structural contradictions.

The October 23 verdict contained structural contradictions. Procedural errors: The court committed notable legal and procedural mistakes.

The court committed notable legal and procedural mistakes. Insufficient evidence: The available evidence did not sufficiently support the findings against their client.

The available evidence did not sufficiently support the findings against their client. Jurisdictional limits: The defense questioned Criminal Court “E’s” jurisdiction over the kidnapping charge.

The defense questioned Criminal Court “E’s” jurisdiction over the kidnapping charge. Forensic disputes: The defense challenged the prosecution’s medical and forensic interpretations.

The prosecution resisted the motion, insisting that the statutory rape conviction was independently supported by the evidence and should not be disturbed because of the jurisdictional issue surrounding kidnapping. Prosecutors also urged the court to preserve the statutory rape conviction while quashing the kidnapping finding and forwarding that charge for fresh proceedings before Criminal Court “A.”

Judge Wesseh’s Monday ruling substantially adopted that approach. Following the decision, the defense objected and announced plans to appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia. That appeal could place important questions concerning the sufficiency of evidence, jurisdiction, and the legal treatment of the separate charges before the country’s highest court.

No Prior Criminal Record, But 50 Years Behind Bars

An aspect of the sentencing proceedings was the pre-sentence and behavioral assessment conducted through the Ministry of Justice’s Bureau of Probation Services. The report, according to information presented in connection with the sentencing, indicated that Jallah had no prior criminal record before the present conviction.

But the absence of a previous criminal record did not prevent the court from imposing the 50-year prison term. The sentencing marks a significant development in a case involving a minor and a defendant who previously served within the National Security Agency, an institution entrusted with responsibilities relating to national security.

Jallah’s former position adds another dimension to the case, particularly the broader public debate over accountability, institutional responsibility, and the protection of children from sexual exploitation. His former government affiliation, however, does not alter the legal standard governing the criminal proceedings.

How the Case Unfolded

The charges stemmed from allegations involving a 16-year-old boy who reportedly performed paid domestic chores at Jallah’s residence in Monrovia:

Late 2025: According to the indictment, the prosecution alleged that the teenager was sexually abused on multiple occasions.

According to the indictment, the prosecution alleged that the teenager was sexually abused on multiple occasions. January 2026: A subsequent incident allegedly involved the boy being transported to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area, where prosecutors said he was confined and sexually abused.

A subsequent incident allegedly involved the boy being transported to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area, where prosecutors said he was confined and sexually abused. Unindicted actors: Two unidentified men were also implicated in connection with the allegations but were not brought before the court during Jallah’s trial.

The trial featured an extensive array of testimonies and evidence:

The Prosecution: Presented 13 regular witnesses and 6 rebuttal witnesses, including the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel, and forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije of the Rwanda Forensic Institute.

Presented 13 regular witnesses and 6 rebuttal witnesses, including the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel, and forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije of the Rwanda Forensic Institute. The Defense: Presented 8 witnesses, including Jallah himself, challenging the prosecution’s account and disputing aspects of the medical, forensic, and DNA evidence.

After considering the evidence and arguments from both sides, Judge Wesseh delivered his October 23 verdict, finding Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping while acquitting him of gang rape. That verdict has since undergone a significant legal adjustment.

The Bigger Legal Question

The case has also drawn attention to Liberia’s legal framework governing sexual offenses involving minors. Under Liberia’s amended rape law, sexual intercourse involving an adult and a person under 18 falls within the statutory definition of rape. First-degree rape involving a minor is treated as a capital offense for purposes of the law’s bail provisions, although that classification should not be confused with an automatic death sentence.

The 50-year sentence now imposed on Jallah places the case among the significant sexual-offense sentencing developments before the Liberian courts. Still, the legal battle is not finished. The defense has announced its intention to challenge the court’s decision before the Supreme Court, while the kidnapping allegation remains available for fresh prosecution before Criminal Court “A.”

For the 16-year-old survivor, the proceedings have already involved months of testimony, investigation, and courtroom scrutiny. For the Liberian justice system, the case presents a continuing test of how the courts balance the protection of minors, the prosecution’s burden of proof, the jurisdiction of criminal courts, and the constitutional rights of an accused person.

One conviction has now produced a 50-year prison sentence. One charge has been sent back for a new fight in court. And another has ended in acquittal. The final chapter of the Peter Bon Jallah case may yet be written by the Supreme Court of Liberia, as the Defense Council has announced an appeal to the Supreme Court for the March Term of Court.

World.title: Liberia Calls for Greater Geographical Balance and Inclusive Recruitment at IMO
World.content:
London, United Kingdom – Liberia’s Maritime Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer of the Liberia Maritime Authority (LMA), Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe, Sr., has called for greater geographical balance, fairness, and inclusivity in the recruitment and staffing structure of the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

Speaking during the ongoing 138th Session of the IMO Council in London, Commissioner Lighe presented Liberia’s official position on the Organization’s latest human resources update and staff data, expressing concern over the persistent underrepresentation of Africa and other developing regions within the IMO Secretariat.

Echoing concerns raised by several African and developing Member States, Commissioner Lighe emphasized that the longstanding geographical imbalance within the Organization remains unresolved and requires more deliberate and practical interventions.



He highlighted that despite Africa being the largest bloc and continues to effect significant participation in international maritime affairs, the continent accounts for only 5% of the IMO’s workforce, while Arab States account for approximately 4%, with other developing regions similarly underrepresented. And the European region accounts for about 45% of the total employment of the IMO thus enforcing the question of balance and equity in the organization workforce.

Commissioner Lighe further raised concerns about existing recruitment practices, particularly the processes through which vacancies are advertised and opportunities communicated to prospective candidates across Member States.

He stressed the importance of ensuring that competent and qualified professionals from Africa and other developing regions have equitable access to employment opportunities within the Organization.

While acknowledging and commending the IMO Secretariat for its ongoing efforts to improve geographical representation, Commissioner Lighe urged the Organization to adopt more proactive and targeted recruitment strategies.

“Liberia encourages the Secretariat to consider targeted recruitment missions and other talent outreach activities to ensure broader inclusion and participation within the Organization’s structure,” Commissioner Lighe stated.

Liberia maintains that a truly global maritime organization must reflect the geographical diversity of its membership, not only in policy formulation and decision-making but also in its institutional workforce.

The Liberian delegation reaffirmed its commitment to promoting fairness, inclusivity, equitable representation, and institutional reforms that strengthen the IMO’s legitimacy and effectiveness as the United Nations specialized agency responsible for international shipping.

World.title: Rethinking Education Investment and Partnership in Africa
World.content:
This photo was taken at the main round table event at the University of Toronto.

At the Liberia–Canada Education Investment and Partnership Roundtable in Toronto organised by the OFFICE-Liberia Trade and Investment Office in Canada, I invited the institutions and individuals gathered in the room to find themselves in Liberiaʼs education story.

Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, contributing writer

It was a deliberate invitation.



We had come to discuss the future of an education system serving more than 1.3 million learners, the reforms already underway, and the contributions that universities, colleges, foundations, businesses, and members of the diaspora could make.

Yet as I reflected on our engagements in Canada, I found myself returning to a question that extends far beyond Liberia:

When African countries seek international investment and partnerships, how do we ensure that the relationships we build strengthen our capacity to determine and sustain our own development?

The question is important to me because resources, however necessary, do not settle the deeper issues of ownership, institutional capability, and accountability. A country may attract considerable investment without fundamentally changing the conditions that made that investment necessary. Similarly, a partnership may deliver everything it promised while leaving the receiving institution unable to sustain or build upon those achievements.

I believe we must take these possibilities seriously. They reveal three closely connected questions that should guide our engagement with prospective partners:

Who defines the problem or need, Who assumes responsibility for addressing it, and What remains when the partnership has fulfilled its immediate purpose?

This photo was taken at Mohawk College in a session with with Mohawk College President Paul Armstrong, Associate Vice President for International Thea Laidman, and Manager for Global Markets Engagement Ricardo Rivera.

The first question is particularly important in the African context, where the way our challenges are represented often influences the solutions that are proposed.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichieʼs reflections on The Danger of a Single Story offer a critical way of thinking about this. Her argument shows us that the stories told about people and places are inseparable from questions of power.

A narrative becomes particularly consequential when it is treated as the definitive account of another personʼs reality.

I see a parallel in how African education systems are frequently presented within international development conversations. The statistics are all too familiar: children out of school, inadequate classrooms, teachers without sufficient professional preparation, and low learning outcomes.

These are serious challenges, and governments have a responsibility to acknowledge them. In Liberia, our emphasis on foundational learning and adult literacy reflects our recognition of persistent learning gaps and our commitment to addressing them through deliberate policy choices and targeted investments.

But the statistics do not tell the whole story.

They reveal educational gaps without necessarily explaining the institutional conditions that produced them. They tell us where learners are struggling but may say little about the teachers working under difficult circumstances, the communities sustaining education despite limited resources, or the public investments already being made.

If we present only the deficits, we risk constructing a narrative in which Africa appears primarily as a place of need and the external partner becomes the principal agent of change. If we present only our achievements, however, we risk obscuring the very inequalities and institutional weaknesses that demand our attention.

Neither approach provides a sufficient basis for effective investment. Our responsibility is to present a more complete account: one that is honest about our challenges, clear about our national ambitions, and equally transparent about the capabilities and resources we bring to the partnership.

This is why the investment case we presented in Canada began with Liberiaʼs development agenda, our education priorities, existing commitments, and the evidence guiding our reforms. We wanted prospective partners to understand the direction Liberia has already established and identify where their contributions could strengthen it. But the power to define the problem is only meaningful if it is accompanied by the capacity and responsibility to shape the response.

Here, I find the work of Zambian economist Dambisa Moyo particularly relevant. In Dead Aid, Moyo challenges the assumption that sustained external assistance necessarily produces sustained development. Her critique raises difficult questions about dependency, political accountability, and the incentives created when governments rely heavily on resources controlled by others.

Her conclusions have generated considerable debate, and rightly so. African countries have benefited from development partnerships that have expanded access to education, strengthened health systems, and supported critical infrastructure. Liberiaʼs own experience demonstrates the

importance of international cooperation, particularly given the scale of our educational needs and the constraints on public resources. I would therefore resist treating the debate as a simple choice between accepting external support and rejecting it.

The more consequential question is what our financing relationships enable governments to become.

Do they strengthen our ability to plan, coordinate, finance, and deliver public services? Do they develop professional and institutional capabilities within the country? Do they reinforce accountability to the citizens whose education and futures are at stake? Or do they create arrangements in which essential functions remain dependent on external expertise, parallel systems, and financing that may not be available indefinitely?

In conversation with Canada Black International Women Excellence Founder Rose Cathy Handy

These are uncomfortable questions because they place responsibility on both sides of a partnership. Development partners must examine whether their funding arrangements strengthen the institutions they intend to support. Governments must confront weaknesses in their own planning, coordination, public financing, and implementation.

We cannot meaningfully demand ownership while avoiding the obligations that ownership entails. In Liberia, this means taking responsibility for the education system long after individual projects conclude. It means understanding what is already financed before inviting new investment, ensuring that different programs reinforce one another, and making difficult decisions about the recurrent costs of the reforms we introduce.

It also means accepting that a signed agreement, a completed project, or an impressive financing announcement cannot substitute for institutional progress.

This brings me to a further question:

What kinds of capabilities should education investment and partnership ultimately develop?

More than half a century ago, Julius Nyerere, in Education for Self-Reliance, challenged African societies to examine the purposes their education systems were designed to serve. He was concerned with the relationship between education, national development, social responsibility, and the realities of the societies in which learners would live and work. His thinking emerged in a particular historical and political context, and no countryʼs educational model should be adopted without examining its limitations. But the underlying question remains important for contemporary Africa: are we developing education systems that equip our people to participate meaningfully in transforming their societies?

In conversation with President and CEO of Atlas International Freight Forwarding Inc. (Atlas Cargo) and Canadian Customs Brokers Inc.

For Liberia, this question has immediate relevance. Our national development ambitions include investment in agriculture, infrastructure, energy, health, industry, and economic transformation. These ambitions require engineers, technicians, educators, researchers, entrepreneurs, and skilled workers.

Yet expanding access to education alone will not guarantee that those capabilities emerge. During our visit to Mohawk College College, I was particularly interested in how technical training connects with industry, practical experience, and employment. It demonstrated the importance of relationships between educational institutions and the environments in which their graduates will apply their knowledge.

For Liberia, the lesson is to examine how such relationships can be developed within our own economic and institutional realities.

A technical training center needs qualified instructors, functioning equipment, relevant curricula, and credible pathways into work. A university partnership should strengthen teaching, research, and institutional competence. Teacher development should result in better professional practice and improved learning.

The value of these investments lies in how the different elements reinforce one another. This is especially important because African countries cannot afford to reproduce systems whose operating costs and technical requirements they are unable to sustain.

A technology partnership, for example, should prompt questions about maintenance, connectivity, accessibility, content, and the capacity of local institutions to manage what is introduced. An infrastructure investment should account for staffing, operations, and the conditions required for the facility to serve its intended purpose. These considerations are sometimes treated as implementation details. I regard them as central questions ofdevelopment.

A partnership that increases a countryʼs dependence on external support may meet an immediate need while creating another long-term vulnerability. Conversely, a partnership that develops local expertise, strengthens public institutions, and improves their ability to solve problems can generate value well beyond its original financing period.

There is also a broader purpose to education that must remain visible within these discussions.

We need education systems that prepare people for productive employment and economic opportunity. But education must also expand peopleʼs ability to think critically, participate in public life, challenge inequality, and exercise meaningful choices about their futures.

The value of a girl completing school, an adult acquiring literacy, or a learner with a disability gaining access to education cannot be fully understood through earnings or labor-market participation alone. These outcomes concern the kind of society we are creating. For this reason, I believe the definition of an effective education partnership must be sufficiently broad to recognize both economic and social value, while remaining sufficiently rigorous to demand evidence of actual results.

That balance is important because if everything is described as impact, accountability becomes difficult. If only immediately measurable outputs are valued, some of the most important purposes of education risk being neglected.

We must learn to hold both considerations together.

As I return to the discussions in Canada, these reflections have practical implications. At our Toronto Roundtable, participants requested 90 days to engage additional institutions, mobilize resources, and consider a coordinated response to Liberiaʼs education priorities. I welcomed that expression of interest and the willingness to undertake further work.

But the true significance of that engagement will depend on what follows. We must ask whether proposed contributions respond to demonstrated needs, whether the institutions involved possess the appropriate capabilities, and whether the arrangements we establish will strengthen Liberiaʼs ability to deliver education.

We must also be honest about the responsibilities we are prepared to assume ourselves. Some partnerships may involve financing classrooms or learning materials. Others may focus on institutional development, applied research, teacher education, workforce training, or technical cooperation. Their structures will differ because the problems they address differ.

What should unite them is a clear contribution to national priorities, shared responsibility for implementation, and a credible understanding of what will remain after the initial engagement.

For me, this is where the perspectives of Adichie, Moyo, and Nyerere converge in a useful way. They approach different questions, but each invites us to examine a dimension of African agency: the ability to represent our realities, take responsibility for our development, and shape institutions that serve the needs and aspirations of our societies.

Their perspectives also challenge African governments to look inward.

We must not allow the legitimate criticism of externally driven development to become an excuse for weak governance, inadequate domestic investment, or poor implementation. National ownership carries little meaning unless it is demonstrated through decisions, institutions, and accountability.

The responsibility is ours to exercise.

I left Canada encouraged by the possibilities for collaboration, but also conscious of the standard to which those collaborations must be held. The question I now carry into our next phase of engagement is the same one that shaped my invitation in Toronto, although I would frame it more precisely.

We have asked prospective partners where they fit in Liberiaʼs education story. We must now determine what we can build together, who will be responsible for sustaining it, and whether that collaboration leaves our institutions more capable of serving our people.

If education investment and partnership are to contribute meaningfully to Africaʼs development, they must expand our capacity to shape our own futures.

That is the measure of partnership I believe Liberia should pursue, and the responsibility we must be prepared to uphold.

Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah serves as Minister of Education, Republic of Liberia.

World.title: LCC, EU Dedicate Trade Facilitation Secretariat Office to Boost Private Sector Growth
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Liberia Chamber of Commerce (LCC), with support from the European Union (EU), has dedicated a renovated office for the National Trade Facilitation Secretariat (NTFS), in a move aimed at strengthening public-private sector collaboration, improving trade procedures, and creating a more conducive business environment in Liberia.

By Francis G. Boayue

The dedication ceremony, held on Thursday, October 29, also recognized logistical support provided by the EU Delegation to Liberia through the Private Sector Development Project, implemented by Expertise France.



Speaking at the ceremony, LCC President O. Natty B. Davis said hosting the Secretariat demonstrates the Chamber’s commitment to bringing government institutions and private businesses together to address challenges affecting investment and economic growth.

“Hosting the National Trade Facilitation Secretariat is a demonstration of our commitment to strengthening collaboration between government and the private sector. We believe that bringing these institutions closer to businesses will help address the challenges affecting investment and economic growth,” Davis said.

He expressed appreciation to the Government of Liberia, the EU Delegation, Expertise France, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and the Liberia Revenue Authority for their support toward the initiative.

Davis emphasized that businesses require clear regulations, consistent policies, and predictable government services to make sound investment decisions, particularly for projects involving substantial capital and long-term commitments.

“Businesses need certainty. Investors must be able to operate within a system where policies are consistent, regulations are clear, and government services are predictable,” he stated.

Referencing discussions at the recent Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference, Davis identified inadequate coordination among government institutions as a major concern for private-sector operators.

He said the Secretariat’s presence at the Chamber would provide an opportunity to strengthen institutional relationships and ensure that business concerns receive greater attention in national trade policy discussions.

Davis also disclosed that the office would complement the Chamber’s Trade Desk, which is expected to improve businesses’ access to reliable statistics, trade-related information, and other services necessary for investment and expansion.

Meanwhile, Dimitri De-Pues, Regional Hub Investment Officer at the EU Delegation to Liberia, welcomed the completion of the renovated facility, describing it as an important milestone in the partnership between the European Union and the Liberia Chamber of Commerce.

De-Pues said the collaboration between the two institutions had lasted nearly two years and reaffirmed the EU’s commitment to supporting the initiative throughout the remaining three years of the project.

“Our commitment to supporting private-sector development in Liberia remains strong. We recognize the importance of working together with the Chamber, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and Expertise France to create opportunities for businesses and improve the country’s trade environment,” De-Pues said.

He stressed the importance of continued cooperation among implementing partners to ensure the project achieves its intended objectives.

Also speaking, Deputy Minister of Commerce and Trade Wilmot A. Reeves, Chairman of the National Trade Facilitation Committee, welcomed the Chamber’s decision to host the Secretariat, describing it as an important contribution to improving Liberia’s business climate.

Reeves explained that the EU-supported Private Sector Development Project promotes business growth through interventions targeting key value chains, including wood processing, fisheries, and cassava.

“Government cannot do it alone. Our responsibility is to create an enabling environment where the private sector can operate, expand, create opportunities, and contribute meaningfully to national development,” Reeves emphasized.

He said the project also prioritizes public-private dialogue and the removal of barriers that prevent businesses from reaching their full potential.

Another speaker, Buku, underscored the importance of private-sector participation in trade modernization, noting that involving businesses early in the reform process helps ensure that policies address practical challenges encountered by operators.

“Trade reforms must reflect the realities of the business community. When the private sector is involved from the beginning, we are better positioned to identify challenges and develop solutions that respond to the actual needs of businesses,” Buku said.

He welcomed the dedicated workspace, noting that it would strengthen the Secretariat’s ability to coordinate activities and communicate business concerns during trade policy discussions.

The National Trade Facilitation Secretariat operates under the National Trade Facilitation Committee, chaired by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Its presence at the Liberia Chamber of Commerce is expected to strengthen engagement with businesses, improve access to trade-related information, and enhance coordination among relevant institutions.

The initiative is expected to contribute to reducing trade barriers, attracting investment, and supporting sustainable private-sector growth.

However, its long-term impact will depend on the ability of the Secretariat and its partners to translate their commitments into practical reforms that improve Liberia’s business and trading environment.
