World.title: Liberian Rights Advocates Urge Abolition of Death Penalty
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE — Naymote Partners for Democratic Development has entered into a partnership with the Civil Society Human Rights Advocacy Platform of Liberia (CSOHRAP) to strengthen human rights monitoring, legislative engagement, and evidence-based advocacy aimed at advancing the abolition of the death penalty in Liberia.

By Francis G. Boayue

The partnership is being implemented under the FCDO Support for the Abolition of the Death Penalty Phase III – A Strategic Advocacy Initiative, through a sub-award agreement effective August 3, 2026, and running through January 31, 2027.



Under the agreement, Naymote will contribute to strengthening civil society engagement with the Liberian Legislature by monitoring legislative developments, gathering and analyzing information on lawmakers’ positions on the death penalty, and developing a standardized legislative scorecard methodology to support evidence-based advocacy.

Adama Dempster, Secretary General of CSHRAP, said Liberia’s continued retention of the death penalty undermines its commitment to international human rights standards and called on the government and Legislature to take concrete steps toward its abolition.

Dempster made the remarks on Monday during a one-day capacity-building training for legislative observers and interns on the Abolition of Death Penalty Project (ADP), legislative engagement and advocacy, organized by SHRAP in partnership with Naymote Partners for Democratic Development, with support from the British Embassy.

He said Liberia was among the first ten countries to ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which seeks the abolition of capital punishment.

According to Dempster, Liberia abolished the death penalty in 2005 but subsequently reintroduced it between 2005 and 2008 following concerns over increasing armed robberies, hijackings, and other violent crimes.

He said the decision was intended to deter criminal activities but had failed to produce the desired results.

“The reintroduction of the death penalty had not reduced crimes at all, and it had not changed society in terms of serving as a lesson for those who are committing crimes daily,” Dempster said.

He argued that Liberia’s commitment to human rights should be reflected in its laws and policies, particularly those concerning the protection of human life.

Dempster cited Article 20(a) of the Liberian Constitution and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as legal frameworks that underscore the protection of life.

He also raised concerns about the possibility of wrongful convictions, particularly given what he described as Liberia’s limited forensic capacity to conclusively identify individuals involved in criminal activities.

According to him, executing a person who is later found to have been wrongfully convicted would constitute an irreversible miscarriage of justice.

“The actions taken under the death penalty are irreversible. If we later discover that an individual was not the person who committed the crime, what do we say to such a person?” he asked.

Dempster maintained that Liberia could adopt alternative punishments, including life imprisonment, while strengthening its criminal justice system and improving prison facilities.

He cautioned against using existing prison conditions as a justification for retaining capital punishment, arguing that prisons should focus on rehabilitation rather than punishment alone.

Dempster said SHRAP and Naymote are intensifying engagement with lawmakers to build support for the abolition of the death penalty.

He disclosed that legislative observers and interns would be stationed at the Legislature to monitor proceedings, track lawmakers’ positions, and document debates relating to the proposed abolition.

According to him, the observers will monitor lawmakers who support, oppose, or abstain from decisions concerning the death penalty, providing civil society organizations with information to guide targeted advocacy.

“The legislative interns’ work will help us to know how to engage individual lawmakers and how to win them over to support this bill that has to do with abolishing the death penalty,” he said.

He added that the initiative would help civil society organizations better understand lawmakers’ positions and develop strategies to engage those who remain opposed to abolition.

Dempster said there was political willingness within the Legislature to advance the issue, noting that the position of the Senate could provide an opportunity for further engagement with the House of Representatives.

He urged lawmakers to reconsider the existing legal framework, arguing that abolishing the death penalty would strengthen Liberia’s human rights credentials and demonstrate leadership in the region.

Dempster further argued that Liberia’s international standing creates an opportunity for the country to demonstrate leadership on human rights issues.

He cited countries across Africa and the world that have abolished capital punishment, including Sierra Leone, Guinea, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire.

He said Liberia should align itself with evolving international human rights standards, particularly as the country seeks to play a greater role in international affairs.

“We need to show leadership by abolishing the death penalty,” Dempster said.

He maintained that the abolition of capital punishment would not weaken Liberia’s justice system but would instead encourage reforms aimed at protecting lives, strengthening accountability, and ensuring justice.

The Abolition of Death Penalty Project 2026 seeks to strengthen legislative engagement and advocacy through the training of observers and interns, equipping them with the skills to monitor legislative proceedings and support efforts to secure the abolition of capital punishment in Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Unity Party Officials’ ‘Unit 2’ Meetings Stir Questions Over Who Wields Power in Boakai Government
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three senior officials of the Unity Party-led government have set tongues wagging after posting photos on Facebook of what they described as late-night strategy sessions with “Unit 2,” a label widely read in political circles as a reference to Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The posts come at a delicate moment for the Boakai administration, which is still facing questions over its request that the European Union withdraw its envoy to Liberia, partly over remarks she allegedly made about the Vice President’s reach into sectors outside his constitutional remit. For many observers, the timing has sharpened a question already circulating in Monrovia: who is really running the country?



The Posts

Youth and Sports Minister Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah captioned her photos: “To be a politician is not the thing… It’s the late-night meetings… Check-In with Unit 2…” She tagged the post #StrategicPartnership, #UnityParty and #PreparingForTheSecondLeg.

Mohammed “Mo” Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation and a former Unity Party Secretary General, posted photos from the same room, writing: “These late-night strategic sessions keep things moving and on course.”

M. Boakai Jaleiba, Vice President for Administration at the National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL), followed with: “After a late-night caucus with Unit-2!”

None of the three posts mentions President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

The EU Backdrop

Earlier this year, the Government of Liberia formally asked the European Union to recall and replace its Head of Delegation, Ambassador Nona Deprez, accusing her of making statements that undermined the country’s leadership, institutions and investment climate.

In a letter signed by Acting Foreign Minister Ethel Davis, the government alleged that the envoy made a series of derogatory and misleading comments during official engagements with Liberian authorities, investors and development stakeholders.

Some of the remarks were reportedly made at the Liberia-European Union Business Forum in Brussels on February 24-25, where the envoy allegedly questioned governance practices within the Liberian government and raised concerns about Vice President Koung’s role in the mining and energy sectors.

Critics of the move argued at the time that calling for the ambassador’s recall did not, by itself, clear the Vice President, and risked leaving the allegation unresolved in the public space.

Loyalty Signals

Against that backdrop, political watchers say the posts read less like routine party business and more like a public declaration of where loyalty lies. The hashtag #PreparingForTheSecondLeg is likely to be read as a nod to 2029, raising the question of whose second leg is being prepared.

The officials’ own histories add a layer of intrigue. FrontPageAfrica previously reported that President Boakai and his immediate circle blamed Mo Ali, Amin Modad, Cllr. Jeror Cole Bangalu and Rep. Clarence Massaquoi for the party’s defeat in Lofa. Massaquoi, now Chairman of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, is Minister Kruah’s spouse. For some insiders, a visible alignment with the Vice President by figures once at odds with the President’s inner circle is hard to dismiss as coincidence.

‘The Prezzo Approved This Meeting’

A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, pushed back on that reading.

“It is my understanding that the Prezzo had approved this meeting. It was primarily to discuss growing disenchantment among the young people in the party. Don’t mind the way it is being projected by the posts,” the official told FrontPageAfrica.

The source conceded, however, that the party’s troubles run deeper. “That, yes, is our biggest problem right now. People want to hold onto their jobs and not pay attention to the party. And even in their jobs, how many of the young people have they brought on board?”

Bad Optics

Critics are less forgiving, noting that most of those in the room owe their positions to President Boakai.

“These are people the President gave jobs. Is he supposed to tell them what to do? Should he provide them money? The optics are bad,” said the source.

Whatever the intent, the episode lands on a government already defending itself against claims that power has drifted from the Executive Mansion. If the meeting was sanctioned by the President, the officials chose to tell the public it was with “Unit 2,” not him. In Liberian politics, that kind of messaging is rarely accidental.

World.title: Liberia: McGill Signals CDC Comeback, Says UP Would Not Have Won 2023 Elections Had He Remained in Government
World.content:
Monrovia – Former Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Nathaniel McGill has reignited political conversations about the future leadership of the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), declaring that the ruling Unity Party (UP) would not have won the 2023 presidential elections had he remained in government.

McGill, who currently represents Margibi County in the Liberian Senate, made the assertion while defending his political influence and electoral support, despite being placed under United States sanctions.

The former minister maintained that his political standing remained intact even after the sanctions, pointing to his election to the Senate as evidence that he continues to enjoy considerable grassroots support.



“If I had remained as Minister of State, the Unity Party would not have won. Despite being sanctioned, the Liberian people still voted for me and elected me as senator. I had the backing of the people,” McGill said.

His remarks come at a politically significant moment for the CDC, which is facing growing internal conversations over whether to retain its current chairman, Janga Kowo, or install a new leader as the party positions itself for a return to power.

McGill further suggested that the Boakai-led administration was already losing its political grip, declaring that the CDC has the political strength and personnel to reclaim the presidency.

“We have men, we have soldiers in the CDC. And we are coming back,” he said.

Political Scorecard and Claims of Unfinished Projects

Beyond his political declaration, McGill sought to challenge the Unity Party government’s development record, arguing that several projects being presented as achievements of the current administration were initiated or negotiated under the former CDC-led government.

He specifically referenced the Roberts International Airport (RIA) Road Project, the agreement for the construction of an overpass bridge, and a diagnostic laboratory at the 14 Military Hospital.

“The RIA Road Project belongs to us. We signed the agreement for the overpass bridge. The diagnostic laboratory at the 14 Military Hospital was also supposed to be dedicated. We completed more roads, yet this government has not commissioned a single one,” McGill claimed.

He argued that, had he remained Minister of State, he would have demanded explanations from the Ministers of Finance and Public Works over the failure to commission completed road projects.

While McGill’s comments reflect the CDC’s attempt to reclaim political credit for projects initiated during its administration, the claims also underscore the continuing political contest between the former ruling party and the government over development achievements.

Kowo’s Leadership Under Scrutiny

But beyond the exchange over political performance, McGill’s comments have drawn renewed attention to the unresolved question of who should lead the CDC as it attempts to reorganize following its defeat in the 2023 elections.

Janga Kowo currently serves as chairman of the party, having assumed the position following the resignation of Mulbah Morlu, who stepped down both as chairman and from the party.

A former Comptroller and Accountant General of Liberia, Kowo inherited the CDC during one of the most challenging periods in its political history.

His leadership has been credited by supporters with helping to keep the party together amid internal disagreements, political uncertainty and the transition from governing party to opposition.

Under his chairmanship, the CDC has remained vocal in its criticism of the Unity Party-led government. However, some partisans have questioned whether his leadership style is sufficiently assertive to reposition the party for a political comeback.

While critics favor a change at the top, others believe removing Kowo could deepen existing divisions and undermine the relative stability he has helped maintain.

The disagreement presents a difficult choice for the former ruling party: whether to prioritize continuity and internal cohesion or embrace a more confrontational leadership capable of energizing its base.

McGill, Koijee Emerge in Succession Speculation

Sources within the party indicate that former President George Weah and some members of the CDC hierarchy are considering possible alternatives to Kowo.

Among the names circulating is McGill, whose close political relationship with Weah and experience in the former administration have fueled speculation that he could be a preferred candidate for the chairmanship.

Although no formal decision has been announced, McGill’s recent remarks, particularly his declaration that the CDC has the political personnel to return to power, have added another dimension to speculation about his possible political ambitions within the party.

Another prominent name is former Monrovia City Mayor and CDC Secretary-General Jefferson T. Koijee, who has built a strong political following, particularly among the party’s youthful supporters.

Koijee rose through the ranks of the CDC Youth League and remains one of the party’s most recognizable and outspoken figures.

His popularity among younger partisans could make him an attractive option for those seeking a more energetic and combative leadership style. However, his inclusion in the succession conversation also raises questions about the political and reputational implications of his continued presence on the United States sanctions list.

McGill, too, remains under U.S. sanctions, creating a potentially complicated leadership choice for a party seeking to rebuild its national and international political standing.

The sanctions do not automatically disqualify either man from holding the party’s chairmanship.

Other Names in the Leadership Conversation

Other names being mentioned include Eugene Lenn Nagbe, a former commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority and special aide to Weah.

Nagbe’s experience in public service and association with the former president have placed him among the personalities being discussed as the party considers its leadership options.

Former House Speaker Jonathan Fonati Koffa has also been mentioned as a possible contender.

Koffa, who previously belonged to the Liberty Party before switching allegiance to the CDC, currently chairs the committee overseeing the construction of the party’s headquarters.

However, sources close to the former speaker say he has no intention of contesting for the chairmanship.

His name nevertheless reflects the broader search within the party for a leader who can command political respect, strengthen internal structures and help bridge differences among competing factions.

A Defining Moment for the CDC

The CDC’s leadership question goes beyond choosing a new chairman. It touches on the party’s identity, its relationship with former President Weah, the influence of its political heavyweights and the strategy it intends to pursue ahead of the next electoral cycle.

Kowo’s supporters see continuity as essential to preserving party unity, while those advocating a change believe the CDC needs a more assertive political figure to rebuild its mobilization capacity and challenge the ruling government.

McGill’s latest remarks have added to that debate, particularly because they come from a former senior official of the Weah administration who continues to command an electoral constituency despite the controversy surrounding his U.S. sanctions.

Whether his declaration signals a genuine interest in the chairmanship or is simply an assertion of his political relevance remains unclear.

What is increasingly evident, however, is that the CDC faces a delicate leadership decision. A poorly managed transition could expose existing divisions, while a carefully negotiated succession could provide an opportunity to rebuild the party’s structures and strengthen its opposition politics.

For now, Kowo remains chairman, and no formal succession process or final decision has been announced. But with McGill, Koijee and other prominent figures featuring in the conversation, the question of who will lead the CDC into its next political chapter is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

World.title: EDITORIAL: BEYOND THE WALK
World.content:
On the last day of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Liberia’s survivors and advocates did what a health system is supposed to do: they told women that cancer is not a death sentence if it is found early. They did it on a short timeline and on goodwill. It is now the government’s turn to match them with money, practical support and imagination.

ON SATURDAY, WOMEN who had been told they were dying walked to show otherwise. Benejane Shaw, ten rounds of chemotherapy behind her, called herself “a living testimony that early detection saves lives.” Florence Tugbeh, who once had no hair, said she could now “shake my head.” They were not asking for sympathy. They were asking their fellow Liberians to get screened.

THEY DESERVE MORE than applause.



Credit Where It Is Due

THE LIBERIA CANCER Resource Initiative, led by Christine E. Brooks-Jarrett, planned this year’s walk on a short timeline and still drew an encouraging crowd. It runs this campaign every year, and insists that awareness must be a year-round effort. Its stated aim is to “break the stigma surrounding cancer and encourage women to prioritize their health and get screened.” In a country where a cancer diagnosis is still whispered about, that is not a small ambition.

DR. DEDDEH SUPUWOOD, a medical oncologist at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center, carries a different kind of weight. She lost her own mother to breast cancer, and she now spends her days trying to make sure fewer Liberian daughters lose theirs. “When you save one woman’s life,” she said, “you are probably saving a whole family.” She is right, and a country that can count on doctors like her, and survivors who will stand up in public and tell their stories, should not leave them to carry the load alone.

A Walk Cannot Carry This Alone

THE LATEST INTERNATIONAL estimates put Liberia’s toll at 4,217 new cancer cases and 2,745 deaths a year. Breast cancer is the most common: 885 new cases and 421 deaths in 2024, roughly 48 deaths for every 100 women diagnosed. Estimated cases are up about 50 percent since 2018. Those figures are modeled, because Liberia has no cancer registry to count its patients properly, and that gap is itself a failure of public health.

THE SYSTEM THOSE women enter is thin. As of the World Health Organization’s last country profile, Liberia had no radiotherapy machines, no radiation oncologists, no mammography units and no national breast or cervical cancer screening program. The Kennedy hospital is described as the only public facility offering specialized cancer treatment. Many patients arrive late, and some stop chemotherapy because they cannot pay. One woman told the Liberian Observer: “My children and I were deciding what to sell next.”

What Government Should Do

THE GOVERNMENT HAS made a start, and it should be credited. Ground was broken in July 2025 for the country’s first radiotherapy center. Officials have bought mammography and imaging equipment, donated chemotherapy drugs to the Kennedy hospital in June, and told the Liberian Observer they are discussing a dedicated cancer medicines budget line. A start is not a system. We urge the President, the Ministry of Health and the Legislature to go further:

Fund cancer by name. Create a dedicated, published line in the national budget for cancer drugs, screening and the completion of the radiotherapy center, and report every quarter on what was spent. Liberia joined other African governments in pledging in Abuja in 2001 to devote 15 percent of national budgets to health; citizens are entitled to know how close the country is, and what share reaches cancer.

Take screening beyond Monrovia. Most of the new equipment sits at one hospital. Mammography, clinical breast exams and cervical screening must reach the counties, with trained staff to read the results and refer the women who need treatment.

Stop making families choose what to sell. Move the key cancer drugs onto the national essential medicines list, as officials say they are considering, and subsidize chemotherapy so that no woman stops treatment because she cannot pay.

Back the advocates in practice.

Groups like the Liberia Cancer Resource Initiative should not have to plan a national campaign on a few weeks’ notice. Offer them grants, free airtime on state media, help with permits and logistics, and a seat at the table when programs are designed.

Count the problem and publish it. Build a cancer registry and release the numbers every year, so that Liberians know how many of their neighbors are being diagnosed and dying, and so that policy follows evidence.

CLLR. TIAWAN SAYE Gongloe told Saturday’s crowd that “corruption starts with C, cancer starts with C.” The budget is where the two meet. Every dollar lost to waste is a drug not bought and a screening machine not installed.

Room for Creativity

THE FIGHT WILL not be won with money alone. The people best placed to reach Liberian women are already in their communities, and government should make room for them to be inventive.

MARKET WOMEN’S ASSOCIATIONS, churches, mosques and radio stations broadcasting in local languages reach women the clinic never sees. Community health workers could be trained to perform clinical breast exams and refer women early. Survivors like Benejane Shaw and Florence Tugbeh could serve as peer guides, walking the newly diagnosed through a system they have just survived. Schools, football clubs and musicians could carry messages about screening and cervical cancer prevention to young Liberians. Mobile teams could visit county towns on market days. None of this has to wait for a new hospital.

THE GOVERNMENT CAN invite these ideas rather than wait for them. A modest innovation fund for community cancer projects, open to local groups as well as hospitals, would let the best ideas grow, and a requirement to measure results would show which ones deserve to be copied.

SATURDAY’S WALK ENDED with games and a plate of dry rice, and a crowd that went home glad. Christine E. Brooks-Jarrett said the fight “requires collective and sustained action.” Government is the largest part of that collective. The advocates have shown the way. It should follow, and it should fund them.

World.title: Burundi AFCON qualifier back at Levy Mwanawasa
World.content:
Ndola’s Levy Mwanawasa Stadium will remain Chipolopolo’s fortress after FAZ’s late attempt to shift the crucial AFCON qualifier against Burundi to Lusaka collapsed on conditional approval deadlines.

FAZ General Secretary Charles Chakatazya confirmed that Zambia will host Burundi in Ndola on 13 November, dashing hopes of an immediate return to the capital Lusaka.

The decision comes as a blow to Lusaka fans who have been starved of senior national team action, with Ndola retaining its grip on Chipolopolo fixtures.

However, in a major boost for Lusaka, CAF has approved the return of international football to National Heroes Stadium, with the Egypt 2027 U-23 AFCON qualifier against Burkina Faso set for 15 November.

Chakatazya said the U-23 fixture marks the reopening of Lusaka to international matches.

“I wish to confirm that the U-23 home match will be held in Lusaka after receiving approval from CAF. We are happy that the U-23 match opens the way to the return of international matches to Lusaka,” he said.

“On the Chipolopolo, we were unable to secure the change of venue given the tight deadlines to fulfil the conditional approval.”

He said FAZ still plans to bring Chipolopolo back to Lusaka in the near future.

With preparations in high gear, Chakatazya has challenged both teams to collect maximum points and appealed to fans to buy tickets via Computicket to make home advantage count.

Zambia faces a tight schedule – the U-23s travel to Ouagadougou on 11 November before hosting Burkina Faso four days later in Lusaka, while Chipolopolo host Burundi on 13 November before the return leg in Bujumbura.

The stakes are high. Fourteen nations will progress from the second round to the decisive third round, where seven winners will join hosts Egypt at the U-23 AFCON – the gateway to the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

World.title: Kalusha pays tribute to  Freddie Mwila
World.content:
Football icon Kalusha Bwalya has paid glowing tribute to late former Zambia national team coach Freddie Mwila, describing him as a true pioneer and torchbearer of Zambian football.

In a tribute, Kalusha says Mwila helped open doors for generations of Zambian players seeking professional opportunities abroad.

He has also hailed Mwila for his pivotal role in rebuilding Zambian football following the tragic Gabon Air Disaster of 1993.

Kalusha recalls that within just 90 days, a new Chipolopolo team was assembled under difficult circumstances, demonstrating remarkable courage and resilience.

He notes that against all odds, that team went on to reach the 1994 Africa Cup of Nations final in Tunisia, where Zambia narrowly lost 2-1 to Nigeria.

Kalusha says that journey was more than a football achievement – it was a symbol of national pride and the determination of a nation to rise again.

“Freddie Mwila was part of that remarkable chapter in our history. His contribution to the game and the generations he inspired will never be forgotten. Rest in peace, Coach, you served Zambian football and your legacy will live on,” Kalusha said.

Mwila remains one of the most decorated figures in Zambian football history. He featured for Rhokana United, now Nkana, and became one of the first Zambians to play professional football abroad when he joined American side Atlanta Chiefs in 1967, later playing for Aston Villa in England.

As a coach, he etched his name in continental history when he led Power Dynamos to the 1991 African Cup Winners’ Cup, making Power the first Southern African club to win a continental title.

He also coached the Zambia and Botswana national teams, as well as Zanaco, Lusaka Dynamos, Nkwazi and Circuit Chiefs.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Global Child Nutrition Forum side workshop on making fish work in school meals, from policy ambition to practical implementation, Ms Kapusana highlighted that fish could add high quality protein and essential micronutrients to children’s diets.

Ms Kapusana noted that buying the fish locally could also contribute to economic growth by supporting fishing communities, small-scale aquaculture farmers, processors and other businesses in the aquatic food supply chain.

She called on participants that comprised the private sector, researchers and governments from various countries to share practical experiences and develop recommendations to strengthen supply chains and partnerships in school meals programmes.

The side workshop, was convened by the Zambian government in collaboration with WorldFish, aimed at turning aquatic foods into school meals.

In his closing remarks, the Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Educational Services, Dr Kelvin Mambwe reaffirmed government’s commitment to including aquatic foods such as kapenta to school meals.

In a separate side plenary, Chairperson for the United Nations Food System Coordination Hub, Scientific Advisory Committee, Shakuntala Thilsted, called on governments to take deliberate steps in including aquatic foods in the school meals programmes.

Dr Thilsted outlined some call to action in strengthening research on diverse aquatic foods for school meals.

The school meals programme aims to improve learners’ nutrition, health and educational outcomes, while supporting local agri-food economies and poverty reduction.

World.title: FIC uncovers mineral smuggling syndicate
World.content:
The Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) has uncovered a mineral smuggling syndicate involving approximately K1 billion, in which foreign currency was allegedly smuggled into Zambia through illicit mineral transactions.

FIC Director General, Clement Kapalu, says the illegal transactions occurred between 2022 and 2024 and involved copper, gold and gemstones which were exported without payment of the required taxes and duties.

Mr Kapalu has explained that the minerals were moved out of the country without following established customs procedures, resulting in significant revenue losses to government and threatening the integrity of the country’s financial system.

He disclosed this when he officially opened a three-day workshop on gold supply chain practices in Lusaka today.

Mr Kapalu said unregulated gold mining and trading created opportunities for criminal networks to exploit weaknesses in governance and regulatory systems to facilitate illicit financial flows.

He stated that Zambia’s overall money laundering risk had improved from medium to high, following the revised National Risk Assessment on Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Proliferation Financing launched in March, this year.

However, Mr Kapalu said the assessment had also identified regional extremist groups that posed a security threat and were suspected of financing some of their activities through minerals, including illegally mined gold.

He said the connection between gold trading and terrorist financing was a growing concern that required stronger oversight and collaboration among law enforcement agencies, regulators and other stakeholders.

Mr Kapalu further expressed gratitude that the Bank of Zambia had incorporated gold into the country’s international reserves and was expanding its domestic gold purchasing programme to include small-scale producers.

He said although the development presented significant economic opportunities, it also created avenues for criminal networks to exploit weaknesses in the gold supply chain.

Mr Kapalu noted that gold is particularly attractive to criminals because it was valuable, durable, easy to transport and could easily be smuggled across borders.

He stated that gold can be used as proceeds of crime, a commodity for trafficking or a means of payment for illegal activities, including the trafficking of arms, drugs and financing of conflict.

Mr Kapalu said the sharp increase in international gold prices had further heightened its attractiveness to criminal networks seeking to exploit gaps in governance and regulation.

He said as Zambia strengthened her anti-money laundering framework and prepared for the next Financial Action Task Force (FATF) mutual evaluation, institutions needed to demonstrate their capacity to identify financial crimes and effectively enforce existing laws.

Mr Kapalu expressed hope that the establishment of the Zambia Cyber Agency and the Mineral Regulation Commission would help address illicit financial transactions associated with digital platforms and strengthen regulation of the mining sector.

Speaking earlier, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) Project Coordinator, Lindy Muzila, said international cooperation is critical in addressing mineral smuggling and other organised financial crimes.

Ms Muzila said Zambia’s presidency of the Asset Recovery Inter-Agency Network for Southern Africa (ARINSA) provided an opportunity to strengthen regional collaboration and facilitate cross-border investigations.

Ms Muzila said the network enabled law enforcement practitioners from different jurisdictions to exchange information and provide assistance in investigating transnational crimes.

She also emphasised the importance of involving the private sector in combating illicit financial flows, noting that businesses played a critical role in identifying and addressing suspicious transactions.

Ms Muzila thanked the World Gold Council for supporting the workshop through technical expertise and financial assistance.

Meanwhile, World Gold Council Senior Policy Lead, Levy Pezulu, said transparency, traceability and responsible market access were essential in combating money laundering, illicit financial flows and gold smuggling.

Mr Pezulu said strengthening governance and responsible sourcing would enable Zambia to unlock the economic potential of artisanal and small-scale gold mining, while ensuring compliance with international anti-money laundering standards.

He pointed out that the Council remained committed to working with Government, regulatory institutions, law enforcement agencies, mining stakeholders and local communities to promote a responsible and internationally competitive gold sector.

World.title: Fube ordered to pay K100,000 or serve prison sentence
World.content:
The Lusaka Magistrates’ Court has ordered that Binwell Mpundu’s surety former Chilubi Member of Parliament, Mulenga Fube, pays a sum of K100, 000 bond amount or serve a prison sentence of six months for the non-appearance of former Nkana Member of Parliament before court.

Mr Fube, a surety in a case in which Mr Mpundu is facing one count of seditious practices, is expected to account for the accused person’s failure to appear before court.

The media reports that In October last month, Principal Magistrate, Webster Milumbe, issued a bench warrant against Mr Mpundu for the second time after he failed to appear in court.

The court also directed Mr Fube and former Kamfinsa Member of Parliament, Christopher Kang’ombe, to show cause as to why the accused person had failed to attend court.

Magistrate Milumbe subsequently adjourned the matter to today, November 3, 2026, and ordered that Mr Fube be brought before the court.

The matter was therefore before court for Mr Fube, a surety to give account of the whereabouts of Mr Mpundu, to which he indicated that Mr Mpundu did not reveal his location to him.

The Court told Mr Fube that in an event that he decides to pay, he should pay as and when he has the money so that he can be discharged as a surety.

Mr Milumbe has since ordered that Christopher Kang’ombe has up to November 23, 2026 to appear before court and explain Mr Mpundu’s whereabouts.

Mr Mpundu’s charge stems from a Facebook post allegedly published on December 20, 2024, in which he is accused of urging members of the public and politicians to acquire firearms for self-defense.

World.title: Ndola Council probes squash club land encroachment
World.content:
Ndola City Council says it is investigating a matter in which a Lebanese business investor has allegedly encroached on land belonging to Ndola Squash Club.

The investor, who runs food outlets, has reportedly razed down the club’s perimeter fence after procuring land said to have previously hosted old council toilets.

Ndola Town Clerk Stanley Mbewe confirmed the development in an exclusive interview with Lusaka Times Sports.

Mbewe said Council has received a complaint from Ndola Squash Club and is engaging both the club management and the developer.

“We have received that concern from Ndola Squash Club regarding a land dispute. We wish to appreciate that even the Squash Club doesn’t have a title but that person who is developing land has a title,” Mbewe said.

“So, we are reviewing the title to see if he has really encroached or not. We have taken the matter to the Ministry of Lands. Once an appropriate decision is made we will be able to communicate whether the developer has encroached or not.”

He added: “If he has encroached he will be told to go back to where his title is and we also want to establish how he acquired the title. We are engaging both sides so that we come up with an amicable solution.”

Meanwhile, the Chapter for the Revival of Ndola City has accused the Council of having a malicious and irresponsible scheme against prime sports facilities by encouraging foreign investors to encroach on their land.

Chapter President Chungu Kapema said Ndola lacks adequate functional sports facilities and the Council should not aid illegalities at the expense of sports development.

Kapema cited a similar attempt at Ndola’s Kwacha Centre where the Council allegedly wanted to sell land to a foreign investor to set up a filling station.

He called on residents to object to the illegality and petition the Town Clerk to stop the development.

“All this has been done without presenting any documentation to prove so and without engaging Ndola Squash Club management,” Kapema said.

World.title: Stakeholders extolled for ballot paper inspection
World.content:
Kanchibiya District Electoral Officer, Julius Katuka, has commended political party representatives and other stakeholders for witnessing the inspection of ballot papers ahead of the November 5, 2026 Lubaleshi Ward By-Election.

Mr Katuka said stakeholder participation in electoral activities was important in promoting transparency and building confidence in the electoral process.

Speaking in an interview with the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS) after the inspection exercise held today, Mr Katuka encouraged political parties and other stakeholders to actively participate in all stages of the electoral process.

He said stakeholders were free to witness electoral activities conducted by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) as part of efforts to ensure transparency.

Mr Katuka further assured stakeholders that adequate security measures had been put in place at every stage of the electoral process.

He said the Commission remained committed to conducting free, fair and credible elections.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) District Secretary, Peter Bwalya, expressed satisfaction with the ballot paper inspection exercise.

Mr Bwalya said the participation of political party representatives in the exercise was important in promoting openness and accountability.

And National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) representative, Maybin Chibende, also expressed satisfaction with the exercise, saying stakeholders had been given an opportunity to witness the electoral preparations.

Meanwhile, Citizens First (CF) Party representative, Webster Chanda said the exercise had given stakeholders confidence in the preparations for the forthcoming by-election.

The Lubaleshi Ward By-Election which was necessitated by the death of UPND before the August general election is scheduled to take place on November 5, 2026.

World.title: Nchelenge Council receives funds for revenue enhancement
World.content:
Nchelenge Town Council has received K400,000 from the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) towards the implementation of a revenue enhancement plan aimed at improving revenue collection and reducing revenue leakages.

‎

Council Secretary, Benson Malama says community members have already been sensitised on the initiative, while data collectors have also been trained.

‎

‎ Mr Malama says data collection has since been completed, with the remaining process being consolidation of the data before it is submitted to Chipata City Council for review.

‎

‎He says the initiative is expected to improve revenue collection and accountability once implemented.

‎

‎“Once this plan is implemented, we expect to reduce revenue leakages and maximise revenue collection because payments will be deposited directly into the council’s account,” Mr Malama said.

‎

‎He notes that the system will also help reduce manpower costs while making it convenient for residents to pay for council services.

‎

‎“People will be able to pay for services from the comfort of their homes, and monitoring will be much easier because all businesses will be captured in the database,” Mr Malama said.

‎

‎Nchelenge Town Council is among five local authorities in Luapula Province that have received support from UNICEF for the revenue enhancement initiative.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 3, 2026
World.content:
press review

US to Cut South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA Trade Deal

U.S. President Donald Trump has notified Congress of plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective 1 January 2027, after a review found both countries failed to meet the programme's eligibility requirements. The US cited trade and investment barriers, national security and foreign policy concerns, with additional concerns over corruption in South Africa and human rights, political pluralism and workers' rights in Rwanda. The decision comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with Rwanda also facing US sanctions over its alleged support for M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo. South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the move as unfortunate, saying Washington had raised new concerns not part of ongoing trade negotiations. He said the government would continue diversifying export markets to protect jobs.

Uganda Begins Withdrawal of Troops from Somalia After 20 Years

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly 20 years of military involvement. The first group of soldiers is already returning home. The phased withdrawal, announced by the country's military leadership, is expected to be completed by the end of 2027 and will include troops serving under the African Union mission. Uganda was the first African country to deploy forces to Somalia in 2007 under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), helping government forces push al-Shabaab militants out of Mogadishu and other strategic areas. Uganda's army spokesperson Chris Magezi said the withdrawal would allow Somalia to assume full responsibility for its security. The move follows talks between Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, during which Somalia reportedly asked for an extension of Uganda's military presence. The withdrawal comes as the AU's current mission faces uncertainty over future funding and ongoing efforts to build up Somalia's security forces.

UNESCO Warns 86% of Journalist Murders Worldwide Remain Unpunished

UNESCO has warned that 86% of crimes committed against journalists worldwide remain unpunished, highlighting persistent threats to press freedom and the safety of media workers. In a report released on the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists, the UN agency said more than 1,600 journalists had been killed globally over the past 20 years, with local journalists accounting for nine out of every ten victims. Africa continues to face serious challenges, with journalists in countries such as Somalia, Uganda and the Sahel region exposed to killings, intimidation and online harassment. Reporters Without Borders recorded two journalist deaths in Africa this year, in Uganda and Somalia, with neither case resulting in arrests or convictions. UNESCO also raised concerns about the growing use of social media campaigns to discredit journalists and warned that reporters are increasingly being targeted in conflict zones, including through drone attacks. The agency called for greater accountability and protection for journalists, stressing that press identification does not guarantee their safety.

Tensions Flare at Inquiry Into Malawi's Deadly Plane Crash

A parliamentary inquiry into the plane crash that killed former Malawian Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others descended into heated exchanges after independent campaigner Christy Lwara clashed with lawmakers over his testimony on the military's handling of the search operation. Lwara told the Ad Hoc Parliamentary Committee that he was dissatisfied with the military's response, questioning why soldiers allegedly stopped people from proceeding to Kasangazi, citing fuel shortages. He said his discussions with officers had led him to believe the aircraft had crashed in the area, prompting him to continue searching there. However, lawmakers challenged his account, accusing him of giving contradictory statements about the search operation. The questioning escalated into personal insults between Lwara and MPs George Jivason Kadzipatike and Joshua Malango, forcing committee leaders to repeatedly intervene to restore order. Committee chairperson Macmillan Water Nyamilandu Manda said he was frustrated by the conduct and warned members that the enquiry could not continue in such an atmosphere. The confrontation comes as lawmakers continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding one of Malawi's deadliest aviation tragedies.

Renewed Tigray Conflict Threatens Ethiopia's Economic Recovery

Ethiopia's strong economic growth prospects are facing renewed uncertainty as escalating tensions in the northern Tigray region threaten to undermine the country's recovery from years of conflict. The International Monetary Fund forecasts economic growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year, driven by agriculture, mining and electricity generation. The conflict caused huge damage to infrastructure and great economic losses. Increased military spending may divert resources away from infrastructure, education and social services, discouraging investment and cutting government revenues, according to financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed. If the conflict starts up again, there is a danger of increased military spending. More instability could also exacerbate inflation, shortages of foreign currency and pressure on the national currency. Agriculture and tourism are highly susceptible to insecurity, disruption of transport routes, poor rainfall and climate-related crop challenges that threaten livelihoods and production. Analysts warn that a prolonged conflict could reverse economic gains and place additional pressure on already struggling households.

Close 

Five Arrested Over Attack on South African Farmer

South African police have arrested five suspects in connection with a brutal attack on a 50-year-old cattle farmer, Donovan Marx, at his farm in Ventersdorp, North West. Marx was ambushed by masked attackers during a house robbery last Wednesday, shot, stabbed, and had his ears cut off before the suspects fled with three firearms and his vehicle. Police said the attackers first tied up a farm worker before assaulting Marx when he returned home. The worker later managed to free himself and alert authorities. Marx remains in hospital and may require prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his. His family has welcomed the arrests, saying the legal process must now take its course. The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, are expected to appear in court facing charges including house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack, while Parliament's police committee chair Ian Cameron called for a thorough investigation and prosecution.

World.title: South Africa: Cape Town Taxi Rivals Agree to Seven-Day Truce - South African News Briefs - November 3, 2026
World.content:
press review

Cape Town Taxi Rivals Agree to Seven-Day Truce

Rival Cape Town taxi associations, the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association (CATA) and the Cape Organisation for the Democratic Taxi Association (CODETA), have agreed to a seven-day truce, reports EWN. This comes after months of deadly violence that has claimed about a dozen lives and disrupted public transport. The agreement is aimed at restoring calm along the Delft-Langa-Epping corridor, where tensions have been fuelled by disputes over unlawful taxi operations. Both associations have also committed to an independently facilitated process to address the underlying causes of the conflict, with a follow-up meeting with government. The South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO) has welcomed the agreement, saying it is important to protect commuters, drivers and taxi operators.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

IEC Warns Voters Against Photographing Marked Ballots

The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has reminded voters of the rules at voting stations ahead of the Local Government Elections, reports SABC News. It warned that taking photographs of marked ballot papers is strictly prohibited. Deputy Chief Electoral Officer Masego Shiburi said voters must mark their ballots in private and follow the instructions of election officials. The commission has also warned against campaigning, canvassing, intimidating or attempting to influence voters inside voting stations. It further urged the public not to intimidate electoral staff or take and share unauthorised photographs of officials on social media. Shiburi said that voting booths are positioned to protect ballot secrecy and prevent voters from being pressured into photographing their choices in exchange for favours or other benefits.

SAHRC Urges Urgent Action to Fix Gauteng Water Crisis

The South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) has called on Gauteng municipalities and water service providers to urgently rehabilitate failing wastewater treatment plants and improve access to reliable water and sanitation services, reports EWN. The appeal follows the release of the commission’s report on water and sanitation service delivery in the province, which highlights serious challenges affecting water infrastructure and security. The commission found that approximately 1.5 billion litres of water are lost daily in Gauteng due to leaks. While acknowledging the substantial support provided by the Department of Water and Sanitation to the province's water sector, SAHRC commissioner Henk Boshoff warned that greater attention must be given to protecting and rehabilitating water resources. The commission raised concerns about the deteriorating condition of the resources on which Gauteng's long-term water security depends.

World.title: Nigeria: The Assassination of a Peacemaker
World.content:
blog

An Islamic preacher's brutal after-dark execution is a tragic reminder of what is at stake in the struggle to vanquish jihadism in northern Nigeria.

It tells you everything you need to know about the moral confusion surrounding the jihadist insurgency that has throttled vast swaths of northern Nigeria that Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka, the respected Islamic cleric who was gunned down outside his Dutsin-Ma, Katsina state residence last week by two armed men on a motorcycle, is being described by sections of the media as "controversial." For, if Malam Masussuka was "controversial," it raises the legitimate question of what to call his assassins.

Prior to his assassination (a friend of the cleric, one Adamu Abubakar, also lost his life), Mr. Masussuka had received numerous death threats, including on social media, from those who wanted him to stop doing what he was doing: preaching against extremism, contesting conservative interpretations of sections of the Quran and Hadith, and generally being a voice for theological moderation and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians in the northern region of the country. In June 2025, Mr. Masussuka was honored for his efforts with a Peace Ambassador award by the Abuja-based Network for Good Governance and Transparency. Receiving the award, Mr. Masussuka reiterated the keynote of his advocacy as reorienting Nigerians "to embrace peace and unity" and challenging "hate speech and extremist ideologies."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

If Mr. Masussuka's message of peace and tolerance was music to some ears, there were others who bitterly resented what he stood for and were desperate to have him removed from the scene. For example, in November 2025, just five months after he was honored for his peacemaking interventions, Mr. Masussuka received an official summons from the Katsina state government "for questioning over allegations that his sermons contravene established principles of Islamic law." At the time, Mr. Masussuka had also complained to the government that he was being insulted by members of Jama'atu Izalatil Bid'ah wa Ikamatis Sunnah--commonly known as Izala or 'Yan Izala.

Last week, though, it wasn't an Izala member who finished off Mr. Masussuka and his friend. Rather, it was gunmen deputized by a different extremist group, Jama'atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis-Sudan (meaning "Vanguard for the Aid of Muslims in Black Africa"), popularly known as Ansaru, who did. We know this because the group has claimed responsibility through a four-minute video obtained by Premium Times, a leading Nigerian newspaper. In the video, the terror group did not mince words about why they decided to eliminate Mr. Masussuka: because he was "an (arnai) infidel, not a Muslim. He was contracted to disrupt Islam and confuse Muslims." While it is not clear from Ansaru's video who or what entity they believed had "contracted" Mr. Masussuka, what is beyond dispute is the group's bloodcurdling warning to "other infidels" who "belittle the Hadiths of the Prophet": "You should repent. You should stop, or else we are coming for you." Translation: Ansaru is coming for you if you dare insist that (Nigerian) Muslims and Christians should peacefully coexist.

For some time now, the origins of the decadeslong jihadist violence in northern Nigeria and much of the Sahel have been a subject of intense litigation. While some scholars and analysts have insisted that the violence has nothing to do with religion and that it is best seen as an expression of legitimate grievance against failing states, others (I belong to this group) have argued that not only is the violence mobilized by various terror groups ultimately religious in essence, neither the violence nor the totality of their praxes can be understood without recourse to this basic and inextricable religious factor. The latter position does not dispute the need for investment in good governance, or that such will not work to vitiate the appeal of terror groups to disaffected young men; the argument has always been that after all is said and done, we need to face the reality that there are those who engage in violence because they see it as a religious obligation. For such people, no amount of investment in good governance or infrastructure will do. If that were so, there would be zero extremism in societies where social opportunities are abundant, relatively speaking. As a matter of fact, part of what Islamist groups take exception to (and they could not be more transparent about this) is the very apparatus of the modern state that seeks to pacify and draw them into its fold. Their grouse, not to put too fine a point on it, is unbelief, not the poverty of good governance.

This is where the late Malam Masussuka comes in. The reader will notice that he was abused, threatened, and ultimately assassinated, not for his extremism, but because he disavowed extremism. In other words, Mr. Masussuka lost his life because he preached moderation and peaceful coexistence, and we need no further confirmation than the video message from Ansaru. How in the world this makes someone "controversial" (looking at you, BBC) is beyond me.

For context, Mr. Masussuka is not the first Islamic cleric in northern Nigeria to be silenced for good by armed gunmen. In May 2025, Islamic scholar Sheikh Mustapha Aliyu was brutally murdered by armed bandits who had earlier abducted him. Around the same time, Chief Imam Alkali Salihu Suleiman was killed by his abductors in the northwestern state of Zamfara. Sheikhs Jaafar Mahmud Adam and Auwal Albani Zaria, both respected Salafi scholars, lost their lives in similar circumstances in 2007 and 2014, respectively.

Nor, crucially, is this Ansaru's first rodeo as far as eliminating its ideological adversaries is concerned. Since its emergence as a splinter faction of Boko Haram in 2012, the group has been linked to several high-profile attacks and kidnappings across the country. These include the 2012 prison break in Abuja, the ambush of a Nigerian military convoy in 2013, the kidnapping and subsequent execution of seven foreign construction workers during the same year, and assaults on military bases leading to the execution of dozens of Nigerian army personnel in August 2020 and April 2022.

Ansaru is officially proscribed and designated as a terrorist organization by Nigeria, the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

All of which raises an interesting question: If Ansaru and the many cognate terror groups currently active in Nigeria and across the Sahel have not been shy about their aims, why is it that many commentators continue to play the ostrich, attributing to terror groups moral and political objectives that they unambiguously deny? One reason is that many are wary of antagonizing Muslims--especially Muslim minorities in Western countries. Such people wrongly equate condemning the rampages of Islamists with taking sides with alleged Islamophobes. Nothing could be further from the truth. Indeed, refusing to back moderates like Malam Masussuka only allows religious bigots in northern Nigeria--and elsewhere--to avoid confrontation with their own demons.

Close 

Failure to decisively champion the Masussukas of this world has another regrettable consequence. It lets bigots get away with not just bad but objectively regressive arguments. Those of us who care about modernity and its amenities can ill afford not to speak up against the plague that is Islamist terror, which, drilled down to its essence, is a rejection of life, value pluralism, and the right of the individual to choose what is best for him (and vitally, change his mind) in matters of faith. What this means is that, from the standpoint of the Islamist terrorist, we should all be "infidels." This particular point bears emphasizing because, if past experience is anything to go by, it really does not matter whether or not we are interested in Islamism. Islamists are interested in us, and there is no better antidote to their poisonous ideology than standing our argumentative ground and taking sides with and empowering moderates and peacemaking agents like the late Mr. Masussuka.

In the meantime, one would hope that this tragedy is the final nail in the coffin of the risible argument that violence in northern Nigeria has nothing to do with religion. As should be obvious by now, no amount of wishing Islamism away would make it disappear.

World.title: Africa: Women Still Shut Out of Power As Gender Bias Undermines Africa's Democracy
World.content:
Discriminatory social norms, unequal power relations and growing gender-based violence continue to undermine women's participation in political leadership across Africa, despite progress in representation and the adoption of laws promoting gender equality, United Nations and European Union officials have warned.

Speaking at the opening of a two-day Inter-Regional Dialogue on Advancing the Transformation of Gender Social Norms to Enhance Women and Youth Participation and Representation in Leadership and Decision-Making in Zanzibar, UN Women Representative in Tanzania, Julia Broussard, said women's political representation remained disproportionately low, with entrenched attitudes continuing to influence who gets opportunities to lead.

Broussard said women occupy just over a quarter of parliamentary seats across sub-Saharan Africa, while in Tanzania they account for approximately 38 per cent of Members of Parliament.

However, she warned that progress in representation had not necessarily translated into equal influence in decision-making spaces.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Beyond the numbers, discriminatory social norms and unequal power relations continue to shape who is seen as a legitimate leader, whose voice is heard and whose contributions are valued," she said.

Citing the OECD's 2023 Social Institutions and Gender Index, Broussard said 43.9 per cent of Tanzanians believed men made better political leaders than women, highlighting the attitudes that continue to reinforce gender inequality in public life.

She said such perceptions had practical consequences, affecting the opportunities women receive, the support they can mobilise and their ability to influence decisions.

Women who venture into politics also face violence and intimidation, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which further discourages their participation.

Tanzania's Minister for Community Development, Gender, Elders and Children, Saada Mkuya Salum said women aspiring to political leadership continued to face social scrutiny and criticism that often left them with little opportunity to defend themselves.

"It's not easy at all. They will write. They will comment. They will do everything. And you don't have a chance actually to explain," she said.

She added that although progress had been made in empowering women, the systems and attitudes that historically excluded them remained firmly entrenched.

"So even the journey, women journey much as enhanced, are empowered somehow, but the journey has never and I believe it's not going to be that easy because of these systems that have been rooted," Mkuya said.

The Minister said Tanzania was proud of the progress made but warned that discriminatory social norms, weak institutional support and inadequate assistance for female candidates continued to undermine meaningful participation.

"We're proud of progress but they also tell us that when we are heading into the right direction we are not there yet and we will not get there as long as deep-rooted discriminatory social norms, institutions that support women's advancement and inadequate support for women candidates continue to restrict their participation," she said.

Mkuya also highlighted the additional burden placed on women by traditional household and caregiving responsibilities, which often leave them with less time and resources to build political networks, mobilise support and pursue leadership positions

European Union Ambassador to Tanzania and the East African Community, Jean-Marc Pisani, echoed the concerns, arguing that women's underrepresentation was not primarily a question of legal frameworks or leadership capabilities, but of deeply rooted social attitudes and the failure to translate commitments into practice.

Pisani said women held an average of 27 percent of parliamentary seats and 26 percent of local government positions across sub-Saharan Africa.

Regional disparities remain significant, with women accounting for approximately 31 percent of parliamentary representation in East and Southern Africa, 20 percent in Central Africa and 16 percent in West Africa.

Rwanda, where women hold 64 percent of parliamentary seats, demonstrates what can be achieved through political will and strong institutions, he said.

"Norms are not a cultural footnote to democracy. They determine who can take part in it," Pisani said, pointing to research showing that about half of the world's population still believes men make better political leaders than women.

He warned that violence against women in politics was increasingly moving into digital spaces, where abuse, threats and disinformation targeting female candidates and leaders were becoming additional obstacles to their participation.

"These are not private harms. They are attacks on democracy itself," he said.

Both officials called for a broader approach to gender equality, arguing that increasing the number of women in political institutions would not be enough without addressing the social and institutional barriers that limit their influence.

Broussard called for more inclusive political institutions, gender-responsive media coverage and the active involvement of men and boys in challenging discriminatory attitudes.

She also highlighted the importance of recognising young people, particularly young women, as agents of change rather than merely future leaders.

Pisani similarly urged men to take an active role in dismantling barriers by supporting women's political ambitions, speaking out against harassment and sharing decision-making power.

He also challenged journalists to examine how media narratives shape public perceptions of leadership and influence what girls believe they can achieve.

Close 

"The stories a society tells about leadership shape what its girls believe they can become," he said.

The two officials also pointed to ongoing interventions aimed at translating gender equality commitments into tangible improvements.

Broussard highlighted Tanzania's legislative reforms, including the recognition of violence against women in politics as an electoral offence under the Presidential, Parliamentary and Councillors Election Act.

She also cited initiatives supporting women parliamentarians through partnerships involving the Uwongozi Institute and the European Union, as well as community engagement programmes with the Tanzania Media Women's Association (TAMWA).

Pisani said the European Union had committed €90 million to its Gender Transformative Action programme, Breaking the Glass Ceiling, which supports gender-responsive policies, legal empowerment and community-level efforts to challenge discriminatory social norms.

The dialogue, bringing together participants from 23 countries, including journalists, women in politics and community leaders, is being convened by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA), with support from the European Union and UN Women.

The meeting seeks to facilitate exchanges on practical strategies for transforming gender norms and strengthening women's and young people's participation in leadership and decision-making.

World.title: Kenya: IG Kanja Denies Police Custody of Missing Tanzanian Activist Twaha Mwaipaya
World.content:
Nairobi — Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has denied that security officers arrested or detained missing Tanzanian activist Twaha Mwaipaya, even as he faced questions in the High Court over investigations into a wave of abductions.

Appearing before the Milimani High Court on Tuesday, Kanja told Justice Alexander Muteti that Mwaipaya had never been in police custody anywhere in the country, distancing the National Police Service from his disappearance.

"My Lord, I'd wish to inform this court we don't have the subject in our custody throughout the Republic of Kenya," Kanja said.

He also denied knowledge of any arrest involving the activist by officers from the National Police Service, insisting that police could not have removed someone they had never detained.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

However, Kanja confirmed that a report on Mwaipaya's disappearance had been lodged at Ruai Police Station and that investigations were ongoing.

The Inspector General's appearance came amid mounting pressure on security agencies to account for the activist, who was reportedly abducted on October 25 in Kamulu, Machakos County.

The court had directed police to produce Mwaipaya, dead or alive, following an application by human rights organisations led by Vocal Africa.

Kanja maintained that police treat reported abductions as criminal offences and initiate investigations whenever such incidents are reported.

"Not at all, we don't abduct and make people disappear," he told the court when questioned about allegations of police involvement in enforced disappearances.

"Any abduction is to be treated as an act of criminality," he added.

However, his assurance that investigations were underway faced questions over whether authorities had made progress in identifying and prosecuting those responsible for abductions.

During cross-examination, lawyers challenged Kanja to name individuals who had been arrested and brought to justice over abductions reported in the country.

Asked whether he could identify any perpetrators who had been held accountable, the police chief said several investigations were still ongoing.

"We have got many cases that are running even now. Investigations are still ongoing," he said.

Pressed further on whether any suspects had been brought to book, Kanja described the investigations as tedious, saying they involved extensive work.

He acknowledged that some cases could have been concluded but said he would need more time to provide details.

Close 

The police chief nevertheless maintained that Kenyans had confidence in his leadership, arguing that the country remained safe and secure.

"From north to south, from east to west, this country of ours is safe and secure. The properties of people are safe and secure. That is why Kenyan people are confident in the Inspector General," he said.

The activist was reportedly seized at around 2pm on October 25 while travelling in a taxi to visit friends in Kamulu.

Amnesty International Kenya and the Defenders Coalition said the individuals involved were travelling in three vehicles, including a Toyota Land Cruiser hardtop, and called on authorities to urgently establish his whereabouts and guarantee his safety.

The High Court is expected to give further directions on the petitioners' application as the search for Mwaipaya continues.

World.title: Uganda: Uganda Arrests Former Army Deputy Chief
World.content:
Former deputy chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu has been arrested over allegations of destabilising the country.

The Ugandan military has announced the arrest of its former deputy chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu over allegations of destabilising the country.

In a post shared via X, Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF)'s acting spokesperson Chris Magezi said Elwelu had been arrested on Monday, November 2, describing him as a "renegade" officer who was involved in subversive activities.

Recently, Uganda's defence chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said he had stripped Elwelu of his Lieutenant General rank and demoted him to a private.

According to Magezi, security forces recovered 15 guns in Elwelu's possession, military fatigues, and two pick-up trucks.

"Elwelu has been on the run over involvement in subversive activities and plans to destabilise Teso," Magezi said.
