World.title: NBC News Exit Poll: How it works and how we use the results on election night
World.content:
Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.

An exit poll is a survey of voters taken as they leave (or exit) their voting location. Unlike public opinion polls ahead of elections that predict whether respondents will vote, exit polls capture the views of voters in person on Election Day. The exit poll also reflects the views of people who voted early or by mail — we take steps to reach those voters by phone and by mail, as well as online.

Here’s how exit polls work, where they are conducted and how NBC News will be using the results on election night and in the days after.

Who conducts the exit poll?

For this year’s midterm election, exit polls are being conducted by SSRS, a survey and market research firm, on behalf of a group of news organizations: NBC News, ABC News, The Associated Press, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and MS NOW. The companies receive the same data, and NBC News then independently analyzes and reports on the exit poll results.

What questions are asked?

The national exit poll asks respondents whether they voted for the Democratic or Republican House candidate in their district, and in many states the poll also asks which candidates voters supported in Senate and governor’s races.

In addition, the poll usually includes a number of questions about voters’ views, such as, “What is the most important issue facing the country?”

The other key component of an exit poll is asking about voters’ demographics, such as age, gender, race and education level.

These types of questions help illustrate how different groups of people voted and what mattered to them. Demographic data is also used to weight the exit poll — that is, to make sure the poll reflects the demographics of the electorate as well as the election results.

The national and state exit polls include some different questions, to capture voters’ views on local issues and candidates.

The news organizations jointly determine how the exit poll will be conducted and develop the questionnaire together.

How are exit polls conducted?

The in-person Election Day exit polls are surveys that voters in scientifically selected precincts are asked to fill out as they leave their polling place. The paper forms have about 25 questions.

This year, interviewers will be stationed at over 450 polling locations in 15 Senate battleground states. Each interviewer follows local rules about where they can stand outside the polling location.

The exit polls also include a pre-election survey to capture voters no matter how they participate, whether early, by mail or on Election Day. Before Election Day, respondents are surveyed through methods including mailed invitations, telephone and text interviews and online surveys. Interviewers then follow up with respondents to confirm that they voted and whom they ultimately voted for.

Respondents can complete the poll in English or Spanish.

On Election Day, interviewers count the people coming out after they have voted and are instructed to offer questionnaires to every third person or every fifth person, for example, from the time polls open until polls close.

Interviewers phone in the results from the questionnaires to a data center three times during the day. Those results are tabulated with the pre-election survey results, and the exit poll is updated throughout the day as new data is collected.

Are exit polls anonymous?

Yes. In person, voters fill out the questionnaires themselves and deposit them in boxes, so their answers, like their actual ballots, are secret. Interviews conducted by mail, by phone and online do not retain any personal information about the voter who was interviewed.

Which states will have exit polls?

In addition to a national exit poll, which captures voters in all 50 states, there are also state exit polls this year in 45 states that have consequential Senate and governor’s contests.

How many people are interviewed?

The national exit poll sample will include over 75,000 voters at voting locations, online and by telephone.

In 15 states, interviewers will be stationed outside at least 30 randomly sampled voting locations. In the remaining states, interviews are conducted via phone, online and mail.

The sample size in each of these states will be about 4,000 voters: Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin.

The sample size in Alaska will be about 3,000 voters, and it will also include interviews from voters at early-voting locations before Election Day.

All other states with exit poll results for Senate and governor’s races will include between 500 and 3,000 voters.

How do we use exit polls?

The NBC News Decision Desk uses some exit poll data to help project race outcomes on election night, but the exit poll is primarily used to help tell the story of the election.

The data gives viewers and readers real-time insight into what motivates voters and how they feel about the country. It’s the nation’s first look at who is turning out to vote this year and what is driving their choices.

What does NBC News report and when?

NBC News does not report any exit poll results before 5 p.m. ET on election night, and no exit poll results that may indicate the outcome of a race are reported until after all the polls are scheduled to close in that state. As election night goes on and interviewers on the ground call in more exit poll results, the data is updated and reweighted in real time.

World.title: Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?
World.content:
In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.

Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term.

Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time.

Of course, no one, including the Decision Desk, will know what will unfold until election night, but we will have a good sense possibly early in the night of how the contests are trending. The answer of when we could call control in both the House and Senate depends not only on how states count their votes, but on how close the races will be.

When we could know Senate control

Senate control will likely come down to the eight races that NBC News rates as either toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas) or lean Democratic (Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire).

Assuming that Democrats win the states NBC News currently rates as “Likely” Democratic (which includes flipping North Carolina’s Senate seat from red to blue, and keeping Georgia in their column), Democrats still need to win five of these eight contests.

Some of these states are quick to count their ballots, and others are perennially slow. If some of these Senate contests are as close as we expect, calling control of the Senate as a whole could take us into the early morning hours of Wednesday, regardless of who wins those individual races.

It is also a real possibility that Americans will wake up at a slightly more reasonable hour on Wednesday without a majority decided, even if we have a good sense of who will ultimately win. And if Senate control comes down to the outcome in Alaska, we’ll all be here awhile.

In that case, it will take a couple of weeks to know who won the majority thanks to the state’s ranked choice voting system. Past elections offer a useful guide to how quickly we expect to see votes counted in each of these states, even if the timing Tuesday night is not exact. Let’s look more closely at each of these categories — the fast-counting states, the slow-but-steady states, and the ranked choice wild cards.

The fast counters

Votes in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas were counted fairly quickly in 2024. We expect over 80% of the vote in those states to be counted by midnight Eastern time. If those historical patterns hold, there is a good chance that those Senate races will be called. And some of these calls may come in before midnight if there is some spread in the races as some recent polls suggest.

But Democrats must win five of these battleground Senate races to take a majority, which means that even if they win all four states here, NBC News would still not be able to project control of the Senate.

The steady counters

In two of the key battleground states, New Hampshire and Michigan, nearly all votes will be counted over the course of election night, but more steadily and slowly than the fast counters. Here, elections are administered by towns and municipalities, not by counties. This results in a more decentralized and variable counting process that lasts until early morning, or even midday Wednesday. How quickly these races are called really depends upon the margin of the race.

Earlier in the election cycle, polls suggested both these races would be close. Recent polls favoring the Democratic candidates and what appears to be a Democratic advantage in the early vote in Michigan mean there’s a wide range of timing possibilities there.

If the nationwide Democratic momentum translates to results, New Hampshire could possibly be called before midnight. But that seems to be highly unlikely in a place like Michigan, where Wayne County, home to Detroit, often releases large batches of votes between midnight and 3 a.m. ET. This is such a significant source of ballots that statewide races in Michigan often cannot be called without Wayne County’s results.

The takeaway here is that if the Senate races in these states are close as the polls have indicated all along, it’s unlikely that calls will come before the early morning hours. But it all depends upon how far apart the two candidates are in the state, and we won’t know that until tonight.

The ranked choice states

Maine and Alaska are the slowest counters of the group. As in New Hampshire, Maine’s elections are administered by towns, each with their own schedule for tabulating ballots and releasing results. In Alaska, mail ballots from remote corners of the state can arrive up to 15 days after the election. If these historical patterns hold, there will not be enough votes counted on election night to call a close race in either state.

In 2024, the presidential race in Maine was called on Wednesday at 4:40 p.m. ET, and in Alaska on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points, while Trump won Alaska by 13 points. It’s possible the margins in this year’s Senate contests could be much closer.

There is a second complication in Maine and Alaska that could cause even more delay in knowing which party will control the Senate. These states both use ranked choice voting for their Senate races, in which voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of more than 50% of voters, the winner will be determined by ranked choice tabulation, in which the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their votes are reallocated based on voters’ next-most preferred candidates.

In Alaska, the ranked choice tabulation occurs 15 days after Election Day. Maine does not provide official guidelines on when its ranked choice tabulation will occur, but in June, the ranked choice results were released 10 days after Maine’s primary election.

In either case, if one or both of these seats are needed to win a majority, we may not know until the next day, or even for several weeks, which party will control the Senate.

What about the House?

Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to flip control of the House, and they’re heavily favored to succeed. But the size of that majority depends on how much voters shift their support toward the Democrats and away from Republicans.

A recent NBC News Decision Desk analysis shows evidence that this nationwide shift could be big enough to produce a historically large majority for the Democrats — or it could be sufficiently small that either party could end up with a razor-thin majority. (The House is made up of 435 seats, all up for re-election every two years, and 218 seats are needed for control.)

The size of that majority for either party matters significantly to our ability to project control of the chamber. The smaller the final size of the majority, the longer it will take for the Decision Desk to be certain of who will control the House.

If current polls are overestimating Democratic support and the size of the House majority for either party is small, the 2022 and 2024 elections provide some idea of timing.

During the 2022 midterms, it took the NBC News Decision Desk eight days after Election Day to project that Republicans would win a slim majority. This call came as the Decision Desk projected the Republicans would win California’s 27th District, their 218th win. The ultimate size of their majority was nine seats.

In the 2024 election, the Republicans won an even smaller majority — just five seats. This election also took until the second Wednesday after Election Day for the Decision Desk to project the 218th seat for the Republicans.

If the size of the Democrats’ or Republicans’ majority this year is a single-digit number of seats, we expect it to take days or weeks for either party to reach 218 seats.

Just like the Senate elections, the House elections in Maine and Alaska use ranked choice voting to determine a winner. If control of the House hinges on Maine’s 2nd District or Alaska’s lone district, we may have to wait until ranked choice tabulation occurs 10 to 15 days after Election Day.

On the other hand, if current polls end up being close to accurate, Democrats would be poised to win at least 230 seats, according to the recent Decision Desk analysis. This could speed up when we know control.

Throughout the night, the NBC News Decision Desk uses a statistical model to estimate the total number of seats that the Democrats and Republicans will end up winning. It is possible that NBC News will report this estimate on election night. The House model relies on past and current vote counts; it does not use any polling, including exit polls, in its estimation.

Early House indicators with clues for timing

Elections in states with early polling close times or that count their ballots quickly can also provide an indication of where things may end up. Kentucky’s 6th District, which Trump won in 2024 by 15 points, is a good example of an early bellwether district. The Republican-held district has its polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and in 2024 it reported nearly 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m.

While the Democrats do not need their candidate, Zach Dembo, to win this district to earn a majority, a low-single-digit win by the Republican candidate, Ralph Alvarado, is a favorable signal for the Democrats’ chances of winning the House. If Dembo were to win this district, it would likely foretell a Democratic tsunami, as there are 267 districts nationwide where Trump performed more poorly on his way to the White House. And if Alvarado were to win by a margin close to or in the double digits, it may suggest that neither party will end up with a large majority.

Florida, which tends to report its votes quickly, also has several congressional districts worth paying attention to early in the night. One of these is Florida’s 25th, where Democrat Jared Moskowitz seeks re-election in a district that Florida Republicans redrew to favor Trump by 9 points. If Moskowitz loses to Republican Scott Singer, it would be a major victory for Republicans and may foreshadow the party holding on to House control. If Moskowitz wins comfortably, it may signal a large Democratic wave.

Florida’s 14th District and Florida’s 22nd District are also Democratic-held toss-ups that Republicans redrew to be districts Trump would have won by 10.5 points. Given how quickly Florida counts its ballots, these two districts may be the first toss-ups NBC News can project. If one party were to win both of these districts early in the night, that party could very well end up with the majority.

World.title: Floods and severe weather beset parts of the U.S. on Election Day
World.content:
Flash flooding, heavy rainfall and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the United States to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races.

At least 21 polling locations were moved across eight Florida counties — including Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties — after intense rainfall caused flash floods Monday and into Tuesday morning.

Roads were impassable in several parts of the state’s Atlantic coast after a storm dumped as much as 22 inches of rain in 24 hours in a storm that “exceeded everyone’s expectations,” as one forecaster put it.

Severe storms were moving across Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas overnight. Forecasters issued a tornado watch that lasted until about 2:45 a.m. local time Tuesday.

Forecasters were also predicting possible flash flooding in parts of Alabama, Tennessee, Arkansas and Mississippi on Tuesday, as that storm system continued to travel east. A flood watch remained in effect in some parts of Florida, though rainfall rates were slowing.

“Areas affected by catastrophic flooding remain extremely sensitive to any additional rainfall,” forecasters wrote in a Tuesday morning discussion.

In Oklahoma, a tornado Sunday forced Cimarron County officials to change one of its polling locations. The tornado, which had peak winds of about 100 mph, snapped tree branches, damaged the roof of the Keyes Community Center and collapsed a wall, according to a damage survey report from the National Weather Service.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

In an emergency request, county election officials said the tornado caused “considerable structural damage” to the community center “rendering the polling location unsafe.”

And after historic flooding in the Four Corners region, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre M. Henderson declared a state of emergency and issued a special accommodation that will allow voters registered in San Juan County who are isolated by floodwaters to request and return ballots electronically.

The Colorado secretary of state is allowing a similar measure for voters — allowing votes online — in La Plata and Archuleta counties, according to 9 News.

More election day surprises could be in store.

Experts say inclement weather has suppressed voter turnout in past elections. In research of elections from 1948 to 2000, researchers observed a modest drop in turnout during unusually intense rain storms.

“What we found was that for every inch of rain that a county received above its average amount of rainfall, voter turnout went down about eight-tenths of 1 percentage point,” said Brad Gomez, an associate professor of political science at Florida State University.

But experts said the effect of rain on turnout is diminishing over time as more people choose to vote early or vote by mail, and they said it’s hard to predict what effect the inclement weather will have, if any, on key races.

In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in seven counties along the Atlantic seaboard that are being hit with flash flooding and extreme precipitation.

Damage in parts of Colorado remains widespread after heavy rain and flooding, with first responders searching for people who may be stranded across the area, including by helicopter.

A vehicle is submerged on the Piedras River in Arboles, Colo., on Monday. Gregory Bull / AP

People with homes along the Animas River in southwestern Colorado were also facing evacuation.

Record rainfall was also reported in usually dry Arizona, causing deadly flooding and power outages.

The brief closure of two voting centers in Maricopa County sparked a chorus of conspiracy insinuations online Monday. Two out of the 254 polling locations in the county had to be temporarily shuttered “due to power related issues,” election authorities announced on social media.

An overturned mobile home and other debris in the Verde River as severe flooding rushed through an RV park in Camp Verde, Ariz., on Monday. Ross D. Franklin / AP

The two polling locations have since been reopened, authorities said, but some online used the shutdown to allege impropriety in the competitive swing state.

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs issued a statewide emergency declaration Monday after recently issuing an emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties. The governors of New Mexico and Colorado also asked President Donald Trump to declare a major disaster to receive federal funding assistance.

World.title: Trump sets the stage for potential GOP losses, says party ‘gave this a very strong shot’
World.content:
In an election-eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said Republicans “gave this a very strong shot” while acknowledging that historically, the president’s party “doesn’t win the midterms.”

“This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime,” Trump said Monday in his final major speech before the midterm elections Tuesday. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump’s “closing message” before voters make their final trips to the polls, Trump spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool.

Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, a key focus and fascination of his second term.

Speaking about the election, he touted what he considered economic wins, saying that “personal incomes are the highest in history” and that “the poverty rate is at an all-time record low.”

But, he said, “it all doesn’t matter if we’re going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election ... just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” he continued. “Now, that doesn’t happen, because usually, whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad — for some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

Trump derided Democratic candidates and falsely said some were jihadists or members of the Muslim Brotherhood. He said they are “all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy costs skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world, hoping to get them to be able to vote.”

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Trump referred to Alaska’s Senate race and last week’s report by The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent. Peltola has denied having been aware of the reported scheme.

“They got somebody named Dan Sullivan to run against Dan Sullivan,” Trump said. “It’s corrupt. It’s really a fraud, fraudulent election.”

Asked by NBC News after his remarks whether he would consider resuming strikes on Iran after the election, Trump said, “No.”

Trump closed out a 28-rally swing through the U.S. to campaign for Republican candidates Sunday. He traveled for 25 days in the final month of the campaign, visiting 19 states. He held his final rallies outside Washington on Sunday, with one in Kansas and the other in Iowa, both states with competitive Senate races.

Trump is scheduled to participate in several tele-rallies for the midterms from Washington on Monday. On the final day of the 2018 midterm election cycle, by contrast, he held in-person rallies in three states.

“We’ve got some big races tomorrow,” Trump said in his remarks. “I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow’s Election Day, more traditional.”

Asked Sunday why he chose to speak at the Reflecting Pool, Trump told reporters: “Just to show how beautiful it is. It’s been finished. It was vandalized badly. We have cameras all over the place now for the vandals.”

On Monday, he stood next to a poster that said, “Back, and more beautiful than ever.”

“We’re booming like we’ve never boomed before,” he said. “We’ve cleaned hundreds of sites of graffiti, fixed over 2,300 lighting fixtures in Washington, D.C., cleaned and renovated over 83 statues and fountains and monuments, removed hundreds of squalid homeless encampments.”

In addition to the Reflecting Pool between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II Memorial downtown, Trump highlighted other construction projects he launched, including the White House ballroom, a White House helipad, a new golf course in the city and a triumphal arch, among other projects.

Trump appeared to joke at one point that the Reflecting Pool would be named after him.

The Reflecting Pool has been closed since July after additional renovations had to be made when the bottom coating peeled and algae formed, tinting the water green.

The National Park Service announced recently that it was extending the closure of the pool and the areas surrounding it until Nov. 20.

After the initial renovation process began in June and it first reopened to the public, Trump accused multiple people of “destroying” the pool.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Washington charged former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with destruction of property during a June 19 visit. In late July, the U.S. attorney’s office, led by Jeanine Pirro, dropped the case, citing information it had obtained that undermined “the evidentiary basis for the indictment.”

World.title: In top Senate race states, gas and grocery costs rose faster than the national average
World.content:
From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.

In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.

But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters.

These frustrations aren’t confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

This has created an opening for Democrats to win majorities in both the House and the Senate. And while the House majority is widely expected to shift to Democrats after Tuesday night, the Senate is still very much a jump ball.

Veteran election data analysts are quick to remind the public that as Tuesday’s voting and later counting unfolds, any one of the competitive Senate races could tip either way.

Pain at the pump

In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period.

Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof.

Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16.

In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%.

All three states broke for Trump in 2024. But two years later, they are in play, and Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, will be very closely watched Tuesday night.

World.title: Interactive graphic: Road to a House majority
World.content:
Who will win control of the House?

Democrats enter the final sprint to Election Day as the clear favorites, polls show, though Republicans have money and geography on their side.

Currently, the Democrats hold 214 seats in the House, compared with 219 held by the Republicans, with two vacant seats. Democrats need to net just three seats to gain the majority; the question then becomes, how big is that majority?

The chances that Republicans maintain a majority control appear slim, but that outcome is still possible. The House battleground runs primarily through states and districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, and Republicans attempted to shore up their structural advantage last year through redistricting. Those two factors could prevent Democrats from fully capitalizing on the increasingly favorable political environment even if they flip the chamber.

Explore the interactive below to see how Democrats could build a big majority, or Republicans could hang on.

World.title: U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at the end of the year, Trump says
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the United States to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel.

It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant.

Trump said he and Netanyahu “made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” and that the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”

Speaking in a phone interview with “Fox & Friends,” the president said the idea was Netanyahu’s — the Israeli prime minister has previously floated tapering American aid over the next decade. Netanyahu’s office declined to comment Tuesday.

“We’ll help Israel if they need it — you know they’ve been a great ally,” Trump said, adding that the Israeli government was “fine with it because, you know, they have become a very successful country” and “they don’t need” the money.

The president was speaking while voters were heading to the polls for the midterm elections. U.S. military aid to Israel and Israel’s use of American weapons in Gaza and the West Bank has become one of the most contentious issues during the campaign.

The president appeared to acknowledge a political dimension to the decision, saying, “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.”

“I don’t like that because you know it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target,” he said.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump added, referring to Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan progressive Democratic Senate nominee, who has forcefully criticized Israel and U.S. foreign policy during the campaign.

The price of Brent oil slid 3% to $101 in response to Trump’s comments, its lowest level in more than three weeks, as investors and traders viewed the comments as potentially further evidence that the Iran war could be ended without escalation. It ticked back up to $103 as of noon ET.

The initial drop added to oil’s biggest one-day decline in three months Monday, after Trump told NBC News that he was not planning to attack Iran after the midterms.

Complex aid picture

The U.S. has agreed to give Israel $3.8 billion annually as part of a “memorandum of understanding” between the two countries signed in 2016 under then President Barack Obama. That agreement took effect in October 2018 and specifies $3.3 billion a year in military financing grants and $500 million a year for joint missile defense. It is due to expire in 2028.

Almost all of that money must be spent on purchases from the U.S.

But the total amount is much higher, with American military aid to Israel greatly boosted following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and subsequent Israeli assault on Gaza.

In the two years after October 7, the U.S. spent at least $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to a paper by William D. Hartung, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank based in Washington, D.C.

World.title: Poland launches major security operation along border with Russia
World.content:
Berlin — Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the country's national police chief said, and the Polish prime minister said the effort may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation targeting the NATO member.

Additional police and counterterrorism units, as well as troops from the elite military special forces unit GROM, have been deployed as part of the operation, which national police chief Marek Boroń said would run from Monday until at least Nov. 8.

Polish and allied intelligence agencies had warned of possible sabotage operations and provocations during the first half of November, particularly along Poland's border with Kaliningrad, and including possible border incursions by armed groups.

Those warnings had already put domestic security agencies on high alert even before the additional security forces were deployed to the northeast regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.

Tourists stand next to a razor-wire fence along the Polish-Lithuanian border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, near the village of Grzybina, in Poland's Podlaskie province, near the Suwalki Gap, Sept. 26, 2026. Sergei GAPON/AFP/Getty

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Tuesday that suspicious movements were observed overnight near Kaliningrad, including individuals carrying flashlights close to the border area.

He said the quick reaction by Polish security forces may have prevented an unspecified provocation this week.

"We very quickly mobilized the necessary security forces and means on site, and we successfully prevented any attempted acts of provocation, if that was the intention. Of course, we will never be able to completely confirm that," Tusk said Tuesday, adding that intelligence had pointed for weeks to possible "acts of diversion or more serious provocation" against the European Union, including "the intrusion of armed individuals into Polish territory."

A special command center was set up at Polish national police headquarters to coordinate the new security operation.

The goal is to protect the public, detect suspicious activities early, and prevent attacks on critical infrastructure, the police said Tuesday.

Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad, bordered only by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic Sea to the west, is of considerable military and strategic significance. It is widely believed that Russian security agencies, including the FSB and GRU intelligence agencies, have a presence in the territory in eastern Europe.

A map shows some of the Eastern European NATO states that border Russia's Kaliningrad exclave, with the Suwałki Corridor between Lithuania and Poland labeled. Peter Hermes Furian/Getty

To the immediate east of Kaliningrad is the strategically important Suwałki Corridor — the only land border connecting the Baltic NATO states with the rest of the alliance, where Poland and Lithuania share a short border sandwiched between Russian and Belarusian territory.

Polish authorities had not published any evidence of specific plans for an act of sabotage or an attack originating from Kaliningrad by Tuesday afternoon, but the alert comes after months of sabotage, air incursion and other low-level incidents across Europe blamed largely on Russia.

During a joint news conference with Lithuania's prime minister on Oct. 13, Tusk referred to a conversation he had recently had with NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich, and said it had reinforced his own concerns about increasing threats of sabotage, including possible provocations involving aircraft or attacks on border crossings.

At about the same time, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture of the security threats facing the U.K. and Europe, and he said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one."

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.

"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Among the numerous incidents attributed to Russia across Europe this year alone, there was a fire in August at a Polish factory that produces drones and other military components, and an arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station that Polish officials blamed directly on Russia in September.

Russian drones have also crossed into NATO airspace in Eastern Europe repeatedly during the war in Ukraine, and just this week the U.K. Royal Navy said it had intercepted a Russian spy ship off the far northern coast of Scotland.

The navy said helicopters were dispatched to track the intelligence-gathering ship, which was "closely monitoring" a NATO exercise taking place near Scotland's Outer Hebrides islands.

World.title: Here's when polls close for 2026 midterm elections today
World.content:
Millions of Americans will be casting their votes in person in the 2026 midterm election on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Polling times vary by state. States will begin reporting election results after their polls close.

Forty-seven states and the District of Columbia offer early voting options, with the exception of Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire. Eight states and Washington, D.C., automatically send a mail-in ballot to every registered voter, although voters generally can still choose to vote in person. Over 57 million voters have already cast their ballots early this year.

If you are in line to cast your ballot before a site closes, you have the right to remain in line and vote. View a list of voter rights from the ACLU here.

World.title: Soaking rain to start the week in Minnesota; colder days ahead
World.content:
Scattered rain showers will continue on Election Day in the Twin Cities, with highs expected in the 60s.

The steadiest rain is forecast west and north of the Twin Cities. Patchy showers are expected in the metro, with 0.25 to 0.60 inches of rain possible Tuesday.

More showers will move through Tuesday night and Wednesday, with rain gradually winding down. A few lingering showers could stick around Thursday.

Clouds and showers are expected to clear out Thursday into Friday, bringing a cooler but drier Friday with some sunshine.

World.title: Bodycam video shows moments after National Guard fatally shot man
World.content:
Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.

A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer's body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops, "Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?"

The Shelby County District Attorney's Office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the July 5 shooting of Tyrin Johnson.

Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson's family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and National Guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him.

André C. Wharton, an attorney for Johnson's family, noted the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself. The footage also doesn't show Johnson's initial encounter with the guard members.

"This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable," Wharton said in a statement, reported by CBS affiliate WREG.

Wharton said a "critical question" investigators must answer "is what happened in the immedate moments before Tyrin was shot in the back."

"The videos released today underscore why our Constitution protects every person from unreasonable searches and seizures. Whether force was unreasonable must be decided by a careful, unbiased investigation of the facts, and this case is no exception," Wharton said. "The footage released today unfortunately does not capture the full sequence of events, including the active threats Tyrin was reportedly facing prior to being shot by the task force."

The attorney also asked for the public's patience as he and his team "work tirelessly to obtain all critical, objective evidence."

The guard members were part of a federal task force created by President Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democrat-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee had deployed the Guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

A banner for shooting victim Tyrin Johnson is seen on July 17, 2026, in Memphis, Tenn. AP Photo/George Walker IV, File

District Attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death.

A spokesperson for the Tennessee National Guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time.

Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots around 4 a.m. when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot.

Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun.

The video, which is blurry from the officer's movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises.

A Tennessee National Guard report obtained by The Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who "rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them." Both guard members fired their service weapons — M17 handguns — and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated.

Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting "Hands!" and "Turn over!" as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk.

Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said.

At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man's shirt just before the video ends.

World.title: Cruise canceled after Coast Guard detains ship in Miami, officials say
World.content:
MSC Cruises canceled the voyage of its MSC Poesia cruise ship after it was detained by the Coast Guard at the Port of Miami, the cruise line confirmed to CBS News on Tuesday.

A source familiar with the matter told CBS News more than 2,000 people were on board the ship.

MSC Cruises said the cancellation happened because of a "regulatory matter" that arose before departure. The cruise line said it was unable to resolve the issue in time to set sail.

"We have made the difficult decision to cancel the current sailing," MSC Cruises said in a statement. "We recognize how disappointing and frustrating this news is for our guests, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption to their holiday."

Guests will receive a full refund of their cruise fare, MSC Cruises said. The cruise line also said it was helping people get back home.

The cruise ship MSC Poesia in the Baltic seaside resort of Warnemünde. Stefan Sauer/picture alliance via Getty Images

Before Tuesday's cancellation, the Coast Guard said in a statement to CBS News on Monday its teams "are verifying the cruise ship's compliance with international standards and U.S. regulations."

The Coast Guard's Miami sector detained the ship for inspection on Sunday.

"The Coast Guard is tasked with verifying safe and secure commerce. It is the Captain of the Port's priority to ensure the safety of passengers, crew, the vessel, and the environment," the Coast Guard said.

In an earlier statement, MSC Cruises said the company was fully cooperating with authorities.

MSC Cruises says the MSC Poesia has a capacity of more than 3,200 passengers and over 1,000 crew members.

World.title: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
World.content:
For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.

Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.

This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."

They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.

Sponsor Message

"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."

Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.

"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."

Loading...

The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.

Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.

Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.

Sponsor Message

This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.

Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.

"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"

Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.

"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.

This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.

"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.

"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."

Sponsor Message

She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.

NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.

World.title: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
World.content:
Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia

toggle caption i Ben Curtis/AP

MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.

The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.

An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.

Sponsor Message

The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.

India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.

The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.

The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.

Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.

The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.

Sponsor Message

The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.

In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.

The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.

Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.

International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

The Associated Press reports that the U.S. conducted defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz last night, including Qeshm Island, which is a key launch point for Iran's strikes. While NPR could not independently confirm the details, Iran reported explosions on the island. This pattern of strikes has occurred several times in recent months, coinciding with heightened Iranian attacks on shipping vessels in the Strait.



🎧 Iranian officials say they prefer to return to negotiations. The country has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days ahead of the seven it proposed in September, if the U.S. re-engages in talks, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi says. The Iranian inflation rate is around 90%, and residents are facing dire economic conditions alongside fears of potential bombings. As winter approaches, officials are urging millions of Iranians to conserve energy to avoid soaring natural gas prices. They say the country's natural gas networks are unstable due to damage from the war. Al-Shalchi says Tehran is hoping it can wait out the U.S. election and possibly see Trump's party lose control of Congress.

Sponsor Message

A Massachusetts judge is considering a motion to dismiss the case against Lindsay Clancy. Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan will announce his decision later this month. In court yesterday, Clancy's attorney requested that the judge dismiss the case or initiate a new trial. Clancy faces first-degree murder charges for the 2023 deaths of her three young children in their Duxbury home. The trial ended in a mistrial in September when jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The Plymouth County district attorney's office has not disclosed its next steps, including whether to seek a new trial or pursue lesser charges. In a recent motion, prosecutors stated they aim to "pursue justice" for Clancy's children.

Picture show

toggle caption i George Steinmetz/©2026 George Steinmetz

The Siena Drone Photo Awards showcase aerial views of our planet each year, highlighting landscapes and human stories often hidden from view. Photographer George Steinmetz won the top prize of 2026 for his photo titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal," which captures a stranded vessel off the coast of Bangladesh. The image depicts workers around a partially dismantled tanker designed for transporting liquefied natural gas. The photo illustrates the country's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe are dismantled, and their materials are repurposed. See Steinmetz's work and some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs from countries in the Global South.

Behind the story

by Jonaki Mehta , education correspondent focused on disabilities and learning differences

toggle caption i LA Johnson/NPR

For half a century, America hasn't had enough special education teachers. It's a shortage that's only gotten worse as the number of students with disabilities grows rapidly — 8.2 million according to the most recent federal count, or about 1 in 6 students.

Research explains some of why these roles are so hard to fill: These teachers enjoy working with students but spend more time on legally required paperwork and tasks other than teaching. They often don't get paid more despite having more responsibilities than many other teachers. And because there's such a widespread shortage, the teachers who stay in the profession are often handed a bigger load.

Sponsor Message

NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear directly from educators, so NPR senior producer Lauren Migaki and I have been exchanging voice memos with more than a dozen teachers from big and small districts around the country. So far, they've shared tales of joy when a student found success, tearful moments when they felt like they had failed, and waking up before dawn to make sure they were prepared.

For example, Jeffrey Carroll, who teaches in Newport News, Va., said last year, he was teaching students across three grade levels and multiple subjects: second, fourth and fifth. It meant he was constantly running from one classroom to the next. "I just didn't feel like I was teaching, I was never in a class long enough to be a meaningful part of it." This year, he was relieved to only be teaching across two grade levels. "It's been good to support my students in the classroom. I get to do some co-teaching. The lesson plans come to life."

Lauren and I will stay in touch with these teachers throughout the rest of the school year and visit some in their classrooms to get a better understanding of what it takes to do this essential job.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Photo by Scott Suchman-NSO/KC1CT22

The National Symphony Orchestra is currently without a home while its Kennedy Center venue is involved in a federal court dispute. The NSO faced a new reality when it had to find six alternative concert venues in the Washington, D.C., area while hoping to maintain its budget amid ongoing controversies. After entertaining visitors for decades at the St. Louis Zoo, Raja, a 10,000-pound Asian elephant, has moved to new stomping grounds at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden. (via STLPR) The Commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia have filed a lawsuit to stop the construction of Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall triumphal arch.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Death toll hits 29 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with 48 still missing
World.content:
Death toll hits 29 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with 48 still missing

toggle caption i Ukrainian Emergency Service/via AP

KYIV, Ukraine — The death toll from a Russian attack in southern Ukraine on a site where people had gathered to receive humanitarian aid rose to 29 on Tuesday, with 48 still missing, as a wave of overnight strikes targeted power plants across the country, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people.

Dozens of rescuers and volunteers continued to search the cratered blast site of a destroyed aid facility and shelter in Komyushuvakha, a village in Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region, hoping to find missing residents alive under the rubble. Instead, more bodies were pulled out and carried away in white plastic sheeting.

"The scale of the tragedy is terrifying," Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region's military administration, wrote in an online post. "This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war."

toggle caption i Danylo Antoniuk/AP

Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections.

Sponsor Message

"The Russians think America won't notice this signal of theirs," he said. "But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes."

Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia where Russian bunker-busting bombs, filled with nearly 1.5 tons of explosives, were used in Monday's attack.

The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Semikin said Tuesday. At least five people were hurt.

toggle caption i Ukrainian Emergency Service/via AP

In the northeast region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said.

A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients were transferred to other medical facilities, head of the regional military administration Oleh Syniehubov said.

In the Dnipro area, rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble Tuesday morning, after a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17, local authorities said.

The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital. Patients were transferred to other hospitals, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Tuesday that it had shot down 856 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones were fired toward the Russian capital.

Sponsor Message

A Ukrainian drone attack wounded two employees at an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, regional Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev said Tuesday. He added that there was damage to the refinery's infrastructure.

Rolling blackouts have been instituted in the south, west and east of Russian-occupied Crimea following attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow-installed officials said Tuesday.

World.title: Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go
World.content:
Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go

toggle caption i Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House on Tuesday. If they do, will their majority be built upon a blue wave or a tiny trickle? A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.

Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress, and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.

Sponsor Message

So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:

Early polls closing

The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 6th Congressional District (KY-06) and Indiana's 5th (IN-05), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.

Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.

Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.

Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.

Sponsor Message

Other races to watch: FL-27, NC-11, SC-01, VA-01

Last-minute big spending

In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07, where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10, where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.

New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 could be one of the rare Republicans who holds on to his seat thanks in part to his party's ad spending advantage in the closing stretch against Democrat Cait Conley.

Three of Iowa's four House races, IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 are on the list of most expensive, in part because of the competitive governor and U.S. Senate races that are also on the ballot and driving up turnout.

Other races to watch: CO-08, PA-01, WA-03, WI-03

Redistricting

This year's Supreme Court decision rolling back part of the Voting Rights Act led to many Republican-led states redrawing their House maps to eliminate districts that favor Democrats in a typical election year – but this year is not typical.

Now, the political environment has deteriorated so much that seats like AL-02, held by Democrat Shomari Figures, OH-09 held by Democrat Marcy Kaptur and NC-01 held by Democrat Don Davis are all considered toss-ups at best and favoring the Democrats at worst for Republicans.

In Texas, Latino voters seem poised to swing back to Democratic candidates and could prevent Republican Eric Flores from flipping the seat held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 or Tano Tijerina from unseating Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar in TX-28.

Sponsor Message

Other races to watch: CA-22, FL-09, FL-14, TX-35

The outer edges of the map

As results continue to be reported, one thing to watch is how far into conservative communities the increased support for Democrats can go.

One race that has received a surprising amount of ad attention is in Arkansas's 2nd district (AR-02), where incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill faces a well-known challenger in Democrat Chris Jones. By the time polls close, closer to $10 million will have been spent in the final months on the Little Rock-based seat that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.

There are also many districts in states that redrew their maps where the Republican gerrymander could backfire, like Ohio. In both OH-10 held by Republican Mike Turner and OH-15 held by Republican Mike Carey, Trump won by closer to 10 points in 2024. They're also in a state with competitive governor and Senate races and stretch between the suburbs and exurbs of Dayton and Columbus with an electorate that could swing away from the GOP.

The margin in North Carolina's Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is expected to win against former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, could determine if races like NC-03 are in play as well too. Rep. Greg Murphy's district absorbed more Democratic-leaning voters after the latest map redraw.

Other races to watch: NC-09, NY-21, TN-09, WA-05

World.title: From 'model minority' to target, anti-Indian hate on the rise
World.content:
From 'model minority' to target, anti-Indian hate on the rise

toggle caption i Laura Bargfeld/AP

A 19-year-old man's alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago last month is drawing attention to a recent and steep rise in anti-South Asian and anti-Hindu hate. Police in Palatine, Ill., announced that on Oct. 11, a college student and Taco Bell cashier named Alexandros Paporakis tried to carry out the attack at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Ill., roughly 40 miles west of Chicago. They said the plot was averted by a jammed gun.

"Something of this scale … has not been directed at South Asians before," said Rohit Chopra, professor of communications at Santa Clara University and visiting fellow at the Center for South Asia at Stanford University.

Sponsor Message

Two decades ago, the predominant narrative about Indian immigrants to the U.S. was glowing, describing the relatively small population as a "model minority." But Chopra says that over the last four years, a combination of growing anti-immigrant populism, economic anxiety and rising political visibility have dramatically changed the script. Today, he said, online and political discourse more often depict Indian Americans and a broader community of people of South Asian descent in conspiracist, degrading and dehumanizing ways.

"It's become a question of who is American, and deliberately trying to keep the Hindu- and Indian-American community out of those conversations entirely with these sort of preconceived notions and bias against the community," said Prasiddha Sudhakar, a board member of the Network Contagion Research Institute. Sudhakar was formerly a researcher at the NCRI who coauthored some of that organization's reports on the topic.

Most concerning, said Sudhakar and Chopra, is that the toxic online rhetoric they have documented has moved from fringe social media platforms to mainstream ones in a short period of time. And, they said, they see strong connections between online hate and offline violence.

"It didn't start off as mainstream, maybe even like a year or a few years ago. You still saw it on the internet," Sudhakar said. "But what has actually become more important now is that this is reaching many different parts of society in a scale that we've never seen before."

Sponsor Message

A massacre averted

Paporakis has been charged in Illinois with making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a rifle, both felonies. Police said his coworkers called to report the attempted massacre. One of them, according to an affidavit filed by a Cook County assistant state attorney, had spoken by phone with the defendant shortly after the attempted attack. The affidavit further states that Paporakis had also sent that coworker messages, including an eight-page document he had written outlining his motivation for the alleged plot.

Later that day, police said that a search of Paporakis' apartment turned up a bag containing an AR-style rifle, 300 rounds of ammunition, eight loaded magazines, one loaded extended magazine and body armor. They also found a gas can and items bearing Nazi symbols and anti-Indian slurs.

"The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated," said Palatine Police Chief William Nord at a press conference.

Court filings state that the written document was filled with "derogatory and racially charged slurs" directed at "people of Indian ancestry, Jews and African Americans," and that it described those groups as "subhumans." It also indicated that the defendant had settled on the temple location two months prior, but had been planning an attack for two years. In the writings, the defendant allegedly described himself as "a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day."

The day that the defendant allegedly went to the temple coincided with the beginning of a major Hindu nine-day festival. Among the many in attendance were U.S. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi , D-Ill., and his family. Krishnamoorthi has since called for the FBI to investigate the incident as a federal hate crime.

Grafting antisemitic conspiracy theories onto a new group

Sudhakar, whose research was published through the NCRI, said that fringe social media spaces such as 4chan and Gab were the original loci of denigrating and dehumanizing rhetoric about Indians and South Asians. But around 2022, Sudhakar said, her research started to see some of the negative attitudes morph into full-blown conspiracy theories. One of them was a baseless theory about a "Brahmin Organized Government."

Sponsor Message

"This is the idea of, oh, there's like this elitist group of people that are of high class, high privilege that are sort of occupying the entire government, that this is all like some sort of secret ploy," Sudhakar said.

The term echoes the conspiracy theory of the "Zionist Organized Government," or "ZOG," widely espoused by neo-Nazis. This baseless narrative posits that a cabal of powerful Jews runs global affairs, and closely ties with the Great Replacement Theory. It claims that Jewish puppetmasters are deliberately diluting the power of white Christians by promoting immigration, interracial relations and diversity.

Sudhakar said the main distinction is that the anti-Indian conspiracy theories center more heavily on fears over immigration and jobs, rather than changing demographics. Just as the narratives position people of Indian origin as all-powerful, they also invoke dehumanizing tropes about Indians as "dirty" immigrant "invaders" being brought to the U.S. to displace technology sector workers.

"What we saw was that what began as sort of this anti-Hindu meme that began on 4chan started moving into these mainstream platforms [like X]," she said. "And every time that you'd see Indians or anyone of Hindu origin kind of gain prominence, that these same code words would also be increasing."

Sudhakar said those spikes coincided with events such as Parag Agarwal's appointment as CEO of Twitter, Sriram Krishnan's selection as former White House policy adviser on Artificial Intelligence and the installation of Usha Vance as second lady.

But 2025, said Sudhakar, was when online anti-Hindu and anti-Indian hate truly mushroomed. Chopra, the professor at Santa Clara University, found the same, in research co-authored for the Center for the Study of Organized Hate. It found that between January 2025 and June 2026, anti-South Asian hate speech on the social media platform X was 240% higher than it was in January 2024.

Sponsor Message

"I think the right has very effectively succeeded in making the H-1B visa issue a political hot button," Chopra said, noting that Indian nationals account for more than 70% of H-1B visas. "Every time there was some development to do with the H-1B visas or a remark that might be made by a figure in authority, you'd find a spike in hate online on X."

A community new to fighting back

Since the alleged temple massacre was disclosed to the public, calls are growing within the Hindu and Indian communities in the U.S. to speak more vocally about racism. Congressman Krishnamoorthy released a video urging the community to become more engaged. Chopra said that in some ways, the rapid uptick in anti-South Asian hate online has been possible because there has been little organized opposition.

"The South Asian community is particularly vulnerable for, I think, a number of reasons. One is this combination of high median income of certain groups of visible success … combined with the fact that it does not have significant political power," Chopra said.

The rise of Indian Americans on the political stage in recent years has been significant, given that estimates put the community's population only around 5 million. These figures include Usha Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel, former Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard, Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and former GOP presidential candidate Nikki Hayley. But Chopra said that these milestones do not equate to the political power of an organized constituency.

"It doesn't have the kind of political power that can … significantly shift elections, Chopra said.

Additionally, explicit racism directed at South Asians has become disturbingly evident within the political arena, Chopra said. In September, a Republican candidate for statewide office posted a screenshot to X of cheering University of Texas football fans after a team victory. It featured a crowd of revelers that included many of South Asian and Asian origin, with the candidate's comment that "social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It's everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine."

Sponsor Message

The Department of Homeland Security also set off controversy when it shared an image of a poster captioned "Transformers," with an image of a Sikh man and the words "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr. Singh." The message was understood to refer to an August 25 tragedy, in which a commercial truck driver of Indian nationality illegally made a U-turn on a Florida highway, and killed three people. After a backlash, DHS took the post down.

But while calls are mounting for the community to organize, there are unique challenges. For one, said Pushpita Prasad of the Coalition of Hindus of North America, Hindu temples do not serve quite the same function as houses of worship do in many other religions.

"We don't belong to temples and we are not part of congregations," Prasad said. "So for us, organizing and finding our voice and sharing information is that much harder."

Additionally, Prasad noted that the economic and professional success of many people of Indian origin in the U.S. masks the uncertainty many may feel about their long-term status in the country. According to the Pew Research Center, two-thirds of the Indian population in the U.S. are immigrants, and of those, nearly half are not naturalized citizens.

"If you happen to come from India, you will find that a lot of Hindus who may be very well off have a great job, seem very well established, they're not really able to speak because they're in that weird sort of immigration limbo," Prasad said. "So that's another reason why a community that seems well off, at least in media chatter, is not as vocal or as organized as it probably should have been."

World.title: How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election
World.content:
