How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election

Voters are voting, ballots are being counted and results are starting to come in for 435 House races, 35 Senate races and 36 gubernatorial contests as well as ballot measures and thousands of state legislative seats. But how will NPR call races on election night? Determining a winner in any of the many races across the country is a big job. That's why NPR partners with the Associated Press — and has for many years — to ensure that races are called accurately.

The Associated Press has been calling races since 1848 and even now, nearly 180 years later, the process for making those calls is pretty simple. Here's how the AP explains its race calling process:

Sponsor Message

Race callers collaborate with analysts who focus on statewide races, such as those for U.S. Senate and governor, and elections for the U.S. House of Representatives. The decision editors on AP's Decision Team sign off on every race call for president, U.S. Senate and governor, as well as races of significance for U.S. House.

Together, they are looking at far more than just the overall vote totals. They study the incoming vote county by county. In states where the information is available, they look at the vote by type of ballot: cast in person at polling places, or in advance by mail or in person. They are also in constant contact with AP's vote count team, in search of the latest information about what's been counted so far and how many ballots may still be left to count.

Once AP has an idea of how many ballots are outstanding versus how many have been counted, their staff can start to tabulate the likelihood of a certain winner being victorious in a certain contest based on a lot of different factors: where the ballots that are outstanding are coming from, what the makeup of those communities looks like and even, how the individual chose to vote.

Sponsor Message

For NPR's part, once the AP calls a race, we will alert our broadcast and digital audiences on air as part of special coverage and online through digital stories. We also ensure that our hundreds of member stations also have access to that information. We will use AP's data to populate our election results pages so viewers can keep track, in real time.

How are races called when not all votes have been counted?

But sometimes, races might be called without all — or even most — of the vote counted. How is that possible?

The Associated Press explained in 2024 that it uses that same calculation of ballots, external factors and other data to inform its decisions.

In almost all cases, races can be called well before 100% of the votes have been counted. The AP's team of election journalists and analysts will call a race as soon as a clear winner can be determined. That may sound obvious, but it is the guiding principle that drives the organization's election race-calling process.

The AP's race calls are not predictions and are not based on speculation. They are declarations based on an analysis of vote results and other election data that one candidate has emerged as the winner and that no other candidate in the race will be able to overtake the winner once all the votes have been counted.

It sounds simple, right? The AP won't call races until "a clear winner can be determined." But that doesn't always require all of the votes for every precinct for every race. Sometimes it's all about the math: can this candidate feasibly win with the votes outstanding in the places they are yet to be counted? And that raises another, really important point.

The AP – and therefore NPR – will not project races. The team at the AP will wait until it has certainty to call raises and that is why its race calls are trusted by hundreds of news organizations, including NPR. Because they wait until there is surety, even if it means waiting just a bit longer to be sure.

Sponsor Message

On an ethical note, NPR will not make race calls just because a candidate declares victory, nor will NPR use a concession speech or statement to make a race call either. That is true of the Associated Press as well:

AP does not make projections or name apparent or likely winners. If our race callers cannot definitively say a candidate has won, we do not engage in speculation. For example, AP did not call the closely contested race in 2000 between George W. Bush and Al Gore – we stood behind our assessment that the margin in Florida made it too close to say who won.

AP only calls a race when we are fully confident that race has been won – defined most simply as the moment the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory.

When AP makes a race call, we back it up with transparent reporting into the research and analysis that led us to say with certainty who has won. This explanatory journalism is as much a hallmark of our coverage of U.S. elections as the race calls themselves.

World.title: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's midterm election day in the U.S.

Just a small handful of battleground states and districts will decide whether power in Congress shifts from the Republicans to the Democrats for the remainder of U.S. President Donald Trump's time in the White House.

The Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to get a majority in the 435-member House of Representatives, a target that polling analysis suggests is well within reach.

What's less certain is whether the Democrats will take the Senate.

To achieve a 51-49 Senate majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats. That requires flipping at least two states Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas or Kansas.

Here's a look at the pivotal races to watch in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Senate: Maine

U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican representing Maine, speaks with gun shop owner Rick LaChapelle at a campaign stop in Lewiston, Me. on Oct. 21. (Robert F. Bukaty/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Susan Collins vs. (D) Troy Jackson

Collins has held this seat for 30 years, even though Maine has not voted for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988.

Collins has kept winning elections by persuading enough Democrats that she gets results for Maine in Washington. Most recently, she took credit for Trump's moves to exempt certain Canadian products used by Maine businesses from the crushing 50 per cent tariffs he'd imposed in late August.

The question is whether Maine voters will punish Collins for being a Republican this time or reward her for the occasions when she stood up to Trump.

Her Democratic Party opponent is a former logger turned politician from a small town in northern Maine. Jackson entered the race only in July after the original nominee, Graham Platner, stepped down amid allegations he had sexually assaulted a former partner.

Key issues: Trump's posture toward Canada has led to a sharp drop in Canadians crossing the border to visit Maine. His war in Iran triggered a 74 per cent jump in the price of furnace oil, which roughly half of all households in the state use to heat their homes.

Senate: Michigan

Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is putting U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada on the ballot in Michigan in the midterms. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

Candidates: (D) Abdul El-Sayed vs (R) Mike Rogers

This seat was thrown open by incumbent Democrat Gary Peters' decision not to seek re-election. If Democrats can't hold Michigan, their path to a Senate majority becomes significantly tougher.

El-Sayed is a medical doctor and staunch progressive who was born in the U.S. to Egyptian immigrant parents. Since winning the Democratic nomination in August, he has become a frequent target of Trump's attacks.

Trump launched an Islamophobic rant against El-Sayed during a rally in the border town of Port Huron, Mich. on Oct. 25, calling him a "jihadist" several times. Trump warned that a Democratic win in the midterms would bring "hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror."

Rogers, a former FBI agent who served in the House for 14 years, has attempted to put some distance between himself and Trump on Canada-U.S. relations. He launched a new ad this month in which he said, "We need to end this tariff war now," while sitting in a sports bar with a Labatt beer.

Key issues: Trump's tariffs on Canadian products and the breakdown in trade talks are causing upheaval in the auto industry, Michigan's economic engine. Michigan residents have faced higher tariff costs per household than any other state, according to a recent study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

Senate: Ohio

Trump listens as Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio speaks at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Oct. 12. (Gene J. Puskar/THe Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Jon Husted vs (D) Sherrod Brown

Husted was appointed to the seat in 2025 to replace JD Vance when Vance became Trump's vice-president. Before that, Husted had a lengthy career in state politics, holding elected office since 2001.

Trump has recently commented frequently on the 59-year-old Husted's athletic physique, including at events outside of Ohio.

"I examined his ass," the president said at a rally in Kentucky on Oct. 17. " I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I'm still recovering."

Brown has been in politics for more than 50 years, first elected to the state legislature just before his 22nd birthday. He held Ohio's other U.S. Senate seat from 2007 until losing his re-election bid in 2024.

Brown has long advocated targeted tariffs to protect U.S. manufacturing jobs but has consistently criticized Trump's sweeping tariffs, including those on Canadian goods, as ineffective and inflationary.

Key issues: Ohio is a often considered a bellwether state, so the issues top of mind for voters there mirror those resonating across the country: the rising cost of living and whether Trump's war against Iran and his tariffs are to blame. Concern over the spread of data centres is also emerging as a local issue that could affect the statewide race.

Senate: Texas

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, right, greets a supporter at a campaign rally in Allen, Tex. on Oct. 19. Paxton is the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, running against Democrat James Talarico. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Candidates: (R) Ken Paxton vs (D) James Talarico

Democrats haven't won a U.S. Senate election in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born.

Yet polls suggest Trump himself has put the seat at risk by rejecting incumbent Sen. John Cornyn and endorsing Paxton — the state's scandal-ridden attorney general — as the Republican candidate.

A Republican loss in Texas would be the most significant midterm repudiation of Trump in the country. Paxton seems to realize the burden.

"I'm not exaggerating when I say if we lose Texas, we lose America," he told an Oct. 19 rally in Fort Worth.

In their campaign stump speeches, the rivals describe each another in extreme terms. Talarico calls Paxton "the most corrupt politician in Texas," while Paxton says a vote for Talarico is "a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now."

Key issues: The Latino community accounts for roughly one in every five eligible voters in Texas. It supported Trump in record numbers in the 2024 presidential election, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) targeting thousands of non-criminals who've been in the U.S. for years could swing many of those voters toward Talarico.

Senate: Iowa

Iowa Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee Josh Turek on Oct. 13 in Des Moines, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Ashley Hinson vs (D) Josh Turek

Both parties believe they've nominated appealing candidates in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst.

Hinson was a TV reporter and anchor before winning a House seat in 2020. Turek is a three-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball who was born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam.

Both candidates have tried to persuade Iowa voters they aren't beholden to their party or its leadership. Hinson has said she will stand with Trump on issues such as border security but stand up to him when she believes his policies are wrong for Iowa.

Turek, campaigning in a state that hasn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 16 years, has described himself as "proudly a moderate" and said he and Trump could agree on many issues.

Key issues: Farmers are a major voting bloc in Iowa and rely on diesel to fuel their equipment. For months, Trump brushed aside concerns about soaring fuel prices, driven largely by the war with Iran. Less than two weeks before election day, he announced $8 billion US in one-time payments to farmers to offset diesel costs.

Other notable Senate races

North Carolina appears poised to be the mostly likely state for Democrats to flip.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is retiring, Trump only carried the state by three percentage points in 2024, and Democratic candidate Roy Cooper served 16 years as North Carolina's attorney general and two terms as governor.

His opponent Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, is a political backroomer who has never held elected office.

Alaska has sent only one Democrat to the U.S. Senate in the past 50 years. But there are clear signs the Republicans are worried this time.

At Trump's behest, the Department of Justice launched a lawsuit seeking to bar the state from certifying the election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. The ostensible reason: there is also an independent candidate on the ballot named Daniel J. Sullivan.

The tight Alaska race took on even more uncertainty last week after a bombshell New York Times report that Sullivan the independent was recruited into the race by a Democratic operative from Ohio.

The Democratic candidate is Mary Peltola. She and Minnesota Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan could become the first Indigenous women elected to the U.S. Senate.

In Kansas, no Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election since 1932.

Yet polls suggest that could change in 2026. Similar dynamics are at play in Kansas as in Iowa: farmers are upset by soaring diesel prices triggered by the Iran war and rising input costs resulting from tariffs.

Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is up against Democrat Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a megachurch.

WATCH | What a Democrat sweep of both House and Senate would mean for Trump: What happens to Trump if the Democrats crush the midterms | Duration closed caption 4:57 With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections threatening Republican control of Capitol Hill, CBC’s Ellen Mauro breaks down how a shifting balance of power could challenge President Donald Trump’s agenda — and the key tools he can use to counter Democratic opposition.

House races to watch

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for election.

However, various websites that analyze U.S. politics — including the Cook Political Report, the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, Decision Desk HQ and 270toWin — currently rate no more than 53 of them as truly competitive.

Here are a few of the key Republican-held districts Democrats are targeting in their effort to take control of the House.

Virginia 1st district: (R) Rob Wittman (incumbent) vs (D) Shannon Taylor

Polls close in Virginia at 7 p.m. ET, so this race could provide one of the earliest indications of what kind of a night it will be for Republicans and Democrats. The district, which stretches from the suburbs of the state capital, Richmond, to the historic city of Williamsburg, was flagged by the Washington Post as one of the "bellwether races to watch" in the midterms.

Pennsylvania 7th district: (R) Ryan Mackenzie (incumbent) vs (D) Bob Brooks

This district, centred on the working-class city of Allentown, has swung between Democrats and Republicans four times since 2006. Latinos make up nearly one-quarter of eligible voters. Mackenzie won the seat in 2024 by a one-point margin. Brooks is a former firefighter who has never held elected office.

New York 17th district: (R) Mike Lawler (incumbent) vs (D) Cait Conley

Lawler's pitch to voters in this Hudson Valley district includes what he has called his "strong working relationship" with Trump as a way to get things done in Washington. Conley is a West Point graduate who served in Iraq and Afghanistan and is making her first run for office. She has put her military background front and centre in her campaign advertising.

Democrat Bobby Pulido, a famous singer among the Latino community, is trying to unseat Republican Monica De La Cruz in the race for the 15th Congressional district of Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Texas 15th district: (R) Monica De La Cruz (incumbent) vs (D) Bobby Pulido

Democrats recruited a star candidate for this South Texas race: Pulido is a two-time Latin Grammy Award winner. De La Cruz tried to dismiss him as unserious by saying the election " isn't about who you want performing at your niece's quinceañera." Pulido seized on the remark by taking his campaign to quinceañeras, the traditional celebration of a girl's 15th birthday.

Ohio 7th district: (R) Max Miller (incumbent) vs (D) Brian Poindexter

This district in Cleveland's western suburbs wasn't originally a prime target for Democrats. That changed after Miller's ex-wife — the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno — accused him of physical abuse, including throwing boiling water at her and holding a gun to her head. Miller has denied the allegations.

Poindexter is an ironworker and city councillor in the working-class community of Brook Park.

Michigan 10th district: (R) Michael Bouchard vs (D) Christina Hines

This race in Detroit's northern suburbs is open because incumbent Republican John James is running for governor. Bouchard is an Army veteran whose ads have focused on being tough on crime and securing the southern border.

Hines is a former prosecutor who boasts of having put " hundreds of predators, murderers, and pedophiles in jail ."

World.title: 7 Montreal police officers have been fired after misconduct allegations. What comes next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In an interview on CBC's Daybreak Tuesday morning, Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher called the move to simultaneously fire seven Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) officers "historic," saying it had never been done in the city before.

On Monday, Dagher had announced the administrative dismissal of five officers from Station 39, as well as two officers from Station 21, in connection with allegations of discriminatory and racist behaviour, as well as derogatory acts.

On Tuesday, he said accountability was important not just to the public, but also to the rest of the force.

"I want to make sure that some part of the culture of the police stays, because there was magnificent, good work being done by police officers," he said.

Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher says efforts have been made to weed out the 1% of police officers who deliberately tarnish the uniform. (CBC)

He said the dismissed police officers will not receive compensation in connection with their dismissals, and they will be required to disclose that they had been the subject of an investigation which resulted in their termination if they sought employment with another police force.

Further action regarding the seven officers could come as the result of other investigations, including the possibility of criminal charges.

Demonstrators kneel outside Station 39 in Montréal-Nord during a protest over allegations of racist conduct involving SPVM officers under investigation. (Paula Dayan-Perez/CBC)

The SPVM has forwarded a file to the Directeur des poursuites criminelles et pénales (DPCP) for it to review charges related to allegations of discriminatory and racist acts against police officers at Station 39.

"We've been digging and digging and digging to find out those kinds of stories, allegations," Dagher said. "We didn't find any more after six, seven months."

Last week, however, it was revealed that the DPCP is investigating another Station 39 officer who, according to Radio-Canada sources , allegedly deleted evidence from a victim's phone in a case of domestic violence in 2025.

When an officer flagged the deletion to her superiors the issue was initially ignored, according to Radio-Canada.

Dagher said that a new action plan is underway to rebuild trust, and that community consultations will be undertaken, especially with people served by Station 39, the station where the majority of the fired officers had worked.

WATCH | Montreal Police Chief Fady Dagher says community consultations to come: Montreal police chief reveals more about what led to 7 SPVM officers getting fired | Duration closed caption 8:44

The plan, which is expected by the end of December, will outline revisions to the force's recruitment, training and promotion processes.

Dagher said that despite a series of allegations, the SPVM's most recent annual review was the best in the city's last 15 years.

But according to Alain Babineau, former Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer and director of a racial profiling and public safety at the Red Coalition, action on the seven fired officers could have come sooner.

Montrealers protests police misconduct on Oct. 24. (Kwabena Oduro/CBC)

"There's been plans over the last 20 years. Every five years the SPVM has come up with a plan to curb racism, discrimination," he said. "People are tired of plans."

He said that rather than praising police officers for doing work they're expected to do, Dagher should spend time reassuring the communities his officers serve.

"This is not seven bad apples," Babineau said. "Until you actually dismantle the system that has produced those folks, that had allowed those folks to perpetrate these criminal acts, then you can't be totally satisfied."

World.title: Deadly fire at CFB Wainwright renews compliance clash between oil operator and Alberta regulator
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The deadly fire that swept across the Wainwright, Alta., military base has renewed a months-long regulatory battle between the provincial energy regulator and an oil and gas company.

Military officials have said there is no evidence that energy infrastructure was involved in the grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17, which killed four soldiers and injured dozens more.

But in the weeks since the tragedy, Calgary-based Sumerian Oil and Gas has been speaking out against the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) about recent enforcement issues that led to hundreds of Sumerian wells on the military base being seized days before the fire.

In a series of public statements shared on its website and with CBC News, company officials allege that the AER failed to ensure the wells were secured before the fire.

They say Sumerian staff were the first to alert the regulator that night about the risk the wells could pose as the flames spread. As of Tuesday, the company website appeared to have been taken offline.

Officials with the AER have not responded to questions about the status of Sumerian's wells on or since the night of the training disaster. They also declined to comment on how the wells have been managed since Sumerian lost access and the assets were placed under the care of the Orphan Well Association (OWA) on Oct. 5.

'New compliance issues'

In a statement to CBC News Friday, Lars DePauw, president of OWA, said the agency has secured Sumerian’s wells at CFB Wainwright.

DePauw did not answer questions about when that work was completed or whether it happened before or after the fire.

“All Sumerian wells on CFB Wainwright have been inspected and shut in,” the statement said. “We continue to work on the new compliance issues we have identified. The OWA was not involved in any emergency response activities during the recent fire.”

OWA previously told CBC News that the AER’s Oct. 5 order against Sumerian was due to “significant non-compliance issues.”

While there are operational oil and gas wells scattered across CFB Wainwright, military investigators have said there is no indication that the fire was caused by oil or natural gas infrastructure, or that a gas line was struck. In response to questions about Sumerian’s assets on the base, military officials said there is no new information to share and the investigations remain active.

Call for ministerial review, legal challenge

Sumerian officials assert that the AER has unfairly targeted its operations for months. They have pledged to launch a regulatory appeal and seek a court injunction in an attempt to regain operational control of their assets.

The company has also asked Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to launch a ministerial review into the regulator’s conduct. Jean’s office has not responded to repeated requests for comment.

In a series of statements issued after the Wainwright fire, Sumerian said it lost custody of its wells on the base two weeks earlier and hasn't had access since.

In the AER order on Oct. 5, all of Sumerian’s assets, including more than 300 well licences on CFB Wainwright, were placed under the care of the OWA.

The order followed a string of enforcement actions, unpaid regulatory fees and a pair of crude leaks that allegedly went unaddressed in Wainwright and Killam.

The order required the OWA to shut in the sites within 14 days, a timeline Sumerian officials had warned the regulator was impossible due to the complicated process required to access sites on an active military base.

“So far as Sumerian can determine, between Oct. 5 and Oct. 17 the OWA did not attend a Sumerian site on the range, shut in no well, and isolated no pipeline," the company told CBC News in a statement.

Sumerian officials said they called the OWA emergency line the night of the fire to report that the company's wells were “inside the fire area.”

“On the evening of Oct. 17, the OWA’s designated contact advised Sumerian that none of the Sumerian wells on the range had been shut in and that the OWA did not plan to attend the base until Oct. 27,” the company said in a statement posted to its website last week and emailed to CBC News.

Military officials have said the fire resulted from a training exercise, was initially reported on the base's grenade-launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter — and quickly spread in strong winds.

Three separate investigations are underway, and, among other things, will look at the threat assessment of the fire.

In a statement to CBC News Wednesday, the AER declined to comment on Sumerian’s allegations and said it is unable to answer questions related to the Wainwright incident while it is under investigation.

Mandy Olsgard, a risk assessment specialist and former senior environmental toxicologist with the AER, was critical of Sumerian’s attempts to regain operational control.

The AER's order followed well-documented issues that raise legitimate concerns about the adequacy of environmental management under Sumerian, she said.

Rather than invoking a tragedy of unconfirmed cause to undermine the regulator's credibility, Sumerian should provide evidence that outstanding environmental protection obligations have been met, she said.

"They clearly were not managing their wells in a manner that was sufficient for the Alberta Energy Regulator and that's why they no longer have control of them."

Previous sanctions

Sumerian’s regulatory disputes date back to November 2025, when it acquired the assets of Cleo Energy Corp., which had been in receivership for more than a year while its operations racked up a series of enforcement orders.

The AER did not oppose the initial acquisition, but enforcement disputes continued to arise.

The regulator first ordered Sumerian to suspend operations in July, but the company challenged the order and was granted a temporary stay in the Court of King’s Bench.

When announcing the Oct. 5 order , the AER said it had authorized the OWA to suspend the wells and facilities out of concerns Sumerian “may not be able to provide reasonable care and measures” to protect public safety and the environment.

'Licence loss as a last resort'

The company, however, claims it was not given enough time to fix years-old operational issues before the AER clamped down and seized its assets.

Sumerian asserts that the AER violated its own principles of "education first and proportionate enforcement," punishing the operator for pre-existing conditions on unworkable timelines.

Sumerian claims the AER repeatedly miscalculated compliance and security obligations by attributing third-party or non-existent assets to Sumerian. Along with the company's call for a ministerial review, Sumerian is also demanding a regulatory audit of their assets.

“The deficiencies pre-date the restructuring, and the AER knew it,” the company said in a public statement about its dealings with the regulator.

“The company’s position is that the enforcement rests on conditions that pre-date its ownership, contradicts the AER’s own documents, and runs against the AER’s published policy of proportionate enforcement with licence loss as a last resort.”

Oil assets 'dotted' across Alberta

Olsgard said the adequacy of Sumerian's environmental management and its ability to meet regulatory obligations should be assessed on their own merits.

She said, however, the case is a reminder of the need for clear emergency management protocols for the thousands of abandoned and orphaned energy sites scattered across Alberta, and the dangers these operations, if left unsecured, could pose when seasonal wildfires spark.

"We are a petro state, and these are dotted all over our province," she said. "And given the increasing intensity and magnitude of forest fires, this should be something our provincial government is looking into.”

World.title: PWHL star Sarah Fillier expected to play for Canada at world championship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian star Sarah Fillier is expected to play at the world championship as Canada looks to reclaim gold from the United States.

Fillier left Friday's pre-tournament game against the U.S. after going into the boards awkwardly. The Canadians went on to lose that game, 4-0.

The New York Sirens forward looked to be clutching her right shoulder or arm as she exited the game. The team has described the ailment as an upper-body injury.

Canadian GM Danièle Sauvageau said Fillier is considered day to day, so it's not yet clear when she may suit up for Canada. The team's first game is against Sweden on Friday at 9 a.m. ET in Denmark.

"Things are looking good, so it's a question of day by day," Sauvageau told CBC Sports on Tuesday. "It's on a good track, a positive track."

Fillier scored the game-winning goal and added an assist in Canada's 5-3 pre-tournament win over the U.S. last Wednesday, which ended an eight-game American winning streak that dated back to February 2025.

That she hasn't been ruled out for the tournament is a big win for the Canadians, who rely on Fillier to drive offence on the top line and first-unit power play. Sauvageau described her as a "young veteran" on an increasingly younger Team Canada.

At the Olympics, Fillier finished second in team points (six in seven games), behind Daryl Watts.

Rebuilding for 2030

Canada also has 20-year-old Colgate University forward Alexia Aubin practising with the team in Denmark, but that is unrelated to Fillier's injury. The decision to bring Aubin as an alternate was made before Fillier was hurt.

WATCH | Canada falls to U.S. in pre-tournament game: Canadian women's hockey team loses exhibition to U.S. ahead of world championships | Duration closed caption 2:12 Sarah Fillier left the pre-world championships exhibition game early with injury, and the Americans scored a pair of power-play goals defeating Canada 4-0.

An alternate can replace an injured player at any point during the tournament, assuming the injured player can't return for the rest of the tournament.

But Aubin was also brought to get experience with the team, as the Canadians rebuild ahead of the 2030 Olympics in the French Alps.

"We want to expose as many players as possible in order to be the most prepared," Sauvageau said.

The Canadians looked disconnected in Friday's game, struggling to break the puck out cleanly and generate high-danger chances. The Americans outshot them, 32-13, and Canada's penalty kill yielded two goals on five opportunities.

But the Canadians are keeping the bigger picture in mind, with so many new, young players getting their first crack at international play on the senior team.

"It is an exhibition game," Sauvageau said about Friday's loss. "It is a game that, again, we need to expose, we need to try different things. Of course, Team USA played very, very well and this is what we expected. But at the end of the day, we need to play games in order to get better and to create cohesion, and give the players the experience that we're going to continue to build on."

World.title: Ottawa wants us all to have emergency supplies for 3 days. The good news is, that number hasn't changed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Public Safety Canada is maintaining its longstanding advice for Canadians to be prepared to go at least three days without running water or electricity, following recent calls in the U.K. and other countries for their residents to do the same.

"Canadians have been encouraged for many years to ... be ready to take care of themselves and their households for a minimum of 72 hours during an emergency," Zarah Malik, a spokesperson for Public Safety Canada, said in a statement to CBC News.

Some U.K. retailers reported spikes in sales of essential goods after London launched its Be Ready campaign on Oct. 22. Officials warned that cyberattacks and severe weather could disrupt essential services, and encouraged residents to stockpile 72 hours of supplies including non-perishable food and bottled water.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house."

Officials in Normandy, France, posted on social media on Oct. 27 that residents should prepare a bag containing essentials for 72 hours. "Don't wait for the emergency: prepare now!" the post reads.

And Japan launched a new national agency focused on disaster management on Monday which, as one piece of a much broader plan focused largely on earthquake preparedness, urged residents to evaluate their evacuation procedures and stock up on water and portable toilets for at least three days.

There is no indication that any of those announcements were co-ordinated or are connected to a particular expected event, but the timing has set off some speculation online.

Prep for one week: expert

Suzanne Bernier, faculty member of the Disaster Recovery Institute of Canada, says governments have been putting out the same messaging for at least three decades but it's a good time for an update.

She says it makes sense that the messaging is becoming more prominent, as natural and human-caused disasters are increasing, people are living in areas that used to be unpopulated and cyberattacks are becoming common.

A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food, echoing a similar ‌attack in France last month.

"We're just seeing that it doesn't really matter where we are, everywhere is a target. But particularly of concern is the cyberattacks on critical infrastructure," said Bernier.

"It's just a matter of time before everybody is either indirectly or directly affected by a cyberattack."

She encourages Canadians to aim for at least seven days' worth of supplies.

WATCH | Expecting the unexpected: Getting prepped to deal with emergencies | Duration closed caption 4:11 Emergency Preparedness Week aims to educate people about how to ready themselves for the unexpected, whether it’s a house fire, severe weather or a power outage. Thunder Bay Fire Rescue encourages residents to take a few simple steps now that could make all the difference later.

"We need to really be preparing people for ... potentially not being able to have anybody respond to you or save your family within that first week," she said, adding people should also have a go-bag ready in case of evacuation.

Public Safety Canada says 72 hours is a minimum recommendation and notes it could take more time for some areas to restore basic services, or for emergency workers to reach all affected residents.

The government agency gives more detailed preparedness advice on its website.

Europe has generally ramped up its emergency preparedness messaging over the last two years. The European Commission's Preparedness Union Strategy, released in March 2025, warns of growing geopolitical tension and threats from natural disasters.

Scott Cameron, co-founder of Emergency Management Logistics Canada, says Canadians should also be paying more attention to emergency preparedness, given talk of national sovereignty and growing climate-related concerns, including recent mass evacuations from wildfires and floods.

Cameron says stockpiling for 72 hours is a good idea for personal preparedness, but more work needs to be done on a community level, like identifying local supply chains and resources.

"Where is our local, our community capacity and resilience, to move beyond 72 hours?" he said. "And what are we as Canadians all prepared to be able to help with, as opposed to being the recipients of aid?"

World.title: New company wants to stop northern permafrost slumps with special blanket
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new company that wants to stop permafrost slumps from further erosion says it’s growing its business after testing its product near Fort McPherson, N.W.T., this past summer.

Former Tetlit Gwich’in chief James Ross and academic and entrepreneur Cansu Culha are co-founders of PermaC Land and Environment Inc. The company was incorporated in January and the team spent the summer putting their product — dubbed the “green blanket” — to the test.

“We went out and did the work and learned a lot,” said Ross, who describes the green blanket as a profitable way of healing the land. “Now I have a scientifically proven model of how we can effectively slow down and help these slumps.”

The green blanket is made of biodegradable material that’s laid on top of a retrogressive thaw slump — a kind of landslide that happens when permafrost thaws. The idea is it traps cold in the ground and prevents heat from getting in, while also using a layer of seeds and cuttings to bring back native plants, to try and prevent the gouge in the ground from getting bigger.

James Ross, left, and Cansu Culha co-founded PermaC. They incorporated the company in January and have filed a patent together for their green blanket product. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

Culha, who is an adjunct professor at the University of British Columbia, wouldn’t say what, exactly, the blanket was made of saying she had to protect the intellectual property of her company. However, she described it as being made of “wooded fibres” and other erosion control materials.

And, she said, testing it out this summer was a success.

Culha said her team deployed the green blanket on two retrogressive thaw slumps — one stable, the other growing — around 50 kilometres down the Dempster Highway from Fort McPherson in June. The stable slump demonstrated the green blanket did not trigger erosion itself, she said.

The other slump was partially covered to compare the difference between the two sides. Culha said the part of the slump that wasn’t covered retreated five metres, while the land that was covered stayed intact. At the edge of the blanket the land retreated less than one metre, something Culha said was expected because the land next to it was still eroding and exposed the side of the protected area to warm air.

Culha helps deploy her green blanket product on a retrogressive thaw slump near Fort McPherson, N.W.T. this past summer. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

Culha said a critical part of her solution is also reintroducing the “very protective” tundra vegetation.

“We believe that the long-term solution is not necessarily to control erosion through these fibres, through these blankets. But rather, it's to bring in native plants that can naturally do the restoration of the lands.”

The problem

Steve Kokelj is a senior permafrost scientist at the Northwest Territories Geological Survey. Not only has he long studied the slump where PermaC has deployed its green blanket, but the company has consulted him on the project as well.

He says permafrost has different characteristics or personality, depending on its history.

The Peel Plateau — where the product was tested — consists of permafrost that’s made up of leftover glacier, and is sometimes made up of 70 to 80 per cent ice, he said.

That’s why when it thaws, the land slumps and settles.

Culha said the green blanket was deployed on part of a retrogressive thaw slump. The part that was left uncovered retreated by five metres, while the part that was covered remained intact. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

“A retrogressive thaw slump … they basically start to grow relatively small, when some sort of small erosion or a small landslide exposes the ice and the permafrost, and then that ice thaws in the summertime and the disturbance grows over time.”

Kokelj said a retrogressive thaw slump can “live” and continue to grow for decades.

They can dump huge amounts of sediment into rivers and lakes. Ross said they also pose a risk to infrastructure, and harvesters who travel the land as well.

David Kay, a Gwich’in harvester and sub-chief of the Tetlit Gwich’in Band Council, has seen evidence of this first-hand. Travelling through the mountains, he said he’s seen a lot of erosion alongside creeks and all over the land.

Though he hasn’t had any close calls himself, he’s heard of harvesters chasing animals by snowmobile who have narrowly avoided the steep drop of a slump that’s hard to see.

‘A prudent idea’

Culha said the intent of the green blanket is to stop that positive feedback loop that allows slumps to grow.

“By protecting these slumps from growing further we’re protecting the infrastructure, we’re protecting the streams, the eco-system, as well as preventing the release of carbon, greenhouse gases such as methane, and CO2,” she explained.

Steve Kokelj is a senior permafrost scientist at the Northwest Territories Geological Survey. Not only has he long studied the slump where PermaC has deployed its green blanket, but the company has consulted him on the project as well. (Liny Lamberink/CBC)

In a warming North, Kokelj said the green blanket is a strategy worth pursuing.

“The idea of an insulative blanket is, you know, it seems like a prudent idea. I think coupling that with other things like managing snow, managing drainage, I mean, these are all sort of innovations and ideas that we're going to have to use,” he said.

However, the size of the slump upon which it's deployed will make a difference, he said.

He said it would not be possible to stop erosion of a thaw slump that’s already displaced millions of cubic metres of material. Where there’s likely to be success, he said, is on small disturbances that are just getting started.

Culha said the blanket was deployed in two spots outside of Fort McPherson, N.W.T. One was a stable retrogressive thaw slump, and the other was a slump that had been growing summer after summer. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

Kay described PermaC’s solution like a band-aid on the land. He’d like to see the green blanket deployed broadly on Gwich’in lands.

“The land that we have out there is, you know, really unique and beautiful,” he said. “I really think this PermaC company is gonna help us heal the land … I hope it goes a long way.”

Culha wouldn’t say whether PermaC had clients yet. She said the company’s next steps are to think about commercialization and to grow its team.

World.title: 24 hours in Antigua: Mark Carney's priorities at this year's Commonwealth summit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's oft-stated determination to keep his government focused on what Canadians can control could be tested today, as he meets with leaders from the 55 other member countries of the Commonwealth in Antigua.

As he boarded his flight with his wife Diana on Monday, Carney gestured as if he couldn't hear reporters yelling for clarification on where things stand following his conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend.

Trade negotiations could return to a full boil, but for now they remain on a back burner while the White House focuses on the verdict about to be rendered by American voters in their midterm elections .

The future of the Canada-U.S. relationship hangs so heavy over the Carney government's agenda that it could be hard to focus on anything else. But this week's Commonwealth talks are the first in a series of multilateral summits this month where Canadian officials will pursue alternative partnerships in trade, security and diplomacy.

WATCH | Carney says summit taking place at crucial time: Commonwealth summit taking place 'at crucial time,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:26 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking during a meeting with prime minister of host country Antigua and Barbuda Gaston Browne, called the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting a 'unique gathering' of 56 nations representing 2.7 billion people.

Here are five things to watch for:

1. Push to double intra-Commonwealth trade

The Commonwealth has three main priorities leading up to 2030: democratic resilience, economic resilience and environmental resilience.

On that first priority, ministers, including Foreign Minister Anita Anand, met Sunday to welcome the restoration of an elected government in Gabon, the central African country which had its membership partially suspended following a military coup in 2023.

But the main focus at this summit is trade partnerships: specifically the association's ambition to lower trade barriers and double trade between member countries by the time they meet for their next biennial summit.

That dovetails perfectly with the Carney government's attempt to pivot away from the U.S.

"I think people don't realize the economic clout of the Commonwealth. There's almost a trillion dollars of trade," said Arif Lalani, a former diplomat who served as a senior official the last time a Canadian prime minister attended the Commonwealth summit, in 2022.

"There are studies which show that it's cheaper to do business between Commonwealth countries because we have the same practices, same language, generally the same set of regulations. So it's definitely a place to pursue the economic diversification agenda," Lalani said.

WATCH | What the Commonwealth could offer Canada: Carney should see Commonwealth as trade opportunity: secretary general | Duration closed caption 0:57 With Prime Minister Mark Carney heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting, Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey tells CBC's Janyce McGregor that Canada should consider the association of 56 member states as an alternative trading option.

His fear, however, is that the Commonwealth's "relevance is growing faster than its capacity to deliver."

Leaders need to get more outcome-oriented on trade, he said. He agrees with Carney's efforts to expand this focus to defence and security co-operation too.

At a time when conflicts over choke points like the Strait of Hormuz are restricting global trade, "Commonwealth countries have a lot of coastline, they have strong navies, and so I think there's something that can be done to increase maritime co-operation," Lalani said.

2. Evolving Caribbean relationships

This is Carney's first trip to the Caribbean as prime minister.

That diplomatic deficiency will be addressed this morning in a bilateral meeting with this year's Commonwealth host, Antigua and Barbuda's Prime Minister Gaston Browne, followed by a working breakfast Canada is hosting for all the Caribbean leaders attending this year's summit.

While not a complete gathering of CARICOM leaders, officials briefed reporters that this breakfast is a chance to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Diana Fox Carney are met by a greeting party as they arrive in Antigua. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Vandana Kattar, who worked in the prime minister's office under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, says Carney's approach so far makes sense to her.

"Multilateralism is important to him," she said. Carney went after some of the bigger pieces of his puzzle first, she reckons — pursuing the "low-hanging fruit" of a closer relationship with Europe , attempting to resolve tariff tensions with China .

"Those are big pieces of the puzzle that he's been able to put together," she said. But he also needs to fit smaller pieces into that puzzle, like nurturing Canada's relationships in the Caribbean, "otherwise that doesn't complete the whole picture."

3. Climate finance commitments

"You can't go to the Caribbean countries and not talk of climate resiliency," Kattar said. "They're the ones impacted the most."

Canada's already contributed $4.65 million over three years to the Commonwealth's climate finance access hub to help small island states. It's also made a bigger $13-billion commitment to support all developing countries adapt to the consequences of climate change — like stronger and more frequent hurricanes — over the next five years.

Canada hopes to amplify the voices of smaller Commonwealth partners on climate issues, officials told reporters prior to the trip.

"That's what actually builds the trust, and that's what ensures that Canada is seen as a reliable and a trustworthy partner that actually listens to the concerns of their partners and [is] not just forcing their own agenda onto them," said Climate Action Network's Soomin Han.

Han believes conversations on climate financing between big and small Commonwealth partners might be more productive than at United Nations climate conferences, where a few large countries can block progress.

"Countries should not have to take out more debt simply to survive a crisis they contributed comparatively little to creating," she said.

4. Tensions, debate on reparations

While the Commonwealth has 56 members, King Charles is the head of state in only 15 of them. Half of those are Caribbean countries, and for the week leading up to this summit, he's been touring the region , amid ongoing political pressure for the Crown and the government of the United Kingdom to apologize for its historical role profiting off the slave trade in British colonies .

So far, the King has acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond," but he has not apologized.

Canadian officials briefing reporters prior to the trip said Canada acknowledges the generational and lasting impact of slavery, and supports "open and respectful dialogue" on reparations, but noted there are a "diversity" of perspectives on reparatory justice among Commonwealth members.

WATCH | Britain's role in transatlantic slavery under scrutiny: King Charles will confront 'shameful aspects' of Britain's role in slavery | Duration closed caption 8:13 King Charles III will confront 'shameful aspects' of Britain's history with 'unflinching honesty' when he addresses Commonwealth leaders next week, amid renewed scrutiny of Britain's role in historical transatlantic slavery. The comments resurfaced after Prime Minister Andy Burnham revealed he was open to the U.K. formally apologizing for its role in the trade but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Nicholas Marcus Thompson, an advocate for reparations for Canada's Black communities , says the current U.K. government's opposition to negotiating reparations for slavery is "simply a non-starter" for Caribbean nations.

"Reparations is not giving away a freebie. It's repaying what you took, right? Wealth extracted from enslaved Africans built businesses, financial institutions, universities," said Thompson, who is also the president and CEO of the Black Class Action Secretariat.

"It would have been billions of dollars in today's currency."

5. The Trump factor

Former diplomat Lalani said he believes Canada is heading into this summit with more credibility than it's had in the past, thanks to the "provocative vision" Carney laid out in his speech on middle powers at the World Economic Forum in Davos last winter.

Carney's conversations today won't be limited to people he's close to, like Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. It's also a chance to talk to leaders with whom he doesn't have full agreement — without being overshadowed by superpowers like the U.S. or China.

"Canada can have a discussion with other countries without the baggage of having the United States at the table," he said.

"The biggest destabilizing power in the world right now is the United States. … That requires a candid discussion."

World.title: Man wearing Nazi uniform while kids went trick-or-treating was 'disturbing,' woman says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story includes a picture of a swastika.

A Halifax-area woman says she was disturbed to see a man wearing a full Nazi uniform while trick-or-treating with children on Halloween.

Cole Harbour, N.S., resident Paige Hoveling told CBC Radio's Information Morning Nova Scotia she was out with a group of children and adults when her son spotted the man.

"My 10-year-old said, 'Hey, mom, there's someone dressed up as a German general,'" Hoveling said.

"My husband and I and the adults that we were with looked up and we went, 'No buddy, that's a Nazi. And that's not OK.'"

She said the man was pushing a stroller and appeared to be accompanying children who were trick-or-treating. He looked like he was wearing an eyepatch and a Nazi uniform, including a swastika armband, she said.

"If you think of a Nazi in any Hollywood movie you've seen, that's what it looked like," she said.

CBC News spoke with two other residents, who didn't want to be interviewed, but who saw the man on Halloween and confirmed the photo was real.

A witness said the man was wearing a full Nazi uniform and pushing a stroller on Halloween as kids went trick-or-treating on the residential street in Cole Harbour, N.S. (Paige Hoveling)

Hoveling said her group decided to stay away from the man.

"It is disturbing," she said. "I don't know if this guy thought it was a joke or if he actually believes in this, but either way, it's really disturbing to see symbols of hate like that in our community.

"And we're such a small, tight-knit community here."

She said she talked to her son afterward and explained to him why the costume was not acceptable.

Hoveling said she searched online to try to determine if police should be called. But she found the legislation vague and wasn't sure if she should call the police non-emergency number.

The federal government’s Bill C-9, also called the Combatting Hate Act, came into effect in July and makes it a crime to promote hatred against identifiable groups in public using certain terrorism-related or hate symbols.

The law specifically targets two Nazi symbols — the swastika, also called the hakenkreuz, and the SS lightning bolts — and symbols associated with the federal government’s list of terrorist entities.

Wayne MacKay, professor emeritus of law at Dalhousie University's Schulich School of Law, told CBC News the legal definition of promoting hatred is narrow.

"They make a point of saying it has to be vilification and detestation," MacKay said. "Hurt feelings and offences are not enough. And that is in order to protect free speech."

"From a law point of view, it's not likely to produce either civil or criminal consequences for the parties involved."

In an email to CBC News, the RCMP said it received a complaint about the costume on Nov. 2.

It said determining whether a Criminal Code offence occurred would require an investigation.

Investigators would need to collect evidence of the "willful promotion of hatred and reach the threshold of reasonable and probable grounds."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics
World.content:
The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:29 UTC Full article

Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”

Pope Leo XIV will arrive in Buenos Aires on Sunday on a visit that Javier Milei’s government presents as strictly pastoral, but which takes place amid tension with Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy, one of the most critical voices against the president’s austerity policies. The pontiff will begin a tour in Uruguay on Friday that will continue in Argentina from November 8 to 11 and end in Peru.

“The Pope belongs to all Argentines, not to a political party or a political colour,” presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, who led negotiations with the Church and the Vatican, has repeatedly said. The secretary of worship, Agustín Caulo, insisted it is “an apostolic tour” and that “this should not be politicised”. Authorities expect some 7 million people to follow the Pope in Buenos Aires, Claypole, Luján and Córdoba, in what Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva described as “the largest operation in our history”.

The underlying differences are well known. Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”. A study by sociologist Sol Prieto of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet) of documents published by the Argentine Bishops’ Conference between January 2024 and September 2026 found that 42 of the 44 referring to public policy, or 95%, take “a critical position”, on issues such as the social situation, the environment, institutional quality, the lowering of the age of criminal responsibility and a decree curbing migrants’ rights.

Ten days ago, when Milei questioned the idea that many people cannot make ends meet, the president of the Bishops’ Conference, Marcelo Colombo, replied: “That people cannot make ends meet is a fact of reality, not something that needs to be proven.” The Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge García Cuerva, said the Pope “will find a wounded Argentina”. “There is no affinity, but a very strong aversion between most Argentine bishops and Milei’s government,” said researcher Fortunato Mallimaci, who identifies opposition to abortion as one of the few points of agreement.

According to El País, the government sought to limit mass gatherings but the Vatican’s position prevailed, and the Pope will celebrate open-air Masses.
