Two events are particularly uncomfortable for the government, according to the newspaper: the meeting with trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina and the visit to the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities, one of the sectors hardest hit by spending cuts. The place of Vice President Victoria Villarruel, estranged from Milei, at official events also remains undecided.

World.title: Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”
World.content:
Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:18 UTC Full article

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government

The president of the Madrid regional government, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, on Monday awarded the region’s International Medal to Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who is in the Spanish capital for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government. “On both sides of the Atlantic we defend the same things,” Ayuso said at the ceremony.

“We are free nations and we defend our governments and liberal democracies and the rule of law, which will not yield to authoritarianism,” said the People’s Party leader, who contrasted Chile with Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Ayuso praised Chile as “an example of what a nation can achieve when it trusts its citizens” and highlighted Kast’s “commitment to freedom, security, prosperity and the defence of institutions”. “We do not want citizens dependent on power; we want them to be masters of their own lives,” she added.

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government. “It is the first duty of the state. And when the state fails in that duty, the most vulnerable pay. Without security there is no order, without order there is no peace and without peace there is no freedom.”

The Community of Madrid’s International Medal, created in 2017 and purely honorary, is awarded on the regional president’s personal initiative. Previous recipients include Argentine President Javier Milei and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa; Venezuelan opposition leaders Juan Guaidó and Edmundo González; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky; Pope Leo XIV; and the United States, for the 250th anniversary of its independence. Manuela Bergerot, spokeswoman for Más Madrid in the regional assembly, accused Ayuso of turning the award into “the membership card of her far-right international”. A group of demonstrators protested outside the regional government headquarters.

Kast began the day with a private meeting with Vox leader Santiago Abascal, with whom he has close ties, and plans to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during the summit, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra.

World.title: Corruption joins the cost of living as a top concern for US voters
World.content:
Corruption joins the cost of living as a top concern for US voters

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 00:31 UTC Full article

A Fox News poll published in October found that 88% of voters say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about corruption in government

The United States votes on Tuesday in midterm elections in which corruption has emerged in the final stretch as one of voters’ main concerns, second only to the cost of living, according to several polls. At stake are all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of the 100 Senate seats and numerous governorships and state legislatures.

A Fox News poll published in October found that 88% of voters say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about corruption in government. Another survey, by Harris for Britain’s The Guardian, found that nine in ten Americans consider it a problem and that 76% believe public officials care more about enriching themselves than improving people’s lives. According to that study, only the cost of living weighs more heavily than corruption in voting decisions, ahead of immigration and healthcare.

“Just six months ago, corruption was not a top issue for voters. A few days out from the midterms, it has absolutely become one of the issues,” pollster Frank Luntz said. The Brennan Center for Justice estimates that references to government ethics in campaign ads have reached their highest level in 14 years: about 24% in House races and 16% in Senate races.

Democratic candidates have focused their criticism on the business dealings of President Donald Trump and his family, particularly in cryptocurrencies, and on private donations of more than US$300 million for the ballroom being built at the White House, including US$25 million each from Apple and Nvidia. Ethics allegations also extend to candidates from both parties: Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, the Democratic Senate candidate in Minnesota over alleged welfare fraud, and the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola in Alaska, under investigation for allegedly promoting a candidate with the same surname as her rival.

More than 51 million people have already voted early, 25% more than in the 2022 midterms. Polls favour the Democrats, who need four more seats to control the House and at least four more to take the Senate, with close races in Michigan, Alaska, Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas. Trump closed his campaign on Sunday with rallies in Iowa and Kansas.

World.title: Falklands representative in London honours the Islands’ fallen at Westminster
World.content:
Falklands representative in London honours the Islands’ fallen at Westminster

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 00:08 UTC Full article

Falkland Islands Government Representative, Richard Hyslop, placing a commemorative cross at the House of Commons Garden of Remembrance

The Falkland Islands Government Representative to the UK and Europe, Richard Hyslop, has placed a commemorative cross at the House of Commons Garden of Remembrance in London in memory of Falkland Islanders killed in both world wars and those who lost their lives in 1982.

The cross commemorates the 22 Islanders killed in the First World War, the 25 killed in the Second World War, and the 255 British Armed Forces personnel and three Islanders killed in the Falklands War, according to a statement from the Falkland Islands Government Office in London.

The Garden of Remembrance, installed each year in New Palace Yard outside the Palace of Westminster, was started in November 2021 by the Speaker of the House of Commons, Sir Lindsay Hoyle, in partnership with the Royal British Legion. It allows parliamentarians and representatives of Commonwealth countries and UK Overseas Territories to plant memorial crosses honouring Armed Forces personnel.

“I was honoured to place a commemorative cross in the House of Commons Gardens of Remembrance in memory of those Islanders killed in both World Wars and those killed in the liberation of the Islands in 1982,” Hyslop said. “We must remember the service and sacrifice of those individuals who gave so much to protect the freedoms we enjoy today, we will remember them.”

World.title: An Oxford professor to sit as the UK's chosen judge in the Falklands dispute in Hamburg
World.content:
An Oxford professor to sit as the UK's chosen judge in the Falklands dispute in Hamburg

2nd Monday, November 2026 - 15:23 UTC Full article

British jurist Vaughan Lowe, emeritus professor of public international law at the University of Oxford, will be the judge ad hoc chosen by the United Kingdom in the case between Argentina and London before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea over hydrocarbon exploitation north of the Falklands. Lowe will make his solemn declaration on Monday, November 9, the day before the hearing.

According to a statement from the Hamburg-based tribunal, the public sitting will be held at 10 a.m. in the main courtroom, where Lowe will make the declaration required under article 9 of its Rules. The tribunal's Statute allows a party that has no judge of its nationality among its members to choose one for a specific case. Lowe, who held the Chichele Professorship of Public International Law at Oxford, is one of Britain's most prominent experts on the law of the sea.

The hearing on provisional measures in the case officially named the Case concerning hydrocarbon exploitation in the South-West Atlantic Ocean (Argentina v. United Kingdom) will take place on November 10 and 11. Argentina requested four measures on October 13, including that the United Kingdom prevent exploitation of the Sea Lion field and refrain from granting new permits. London has said it will take part and challenge any attempt to use the proceedings to settle sovereignty. The sittings will be public and broadcast live on the tribunal's website.

World.title: Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns
World.content:
Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns

2nd Monday, November 2026 - 00:57 UTC Full article

The expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the elections

Argentina’s case against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands “could fall at the first hurdle”: the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, which cannot settle territorial sovereignty disputes, according to Australian law of the sea expert Donald R. Rothwell. The tribunal will hold hearings on Argentina’s request on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg.

In an analysis published by The Interpreter, the Lowy Institute’s publication, Rothwell, professor of international law at the Australian National University, notes that under Article 286 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea the tribunal is only competent to settle disputes “concerning the interpretation or application” of the treaty. Territorial disputes have traditionally fallen to the International Court of Justice.

The problem, he argues, is that Argentina’s case cannot be separated from the underlying question. “If the UK has sovereignty over the islands, then Sea Lion is a legitimate act of exploration and exploitation of the continental shelf. If the Argentine claim over the islands is valid, then the UK’s conduct is in breach of UNCLOS,” he writes. Argentina alleges that the UK is illegally exploiting the continental shelf, that the project will cause environmental damage and that issuing licences aggravates the dispute over the maritime areas. “Absent the underlying territorial dispute, these would all be legitimate issues for ITLOS determination,” the expert says.

Rothwell compares the case with the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, in which the Philippines “neatly sidestepped” the question of sovereignty over disputed features and focused on China’s maritime claims, so there was never a need to determine who owned what. That, he warns, will not be possible in the case of the South Atlantic islands. Even so, he acknowledges that the tribunal “has generally been reluctant to take a narrow view of its jurisdiction” and recalls that, in the maritime boundary dispute between Mauritius and the Maldives around the Chagos Archipelago, it reached a full determination even though sovereignty between Mauritius and the UK was not fully resolved at the time.

The legal expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that President Javier Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the 2027 elections. He adds that US President Donald Trump could intervene, unhappy at the limited British support over Iran; Washington officially remains neutral in the dispute, although Trump has said that position is “under review”. “London will inevitably robustly defend its position on all fronts,” Rothwell predicts, adding that if the case proceeds it will be historic: the first time any aspect of the dispute has gone before an international court.

Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, lies about 200 kilometres north of the archipelago. Argentina bases its claim on succession to Spanish rights and on its occupation of the islands between 1820 and 1833, when they were taken by the United Kingdom; London cites its continuous presence since then and the islanders’ right to self-determination, confirmed in the 2013 referendum by 99.8% of voters.

World.title: Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 15:52 UTC Full article

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of France and Germany on Saturday to protest against the cost of living and deteriorating public services, in mostly peaceful demonstrations that ended in clashes between police and masked groups in several cities. In France, where the third day of protests in a month took place, 565 people were arrested.

According to France’s interior ministry, some 320,000 people took part in about 150 demonstrations across the country, down from an estimated 410,000 the previous weekend. In Paris, 70,000 marched along boulevards on the outskirts to avoid the city centre, some in Halloween costumes. The protests, called by students, trade unions and former members of the “yellow vest” movement, passed off calmly until the end, when masked groups hurled paving stones at police in Paris, who responded with teargas and baton charges. There were also incidents in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, where water cannon were used. Four police officers and a gendarme were injured in the capital. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who had deployed 70,000 officers, denounced an “extraordinary” level of violence and described a petrol bomb attack on a riot officer as “attempted murder”.

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living. The first major day, on October 17, ended with the looting of hundreds of shops in several cities. Students announced new blockades of high schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday, ahead of a trade union demonstration called for November 5.

In Germany, thousands of young people demonstrated in dozens of cities at the call of the group “Gen Z regelt!” (“Gen Z has got this”) “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life”. After largely peaceful marches, police used water cannon in Cologne against protesters throwing fireworks; in Frankfurt at least two shops were looted, according to a Reuters witness, and in Hamburg burning barricades were set up, according to the newspaper Bild.

There were also clashes in Tirana, the capital of Albania, at a new protest demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Police were on alert in Barcelona, over calls from an anonymous TikTok network, and in Italy, after recent clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

World.title: Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London
World.content:
Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension

Nearly a hundred Argentine intellectuals, jurists, historians and politicians have signed a declaration rejecting the transformation of the Falklands dispute into a “national cause” that “admits no dissent”, and criticising Javier Milei’s government for acting with “flagrant opportunism” amid escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

The declaration, entitled “Malvinas and dissent” and published in early October in the newspaper Perfil, is signed by, among others, jurist Roberto Gargarella, constitutional lawyer Daniel Sabsay, former justice minister Ricardo Gil Lavedra, former minister Graciela Fernández Meijide, economist Pablo Gerchunoff, writer Santiago Kovadloff and historians Luis Alberto Romero, Hilda Sabato and Federico Lorenz.

The signatories do not deny the dispute. They accept “the existence of this international disagreement”, with its “diplomatic and legal” dimensions, and acknowledge differing views among themselves, for example on whether the islanders should take part in any negotiations. But they warn that the issue “long ago ceased to be essentially a dispute and became a supposed national cause” that “admits no relevant dissent” and brands anyone who strays from it a “bad Argentine”. “The national cause is, in short, an abuse of state, political, social and cultural authority,” they argue. They particularly criticise Article 111 of the sovereignty defence bill, which in their view established “a vague criminal offence and the criminalisation of dissent”; the government acknowledged in mid-October that it would have to be removed. “On Malvinas, this is all we ask: that unanimity stop speaking in our name,” they conclude.

One of the signatories, Alejandro Cowes, who describes himself as a lawyer, went further in a text posted on Saturday in English and Spanish in a public Facebook group about the islands. Cowes accuses the government of using the “sacred national cause” as “a tool for internal state coercion and domestic political consumption” and revives Argentine political scientist Carlos Escudé’s thesis of the “malignant lie”: the idea that a tough policy will raise Britain’s costs, when to do so Argentina would have to multiply its own against a power with far greater resources. He criticises the sanctions on companies linked to hydrocarbon exploitation and the purchase of F-16 fighters, and concludes that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have “the inalienable right to self-determination”, a position not reflected in the collective declaration.

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension. The sovereignty defence bill secured committee approval on October 27, after sanctions were narrowed in response to US objections, and the ruling party plans to debate it in the Chamber of Deputies on November 12. Two days earlier, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will hold the hearing in Hamburg on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. Milei has reiterated that “the Malvinas are Argentine”, while ruling out “military solutions”.

The claim to sovereignty over the islands is enshrined in a transitional provision of Argentina’s Constitution and enjoys broad public support, as the declaration itself acknowledges.

World.title: Cell phone ban takes effect in Mexico’s primary, secondary schools
World.content:
“Turn off the screen and turn your imagination on!”

With this message, Mexico’s Education Ministry (SEP) announced that, starting Tuesday, the use of cell phones and electronic tablets in public and private schools across the country will be restricted.

The announcement follows a Sept. 18 decision by the National Council of Educational Authorities (Conaedu) to regulate the use of phones and tablets in schools.

Speaking at a Conaedu meeting on Oct. 26, Education Minister Mario Delgado Carrillo said that the move aims to boost student focus, strengthen social interaction at school and promote the responsible use of technology.

“We want to see a return to socializing in the schoolyards, conversations in the hallways and the focus and friendships that flourish in the classroom,” Delgado said. “On Nov. 3, we’re going phone-free in schools.”

The new guidelines restrict mobile device use during classes and recess at primary and secondary schools. At the upper secondary, or high school, level, each institution will establish its own rules through agreements with its educational community and according to the students’ specific needs and context.

The new guidelines resulted from a research and consultation process that involved experts and other members of the education community.

Specialists presented an overview of the international landscape, the addictive nature of certain algorithms and their effects. Regional and university-level forums were also held, involving parents and educators from across the country.

According to Delgado, 81% of educators surveyed (565,000) were in favor of there being “guidelines and rules to guarantee the safe use [of devices] for educational purposes.”

The matter was then brought before the Conaedu, where education officials from all 32 entities in Mexico agreed to implement these measures.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico is on the verge of losing one of its most unique animals
World.content:
The vaquita, or “little cow,” is a species of porpoise only found in the Gulf of California. It is the smallest living cetacean and the most endangered, hovering on the brink of extinction. Not only does it live in a small and once remote area, but it is an elusive animal that tends to come to the surface for a gulp of air and then disappear again.

As a result, the vaquita escaped human detection until 1958, when a scientist examining skulls on the beach realized the porpoises occasionally spotted there were an unknown species. Marine biologists Kenneth Norris and William McFarland first introduced the animal in their article A New Harbor Porpoise of the genus Phocoena from the Gulf of California, published in the Journal of Mammalogy.

In Latin, it was identified as Phocoena sinus, or “porpoise of the gulf,” but its common name is vaquita, or “little cow,” which was how local fishermen had always referred to it.

A first discovery

It would be another 30 years before scientists caught a vaquita, offering them a full account of its appearance. The most notable points, apart from the small size, were the dark eye rings and large fin.

This work helped explain how the genus Phocoena adjusted to an environment that was not ideal. Porpoises generally like cold water, and around 2.5 million years ago a drop in ocean temperature allowed a few animals to migrate along cold water highways into the enclosed gulf.

As the planet once again warmed, they should have either fled the area or faced extinction.

However, their new home was rich in fish, squid and crustaceans, which fed off the nutrients flooding into the sea from the Colorado River. This abundant food supply tempted the porpoises to stay.

They became isolated from other groups and adapted to the warming waters, ultimately evolving into a new species. They became smaller, lost blubber and developed large dorsal fins that acted like a cooling radiator.

Over many generations, their decreasing size not only helped keep the vaquita cool but enabled them to hunt for smaller fish in the bay’s shallow waters. This in turn might have kept them away from predators.

How many vaquitas are there in the wild?

We have no idea how many porpoises once lived in this small area of ocean, although academic studies suggest there were once around 5,000 animals. However, the first comprehensive survey took place in 1997 and estimated a population of just 567 individuals.

That number was already low, and the following decades proved disastrous. By 2007, the population was estimated to have fallen to 150. By 2018, it was less than 19.

While there might be other contributing factors, the deadliest and saddest danger currently comes from fishing. The porpoise is not the target, but fishermen place nets here hoping to catch totoaba, a large fish endemic to the Gulf of California.

Once abundant in these waters, the totoaba is hunted for its bladder, which is used in traditional Chinese medicine and luxury cuisine. As a result, much of the catch is sent to the lucrative Hong Kong market.

But here’s the issue with this practice: When catching the totoaba, fishermen employ gillnets — vertical panels of netting that hang from a line and are indiscriminate in what they catch. In addition to the initial catch, the trapped fish attract predators that also get caught.

As numbers declined, conservationists got desperate. In 2007, a team of scientists published an article in the journal Conservation Biology titled Saving the Vaquita: Immediate Action, Not More Data.

This was motivated by the shocking and disheartening news that another endangered cetacean, the Yangtze River dolphin, had been confirmed as extinct.

VaquitaCPR launched in desperation

Ten years later, an even more desperate step was taken. An international coalition called VaquitaCPR launched a $5 million last-ditch effort to save the tiny porpoise.

If nets could not be removed, then the vaquita would have to be kept away from them. The idea was to place the animals in the safety of floating sea pens. With a $5 million budget, the team captured two porpoises.

A mature female was placed in a sea pen but suffered acute shock and died within hours. The young calf was released after displaying signs of extreme stress and was released. With numbers becoming so critically low, the loss of two animals was a disaster.

Vaquita numbers have continued to drop. The most recent 2024 survey reported that the entire population was down to somewhere between six and eight individuals. Hopefully, this might be a slight underestimation.

Surveys have concentrated on a small area where the vaquita are known to be seen, but work with acoustic detectors suggests they might have a wider range. Even so, we are not looking at more than nine to 11 animals — the edge of extinction.

There are a few hopeful signs, and at the moment the vaquita is benefiting from a considerable amount of attention and goodwill. The Mexican government has implemented a vaquita refuge, where commercial fishing is prohibited.

Cement blocks fitted with metal hooks have been fixed throughout the exclusion zone, which capture abandoned and illegal gillnets.

A combination of monitoring by conservation groups, most notably Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, and support from the Mexican Navy has brought a notable reduction in illegal fishing activity within the protected area.

Science of vaquita still being understood

One recent surprise concerns the animal’s reproduction cycle. It was previously believed that females only gave birth every two years, but that is now questioned.

The best evidence comes from observations of a female called Frida, who is easily recognized by a bent dorsal fin. She was spotted with a calf in 2023 and another newborn in 2024.

In 2025, she was seen with a calf that appeared to be a year old, but was showing physical signs that she may have been pregnant again. If the breeding pattern is changing, this could be linked to less competition between the porpoises for food and might offer a ray of hope for the animal’s long-term future.

Another positive discovery was made by genetic scientists who examined the historical library of DNA collected from porpoises caught in nets over the years. Their work revealed that the species has been isolated for so long that they seemingly adapted to the risks of inbreeding.

This phenomenon has been observed in other species on the verge of extinction, from Bengal tigers to right whales.

Had the current conservation measures been put in place 10 years ago, when vaquita numbers were still in the low hundreds, there might have been some optimism. Now there is a fear that all the good intentions might have come too late.

Helping the vaquita to recover will take years of protection and monitoring. Pushing them into extinction might only require a few months of neglect. There are also new problems looming on the horizon.

New problems emerge for vaquita

While the establishment of a protected area has been generally successful, it only covers a small percentage of the animal’s known range. Most alarmingly, it fails to cover a northwestern zone where vaquita might well be active.

In addition, fishermen continue to place gillnets on the outer edge of the exclusion zone where they might still pose a danger to the porpoises.

Fishing is big business with the ability to lobby the government.

A 225-square-kilometer Zero Tolerance Area established in 2020 is also under attack. The argument is that with their declining numbers, vaquita are no longer found in much of the protected area, so unrestricted fishing could resume there.

There are other dangers building up that might be beyond our ability — or at least our will — to halt. Ever since the great Hoover and Glen Canyon Dams were built, little fresh water has flowed into the gulf. This has changed the salinity of the water and places another pressure on the ecosystem.

Plans to build distillation plants will only exacerbate this problem. Then, there is the whole question of climate change. The porpoises survive here because, over many generations, they have adapted to water that would normally be too warm for them.

How are they and their food source going to adapt to a future in which weather patterns appear to be changing, and doing so far more rapidly than ever before?

The vaquita is still with us, but its survival hangs by a thread.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a master’s degree in history.

World.title: A new road opens in Cancún, better connecting the airport with the hotel zone
World.content:
With an inauguration ceremony led by Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama, the Kukulcán Interchange opened to traffic at 6 a.m. Sunday, cutting travel time between the Cancún International Airport, the Nichupté Bridge and the hotel zone.

The new federal government-led improvement follows the opening of the 11.2-kilometer Nichupté Bridge in May. The bridge, which consists of three lanes and a two-way bike path, connects the city’s residential area to its hotel zone, cutting commuting time by up to 50 minutes. It is thought to handle around 12,000 vehicles a day.

The new connector allows vehicles traveling on Kukulcán Boulevard toward the airport to use an elevated one-way road, while those heading to downtown Cancún can use it to merge onto the Nichupté Bridge.

Traffic heading from the airport to the city’s bustling Punta Cancún area will be directed to a one-way street behind Plaza Kukulcán, while traffic from the Nichupté Bridge to the airport will continue along Kukulcán Boulevard.

The U-turn next to La Joya Hospital will remain closed to general traffic, with access only for local vehicles.

During the opening ceremony, Lezama emphasized that the new road project complements the Nichupté Bridge project and stressed that an opposite lane of the interchange is expected to open in the coming weeks.

President Claudia Sheinbaum has supported the city road project throughout, following in the footsteps of her predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who approved the development of the Nichupté Bridge.

“We secured it; you never hesitated; you always said yes,” Lezama said in reference to President Sheinbaum’s support of the Kukulcán Interchange project.

With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and Excelsior

World.title: Ex-TV host wanted in Mexico for fraud arrested by ICE; she and husband face same charges
World.content:
Inés Gómez Mont — a former Mexican television host who is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement — is in immigration detention in the United States after she was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Miami, Florida, on Friday.

According to ICE, Gómez Mont, a former telenovela actress who became an entertainment show presenter, is being held at the Broward Transitional Center, located in Pompano Beach, Florida. Although she is wanted in Mexico, she was arrested for overstaying her U.S. visa, according to media reports.

La #FGRinforma que, derivado del intercambio de información con el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos de América, este día, en Miami, Florida, fue asegurada Inés “N”, quien cuenta con una orden de aprehensión vigente en nuestro país, por su probable participación en el delito de defraudación fiscal equiparada. Más adelante, daremos mayor información — FGR México (@FGRMexico) October 30, 2026

The Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) acknowledged Gómez Mont’s arrest in a social media post on Friday.

“The FGR informs that, as a result of the exchange of information with the Government of the United States of America, Inés “N” was apprehended today in Miami, Florida,” the FGR said, adding that Gómez Mont is the subject of a valid arrest warrant in Mexico “for her probable participation in the crime of tax fraud.”

Gómez Mont is also wanted on money laundering and organized crime charges.

The charges are related to Gómez Mont’s alleged participation in a shell company scheme aimed at evading taxes, embezzling public money and laundering ill-gotten funds.

The former TV presenter’s husband, Víctor Manuel Álvarez Puga, allegedly led the scheme.

The newspaper Reforma reported that he and Gómez Mont allegedly received 17 million pesos (US $915,000) through a scheme that diverted funds from prison construction contracts. The couple is accused of involvement in an alleged embezzlement scheme linked to Interior Ministry prison contracts worth 2.95 billion pesos (US $159 million).

Álvarez Puga, a lawyer and native of the southern Mexican state of Chiapas, was arrested by ICE in September 2025 over alleged immigration violations. However, he was subsequently released pending further immigration proceedings.

Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga have been subject to arrest warrants in Mexico since 2021. The FGR is seeking the extradition of both suspects, who have lived in Florida for years.

Reforma reported that the U.S. Department of Justice hasn’t begun the required legal proceedings to extradite the couple more than a year after Mexican authorities requested their transfer to Mexico.

Since 2021, Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga were each the subject of an Interpol Red Notice — a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action — but President Claudia Sheinbaum said in September that Interpol had withdrawn the notices. She said Mexican authorities would seek their reinstatement.

Sheinbaum described Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga as “well-known factureros,” or issuers of fraudulent invoices.

Gómez Mont seeks release from immigration detention

On Saturday, lawyers for Gómez Mont filed a habeas corpus petition seeking her release from immigration detention. They also filed an emergency motion aimed at preventing her transfer to another immigration detention center.

Federal Judge Jeffrey Kuntz ordered ICE and other authorities to justify the need to keep Gómez Mont in detention. He ruled that they must do so by this Wednesday. Kuntz denied the request aimed at preventing Gómez Mont’s transfer to another immigration detention facility, saying that he lacked the authority to block such a move.

Reforma reported that Gómez Mont’s habeas corpus petition includes reports about the medical care required by one of her daughters. The purpose of including those reports, Reforma reported, was to justify the need to keep her in the Miami area and to release her from detention while her immigration status is assessed.

Álvarez Puga was released from immigration detention after his lawyers presented a habeas corpus petition in late 2025. He is scheduled to appear before a U.S. immigration judge this month. It remains to be seen whether Gómez Mont’s case will follow a similar path.

With reports from Reforma, El Financiero, La Jornada and EFE

World.title: Mexican-American news executive assumes top Vatican role
World.content:
A 39-year-old woman born in Mexico City and raised in the United States has become the Vatican’s new communications chief — the first laywoman to lead a ministry-level department in the church’s central administration.

María Montserrat Alvarado, whose appointment took effect Sunday, previously served as president and chief operating officer of EWTN News, the news division of the largest Catholic television network in the United States.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Archbishop Nelson Perez (@archbishopperez)

She succeeds Italian journalist Paolo Ruffini, 70, as prefect of the Dicastery for Communication.

Pope Leo XIV, hailed by Mexico when he was elected, announced her appointment in June.

Alvarado takes over an operation encompassing Vatican News, Vatican Radio, the newspaper L’Osservatore Romano and the Holy See Press Office, along with publishing, television, photography and other services.

“It’s enormous,” she told EWTN News.

Alvarado, who goes by the nickname Montse, said she was about 7 or 8 when her family moved from Mexico to the United States. She grew up in Miami and holds Mexican and U.S. citizenship, according to AFP.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in political science from Florida International University, she moved to Washington, D.C., to study for a master’s in political management from George Washington University.

In 2009, she joined the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a Washington-based nonprofit law firm that handles religious freedom cases. She started in communications and rose to vice president and executive director in 2017.

Her work included advocating for Becket’s clients in the media, including Univision, Telemundo, CNN en Español and EWTN (Eternal Word Television Network).

In 2021, she joined EWTN as the founding host of “EWTN News In Depth,” a weekly program. Two years later, she was named president and chief operating officer of EWTN News, overseeing its global, multilingual news operations across television, radio, print, digital platforms and social media — work that brought her into direct contact with Pope Leo XIV and Vatican officials.

She helped prepare the Pope’s live video conversation with young people attending a National Catholic Youth Conference in Indianapolis last year, and also worked with the Vatican on a video introducing the Pope’s first encyclical.

Leo later approached her about leading the department, she said. Though she had not applied, Alvarado said she believed Leo wanted a professional equipped to bridge traditional and digital communications.

“In no way am I imposing a vision,” she said. “I’m very much receiving one and executing it.”

Her appointment comes after years of friction between the conservative Catholic network and Pope Francis. Some EWTN programs criticized Francis, who publicly complained about an unnamed Catholic television network’s attacks on him.

Former Francis collaborators told BBC Mundo that tensions had largely eased after Alvarado took charge of the news operation.

Alvarado is not the first Mexican or woman to lead a Vatican department. Mexican Cardinal Javier Lozano Barragán headed its health care department from 1996 to 2009, and Italian Sister Simona Brambilla has overseen religious orders since January 2025.

With reports from N+, Uno TV, BBC and EWTN News

World.title: Record crowd greets Checo Pérez at Mexico City Grand Prix
World.content:
The return of Mexican driver Sergio “Checo” Pérez to Formula 1 with Cadillac electrified the grandstands at Mexico City’s Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez this past weekend, where the three-day Grand Prix drew a record-breaking 405,363 fans.

According to official reports, attendance surpassed the previous record — set in 2024 with 404,958 — by 405 admissions. It also eclipsed the 401,326-person attendance seen at the 2025 Mexico City Grand Prix, at which Pérez was absent following his departure from Red Bull.

Fans’ enthusiasm began to take shape during the lead-up activities, including Checo’s Show Run along Reforma Avenue on Oct. 28, which drew over 100,000 people.

On the grandstands, Friday saw 102,122 attendees for the practice sessions; Saturday brought in 147,889 for qualifying; and Sunday drew 155,352 spectators for the race.

Pérez marked his 300th Grand Prix with a flying start, but trouble in the pits and a penalty hindered his chances of staging a comeback. After starting in 20th position on the grid, he gained six places during the opening laps, reaching as high as 13th position, but a slow pit stop around lap 32 and a 5-second pit-lane speeding penalty dropped him to 19th.

After Valtteri Bottas’s crash brought out a red flag, Pérez climbed to 14th, but he slipped back to cross the line in 17th position. However, following a 10-second penalty handed to Pierre Gasly for speeding under a yellow flag, he moved up to 16th — though still outside the points. Checo’s former Red Bull teammate Max Verstappen came in first, while 20-year-old Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli finished third, becoming the youngest-ever champion of the F1 season.

Checo acknowledged that Cadillac’s problems during pit stops hindered his participation in the race, especially after having gained several positions after the start.

“We had a very good initial start, but then we had a very bad pit stop — the right-side wheel gun broke down and we lost 4 or 5 seconds — which meant we effectively lost the positions we had gained over the other drivers at the start,” Pérez said after the race.

However, he noted that racing in Mexico City again “was a very special moment.”

“I really missed it last year,” Pérez added.

With reports from El Financiero and Telediario

World.title: Medical tourism lifts Mexico’s Caribbean coast as beach tourism falls 7%
World.content:
While overall tourism in the state of Quintana Roo has contracted this year, medical tourism has demonstrated remarkable resilience, according to data from the Medical Tourism Commission of Coparmex Quintana Roo.

Traditional sun-and-beach tourism has declined almost 7% during the first nine months of 2026 — representing approximately 959,000 fewer travelers — whereas 25,000 healthcare tourists are expected to travel to the Caribbean state this year, generating an estimated economic impact of 200 million pesos (US $10.76 million).

Andrés Jurado Viera, director of the specialty firm My Medical Vacations and president of the Medical Tourism Commission, explained that these visitors are not drawn by the beaches, so problems like sargassum do not affect their travel decisions.

“Their main objective is to access high-quality healthcare treatment at competitive prices, as well as first-rate hospital infrastructure and top-quality medical staff,” he said.

Jurado said the average cost per patient rose from US $11,000 to $13,500 in the last year, a 20% increase due to the exchange rate, but one that still represents savings of up to 80% compared to costs in the United States.

When the trend began 16 years ago, medical tourism focused on plastic surgery and dentistry. Today it encompasses more complex procedures thanks to positive reports of hospital experiences in Cancún.

A Commission report found that the visitor profile stands out for its socioeconomic impact. Visitors register average stays of 11 days or more, which generates higher hotel occupancy and boosts sectors such as gastronomy and transportation.

As a result of sustained demand in this sector (following a decade of double-digit growth), the commission will participate in the first joint working group meeting involving the state Tourism Ministry, the Hotel Association and airport representatives will be held this month to promote the destination in strategic markets in North America and Mexico.

This medical tourism has also triggered hospital investment in the region — both foreign and domestic — as new clinics are being built (including a Wyndham Group medical center in the Riviera Maya), international certifications have been procured and diversification of specialties has noticeably increased.

The United States remains the leading source of patients; Canada saw a slight decrease due to the exchange rate against the dollar.

With reports from Animal Político and El Economista

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: How the water crisis is affecting local businesses, fewer dengue cases and a new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal
World.content:
This past week, business leaders and government officials sparred over whether the ongoing water crisis in the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA) will affect business investment in Jalisco, so we looked at the facts.

Meanwhile, as the rainy season winds down, dengue cases have fallen sharply across the state compared to 2025, and a new “Hecho en Jalisco” (“Made in Jalisco”) seal aims to boost the visibility and cachet of select local products.

Business leader warns investment will suffer due to water quality issues

Speaking to local journalists on Oct. 23, José Medina Mora, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), issued a stark warning to Jalisco state officials.

Medina Mora said he expects investment projects in Jalisco to be negatively impacted by Guadalajara’s ongoing water crisis, noting, “There will be investment decisions in Jalisco, and in Guadalajara particularly, that will be halted until we can offer quality water.”

Medina Mora also blamed local politicians for their failure to anticipate and solve these issues before they became acute.

Later clarifying his comments, Medina Mora said the CCE does not expect the water crisis to spark capital flight from Jalisco but expects new investments to be put on hold due to the increased business risk posed by water contamination.

State and federal government officials swiftly pushed back on Medina Mora’s comments.

Government points to strong FDI as local businesses adapt

Ximena Escobedo Juárez, undersecretary of industry at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce of the Ministry of Economy, cited strong business investment across Jalisco in 2026 as evidence that the business community remains undeterred.

In the first half of 2026, Jalisco attracted US $1.41 billion in new capital, surpassing the US $1.2 billion invested in the state for all of 2025. This contrasts with a sharp decline in foreign direct investment in Mexico’s first half overall.

Yet some economic disruption is undeniable.

With municipal water supplies being rationed over the next six months, many local businesses are scrambling to arrange deliveries from private water trucks to avoid major disruptions to area restaurants, hotels, hospitals and other local service providers.

In addition, manufacturers around Guadalajara have reportedly been supplementing operations with more sophisticated filtration protocols, including on-site chlorination systems, sediment micro-filters and reverse osmosis units. These enhancements are needed to remove heavy metals, sediment and fecal matter from the municipal water that enters their facilities and keep contaminated water from damaging their industrial equipment.

Rainy season ebbs with dengue cases in Jalisco down by 90%

Through Oct. 11, Jalisco has 242 confirmed dengue cases in 2026, ranking 12th nationwide. This represents a massive improvement over 2025, when Jalisco ranked third nationwide for dengue, behind Sonora and Veracruz.

Year to date, there have been two confirmed deaths, with five more under investigation. Last year, the state recorded 10 dengue deaths.

Dengue cases in Jalisco

Year Confirmed Cases Percent change, year over year 2023 941 N/A 2024 20,907 2,122% 2025 2,317 -89% 2026 (through Oct. 11) 242 -90%

Source: Secretaría de Salud

Some strains of dengue are more virulent than others. One of the serotypes that is spreading in Jalisco right now is the most virulent form (serotype 2), which causes dengue hemorrhagic fever. Year to date, both serotypes 2 and 3 of the virus are circulating in Jalisco.

It is a mistake to think that most people get infected with dengue in remote, jungle areas. Rapid urbanization and increased population density have created conditions ideal for mosquito breeding and infection.

Yordi Raúl Portillo Montes, who heads Jalisco’s National Public Health Service, noted that the highest incidence of dengue in the state has occurred in Cocula and Teuchitlán, with coastal areas, including Puerto Vallarta, also at high risk. In the GMA, central Guadalajara, Tonalá and Tlaquepaque have recorded the most cases this year.

While dengue is less common outside of the rainy season, the risk does not fall to zero.

Due to the water crisis affecting Guadalajara, hundreds of families have resorted to storing water in buckets, drums or other containers, which has increased dengue risk in urban areas. In response, health authorities have reiterated the importance of covering these containers to discourage mosquito breeding.

While there is a vaccine for dengue, it can be difficult to access in Mexico, so your best bet is to be proactive and avoid infection.

The new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal aims to promote and protect local products

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Desarrollo Económico Jalisco (@sedeco.jalisco)

In a bid to strengthen the marketing of products made in the state, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) recently announced the launch of the “Made in Jalisco” seal.

The initiative aims to increase visibility for Jalisco-made products with protected designations in foreign markets while ensuring that the economic benefits flow through to local communities where they are made.

The new seal is expected to recognize at least 40 businesses that make products with a designation of origin or geographical indication. Participation will be free, and eligible businesses include companies, cooperatives, workshops and individual producers of tequila, raicilla, Yahualica chili or Sayula cajeta that have authorization from the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI).

However, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) and the civil association El Telar will decide which products are eligible to display the new seal. Applicants will be judged on their history and roots in Jalisco, their products’ distinctive qualities, organizational preparedness and desire for designation of origin protection.

According to state figures, the tequila supply chain supports more than 100,000 families, while raicilla involves more than 80 artisanal producers. Yahualica chili peppers are cultivated by roughly 250 small farmers and collectives, and Sayula cajeta is produced in 21 family workshops.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

Why Is Brazil’s Stock Market Falling Again?

The index is about 19% below its 23 October close of 205,083. It fell 13.9% on Monday 26 October alone and settled at 167,922 on Friday 30 October.

The mood darkened after the central bank’s latest weekly Focus survey, a poll of about 140 institutions such as banks and funds. They now expect inflation of 5.22% for 2026 and growth of just 1.76%.

The same institutions see the dollar at R$5.34 at the end of 2026, up from R$5.07 in the 29 October reading. They expect the policy rate to end the year at 13.50%.

The real, Brazil’s currency, weakened to about R$5.50 per dollar from R$5.44 on Friday, as shown in our real-to-dollar guide.

Seats. Governing National, ACT and NZ First would hold 58 of 121, three short of a majority.

New Zealand heads into the weekend with a country split almost exactly down the middle. In the final 1News-Verian poll, published on 3 November 2026, National leads Labour by one point, four days before the New Zealand general election.

1News is the news service of the state broadcaster TVNZ, and Verian is a polling company. It questioned 1,006 eligible voters between 29 October and 2 November, with a margin of error of ±3.1 points, which means a one-point lead is within the noise.

World.title: Morocco Money Supply Growth Hits 12.2%
World.content:
File photo. Casablanca at sunrise, with the minaret of the Hassan II Mosque on the coast. Most of the 500 Global companies have their head offices in this region.

MOROCCO · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Morocco is a North African kingdom whose central bank, Bank Al-Maghrib, publishes the monthly money data.

What happened Broad money (M3), the total money in the economy, grew 12.2% year on year in September 2026.

The level It reached 2,237.9 billion dirhams (about US$228 billion), after 11.9% growth in August.

The driver Bank credit to borrowers outside the financial industry sped up from 10.4% to 11.2% growth.

The release The data point was due Tuesday 3 November 2026 for the period September.

Morocco’s broad money supply (M3) grew 12.2% in September 2026 from a year earlier, to 2,237.9 billion dirhams (about US$228 billion), according to Bank Al-Maghrib, the country’s central bank. That is faster than August, when growth was 11.9%.

For US readers, the figure shows a Moroccan economy where banks are lending more quickly, a trend that matters to exporters, investors and anyone tracking a fast-growing North African economy. Our guide to why investors now rank Morocco ahead of South Africa gives the wider background.

What Happened

Money supply is the total amount of money circulating in an economy, including cash, bank deposits and other money-like savings. Bank Al-Maghrib, whose headline aggregate is M3 (the broad measure), reported that it rose 12.2% year on year in September 2026 and stood at 2,237.9 billion dirhams (about US$228 billion).

In August the growth rate was 11.9%. Our economic calendar labels this release ‘M2 Money Supply’.

A year earlier, in September 2025, money supply was growing 7.8%. The jump from 7.8% to 12.2% in twelve months shows how much faster money has built up in the economy.

File photo: Casablanca Finance City, Morocco’s financial district. Photo: AyourAchtouk, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

Why Credit Is the Cause

Money supply grows mainly when banks lend, because a new loan creates a new deposit. Bank Al-Maghrib said bank credit to the non-financial sector (borrowers outside the financial industry) accelerated from 10.4% growth to 11.2% in September.

The data reviewed do not say what borrowers used the money for. The data do not break the lending down by borrower, so the size of the increase is the firm fact.

The Trend Through 2026

Growth has stayed in an 11% to 12% band for much of the year. Growth was 11.7% in June, 11.2% in July and 11.9% in August; September’s 12.2% is the fastest of those four months.

The gain is small from month to month, but it points in one direction: more credit, more money.

What It Means for You

For investors, faster money growth backed by rising bank lending signals strong demand for credit. Banks that lend more can earn more, though a credit boom also raises the risk that some loans go bad later.

For exporters and US firms selling into Morocco, firmer domestic demand can mean more local customers and bigger orders. Dollar values here use about 9.8 dirhams per US$, an approximate rate; Bank Al-Maghrib’s reference rate was 9.68 to 9.98 per US$ in early October, so 1,000 dirhams are worth about US$102.

On inflation and interest rates, the usual link is that very fast money growth can push prices up and lead a central bank to keep borrowing costs higher. The figures we reviewed do not say whether that is happening in Morocco, so we draw no conclusion on prices or on the next rate decision.

Travelers need not change plans, because the data do not affect visitors directly. Those who send money to Morocco or hold dirham accounts should note that the dirham moves against the dollar, and a 12% rise in money supply is one of many things that can matter for it.

What Would Change This Picture

Slower borrowing would bring money growth back toward the 11% level seen earlier this year. More borrowers falling behind on repayments would force banks to lend more cautiously.

A decision by Bank Al-Maghrib to raise borrowing costs would also cool lending. The next monthly reading, for October 2026, will show whether September was a peak or the start of a faster run.

What Is Not Known

The use of the new loans is not known to us, nor is how much of the growth comes from deposits abroad or from government borrowing. The figures rest on Bank Al-Maghrib’s September 2026 monetary statistics, as reported by Moroccan financial press.

The September 2025 level is not given in the reports we reviewed. The effect on inflation and on rates is not shown in these figures.

More: Morocco news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How Much Did Morocco’s Money Supply Grow in September 2026?

Broad money (M3) grew 12.2% year on year to 2,237.9 billion dirhams (about US$228 billion). In August the growth rate was 11.9%.

What Caused the Faster Growth?

Bank credit to the non-financial sector accelerated from 10.4% to 11.2%. New loans create new deposits, which lifts the money supply.

What Is Money Supply?

It is the total amount of money in an economy, including cash and bank deposits. When it grows faster than output, prices can come under pressure.

Fact check 1: money supply growth, level and credit growth are Bank Al-Maghrib’s September 2026 monetary statistics, as reported by Moroccan financial press. Fact check 2: the June to August path was compared across sources.

World.title: Cuba Loses Turkish Power Ship Amid Blackouts
World.content:
File photo: Havana’s waterfront at dusk, 2009. The Erol Bey was moored in the capital’s port. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Published Tuesday, 3 November, 9:35 a.m. ET (9:35 a.m. Havana, which is one hour ahead of New York) · Source: Cuba’s Ministry of Energy and Mines, Unión Eléctrica

Cuba has lost one of its last two Turkish power ships while much of the island sits in the dark. The Erol Bey, a floating power plant rated at 63 megawatts, left Havana’s port at about 2:30 p.m. Havana time on Monday, 2 November (1:30 p.m. Eastern Time, or ET), according to several reports.

The departure adds to the strain we track on our Cuba news hub. Our explainer on the Cuba blackout shows why the grid is so fragile.

Key Facts What happened: Cuba lost a 63-megawatt (MW) Turkish power ship, the Erol Bey, when it left Havana on 2 November.

What is unclear: Havana has not said why it left, and the cause is still unconfirmed.

Why it matters: Cuba has had at least eight total grid collapses this year, so every megawatt counts.

What is next: Watch the Belgin Sultan, the last Turkish ship in Havana.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, 9:23 a.m. ET, 3 Nov: US military action against Cuba by 31 Dec, 6.5%.

This story is part of our coverage of the cuba news. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Florida Jails Six in Cuban Smuggling Ring

In plain English A “patana”, as Cubans call it, is a ship with a power station on board that plugs into the shore grid. Cuba rents them from a Turkish company because its own old plants cannot keep the lights on.

A Ship Leaves, and the Lights Stay Off

The Erol Bey belongs to Karpowership, a Turkish floating-power company that has rented ships to Cuba since 2019. Reports say it left Cuba, but Cuban authorities have not confirmed the departure or given a reason.

One Turkish unit, the Belgin Sultan, is still in Havana. Outlets disagree on whether it generates power or serves mainly as a support vessel.

Installed capacity, the 63 megawatts quoted for the Erol Bey, is the most a plant can produce. It is not what it delivers when fuel runs short.

Why the Ships Keep Leaving

The fleet once numbered eight vessels. In September 2025 Cuba’s Energy and Mines Minister, Vicente de la O Levy, said the ships had left because Cuba could not pay.

A Cuban news outlet now blames unpaid bills to Karadeniz Holding, the Turkish group behind Karpowership, but that is its own claim and not an official statement.

Fuel is the other limit. One Cuban outlet reports that the Erol Bey had sat idle for months without it, so the real loss of electricity may be smaller than 63 megawatts.

A Grid That Keeps Collapsing

Cuba’s national grid has suffered at least eight total collapses in 2026. Reports from the island say some provinces have gone up to three days in a row without power. The Turkish fleet has shrunk from eight vessels at its peak to one in Havana, the Belgin Sultan, since 2019.

The government calls the situation critical and extremely tense. Cuba’s old thermal plants, mostly built in the 1960s and 1970s, still supply about 40% of its power.

What It Means for US Readers

The ship’s exit shows how thin Cuba’s power margin has become as Washington and Havana trade blows over energy. For Cuban-Americans with relatives on the island, longer outages mean more calls for money, food and generators.

For investors and shipping watchers, the clue to follow is whether the Belgin Sultan also leaves, which would end Turkish generation in Havana. A ninth total grid collapse, after at least eight this year, would show the margin has gone.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a platform where users trade on real-world outcomes, traders put the chance of US military action against Cuba by 31 December at 6.5% (US$7.7 million traded, 9:23 a.m. ET on 3 November). A separate market puts a US-Cuba economic deal by the same date at 11.5% (US$447,000 traded).

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Neither the Unión Eléctrica (Cuba’s state power utility), the energy ministry nor Karpowership had commented in the reports we reviewed. The reason for the departure, the contract status and any debt owed are unconfirmed.

Nor do we know where the Erol Bey is going or how much power it actually produced recently. No source we reviewed ties the departure to US policy.

More: Cuba news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Erol Bey?

A Turkish floating power plant rated at 63 megawatts (MW). It is one of the ships Cuba has rented from Turkey’s Karpowership group, which began supplying the island in 2019.

Why did the Erol Bey leave Cuba?

Cuban authorities have not said. In September 2025 the energy minister said earlier ship departures were due to Cuba’s inability to pay.

Sources: Cuba’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (remarks by Minister Vicente de la O Levy, September 2025); Unión Eléctrica (unionelectrica.cu); Polymarket (US military action against Cuba, US-Cuba economic deal).

World.title: North Korea Denies US$6.3 Billion Binance Hack
World.content:
NORTH KOREA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening TRM Labs blames North Korea’s TraderTraitor group for a theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance on 29 October 2026.

Why it matters US intelligence assesses that Pyongyang nets at least $1 billion a year from crypto theft and financial crime for weapons programmes.

The numbers Chainalysis counted at least $2.02 billion stolen by North Korea in 2025, and Binance says about $3 billion of the latest haul is frozen.

Who is who TRM Labs and Chainalysis are private blockchain analysts, the FBI is the US federal investigator, and Kim Yo-jong is a senior North Korean official.

What to watch Watch for further OFAC designations and any sign of US and North Korean talks, none of which has a confirmed date.

What it means for you Binance says it will cover every dollar and that customer funds were not touched, but US exchange users should expect closer scrutiny of withdrawals and wallet links.

The North Korea crypto hack at Binance, about $6.3 billion by the count of TRM Labs, would be the largest crypto theft on record, and Pyongyang denies it. For US readers it matters because the FBI, US exchanges and US sanctions law all sit at the centre of the case.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

North Korea is a closed, heavily sanctioned state on the Korean Peninsula, and stolen crypto is one of the few ways it can raise hard currency. This analysis explains the accusation, who makes it, how the theft and laundering work, and what remains unproven, building on the Asia Intelligence Brief.

What Is Alleged and Who Blames North Korea

The Alleged Theft

About $6.3 billion was taken from the crypto exchange Binance on Thursday 29 October 2026, according to the Korea Herald and UPI. The Nextgov report is dated 30 October 2026.

The money moved across 10 blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes, according to the Associated Press. The attackers reportedly compromised several systems, including a Binance engineer’s laptop, to reach a privileged system that allowed large withdrawals.

Binance said it found no sign that a wallet private key had leaked, and that the breach had additional points beyond the laptop.

Who Makes the Attribution

TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence firm, assigns the theft to TraderTraitor “with high confidence”, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. TraderTraitor is a subunit of the Lazarus Group, the label for North Korea-linked hacking units, and is also tracked as Jade Sleet.

Jonathan Levin, co-founder of the analytics firm Chainalysis, said the theft was likely done by the group.

An exchange house on Calle Sarmiento in Buenos Aires (file photo). Photo: Gastón Cuello / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Theft and Laundering Work

The pattern is to target people and privileged systems rather than the blockchain itself. Cybersecurity Dive says this theft matches the Bybit and KelpDAO breaches, and TRM Labs links KelpDAO to the same pattern.

The February 2025 Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion was tied by the FBI to TraderTraitor, according to Nextgov and the Associated Press.

Turning Stolen Tokens Into Cash

According to a summary of TRM Labs findings, the attacker sold about 325 million USDT, a dollar-linked stablecoin, to market makers for about 122,300 ETH. The discount was more than 10%, a price criminals pay to swap tokens that issuers could freeze.

TRM estimates the attacker holds over 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about $2.4 billion beyond the reach of token issuers. The bitcoin is moving through a peel chain, a long series of small transfers that makes tracing slower.

Nextgov reports that $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the hack. He said funds not yet moved are very likely still held by North Korea, and that funds being laundered may already be with Chinese money laundering networks, which is opinion rather than proof.

Past Thefts and the Totals

Estimates of North Korean theft differ by firm, period and method, so each figure below carries its owner. They should not be added together.

Chainalysis, 2026 Crypto Crime Report (December 2025): at least $2.02 billion stolen in 2025, up 51% on 2024, about 59% of more than $3.4 billion stolen worldwide.

Chainalysis, same report: an all-time North Korean total of $6.75 billion.

US intelligence, via Nextgov: at least $1 billion a year from crypto theft and financial crime for weapons programmes.

Cumulative totals also vary by source and date, and the Chainalysis figure predates the Binance theft. If TRM’s $6.36 billion figure holds, this would be a single theft nearly equal to everything North Korea had stolen in all prior years combined, per Chainalysis.

That comparison shows why analysts treat the case as a break from earlier thefts, though no one has yet reconciled the series.

The Denial, the Sanctions and the Stakes

Pyongyang’s Answer

UPI reports Kim Yo-jong suggested, without evidence, that the United States itself could be behind the attack, linking this to US plans to use confiscated crypto for a strategic reserve.

Who Is Who

TRM Labs: a private blockchain analytics firm that attributes the theft to TraderTraitor and tracks the laundering.

Chainalysis: a rival analytics firm whose annual report supplies the main yearly theft totals.

FBI: the US federal investigator.

Binance: the exchange that was hit, led by chief executive Richard Teng and co-founder and co-CEO Yi He.

OFAC: the US Treasury office that imposes financial sanctions.

Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team: a group of 11 states launched in October 2024 to monitor North Korea sanctions after Russia vetoed the UN Panel of Experts in March 2024 and its mandate ended in April 2024.

Sanctions and Freezes

The Korea Herald reported on 29 October 2026 a joint statement by South Korea, the United States, ten other countries and the European Union backing sanctions enforcement and citing findings on North Korean cyber activity and overseas labour. In March 2026 OFAC sanctioned facilitators of North Korean IT-worker schemes tied to nearly $800 million in 2024, The Block reported.

Headlines from around 29 October 2026 point to a further OFAC action on 10 individuals and an entity, but we could not read them, so the details are unconfirmed. The Korea Herald says Seoul has not yet decided whether to join additional sanctions.

Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum’s Security Council moved about 8,425 ETH and 74,559,805 ARB tokens into a frozen wallet. Binance puts the total frozen at about $3 billion.

Business Stakes

Teng said in a video on Friday 30 October that Binance will cover every dollar, and that customer funds were never touched. Binance has reserved over $6.34 billion, with $5 billion of it in the tokens taken.

Yi He said Binance is buying back the stolen altcoins using its SAFU fund and holdings. UPI says 90% was already replenished, but that conflicts with the freeze figures and is unverified.

Binance suspended withdrawals and deposits temporarily, though the Associated Press says deposits were unaffected. We found no figures in our research on Latin American exposure, so we draw no conclusions for the region.

Scenarios

One scenario is stabilisation: issuers and exchanges keep freezing funds, Binance honours its pledge, and the story fades into the sanctions record.

A tipping scenario would be rapid laundering of the unfrozen holdings through networks that US authorities cannot reach. A second would be sharper sanctions if Seoul and others join, which could harden the dispute instead of opening talks.

What It Means for You

If you hold crypto on a US exchange, the reported facts point to no loss at Binance, since it says customer funds were not touched and it will cover the shortfall. The practical risk is indirect, as exchanges face pressure to freeze or trace funds linked to sanctioned actors.

Investors and executives should note that the FBI and OFAC treat North Korean theft as a sanctions and national security issue. Any firm handling digital assets has reason to check whether its counterparties and wallets touch the addresses that US authorities publish.

What Is Not Known

The evidence behind TRM’s high confidence has also not been published in the material we reviewed. It is unknown how much will stay frozen or be recovered, and how much has already been laundered.

The full extent of the Binance breach beyond the laptop is also unclear. Kim Yo-jong offered no evidence for her suggestion about a US strategic reserve, so it has no established basis.

Nor is it known whether talks between the United States and North Korea are really in prospect.

What to Watch

We found no confirmed dates for the next steps in the research. Watch for further OFAC designations and the results of Binance’s own investigation.

A signal of talks from either capital would be the clearest sign of an opening.

Related reading: Why Legacy Bitcoiners Cheer ETF Outflows’ Promise; Between Faith and Fear: The Unseen War on Christians in Nigeria; Unyielding Faith: Inside the Global Struggle for Christian Survival in 2024; more from Crypto.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did North Korea hack Binance?

TRM Labs attributes the theft of about $6.3 billion to TraderTraitor, a Lazarus Group subunit, with high confidence. Pyongyang denies involvement.

How much crypto has North Korea stolen?

Chainalysis counted at least $2.02 billion in 2025 and an all-time total of $6.75 billion in its December 2025 report. Other firms give different totals, and the Binance theft would add to these figures.

How does North Korea launder stolen crypto?

According to TRM Labs, the attacker sold about 325 million USDT to market makers for about 122,300 ETH at a discount of more than 10%. The bitcoin is moving through a peel chain, a series of small transfers that slows tracing.

Will Binance customers lose money?

Binance chief executive Richard Teng said the exchange will cover every dollar and that customer funds were never touched. Binance has reserved over $6.34 billion, and says about $3 billion of the stolen assets is frozen.

What did Kim Yo-jong say?

UPI reports Kim Yo-jong suggested, without evidence, that the United States could be behind the attack.

What sanctions target North Korean hackers?

The Korea Herald reported on 29 October 2026 a joint statement by South Korea, the United States, ten other countries and the European Union backing sanctions enforcement and citing findings on North Korean cyber activity and overseas labour. In March 2026 OFAC sanctioned North Korean IT-worker facilitators, and Seoul has not yet decided whether to join additional sanctions.

World.title: EU-Mercosur Trade Deal and Its 99,000-Tonne Beef Quota
World.content:
BRAZIL · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening The interim trade agreement between the EU and Mercosur has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026, while the wider partnership agreement awaits a court opinion and ratification.

Why it matters South American sellers gain tariff preferences in Europe that US sellers do not have, and the EU has built farm safeguards around the sensitive products.

The numbers The new beef quota is 99,000 tonnes carcass-weight equivalent a year, phased in over five years.

Who is who The European Commission, led by President Ursula von der Leyen, negotiates for the EU, while Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay form the Mercosur side.

What to watch The EU Court of Justice opinion has no date, and the EU decision on relisting Brazilian poultry and honey is expected at the next committee meeting.

What it means for you US exporters of soybeans, beef, ethanol and processed food now compete in Europe against suppliers with lower tariffs, though no measured US loss has been published.

The EU-Mercosur trade agreement has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026, but only its trade pillar is in force. For US readers it matters because South American farm rivals now enjoy tariff preferences in Europe that American exporters lack.
