Of the seven options given, those surveyed only saw China as a less trusted partner than the U.S.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s push for a closer relationship with the EU appears to also have public support.

The survey suggests more than half the British public (54%) back prioritizing strengthening relations with the EU over Commonwealth countries (46%) and the U.S. (29%).

Burnham traveled to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in the Caribbean on Monday as he seeks to build greater economic cooperation with the 56-strong association of countries — most of which are former territories of the British Empire.

World.title: EU to host Ukraine reconstruction talks with US and UK
World.content:
A Ukrainian flag flies above the ruins of buildings in Kam'yanka, Ukraine on Oct. 24, 2022. | Carl Court/Getty Images

France, Germany, the U.K., NATO and the World Bank will join representatives from Washington, Kyiv and the EU in Brussels.

BRUSSELS — The European Commission will host talks on Wednesday with representatives from the United States, Ukraine and key European allies on Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic future, Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho confirmed Tuesday.

The meeting will bring together officials from France, Germany, the U.K., NATO and the World Bank, alongside representatives from Washington, Kyiv and the EU.

An EU official, granted anonymity to speak freely, told POLITICO that the discussions would cover security guarantees for Ukraine, economic support for reconstruction and other issues related to the country's future.

World.title: Eurozone countries to nominate Lagarde replacement by Nov. 6
World.content:
Two other seats of the ECB's executive board will also need to be filled next year, as Isabel Schnabel is joining the IMF in January and the central bank's chief economist, Philip Lane, is set to end his term in May.

At their next gathering on Nov. 9, eurozone finance ministers will discuss the candidates and the process to fill all three open posts of the ECB executive board, an EU official told POLITICO.

However, the ultimate decision on the ECB President will be taken by the European Council, so heads of state and governments.



The two frontrunners to replace Lagarde are Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos and Dutchman Klaas Knot.

World.title: What happened near Kyiv as viral allegations sparked unrest outside National Guard building
World.content:
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) stated it has identified around 100 people who actively participated in unrest outside a building used by the National Guard near Kyiv, which investigators suspect was organised to abduct a serviceman who had left his unit without authorisation.

 

Deputy SBU chief Ivan Rudnytskyi said on Tuesday that searches were being carried out at some of their homes and that investigators were considering detentions and criminal charges. At least one woman has been detained.

The unrest began on Monday, 2 November, in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka, a suburb of Kyiv, where around 100 people gathered outside a private house, according to Suspilne, Ukraine's public broadcaster, following claims on social media that dozens of men were being held against their will in its basement.

Some posts described the building as a “house of horror”, alleging that servicemen were being tortured inside.

It later emerged that the building was being used to accommodate National Guard servicemen, including those who had returned after leaving their military units without authorisation.

The confrontation escalated into clashes with law enforcement officers. Shots were heard and police vehicles were damaged, according to Ukraine's State Bureau of Investigation.

Senior officials, including National Guard commander Oleksandr Pivnenko and Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov arrived at the scene on Monday evening.

Budanov said on Tuesday that it was “already reliably known that yesterday's events in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka did not occur without influence”.

“The specific individuals and initiators of these events will undoubtedly be identified and punished,” he said, adding that the Prosecutor General's Office and relevant authorities had launched an investigation.

Questions surrounding the ambulance

A woman who arrived in an ambulance and presented herself as a medical professional was among those spreading the allegations.

An investigation by Ukrainian outlet Slidstvo.Info found that the Med-Prestige clinic, which the woman claimed to represent, had ceased operations in 2023. Its owner told the outlet that the ambulance used at the scene had been sold in 2024, with the buyers required to remove the company's branding.

According to the deputy SBU chief, investigators believe the unrest was deliberately organised to abduct a National Guard serviceman who had previously left his unit without authorisation and was subsequently detained.

The SBU has opened criminal proceedings concerning obstruction of the lawful activities of the armed forces and unauthorised disclosure of information about military locations.

A separate investigation into mass unrest, initially handled by the National Police, has also been incorporated into the proceedings.

Separate investigation into possible military misconduct

Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi rejected allegations that the property had been used as a torture facility.

Separately, Ukraine's State Bureau of Investigation has opened criminal proceedings into possible abuse of authority by military officials. Investigators are examining the conditions in which servicemen were accommodated, allegations of coercion and the conduct of those involved in the confrontation.

The Office of the Military Ombudsman is also examining how servicemen came to be housed at the property, including questions surrounding their medical examinations and fitness for service. Four servicemen were taken to hospital.

The State Bureau of Investigation warned that conflicting accounts of the incident were circulating, some without sufficient evidence, and said all allegations of possible human rights violations would be examined.

Ukraine's General Staff called for an impartial investigation, stressing that the state must respond to possible misconduct by military personnel while also protecting servicemen from threats and unlawful actions.

It also emphasised that the return of servicemen who have left their units without authorisation must be handled in accordance with the law and with respect for human dignity.

Both the circumstances of the unrest and the allegations concerning the treatment of servicemen remain under investigation.

World.title: Georgia PM offers no way out of EU accession deadlock in Euronews interview
World.content:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze insisted his government remains “very committed” to joining the European Union but offered no convincing explanation of how he intends to revive the country's stalled accession bid, instead accusing Brussels of political “blackmail”.

 

Speaking at the Euronews Enlargement Summit on Tuesday, Kobakhidze repeatedly blamed the European Commission for the breakdown in relations, while refusing to reconsider the controversial laws that helped bring Georgia's EU ambitions to a standstill.

Georgia applied to join the bloc in 2022 alongside Ukraine and Moldova, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But the Commission initially withheld candidate status, citing insufficient progress on democracy, the rule of law and institutional reforms.

“It was a great mistake,” he said of the Commission's move.

"It was extremely unclear because there was no ground for that. The European Commission publicised its assessment, its scores about Georgia and other countries, and Georgia was doing much better than Moldova or Bosnia. But these countries received candidate status."

He accused the Commission of political bias, claiming its decision had fuelled protests organised by opposition groups and NGOs that he alleged were funded by European and other foreign donors.

Georgia eventually received candidate status in December 2023, but relations deteriorated rapidly. Within months, the European Council concluded that the government's actions had effectively halted the accession process.

In November 2024, Tbilisi announced it would not seek to open accession negotiations before the end of 2028 in a unilateral move after the European Commission published a report indicating serious democratic backsliding from the judiciary to media freedom.

Asked why his government had taken that decision despite nearly 80% of Georgians supporting EU membership, Kobakhidze again shifted responsibility to Brussels.

“If the European Commission decides to open the accession talks for Georgia, we would immediately join. It was not us. But of course, the European Commission, which decided to suspend the political dialogue with Georgia,” Kobakhidze said.

“When somebody wants to change anything in Georgia, they should talk with us. But now the problem is that they don’t talk with us. They are not ready for talking with us,” he said.

Pressed on what concrete steps he would take to break the deadlock, Kobakhidze offered little beyond a willingness to hold a public discussion with the Commission.

He maintained that Brussels' assessment of Georgia was false and amounted to political blackmail.

Crucially, he ruled out repealing either of the two laws at the heart of the dispute: legislation on the transparency of foreign influence and a national registry of NGOs, both criticised by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission, which urged the ruling party to reconsider the legislation in two separate instances.

The Venice Commission said in a legal opinion that the goals were not clear, some definitions vague, and criminal penalties disproportionate.

Kobakhidze argued that demanding their repeal violated Georgia's sovereignty.

“The Parliament of Georgia, with dignity, passed the legislation, which is fully in line with international standards,” he continued, accusing the Venice Commission of political bias as well.

He went further, likening Brussels' demands to the Soviet era, when Georgia was obliged to follow directives from Moscow.

“We want to have a different approach with Europe,” he said.

Throughout the interview, Kobakhidze accused the Commission of double standards, political interference and refusing to engage with Tbilisi. Yet he offered no clear route out of the impasse, nor any indication that his government was prepared to address the EU's central concerns.

Asked why Georgia still wanted to join the EU, he replied that he is “optimistic” that the EU will change, not only in its attitude towards Georgia but as a Union as a whole, given the growing geopolitical challenges and economic headwinds it faces.

“We have to agree with each other, the European Union and Georgia, that we want to see a democratic rule of law-based, human-rights based, economically strong and sovereign Georgia in the European Union. If they agree on this, everything will go on,” he said.

The reports by the European Commission have been endorsed by the European Council, representing the 27 leaders that must unanimously agree to a candidate's entry to the EU. In a Council resolution in 2025, EU leaders urged Georgian authorities to end their hostile rhetoric against EU institutions and the EU mission in Tbilisi.

World.title: Montenegro rejects ‘second-class’ EU membership as it eyes 2028 accession
World.content:
Montenegro’s EU minister, Maida Gorčević, has said Tuesday that her country will not accept second-class membership of the bloc, as she eyed accession as soon as 2028.

 

Speaking at the Euronews Enlargement Summit in Brussels, Gorčević said she was confident that all negotiating chapters would be closed this year and that Montenegro could join the EU by 2028.

Montenegro is a frontrunner in the enlargement process and is expected to become the bloc’s 28th member.

“I’m certain that this goal, 28 by 28, is ambitious. Yes, but it is happening, and we are all witnessing it.”

Asked about a proposal for a 15-year transition period for new member states, tied to rule-of-law safeguards, the minister said Montenegro wants full membership.

“We don’t want second-grade membership inside the European Union, because that wouldn’t be fair and that wouldn’t be full membership as well,” Gorčević said. She added that her government was not against additional safeguards.

“If we are for the safeguards to strengthen the European Union and the future membership, yes, we are for that.”

Gorčević also said she was hopeful that the recent elections in Serbia would help the Western Balkans in the enlargement process. In late October, the reformist Serbia’s Student List resoundingly defeated the country's longstanding leader Aleksandar Vučić.

“This shift can also help a little bit to the region, to have the shift in a good direction. We will see in the future and let’s hope on the next, your enlargement summit that we have some more tangible results coming from the region.”

Gorčević said Montenegro was also committed to resolving its dispute with Croatia over grievances related to the Balkan wars. In October, Zagreb circulated an eight-point paper to other EU countries, setting out the issues it wants resolved before Montenegro can join the bloc.

“I’m certain that in the future we don’t want to argue with Croatia. We want to solve the bilateral disputes,” Gorčević said, adding that a solution could also come after Montenegro joins the EU.

“If we manage to find a solution before joining the European Union, why not? But also, let’s be very fair and open. There is still the open dispute to disputes between when it comes to the border between Slovenia and Croatia. I’m certain that the border issue is not going to be an obstacle to Montenegro joining the European Union.”

World.title: Tents return to Lisbon square after Portugal protest victory
World.content:
Portugal's housing protesters celebrated in Lisbon on 2 November after a court ruled that activist Renata Cambra could set up a tent in Rossio Square, where police had cleared demonstrators over the weekend.

 

The decision overturned the automatic 00:30 curfew used by officers to demand that protesters leave, recognising the tent as a symbolic part of the demonstration rather than an illegal occupation of public space.

The Acampada movement is campaigning against Portugal's housing crisis and the laws governing relations between landlords and tenants.

Cambra says house prices have risen sharply, making decent accommodation increasingly difficult to find. She also points to the impact of tourism, short-term rentals and luxury properties on housing costs.

The ruling gives demonstrators a legal basis to continue their protest in Rossio Square.

World.title: The Senate on a razor’s edge: The races that will decide America's midterms
World.content:
Polling stations are opening across the United States in a midterm election that, a year ago, Republicans expected to survive with their Senate majority intact. That expectation has been reduced to a hope.

 

Start with the House of Representatives, where the question is no longer whether Democrats win, but by how much. Prediction markets give them a 95% chance of taking control. The Cook Political Report now rates 222 seats as at least leaning Democratic, four more than the 218 needed for a majority, against 195 for Republicans, with 18 pure toss-ups. A good night for Democrats could see them controlling as many as 230 seats. A great night means the Senate and a blue wave.

The magic number

Republicans hold 53 of the Senate's 100 seats. To take control, Democrats need a net gain of four. Three is not enough: in a 50-50 Senate, Vice President JD Vance casts the tie-breaking vote, just as Kamala Harris did a record 33 times as vice president; however, Senator John Fetterman, the Democrat from Pennsylvania, could muddle certain partisan votes in a 50-50 Senate.

Prediction markets now give Democrats roughly a three-in-four chance of winning the Senate. Cook rates six races as toss-ups, all of them held by Republicans.

The battleground covers 12 seats. Democrats are defending three: Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire. Republicans are defending nine: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

Two of the three Democratic seats look safe. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan leads Michele Tafoya by 5.2 points in the RealClearPolitics average. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas leads former Senator John E. Sununu by eight points in the same average. Michigan is another matter, but we will come back to it.

North Carolina: Abandoned

North Carolina is a swing state, but it leans Republican: it has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in every election since 1980 bar one. With Senator Thom Tillis retiring, it should have been a fair fight.

Instead, national Republicans all but walked away. The Senate Leadership Fund, the party's main Senate super PAC, had planned to spend $71 million backing its candidate, Michael Whatley. It cancelled its remaining ads in early October, after spending more than $30 million. Former Governor Roy Cooper now leads Whatley by eight points in polls from both Quantus Insights and Trafalgar Group, two Republican-leaning pollsters.

Barring an upset, North Carolina will be the Democrats' first flip. That leaves three more to find.

Ohio and Texas: The big prizes

Democrats placed one of their biggest bets in Ohio. Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat two years ago, is running against Republican Jon Husted, who was appointed to JD Vance's old Senate seat in 2025. Brown leads by 2.8 points in the RealClearPolitics average, in a state Trump won by double digits.

Texas would be the bigger upset. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Yet Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton 49% to 47% in the latest Texas Southern University poll—in line with other recent surveys. Still, this is within the margin of error and is effectively a tie. Texas probably isn’t turning blue. Republicans lead every other statewide race in the University of Houston's Hobby School poll, from governor down to railroad commissioner. What Talarico could benefit from is ticket-splitting: voters backing a Republican for governor, attorney general or Congress, then crossing over to the Democrat for the Senate. Republican Governor Greg Abbott wins 93% of Republicans in the Hobby poll. Paxton wins 88%.

Part of the problem for Paxton is Talarico, a disciplined young candidate who has run a strong campaign. The other part of the problem is Paxton. The embattled attorney general, impeached by his own party in the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the state Senate, is viewed unfavourably by 57% of likely voters and favourably by just 42%, according to Texas Southern University. Trump backed him over four-term Senator John Cornyn in the primary. If Paxton loses, it will be a wound Republicans partly inflicted on themselves.

The curious case of Alaska

Alaska votes Republican for president, but it has a long independent streak. It sent Democrat Mary Peltola to the House in 2022. This time, Peltola is challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, and she leads 48% to 46% in the latest New York Times/Siena poll. Again, within the margin of error.

Then came the other Dan Sullivan. The New York Times reported last week that Democratic operatives, including senior Peltola aides and officials at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, recruited Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to run as a spoiler and confuse voters. Ballot-stacking is generally legal, but the optics are terrible. Peltola denies involvement. Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a criminal investigation and the Justice Department sued, unsuccessfully, to stop Alaska certifying the result if Sullivan loses.

A trick meant to take votes from Sullivan could end up costing Peltola the race, or the legitimacy of her win. Expect President Trump to aggressively attack the result should Peltola win.

Kansas: A pastor in the pulpit

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. This year, the Democrats are running Adam Hamilton, the senior pastor of the largest Methodist congregation in the country, against Senator Roger Marshall. Hamilton leads by 4.1 points in the RealClearPolitics average.

Even the Washington Post's pollsters, whose own survey had Hamilton 10 points ahead, caution that Democrats were far more eager to respond than Republicans. But in a state Trump won by double digits, a single-digit race is a warning.

The rest of the map In Maine, Troy Jackson leads Senator Susan Collins by 3.6 points in the RealClearPolitics average—but never underestimate Senator Collins, who has a history of pulling off electoral upsets. Iowa is a coin flip, with Josh Turek at 48% and Ashley Hinson at 47% in the New York Times/Siena poll. In South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham, appointed in July after the death of her brother Lindsey, leads Democrat Annie Andrews by 2.6 points in the RealClearPolitics average. Nebraska offers Republicans the most breathing room, with Senator Pete Ricketts leading independent Dan Osborn by six points in the latest Times/Siena poll.

Michigan: The Republican lifeline?

If Republicans are to hold the Senate, Michigan may be where they do it. It is the only Democratic-held seat in RealClearPolitics' toss-up column, in a state that voted Trump, Biden, Trump. With Senator Gary Peters retiring, a Republican win would force Democrats to find five flips.

The Democratic nominee is Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom Republicans tie to the Democratic Socialists of America. A staunch critic of Israel, he has pledged to oppose further US aid to the country. His platform still includes Medicare for All and abolishing ICE, but on the stump, he has traded the left-wing agenda for a populist pitch.

Some in his own party have been harsher. On Sunday, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed narrowly beat in the Democratic primary, endorsed Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate, after being disinvited from a joint campaign event. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it "a despicable betrayal". Senator John Fetterman, a fellow Democrat, took Stevens' side, saying El-Sayed has "the worst case of little man syndrome I've ever seen". El-Sayed still leads by 5.3 points in the RealClearPolitics average, but data from Trafalgar Group has him just one point ahead. A Republican win in Michigan would be a major upset, but the path to it is narrower than El-Sayed's.

It comes down to turnout

This should have been a year in which Republicans kept the Senate. Instead, dissatisfaction with Washington, the economy and Trump has turned it into a close race that could break either way.

By most metrics, Democrats hold the enthusiasm advantage. Polls have favoured the Democrats nationally, but we have seen that mistake before. The question is which model holds. In 2022, pollsters underestimated Democrats. In 2024, Republicans exceeded most pollsters' expectations.

Both models come down to the same thing: whether that enthusiasm becomes votes. Republicans hope to hold the blue wave at bay. Turnout will turn the tide, one way or the other.

World.title: Hoax bomb threats target four European flights as scares spread across the continent
World.content:
Four passenger flights heading to Poland, Spain and Bulgaria were the target of bomb threats on Tuesday. All of them landed safely and no explosives were found, authorities said.

 

Two of the threats involved flights heading for Warsaw. The first was SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight SK751 from Copenhagen, which landed normally at the Polish capital’s main Chopin airport. One runway there was closed while the aircraft was searched.

“The aircraft landed normally in Warsaw and the passengers have disembarked,” the Scandinavian carrier said after confirming a threat had been made against the flight.

The second was a LOT Polish Airlines Boeing 737 MAX flying from London Heathrow. It had been due at Chopin but was diverted to Warsaw Modlin, the city’s second airport, which was closed after the alert.

“The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found,” Modlin spokesman Adam Szablowski told AFP, adding that the airport had since reopened and was operating normally.

In Spain, airport operator Aena activated an emergency protocol “due to a bomb alert” on a Ryanair flight from Manchester, in northwest England, to Murcia in the country’s southeast. The plane landed without incident, and the emergency plan was stood down after the Civil Guard had checked the aircraft.

The fourth flight was a Wizz Air service from Bergamo in northern Italy. It was inspected after landing in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, at 10:10 CET, according to a spokesperson for Bulgaria’s interior ministry.

The threats came a day after NATO’s air defence alert service raised the alarm over another Wizz Air flight, which was flying from London Luton to Sofia. That plane was diverted and made an emergency landing in Budapest.

“The Hungarian Defence Forces’ Gripen fighter jets took to the air within minutes and ensured the safe landing of the passenger aircraft in Budapest,” Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook.

On Sunday, an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna was also rerouted to Bulgaria after a bomb threat. Nothing was found on board.

World.title: Italy-Albania migration deal could be extended beyond 2029, Rama says
World.content:
Italy's controversial migration deal with Albania could be extended beyond its current term if Rome wishes, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama told the Euronews Enlargement Summit on Tuesday.

 

The agreement allows Italy to transfer irregular migrants to Albania ahead of their deportation to their countries of origin, effectively outsourcing part of its migration management beyond EU borders.

The deal is due for renewal in 2029, but its future could be complicated by Albania’s ambition to join the EU, which would mean the centres were no longer outside the bloc.

“The deal will stay for as long as need be,” Rama said, promising to keep it in force for as long as Giorgia Meloni remains in power.

“So [it could be] 2030, 2040, 2050, until she will be prime minister in Italy,” he joked.

In a playful exchange with Euronews moderator Maria Tadeo, Rama added: “You want to get out a headline against my sister in Rome, I’m not going to give it to you.”

The agreement, signed in 2023, entered into force in March 2024 and runs for an initial five years and is automatically renewed for another five unless either country withdraws. It has sparked controversy in Italy over alleged violations of fundamental rights and its high costs.

The two centres Italy set up in Albania are currently holding fewer than a hundred irregular migrants, according to media reports, as the Italian government does not release figures.

An investigation awarded the European Parliament’s Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for Journalism found that Italy had spent approximately €1 million per person held during the first two years of operation.

The facilities in Shëngjin and Gjadër were initially meant to hold asylum seekers rescued at sea while Italian authorities examined their applications. Following repeated legal setbacks, Meloni’s government repurposed the centres in March 2025 to detain irregular migrants already in Italy ahead of their deportation to their countries of origin.

Rama played down the significance of the arrangement, saying it was not “such a huge deal to occupy the minds in Europe”. A recently approved EU legislation allowes member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc, with five countries now seeking similar agreements with non-EU partners.

Rama added that migration remains a huge civilisational challenge for Europe, and stricter laws will not be enough to manage it.

“This issue is not going away because we strengthen borders,” he said.

World.title: Americans head to the polls for US midterm elections
World.content:
Americans are heading to polling stations across the United States on Tuesday, November 3, for the 2026 midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

 

In Fairfax, Virginia, voters filled out ballots, checked in at polling stations and cast their votes as Election Day voting got underway.

Polling stations are opening at different times across the country due to time zone differences, with voting continuing in some western states yet to open their polls.

Millions of Americans had already cast their ballots ahead of Election Day, with early voting turnout on pace to surpass that of the previous midterm elections.

World.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter
World.content:
South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday amid water shortages, frustration with local services and questions over whether the ANC's support will keep falling.

"We've decided not to vote. At all," Vatiswa Zoya said two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."

These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets, and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.

Many voters will be asking whether they'll have water to shower on election day, as shortages persist Image: Siphiwe Sibeko/REUTERS

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said it was this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.

"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in municipal elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in the national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.

Here are five things to know about Wednesday's election.

1. Water is a key voter issue

Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on election day, as many parts of South Africa experience water supply issues.

In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN, told DW at a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," Adam said. "It is a definite water crisis across South Africa," she added.

In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said that, despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many candidates have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional," Naidu said. "Their promises are always, you know: 'We're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc.' But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access."

2. ANC in decline

Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.

The global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.

South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Naidu said the party had struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly the Millennial and Gen Zdemographics, who now make up the bulk of voters.

"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," Naidu said.

Mbandazayo is one such voter. She is casting a ballot in her second election and said she was looking for a new voice in politics.

"We need change," Mbandazayo said. "I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time."

3. Migration a big talking point

South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.

According to Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, parties such as Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.

"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA," Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen said.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."

"But for what percentage?" Cornelissen said. "I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly."

Those margins may seem low, but, in an increasingly fractured political landscape, parties are fighting for every vote.

According to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC), 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).

4. Election misinformation

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating more than 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.

Asylum-seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.

South Africa election hit by disinformation surge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, said misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard buildup to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot-button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections," he said. He added that there will always be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And, in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC is one of the best electoral-management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.

Bird said social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.

5. Will people make it to the polls?

Municipal election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.

Naidu said the election would ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.

Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.

Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the makeup of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.

Could you still afford to live in Cape Town today? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

World.title: Ukraine war: Merz doubts Russia is serious about a truce
World.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin. Both leaders said the EU needs to be included in peace talks with Russia. Merz also expressed doubts that Russia is serious about seeking a truce.

Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had seen no sign that Russia is serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.

Zelenskyy and Merz both said the European Union must help shape any lasting peace.

Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."

Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.

"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.

Europe must have a say on postwar security

Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.

He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.

Lavrov sets conditions for talks with Zelenskyy at G20 meeting To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.

"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.

He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.

Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians

The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.

Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.

Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.

Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."

On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.

Russian forces struck the aid center twice after waiting for rescue workers to arrive Image: REUTERS

Germany pledges aid ahead of winter

"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.

Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.

"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.

He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.

How has Berlin stepped up security?

The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.

Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.

Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

World.title: China and India achieved diplomatic thaw. Now the border is flaring up
World.content:
Indian authorities have confirmed a new border "face-off" between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh, raising questions about the still fragile thaw in relations between New Delhi and Beijing.

Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.

"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.

"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.

The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.

Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.

Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.

Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.

Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.

It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.

Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China rejects wrongdoing

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.

Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.

"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.

Why do face-offs keep happening?

The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.

"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.

The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.

Finding home in exile: Tibetans in India resist China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China building a hydropower dam in Tibet

Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.

"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."

South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.

According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.

"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.

What is different about the latest developments?

For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.

Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.

"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.

He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."

The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.

A fragile diplomatic thaw

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.

The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.

India builds tunnel in Himalayas to counter China threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.

The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.

Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
World.content:
As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival , which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

Inspired by 'imperfect' divas

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Hassandra out of drag: They are also a DJ and cultural organizer Image: Gönna Ketels/DW

Building community through drag

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

What does the Berlin Pride attack mean for city's identity? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."



"There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

World.title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
World.content:
The Republic of Cyprus long balanced ties between Russia and the West. Now, it is phasing out Russian weapons, expanding defense cooperation with the United States and redefining its place in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.

He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.

But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."

Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.

For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.

The ambassador also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports. Pictured here: US amphibious assault ship USS Wasp docked at the port in Limassol in 2024 Image: Iakovos Hatzistavrou/AFP

It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.

The nonalignment years

The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.

In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III (left), Cyprus became a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 Image: Nicholas Tsikourias/ZUMA/picture alliance

This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.

EU membership

Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.

Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.

The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.

The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.

Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.

Close relations with Moscow

The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.

The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.

The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.

Even after joining the EU in 2004, Cyprus maintained close ties with Moscow. Pictured here: Nicos Anastasiades (left), president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Russian President Vladimir Putin after signing agreements in Russia in 2015 Image: Nikita Shvetsov/Anadolu/IMAGO

Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.

These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.

Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

Turning point in 2022

The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.

"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.

Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.

The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.

Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.

Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian military equipment. Pictured here: Russian-made T-80 tanks in a 2021 military parade in Nicosia Image: Philippos Christou/AP Photo/picture alliance

Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.

What form does the rapprochement take?

The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.

Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.

An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.

The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.

Cyprus and NATO

The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.

The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.

Earlier this year President Nikos Christodoulides said that Cyprus would apply to join NATO 'even tomorrow if it were possible' Image: Nicolas Tucat/AFP

At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."

Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."

Phasing out Russian weapons

The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.

After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.

The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.

Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).

The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere
World.content:
Donald Trump's Republicans control the US Congress, but that could change after the midterm elections. The outcome of the ballot will not only impact domestic policy but also conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.

The outcome of the midterm elections will shape US policy for years — and have repercussions around the globe. Decisions made in Washington affect both US adversaries such as Iran and countries such as Ukraine, which is seeking more support from the United States.

President Donald Trump does not have the final say when it comes to deciding where the United States goes to war or which countries get financial or military aid. While the president wields more power in the US than in parliamentary democracies such as Germany, he does not govern alone — even in the land of opportunity.

The House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of Congress whose composition voters will decide this Tuesday, wield considerable influence. They decide on legislation and government spending and also serve as a check on the president and the intelligence agencies.

The president can veto legislation passed by Congress. Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. The legislature also handles impeachment proceedings. In addition, the president can only appoint Cabinet members, US ambassadors and federal judges from a list of nominees the Senate approves.

Trump’s Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers of Congress, making it easier for the president to govern. But recent polls suggest the Democrats could take control of at least the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate. This could shift the direction of major foreign policy issues.

Battle for US midterm elections heats up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Support for Ukraine

Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in the White House when Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. Alongside Europe, the US stood out as a reliable partner, supporting Ukraine with financial aid, military expertise and, above all, large-scale weapons deliveries.

The situation changed abruptly under Trump. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy famously received a notably frosty welcome during his 2025 visit to the White House. Trump now openly admits that he gets along better with Russian President Vladimir Putin than with Zelenskyy.

The US has suspended sanctions against Russia and reduced financial and military aid to Ukraine. If Democrats win majorities in both chambers of Congress, they could put increased support for Ukraine on the agenda.

"Democrats criticize the Trump administration for not doing enough for Ukraine," Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist and now an editor at Bloomberg Government, told DW. "They can push legislation that would provide more aid to Ukraine."

If Trump vetoed such legislation, the outcome would depend on the balance of power in Congress. But a two-thirds majority could override his veto with support from some Republicans.

Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran War

Trump launched the war against Iran alongside Israel on February 28 without consulting Congress. Under the US Constitution, Congress must approve a formal declaration of war against another country. Democrats have repeatedly voted against the war and even passed a resolution, together with some Republicans, calling for an end to the hostilities. The Trump administration has ignored it.

"I don't think Congress will have huge powers here," said Michael O'Hanlon, director of research for foreign policy at the US think tank Brookings Institution, told DW, but added that Congress could perhaps prevent a major escalation by refusing to fund it.

How USAID cuts could result in higher HIV transmission To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How the midterms could impact development aid

US support for aid projects around the world that help fight Ebola, AIDS and hunger was sharply cut back by President Trump shortly after he began his second term. Among other measures, he shut down USAID, the US agency responsible for foreign development assistance.

Whether a Democratic-controlled Congress could "reactivate" the agency against the president's wishes is questionable. But Congress could push for increased aid spending and investigate the controversial closure of USAID.

"Democrats would have oversight power and use it to scrutinize the closing of USAID," Conradis said. "There will be hearings, and they will drag officials they view as responsible in front of Congress."

Ultimately, the US remains a country with a Republican president. There will be no complete reversal of course. "It's not like if Democrats win control of Congress, everything is going to change. But some things will change because the power dynamics will be different."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Multiple flights to European airports targeted by bomb threats
World.content:
The bomb threats involved two passenger planes bound for Warsaw, a Ryanair flight from London to Spain, two flights to Rome and a flight traveling from Israel to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. No explosives were found.

Polish authorities said they carried out inspections of two passenger planes targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday but did not find any explosives, in a string of bomb threats that hit several European airports.

A bomb alert forced a LOT flight from London's Heathrow to make an unscheduled landing at Warsaw-Modlin airport, prompting the airport to shut down. Operations resumed around midday.

"The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found," airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told the French AFP news agency. "The airport has been reopened and is operating normally."

A SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen also received a bomb threat before landing safely at Warsaw's central Chopin airport, where it underwent a security inspection.

No explosives were found on either plane. It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.

Flights bound for Spain, Bulgaria also targeted

Also on Tuesday, a Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK, to Murcia, Spain, was hit by a bomb threat. It landed safely and underwent checks after all the passengers had disembarked.

The Spanish government's delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed on X that police "ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane."

"The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation," he said.

And in the fourth such incident, the Reuters news agency reported that another flight traveling from Israel landed in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Tuesday after a bomb threat was received via email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, ​BTA news agency ⁠quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.

Later, two more bomb threats also targeted Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino airport, according to Italian media. Air Force jets were deployed as a result. Both threats turned out to be false alarms.

The six threats on Tuesday come after a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was redirected to the Hungarian capital, Budapest, on Monday after it received a bomb threat mid-air.

Similar such incidents have been reported across different European airports in recent weeks, with alerts later turning out to be false.

World.title: Yemen: Houthi clashes near Taiz leave residents in a 'state of panic'
World.content:
Fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Yemeni government forces has intensified around the city of Taiz. Residents face growing shortages of food, water and medical supplies as thousands flee their homes.

Four months into the fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthi movement and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, clashes are concentrated around Taiz in the country's southwest. Yemeni authorities have warned civilians of sniper fire from surrounding hillsides. Houthi forces have also largely blocked the delivery of goods to Taiz, which is under the control of government forces.

Taiz is Yemen's third-largest city, with a population of around 1 million people. However, fighting has displaced around 134,000 people in the Taiz governorate region, according to the International Organization for Migration. The governorate accounts for almost half of the more than 319,000 people displaced across western Yemen, the organization said on November 1, 2026.

"The Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies, basically all things required for hospitals to function properly," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "Even those who can reach hospitals may not be receiving the care they need," she said, adding that it has had a devastating impact on people's health, particularly those with chronic illnesses.

As the Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies into Taiz, even patients who reach a hospital, don't receive the care they need, HRW warns Image: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

Taiz residents scared but steadfast

Ammar, a 45-year-old photographer in Taiz, told DW on Monday that he sees people in a "state of panic" and yet he feels that "the determination not to submit to the Houthis is very strong."

Afnan, the mother of a schoolchild in Taiz, told DW that "neighbors share the little food they have and help each other and many people in Taiz refuse to flee." She and the other residents who spoke to DW asked that their full names not be published, fearing reprisals.

Hanan, a 30-year-old mother of three, said that prices have skyrocketed while there is almost no petrol, cooking gas or drinking water left in the city. "This increases the mental load on people who are already scared by hearing the clashes of the fighting day and night," she said. Despite this, she numbers among those who have decided to stay.

Meanwhile, Nabil Shamsan, the governor of Taiz, told DW that negotiations are underway to bring food, fuel and water back to the city. While it remains to be seen when and under what conditions this might happen, international aid organizations remain extremely concerned.

"Fighting and insecurity around Taiz is making it unsafe for civilians to move freely and also for our staff to deliver aid," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen. "This is preventing us from reaching the 7,000 people we are supporting with emergency tents, blankets and educational activities for displaced children," she told DW, calling on both factions to allow "civilians and humanitarian workers to move safely."

Why is Taiz under siege again?

During the previous Yemen conflict, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered truce in 2022, Ansar Allah, the formal name of the Houthi group, had already laid siege to Taiz in 2015 and 2016. That siege brought the population close to famine and caused a humanitarian crisis, but the Houthis never captured the city.

In turn, Taiz, as a bastion of resistance, represents something the Houthis have struggled to subdue for more than a decade, Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemeni adviser with UK-based advisory firm Coral Core Consultants, told DW. "The city symbolizes a deeply rooted tradition of political pluralism, civic resistance and rejection of the Houthi model of rule," he said, adding that the city's continued resistance is both a military obstacle and a political challenge to the Houthis' claim that their authority across Yemen is inevitable.

The Houthis have laid siege to Taiz before in 2015 and 2016 but never gained control over the strategically important city that connects the country's north and south Image: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

Following the truce in 2022, the Houthis controlled the capital Sanaa, most of northern Yemen and parts of the center, while the internationally recognized government controlled much of the west and the south including the city of Aden. However, fighting reignited in late July and the clashes intensified in September, as the Houthis seized territory from forces loyal to the internationally recognized government.

Control of the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, is contested. The precise territorial situation remains unclear, while the Houthis retain the capacity to threaten maritime traffic. The conflict continues to escalate, alongside an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Data on the number of people injured or killed in Yemen varies because of the ongoing fighting and separate statistics given by the Houthi movement and the government's health authorities. According to the latest WHO Health Cluster situation report, at least 1,677 people had been killed and 7,395 injured as of October 25, 2026.

The majority of people in Taiz decided to stay despite the Houthi siege, shelling and clashes around the clock Image: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

A key battleground in Yemen's war

Meanwhile, seizing Taiz is highlighted as a key strategic step by analysts. "Taiz would give the Houthis a major advantage in consolidating their hold over northern Yemen while opening the way for further expansion toward the south and the Red Sea coast," Al-Omeisy said, adding that controlling Taiz would give them stronger cards in any future negotiations.

"Taiz is far more than simply another military front for the Houthis," he noted.

"However, the Houthis may not actually need to capture Taiz to achieve many of their objectives," Hisham Al-Omeisy said. "If they can isolate the city, sever its remaining supply lines and neutralize it as a military threat, they could consolidate their positions along the western coast while tying down significant government forces," he added.

"My greater concern is that the Houthis could use gains around Taiz to progressively weaken and fragment the anti-Houthi camp, rather than immediately launch a full-scale offensive against Aden," Al-Omeisy told DW, adding that the Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to exploit divisions among their opponents, and those divisions remain one of the government's greatest vulnerabilities.

Edited by: Jess Smee
