World.title: Una red que garantiza buena salud
World.content:
La conectividad ya es una parte esencial de la atención sanitaria. Vodafone Empresas ayuda a organizaciones como ASISA a mantener operativos sus servicios, incluso cuando las circunstancias ponen a prueba toda la infraestructura

Una consulta médica ya no depende solo de la conversación entre paciente y profesional. Detrás de cada diagnóstico hay historias clínicas digitales, pruebas almacenadas en la nube y sistemas que conectan hospitales y especialistas en tiempo real. La sanidad se ha digitalizado a gran velocidad, apoyándose en una infraestructura tan esencial como invisible: las redes de comunicaciones.

Su importancia se hace evidente cuando algo falla. Una interrupción no significa solo quedarse sin internet. Puede impedir el acceso a pruebas diagnósticas, dificultar la coordinación entre equipos médicos, obligar a cancelar operaciones o desviar ambulancias. La actividad continúa, pero la operativa se vuelve más compleja.

Evitar que la conectividad se convierta en un punto vulnerable es una de las prioridades del sector. Vodafone Empresas combina redes fijas y móviles, gestión de infraestructuras, herramientas para garantizar la disponibilidad de aplicaciones críticas y soluciones de ciberseguridad. La experiencia de ASISA, uno de los grandes grupos aseguradores y sanitarios de España, muestra la importancia de contar con una infraestructura capaz de mantener la actividad diaria.

La infraestructura invisible de las redes

La transformación digital de la sanidad no consiste solo en incorporar nuevos equipos o desarrollar aplicaciones más avanzadas. También requiere redes capaces de mover grandes volúmenes de información de forma segura, ágil y sin interrupciones.

Para dar respuesta a estas necesidades, Vodafone Empresas combina conectividad fija y móvil, soluciones IoT, redes privadas, capacidades de edge computing y servicios en la nube. Un ecosistema tecnológico diseñado para entornos complejos, donde conviven múltiples sedes, miles de dispositivos conectados y una exigencia constante de disponibilidad.

José Antonio Martínez, Director de Cuentas Estratégicas de Vodafone Empresas, apunta tres tecnologías que están acelerando esta transformación. La primera es el 5G, que, precisa, “ha ampliado las capacidades de conexión, el ancho de banda y la disponibilidad de las comunicaciones”, facilitando el acceso en tiempo real a imágenes médicas de gran tamaño, como las resonancias magnéticas, que antes se entregaban en soportes físicos.

El 5G ha ampliado las capacidades de conexión, el ancho de banda y la disponibilidad de las comunicaciones José Antonio Martínez, Director de Cuentas Estratégicas de Vodafone Empresas

A ello se suman la inteligencia artificial (IA), que empieza a impulsar la modernización de procesos y servicios en las organizaciones sanitarias, y la nube, “que permite centralizar sistemas, almacenar imágenes médicas y garantizar que los profesionales autorizados puedan acceder a la información de forma rápida y segura desde distintos centros”.

Arquitectura de una sanidad digital

Con más de 3,5 millones de asegurados y una red de hospitales, clínicas, centros médicos y oficinas repartidos por toda España, ASISA depende de unas comunicaciones que deben funcionar de forma ininterrumpida. La gestión de citas, el acceso a las historias clínicas, la coordinación entre centros o la atención al asegurado descansan sobre una misma infraestructura digital.

Para modernizarla, Vodafone ha desplegado una red corporativa inteligente SD-WAN, ha renovado las redes locales de comunicación y ha reforzado la infraestructura WiFi de la compañía. El objetivo es dotar a la organización de una arquitectura más robusta, capaz de responder a las exigencias de una actividad asistencial cada vez más digitalizada.

“Buscábamos entrar en el siglo XXI como merecía nuestra actividad y aprovechar todas las posibilidades que ofrecían los avances tecnológicos”, aclara José Pereira, director de Medios de ASISA. La rapidez de las comunicaciones, añade, es determinante para la toma de decisiones: “Si las señales no llegan o no lo hacen con agilidad, las decisiones no se toman a tiempo, se toman mal o ni siquiera se dispone de la información necesaria para tomarlas”.

José Antonio Martínez, Director de Cuentas Estratégicas de Vodafone Empresas. Cedida por Vodafone

Las consecuencias pueden traducirse en retrasos en consultas y pruebas, dificultades para acceder a información clínica crítica, problemas de coordinación entre equipos y mayores riesgos para la seguridad de los datos. Pero una conectividad adecuada no solo reduce estos riesgos. También amplía las posibilidades de atención. “Cuanto mejor sea esa conexión y mayor la información que podamos intercambiar, más posibilidades se abren. En última instancia, hablamos de la salud y la vida de las personas”.

El día que la conectividad se puso a prueba

El apagón eléctrico de 2025 evidenció hasta qué punto las infraestructuras esenciales están interconectadas. “Existe una estrecha relación entre el sistema eléctrico, las telecomunicaciones y el sistema asistencial”, puntualiza Martínez. Por aquel entonces, ASISA ya contaba con la infraestructura de Vodafone. “Mantener la conectividad fue un alivio y nos permitió seguir operando en un momento especialmente complejo”, recuerda Pereira.

La incidencia puso a prueba la resiliencia de las redes. Vodafone logró mantener operativa su red móvil durante más tiempo gracias a una combinación de planificación previa, capacidad de respaldo y protocolos de emergencia. Según explica Martínez, la compañía tenía más autonomía en sus estaciones base y priorizó los servicios esenciales para prolongar la conectividad. Entre ellos se encontraban clientes estratégicos y organizaciones de misión crítica, como ASISA.

La experiencia también reforzó una idea compartida por ambas compañías: en situaciones de crisis, la tecnología es tan importante como la coordinación. “Existe una relación de colaboración”, afirma Pereira. Martínez coincide: “La confianza nos permite compartir los retos y la innovación nos ayuda a encontrar nuevas formas de afrontarlos”.

Innovar sin bajar la guardia

La IA abre nuevas posibilidades para la sanidad, desde el apoyo al análisis clínico hasta la personalización de la atención al paciente. Sin embargo, su adopción también plantea importantes desafíos. Entre ellos, la protección de los datos, la fiabilidad de las respuestas y el coste asociado a un uso intensivo de esta tecnología.

Mantener la conectividad [en el apagón eléctrico de 2025] fue un alivio y nos permitió seguir operando en un momento especialmente complejo José Pereira, Director de Medios de ASISA

También resulta clave definir en qué ámbitos puede aportar más valor. Como recuerda Pereira, “la IA puede ampliar la información disponible para el médico, pero las decisiones clínicas deben seguir apoyándose en su criterio profesional y en las circunstancias personales, sociales y médicas de cada paciente”.

Martínez coincide en que el coste puede convertirse en uno de los principales frenos a su implantación. Por ello, Vodafone apuesta por lo que denomina IA soberana: modelos que se ejecutan en la propia infraestructura de las organizaciones, reduciendo la dependencia de servicios externos y permitiendo una gestión más previsible de los recursos.

La otra gran preocupación es la ciberseguridad. A medida que la IA amplía sus capacidades, también lo hacen las herramientas de las que disponen los ciberdelincuentes para intentar acceder a sistemas sanitarios, robar información sensible o secuestrar datos. “No tenemos otra alternativa: los ataques pueden producirse en cuestión de segundos y alcanzar un volumen que dificulta la respuesta humana por sí sola”, señala Martínez. En este escenario, tanto los operadores tecnológicos como las propias organizaciones sanitarias tendrán que reforzar sus capacidades de prevención, detección y respuesta para proteger una infraestructura cada vez más crítica.

World.title: Un agente inmobiliario quiere cobrarnos por enseñarnos un piso. ¿Es normal?
World.content:
Pregunta. Vivimos en Zaragoza y queremos comprar un piso. La persona que nos lo enseña nos dice que, en caso de venta, sus honorarios son un porcentaje del valor o una cifra que va desde 5.000 hasta 9.000 euros más IVA. ¿Enseñarnos el piso implica que lo hemos contratado y debemos pagar lo que pide? P. Pérez

Respuesta. Lo habitual es que el servicio de intermediación inmobiliaria sea contratado por el vendedor, que es quien pone la vivienda en el mercado y acuerda con la agencia las condiciones de la venta, incluyendo la comisión a abonar mediante el correspondiente contrato de encargo. Por ello, lo normal es que sea el vendedor quien asuma estos honorarios. El comprador, por regla general, no debe pagar comisiones a la inmobiliaria, salvo que exista un acuerdo previo, expreso y transparente, formalizado mediante la firma de un contrato de mediación.

El mero hecho de que una agencia inmobiliaria le enseñe una vivienda no implica que exista una relación contractual con el comprador ni genera, por sí solo, la obligación de abonar honorarios. La agencia está prestando un servicio al propietario del inmueble, que es quien la ha contratado para gestionar la venta. En consecuencia, la realización de visitas forma parte de los servicios incluidos en dicho encargo.

No obstante, resulta especialmente importante revisar con detenimiento cualquier documento que se firme durante la visita, en particular la denominada hoja o parte de visita. En ocasiones, estos documentos pueden incluir cláusulas o menciones relativas al pago de una comisión por parte del comprador en caso de adquisición del inmueble.

Asimismo, debe tenerse en cuenta que los tribunales vienen considerando que la incorporación de este tipo de cláusulas en una simple hoja de visita puede resultar abusiva y, por tanto, nula, cuando no ha existido una negociación individual previa. En este sentido, el parte de visita tiene como finalidad principal acreditar que la vivienda ha sido mostrada al interesado, pero no constituye, por sí mismo, un contrato de prestación de servicios entre el comprador y la inmobiliaria.

Por ello, si la agencia pretende cobrar una comisión al comprador lo recomendable es que dicho compromiso quede recogido en un contrato específico, claro y debidamente firmado por las partes. Si únicamente le comunican de forma verbal la obligación de abonar las cantidades indicadas, conviene solicitar que le faciliten por escrito un desglose detallado de los importes reclamados y de los servicios concretos que, en calidad de comprador, van a prestarle y justificarían el cobro de dichos honorarios.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Dutch consumers warned not to buy recalled French condoms
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch health authorities have warned people not to buy French condom brands online that have been recalled because of concerns that they tear too easily.

The French government ordered a recall of seven million prophylactics sold under 10 different brand names across the EU.

The ultra-thin products were manufactured in Malaysia by Richter Robber Technology, but French authorities found discrepancies in the quality and thickness of the latex, breaching safety regulations.

The labels range from big brands to smaller producers that make fair trade or sustainable condoms and include Vitalis, Einhorn, ON and Joy Division.

The healthcare and youth care inspectorate IGJ warned consumers and importers not to buy the condoms because of the risk of spreading STIs. It said it would wait to see if further measures were necessary to prevent them being sold illegally.

French and Dutch authorities have advised anyone who has used the condoms to have themselves tested for STIs. Women should take pregnancy tests if their period is late.

The full list is available on the French government’s website for recalled products, Rappel.

World.title: Philips settles sleep apnoea case with US regulators for €288m
World.content:
Health technology giant Philips has paid the US justice department €288 million to settle a long-running lawsuit over its defective sleep apnoea devices.

The Amsterdam-based company included the figure in its quarterly results, which also showed the company’s orders and turnovers growing strongly even though its profits dropped sharply.

CEO Roy Jakobs said the agreement in principle with the US government drew a line under the problems with its Respironics machines.

He said it was a “very important step” that would allow Philips to “get back to focusing on innovation”.

The company had to recall 5.5 million machines and 17 million sleep masks worldwide after it emerged that tiny foam particles could be released during cleaning and then inhaled.

Suppressed reports

US regulators started legal action after Philips was found to have suppressed complaints from customers and reports warning it about the risk of using polyster foam in its masks for five years before it began recalling the machines in 2021.

The company also settled a mass claim by users, some of whom said the foam particles had caused lung and nasal cancer, for €1.1 billion two years ago. Philips did not admit liability for the patients’ health problems.

Philips saw its group sales grow by 3% in the third quarter to €4.4 billion. Profits dropped from €187 million to €28 million, partly reflecting the settlement of the sleep apnoea cases.

In the previous quarter the company posted a €186 million windfall in tariffs repaid by the Trump administration after the United States Supreme Court ruled they had been levied illegally.

Jakobs said Philips was reaping the fruits of investing in AI to make medical devices smarter and more efficient.

AI robots had cut the time for MRI scans to be halved, allowing hospitals to scan more patients in a day and cut waiting lists, the CEO said. “It’s great for the patient and the hospital to reduce the waiting list so that they can now help twice as many people for the same cost.”

World.title: Firework sellers fuming over damp squib compensation plan
World.content:
Fireworks shops are not happy after being told they can claim compensation for lost income ahead of the upcoming ban on fireworks set for New Year’s Eve.

Retailers were told they’re entitled to compensation for lost profit if they sold fireworks for last New Year’s Eve and in at least one December before that. The payout will be based on how much stock they bought in a previous year.

National fireworks foundation Vuurwerkcheck has branded the compensation scheme “as limited as possible”, and reemphasised that it believes the ban will only fuel the trade in black market fireworks, which are often far more powerful and dangerous.

Frans Köhler, chairman of the foundation, said that retailers who rely on winter sales are heading for bankruptcy, and that some have to adapt their businesses to sell other produce, and were given only one year to do so. The cost of those adaptations will be far higher than the compensation, he told broadcaster NOS.

In April 2025, a parliamentary majority voted in favour of a total ban on consumer fireworks. The Senate also voted in favour in July that year, and the law came into force this August.

High powered fireworks, often obtained illegally abroad, cause serious injuries and damage each year. Last New Year’s Eve, 1,239 people were treated for fireworks injuries at A&E departments or out-of-hours GP posts, up 7% on the year before, according to safety institute VeiligheidNL.

At the last turn of the year, it is suspected that a firework may have burned down the 19th-century Vondelkerk in Amsterdam, though not enough forensic evidence could be found to prove this.

World.title: Why renting outside the big cities is the smart move in 2026
World.content:
Moving to the Netherlands for work usually means aiming for one of the big five cities, but in 2026 the smarter search may start just outside them. Supply in the Dutch private rental sector has been shrinking for a couple of years now, and roughly 42% of unregulated listings now ask more than €2,000 a month, up from 36.5% a year ago, according to Pararius.

That pressure is heaviest exactly where most international jobs are: Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, and Eindhoven, the so-called G5. Competing directly for a place in one of those cities has become harder. Living just outside them often hasn’t.

That’s mostly down to the trains. The Netherlands is small and its rail network is dense, so a city 15 or 20 minutes down the line by Intercity isn’t really a compromise; it’s closer to a different neighbourhood with better rent.

Here’s where to look around each of the five.

Around Amsterdam, Haarlem is 15 minutes from Amsterdam Centraal and has its own historic centre rather than feeling like an overflow suburb. Amstelveen has direct tram links to the city and tends to suit families looking for more space. Almere, a little further out at about 20 minutes, offers newer, better-insulated housing at a noticeably lower price per square metre. It’s worth comparing current listings of apartments in Amsterdam to get a sense of the price gap.

Between Rotterdam and The Hague, the two cities are close enough together to be linked by both regular trains and the RandstadRail light rail network, which makes the towns in between especially practical. Delft, a canal city almost exactly halfway between the two, and Schiedam, known for its old distilleries and comparatively roomy housing, are both a short train ride from either city. Either lets you keep both cities’ job markets within reach. See what’s listed under apartments in Rotterdam and apartments in The Hague for comparison.

Around Utrecht, the city’s position as the country’s rail hub makes its satellites unusually convenient. Amersfoort, a 15-minute ride away, has a medieval centre and rents that run well below Utrecht’s own. Zeist and Nieuwegein are quieter and greener, and popular with families for exactly that reason. Current listings of apartments in Utrecht are a useful baseline for comparison.

Around Eindhoven, the Brainport tech region stretches well past the city itself. Veldhoven, home to ASML’s headquarters, Best, and Helmond are all tied into the regional transit network and offer a shorter, often bike-friendly commute straight to the tech campuses. Have a look at apartments in Eindhoven to see how the core city compares.

The financial case is fairly straightforward. Amsterdam averages €28.53 per square metre a month, according to the latest Pararius Huurmonitor. A place like Almere or Amersfoort runs considerably lower, which in practice means a two-bedroom home for roughly what a studio costs centrally. Newer buildings in these satellite towns also tend to carry better energy labels, which can shave €100 to €200 off monthly utility bills compared with an older, poorly insulated city-centre flat. And since most Dutch employers reimburse commuting costs, often tax-free, the extra travel is frequently close to free in practice.

What this means for your search

Before signing anywhere outside the city you work in, run the door-to-door commute through the NS journey planner at the times you’d actually travel, and check with your employer how commuting costs are reimbursed, since arrangements vary. The energy label on a listing is a good early indicator of what your monthly bills will look like.

The usual paperwork still applies outside the big cities: landlords generally expect a gross income of three to four times the monthly rent, so have your employment contract, recent payslips, and a short rental history ready before you apply. Pararius only lists properties from verified, professional agents, and the satellite towns sit right alongside the cities in its search.

You can view all listings here.

World.title: Jetten hopes sweeteners will win opposition backing for budget
World.content:
The cabinet looks set to take its budget for 2027 to the brink after failing to secure support from opposition parties ahead of the crucial votes on the plans next week.

Prime minister Rob Jetten called on opposition parties to “take responsibility” when the budget plans are debated on Wednesday in parliament, where the centre-right coalition is 10 seats short of a majority.

The latest version of the budget includes around €350 million worth of sweeteners to ease the cost of living and address the priorities of parties on the left and right. But both sides say the measures do not go far enough.

The cabinet has abandoned plans for the so-called “tulip tax”, which would have seen VAT on bulbs raised from 9% to 21%, which was a sticking point for the farmers’ party BBB.

Other spending announcements include an extra €10 million to support sustainability measures in agriculture – a demand of the orthodox Protestant party SGP, which has strong support in rural areas, and €15 million for the police and prosecution service.

The latter is a concession to the far-right splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower.

No advance deals

Neither the left-wing opposition block of Pro and Volt nor the right-wing alliance of JA21, SGP and BBB were able to negotiate a deal to secure their support for the budget package.

Instead, the cabinet has opted for a riskier pick-and-mix approach of offering concessions to both sides, in the hope that it can attract enough votes from smaller parties to steer the budget through.

The coalition parties are hopeful they can get the support of a third block comprising the ChristenUnie, 50Plus and Markuszower’s group, who between them have 11 seats in the Lower House.

“I am convinced that we can get the House over the line to support these plans,” Jetten told reporters on Monday.

“We have a responsibility here in The Hague to do good things, and that includes a good tax plan with plenty of improvements for citizens and businesses.”

But in the Senate, the coalition will need to find the support of either Pro on the left or the BBB on the right. The former want to raise taxes on the rich while the BBB are pressing the government to tear up its plans to cut nitrogen pollution from livestock farms.

Box 3 reforms

Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen also negotiated a compromise on the “box 3” income tax plan, which has been one of the stumbling blocks in the negotiations, during an extra cabinet meeting on Monday evening.

Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, wants to replace the taxes on assets in box 3 with a capital gains tax. But the party was not prepared to accept Pro and Volt’s demand to make up the shortfall during the transition period by raising the tax rate for investors.

The Council of State, the government’s constitutional advisory body, weighed in on Monday with a scathing report on the Box 3 reforms, calling the timetable for implementing them “irresponsible”.

Heinen had wanted to switch to a capital gains tax for real estate assets and investments in start-up businesses in 2028 prior to a full changeover in 2030.

The Council of State said the government would have to hire 250 extra staff to administer the new system, at a cost of €31 million, and the tax office would not be able to meet the 2028 deadline.

The cabinet has now delayed the temporary system until 2029, against the Council of State’s recommendation to wait until 2030, which would cost the government more money.

World.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. Tickets go for €6 online, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres

Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work

For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health

The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

World.title: AI pushing more graduates onto benefits, says UWV
World.content:
The rise of AI is likely contributing to an increase in highly educated people claiming unemployment benefits in the Netherlands, according to benefits agency UWV.

The share of people claiming unemployment benefit (WW) who have an hbo college or university education rose from 30% in the first half of 2022 to 38% this year. The agency says this is partly because more people in the Netherlands are highly educated.

The agency reports a sharp number in claims from programmers and software developers. Reorganisation in IT-driven sectors like banking has also played a role.

Claims from highly educated marketing and advertising staff and market researchers have also risen sharply, which UWV says is “probably” linked to AI taking over tasks.

“We increasingly see technological developments, particularly artificial intelligence, as the cause,” UWV board member Judith Duveen told the Financieele Dagblad. “But part of it is also due to geopolitical uncertainty.”

UWV said it expects financial services to lose more jobs than any other sector in the coming years. Several big banks are cutting support staff, such as anti-money laundering teams, partly through digitalisation and AI. Accountants, junior lawyers, translators, copywriters and customer service staff are also listed as under threat.

The tech sector is still expected to add more jobs than any other sector, the report says, as demand grows for AI advisers and data and security specialists despite some programming work being automated.

On Monday, the Dutch central bank DNB published an analysis which found that a quarter of Dutch workers are in jobs where AI can speed up at least half of their tasks. Hbo and university graduates make up 62% of workers in the most exposed occupations, against 45% of the workforce as a whole. DNB said its measure shows where AI can support or automate tasks, not whether jobs will be lost.

World.title: Dual passports issue continues to plague Dutch-based footballers
World.content:
Dutch-born footballers who were called up to play for former colonies such as Suriname and Indonesia are still in limbo over their national status, six months after the “passportgate” crisis first flared up.

Suriname’s parliament passed a law in September enabling players who are selected for the national team to gain citizenship automatically.

But the Dutch immigration service IND said the law passed in Suriname made no difference to the rules on dual nationality in the Netherlands.

“The fact that Surinamese nationality has been obtained by legal means is not enough on its own to qualify for one of the exceptional categories under our law,” a spokesman for the Dutch justice ministry told broadcaster NOS.

The law was intended to settle the question of dual nationality for footballers, which arose last March when NAC Breda challenged the eligibility of Go Ahead Eagles defender Dean James.

James took Indonesian citizenship last year after accepting an invitation to play for the national team, but under Dutch dual nationality rules he was required to give up his original passport.

KNVB investigation

The Dutch football association KNVB launched an investigation into the employment status of players who were called up by countries such as Suriname, Cape Verde and Indonesia. In the meantime it arranged for Dutch-based players to be given temporary work permits so they could keep playing for their clubs.

Losing Dutch nationality also stripped them of their EU citizenship, meaning they would need to obtain visas and meet stricter criteria, such as an annual salary threshold of €600,000, to be eligible to play in the Eredivisie.

Several players have passed up invitations to join the Surinamese squad because of the uncertainty, including Danilho Doekhi of Lazio, Milan van Ewijk of Coventry City and Jayden Oosterwolde of Fenerbahçe.

National team manager Henk Fraser said it was “inexplicable” that players’ livelihoods were being damaged by their desire to play international football.

“Both countries have to get together and clarify the situation,” he told NOS. “This is a straightforward case of people following their hearts and wanting to play for Suriname, but not knowing where they stand.”

“Sports passports”

Some players said they felt misled by the Surinamese football association, which told them they were playing for the national team on “sports passports” that allowed them to remain Dutch citizens.

Former Feyenoord winger Jean-Paul Boëtius said he only discovered after he was first called up for Suriname last year that he had inadvertently renounced his Dutch citizenship as a result.

Shortly afterwards he received a letter from the city council in Rotterdam telling him to hand in his Dutch passport, which he had recently renewed, because it was no longer valid.

“I now have a sticker in my Surinamese passport that says I have a residency permit allowing me to live in the Netherlands,” he told NOS. “But that’s only for a year. It’s a very difficult situation. I want to become Dutch again. I was born and brought up here.”

World.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc. Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32. Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41). However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47). Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU. Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%. “In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27. However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal. He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction. Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget. He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits. Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”. Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura. Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026 Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 However, when PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it recognised the need to move Poland away from coal and towards a mix of renewables and nuclear. Solar energy installations boomed under the PiS government, and the overall share of renewables in the energy mix rose from around 9% in 2015 to a record 29% in 2024. The current government has continued with PiS’s plans to shift towards nuclear and renwables. This year, Poland’s first offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea began generating electricity, with a number of other offshore projects set to follow. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Polish journalist held at Ukraine border and handed three-year entry ban
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two. World.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned from his position, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw. All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS. Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation. All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026 On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021. Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively. While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK. Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau. Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022. On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS. Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”. The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court. It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government. Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own. The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023. This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful. Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law. "On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court. He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal. Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid. While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to. World.title: Poland launches operation along Russian border in response to reports of planned sabotage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026 On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year. Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries. The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology. The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males. The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added. “I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.” Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas. With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps. The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees. “Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.” The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers. Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022 The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out. The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites. World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners. Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki. @PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute. Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted. On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”. Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki. “One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. World.title: Chaos at Poland’s constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia” – sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026 While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added. Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Prezesem @TK_GOV_PL jest nadal Bogdan Święczkowski, a Wiceprezesem Bartłomiej Sochański. Pani Anna Korwin-Piotrowska nie jest sędzią Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026 The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister. She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered. Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening. Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”. Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland. Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”. Our most tracked flight right now: A Polish government aircraft en route to Senegal is now returning to Warsaw. https://t.co/YdLhQmV8pl pic.twitter.com/Dz9KPgI3eI — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 30, 2026 Tusk, however, issued a statement on social media defending what was taking place at the TK. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity. The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures. The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years. Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆 ❓Czym jest OPRO? ✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich… — Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026 Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly. Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days. The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels. Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”. The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly. Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects. EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late. Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU. However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty".
