World.title: “The Art of James Cameron” to Open at Prague’s Municipal House in April 2027
World.content:
An exhibition dedicated to filmmaker James Cameron will open at Prague’s Municipal House (Obecní dům) on April 29, 2027, bringing more than 300 items from the director’s archive to the Czech capital.

Titled The Art of James Cameron, the exhibition will run until October 3, presenting original drawings, paintings, film props, costumes and photographs connected to the Canadian director’s career.



Visitors will also see examples of 3D technologies developed or adapted for his films, alongside multimedia installations and audio commentary in which Cameron discusses his artistic development.

The collection will cover several decades of his work, from early sketches and storyboards to the technical innovations behind some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, including The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic and the Avatar films.

Although Cameron is widely recognised for pushing the technical boundaries of cinema, the exhibition will focus on his work as an artist and illustrator.

His creative process often began with pencil and paper, with early sketchbooks filled with imaginary creatures, futuristic machines and visions of distant worlds.

The exhibition will also explore recurring themes in his films, including the threat of nuclear catastrophe and the risks posed by rapid advances in artificial intelligence.

Cameron made his feature-film debut in 1981 with the action horror film Piranha II. His breakthrough came three years later with The Terminator, followed by Aliens in 1986. He continued to explore science fiction with The Abyss (1989), which follows a team investigating an underwater encounter with an unknown form of life.

His biggest success at the time came with Titanic (1997). The film won 11 Academy Awards and became one of the highest-grossing productions in cinema history, earning approximately $1.85 billion worldwide.

World.title: Prague Music Week Brings Czech and International Music Names to Prague
World.content:
From November 4 to 6, Výstaviště Praha will become a hub for musicians, industry professionals, and fans interested in everything happening both on and off the stage.

The fourth edition of Prague Music Week—themed “Women Shaping the Industry”—will feature keynote interviews with Aneta Langerová and Jana Kirschner, as well as discussions with local artists such as Lenny, Jiří Burian, Eva Saija Burešová, Klára Vytisková, and Ventolin.



A newly confirmed guest is singer Ben Cristovao, who will join a panel addressing the surge of AI-generated music.

International guests include renowned PR expert Fiona Bloom, Sziget Festival Operations Director Ádám Kiss, diversity, equity, and inclusion specialist Brechje Merckx, and representatives from Spotify.

Will also join: Finnish music industry professional Maija Talvisto; Christine Osazuwa—founder of Measure of Music and an expert in music data and analytics; Vasja Veber, co-founder of the leading analytics platform Viberate; Kristina Janušauskaitė, Executive Director of the IFPI European Office.

The event will offer practical workshops, speed-meeting sessions, opportunities to receive feedback on one’s own work, a technology expo, industry awards, informal gatherings, and space for forging new collaborations.

Tickets for the festival portion of the program are available for purchase via the GoOut and NFCtron networks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Music Week (@praguemusicweek)

Conference tickets can be obtained via a voluntary contribution through the NFCtron platform. More information is available at www.praguemusicweek.cz.

Prague Music Week will feature an Expo spanning 2,000 m², showcasing companies and products that are driving the music industry forward.

Throughout the day, attendees can combine conference sessions with exploring new innovations, participating in hands-on activities, and connecting with exhibitors.

The Expo will also include an “Experience Lab,” where visitors can try out new skills and discover the technologies used in producing music events.

World.title: German Rock Legends Scorpions to Play Prague’s O2 Arena in 2027
World.content:
One of the most successful hard rock bands of all time will perform on June 9, 2027, at Prague’s O2 arena.

Fans can look forward to an evening filled with unforgettable hits, iconic guitar riffs, and the electrifying energy that has defined the Scorpions for over six decades.

Led by charismatic frontman Klaus Meine, the band will revisit tracks that have left an indelible mark on the history of rock music, including “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” “Still Loving You,” and the timeless ballad “Wind of Change.”



In 2027, the Scorpions will embark on another extensive world tour titled “Love, Peace & Rock’n’Roll,” following up on their successful “60th Anniversary – Coming Home” anniversary concerts.

The schedule includes approximately thirty performances across three continents—ranging from European festivals and arena shows (including stops in their native Germany) to dates in North and Latin America.

The Scorpions rank among the most significant and influential rock bands in music history. Formed in 1965 in Hanover, Germany, the group has built a global reputation over the course of an extraordinary career, thanks to their unmistakable sound, high-energy live shows, and an ability to connect with audiences across generations. They have sold over 100 million records and performed countless times on the world’s biggest stages.

Their major breakthrough arrived in the 1980s with the albums Blackout and Love at First Sting, which catapulted the band into the global rock elite. It was during this period that hits such as “No One Like You,” “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” and “Big City Nights” emerged—songs that remain an essential part of their live repertoire to this day.

The Scorpions also gained fame for their emotive ballads, most notably “Still Loving You” and “Send Me an Angel.”

A truly special place in their discography is held by the song “Wind of Change,” which became a symbol of the political and social changes at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

Inspired by the atmosphere at the end of the Cold War, the song remains one of the most famous rock ballads of all time.

World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Czech Billionaire Strnad Offers €30 Billion for Ray-Ban Family’s Firm
World.content:
Czech billionaire Michal Strnad has offered €30 billion to acquire Delfin, the investment vehicle of Italy’s Del ​Vecchio family and the key shareholder in eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

News of the offer, which was first reported by Italian newspaper Il Domani, comes amid growing tensions within Delfin, whose investment portfolio includes also large holdings in Italy’s ​financial sector.

Il Domani published a copy of a letter dated October 20 ​outlining the offer.



“I am looking for long-term investment opportunities in companies ⁠operating in, or investing in, businesses positioned at the top of their value chain,” ​Strnad said in the letter said, according to the newspaper.

Delfin “perfectly fits my investment approach and ​strategy,” the letter added.

Jan Osuch, a spokesperson for AKIPIA, which oversees some of Strnad’s investment activities outside the defence sector, said the group did not comment “on market speculation or potential business negotiations.”

Strnad earlier ​this year bought a 14% stake in Italian tyre maker Pirelli, opens new tab from China’s ​Sinochem.

Strnad, 34, heads the family’s defence company Czechoslovak Group (CSG) which listed in Amsterdam earlier this year.

Delfin shareholder Leonardo ‌Maria ⁠Del Vecchio, one of the six children of the late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, confirmed he had been recently informed of an offer for the company received from a foreign investor.

“The work of a lifetime by my father must remain part of ​Italy’s heritage”, he said in a ​statement.

The late Luxottica ⁠founder built his business empire from scratch having grown up in a Milan orphanage.

Delfin’s ownership is divided equally among Del Vecchio’s ​eight heirs: his six children, his widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her ​son from ⁠a previous marriage.

A sale would require a virtually unanimous decision from the heirs, who have become increasingly at odds with one another.

In addition to its stake in EssilorLuxottica, Luxembourg-based Delfin holds stakes in ⁠Italian ​insurer Generali and lenders Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) and ​UniCredit, for a combined current market value of €43 billion.

Delfin declined to comment. A representative for Strnad was not ​immediately available for comment.

World.title: Prague’s Only Christmas MINT Market to Take Place on November 28–29
World.content:
Don’t leave your Christmas shopping until the last minute this year.

On the weekend of 28–29 November, head to Hall 13 at Holešovice Market and discover original gifts directly from the people who made them.

MINT Market will bring together more than a hundred carefully selected brands from across the Czech Republic, offering a relaxed alternative to the pre-Christmas rush in shopping centres.



On Saturday from 10 am to 6 pm and Sunday from 10 am to 4 pm, visitors can look forward to independent fashion, designer jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations, original accessories and plenty of Christmas gift inspiration.

And, of course, there will be the relaxed and friendly atmosphere that has become an essential part of MINT Market. The event is suitable for all generations and admission is free.

The youngest MINT Market visitors and their families can enjoy the beautiful NOOK Family Lounge, featuring high-quality wooden toys, a creative play area, a quiet zone with books and space to relax, as well as facilities for babies and parents, including a changing table and a peaceful place for breastfeeding.

There will also be Christmas-themed creative workshops.

MINT Market has been active for sixteen years. During that time, it has become an important platform for small and emerging creators, often directly from Prague, who are given the opportunity to present their products to a wide audience.

Residents of Prague and the surrounding area thus have several opportunities each year to purchase quality products that are literally made by their neighbors – locally, sustainably, and with an emphasis on honest craftsmanship.

MINT Market is not just about shopping. Since 2010, the project has been run by a team of people who systematically support small and local brands and are the only ones bringing high-quality Czech design to more than twenty cities across the country.

What started as a small project has gradually grown into a community of more than 1,500 creatives and a platform that has hosted over 450 events and welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors.

World.title: Czech Government Proposes Voluntary TV and Radio Fees Without State Budget
World.content:
People in the Czech Republic could soon be allowed to decide whether they want to pay television and radio licence fees under a new funding model being prepared by the government.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the Finance Ministry is working on a system that would make contributions to Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) voluntary while ensuring the two public broadcasters receive a guaranteed level of funding.

The proposal is expected to be discussed by the coalition council on Monday.



For now, however, the existing system will remain in place. Although the government had initially hoped to introduce changes at the beginning of 2027, Babiš said the legislative timetable makes that unlikely.

Under parliamentary rules, the bill requires a 60-day review period before moving forward. That means its second reading would fall during the Christmas period, delaying further debate until at least January 2027.

The proposed changes have already sparked political and public opposition.

On October 24, the Chamber of Deputies approved in its first reading a proposal to abolish television and radio licence fees. The governing coalition, made up of ANO, SPD and the Motorists party, added the measure to its priority legislative agenda. The vote took place early in the morning after a lengthy parliamentary debate.

Opposition parties have warned that changing the funding system could expose public broadcasters to greater political pressure. Government representatives have rejected those concerns, saying the planned reform does not threaten democratic standards.

Babiš has said the final model must comply with European requirements concerning the independence of public media and predictable funding.

The issue has also prompted demonstrations. On October 25, thousands of people gathered in Prague’s Old Town Square for a protest organised by the Million Moments for Democracy movement.

Participants expressed concern that changes to the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio could increase political influence over the broadcasters.

World.title: Prague Welcomes a Week of Polish Films and Culture
World.content:
Prague will host a week of Polish cinema and culture from November 9 to 15, as the 3Kino – Polish Film Festival Prague returns for its 13th edition.

The festival will screen 13 feature films representing contemporary Polish cinema, with a program that also includes theater, stand-up comedy, exhibitions, music and events for children.



This year’s festival opens with The Doll (Lalka), directed by Maciej Kawalski. Based on the classic novel by Bolesław Prus, the film is among the most expensive Polish productions ever made and takes audiences to 19th-century Warsaw.

The story explores love, ambition and social divisions, with Marcin Dorociński, one of Poland’s best-known contemporary actors, in a leading role.

Freedom will be the central theme of this year’s edition. The festival will explore the idea through historical events as well as everyday life, personal relationships and decisions that can alter a person’s future.

The program extends beyond the cinema. Visitors can attend theatrical performances, stand-up shows and exhibitions, while this year’s edition will also put a special focus on Poland’s Lower Silesia region.

Among the accompanying events is the opening of photographer Rafał Pawłowski’s exhibition Shadows of Sounds. Another exhibition will mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, featuring a selection of Polish film posters.

The festival aims to bring Polish culture to audiences across Prague, with screenings and accompanying events taking place at several venues throughout the city.

Ticket sales are now open, and the full program is available on the festival’s official website.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán shares the deadline set for Hungary to stop importing Russian gas
World.content:
Hungary’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Anita Orbán, has shared the deadline for phasing out Russian natural gas. The statement comes as Budapest explores alternative energy supplies and seeks to strengthen its role as a regional oil and gas hub.

FM Anita Orbán shared her views on Russian energy

In an interview with Telex, the foreign minister was asked whether Hungary could continue accessing Russian gas in the future. Citing the European Union’s timetable, she claimed “the EU has set a clear deadline for phasing out Russian natural gas, which is autumn 2027,” she said.

The minister also discussed efforts to diversify the country’s oil supply. Hungarian energy company MOL is working to prepare its refineries for the potential import of non-Russian crude through Croatia’s JANAF pipeline, which could provide an alternative route from the south.

The United States has granted Hungary a temporary exemption from certain sanctions affecting Russian oil imports, with a deadline of 21 November. Orbán said the exemption concerns oil purchased from Russian companies Lukoil and Rosneft, and that MOL is working on the necessary technological adjustments to enable sourcing from other suppliers.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in the parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

MOL’s potential acquisition of Serbian oil company

Another key issue concerns MOL’s potential purchase of Gazprom’s stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company, which owns the country’s only oil refinery. The US Office of Foreign Assets Control has granted an exemption allowing negotiations with Gazprom to continue until 11 December.

Foreign minister Anita Orbán she could not comment on ongoing business negotiations, but indicated that Serbian, Russian and Hungarian parties all appeared strongly committed to completing the transaction by the deadline. She added that the acquisition could strengthen Hungary’s position in regional energy infrastructure discussions, including those involving the JANAF pipeline.

Anita Orbán described Hungary as a potential major transit and distribution centre for both natural gas and crude oil. She pointed to the country’s extensive storage capacity, connections with six neighbouring countries and MOL’s influential regional position as factors that could support energy supplies to other states.

Stay up-to-date: Leading Czech magazine portrays Viktor Orbán in handcuffs

Strategic interests stay unchanged

The foreign minister also addressed Hungary’s recent diplomatic engagement with the United States. During her visit to Washington, Orbán and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed two declarations of intent, one on energy cooperation and another on joint efforts against terrorism.

Anita Orbán described the visit as the result of a broader confidence-building process and said its swift organisation demonstrated that Washington regarded Hungary’s new government as a partner and ally. Asked whether the Tisza-led government was continuing certain policies pursued by its predecessor, she emphasised that some national priorities transcend changes in government.

“There are strategic interests that do not change with a change of government, such as the security of the country,” she said. The comments underline the challenges facing Hungary as it navigates EU energy policy, sanctions and regional supply arrangements while seeking to maintain energy security.

World.title: Hungary elects new chief public prosecutor after years of controversy – who is Péter Fejes?
World.content:
Hungary has a new chief public prosecutor. Parliament elected Péter Fejes to the nine-year post on Tuesday, with the experienced prosecutor promising to restore public trust in an institution that has faced serious criticism over its independence and handling of politically sensitive cases.

Fejes received 139 votes in favour and six against in a secret ballot. Following his election, he acknowledged that some decisions made by the prosecution service in recent years had rightly damaged public confidence, and issued an apology on behalf of the organisation.

Speaking at a press conference, he said:

“On behalf of the prosecution service, I apologise to society for certain decisions – and failures to act – which have rightly and justifiably offended the public’s sense of justice.”

He also apologised to former colleagues who had devoted their lives to the institution but had felt compelled to leave.

Péter Fejes and Hungarian President András Baka. Photo: MTI

Nearly 40 years in the prosecution service

Fejes, who describes himself as a native of Szombathely in western Hungary, graduated in law from the University of Pécs and was appointed as a prosecutor in 1988.

He began his career at the local prosecutor’s office before moving to the Vas County Chief Prosecutor’s Office. There, he became a group leader and later served as the organisation’s spokesperson, becoming one of its best-known public faces.

In 2008, he was appointed chief prosecutor of Veszprém County. However, his career took an unexpected turn in 2012, when then-chief public prosecutor Péter Polt dismissed him with immediate effect and without giving a reason, Telex reports.

Fejes subsequently continued working as a subordinate prosecutor at the Győr Appellate Chief Prosecutor’s Office. His final position was deputy chief prosecutor for criminal law at the Vas County Chief Prosecutor’s Office. He retired in 2025 after almost four decades of service.

Péter Fejes and András Baka. Photo: MTI

High-profile criminal cases and academic work

Over the years, Fejes has been involved in several major criminal cases that attracted nationwide attention.

His first nationally known case was the 1998 child murder in Körmend. He also supervised the investigation into the murder of Romanian handball player Marian Cozma in 2009. However, he considers the proceedings against those responsible for the 2010 red mud disaster one of the most important cases of his career.

Beyond his prosecutorial work, Fejes remains active in academia. He teaches criminal law and sports law at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) and Pázmány Péter Catholic University. He is also a devoted supporter of Szombathely’s Falco basketball team and holds a senior position in the European Wine Knights organisation.

If you missed it: Hungary makes 24 December a public holiday starting this year

Plans for a major overhaul

Before his election, Fejes told Válasz Online that the prosecution service needed immediate and far-reaching personnel and organisational changes.

His proposals include reducing the size of the Office of the Prosecutor General, reviewing the role of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office of Investigation, addressing significant salary differences and making a prosecutorial career more attractive.

He described the organisation as morally shaken and professionally stalled, pointing to a lack of trust and prolonged vacancies in senior positions.

Fejes also suggested that cases should be reopened where new evidence emerges, saying that some files may need to be “dusted off”. He believes senior prosecutors should be more visible in public, with important decisions explained by the people responsible for them rather than communicated solely through official statements.

A difficult task ahead

The new chief public prosecutor inherits an institution whose reputation has been seriously damaged. Under Péter Polt, who led the service for years, critics repeatedly accused the prosecution of failing to pursue corruption allegations involving government politicians and business figures close to the former administration.

The leadership crisis deepened in 2026. Former chief public prosecutor Gábor Bálint Nagy resigned in July, while the former head of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office of Investigation, Pál Fürcht, had already stepped down in June. Fürcht subsequently alleged that investigations into politically sensitive cases had been influenced by the Office of the Prosecutor General.

Fejes now faces the challenge of restoring confidence in the institution and demonstrating that prosecutors can operate independently, regardless of political interests.

World.title: Hungary’s Foreign Ministry abruptly sacks foreign policy institute chief over links to previous government
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed Botond Feledy as head of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs (MKI) with immediate effect, citing a loss of trust over his previous working relationship with the former government. The unexpected decision comes less than three months after his appointment, when he was tasked with rebuilding the institute’s professional reputation after years of political controversy.

The dismissal was announced on Monday evening by György Velkey, the ministry’s parliamentary state secretary. According to the statement, the ministry had only learned a few days earlier about Feledy’s professional relationship with the previous government, which had lasted for years and continued into the spring of 2026.

“Based on the information received by the ministry, we are terminating Botond Feledy’s managerial appointment with immediate effect due to a loss of trust,” Velkey said.

HUF 84 million in contracts with Lázár’s ministry

The controversy centres on contracts between Feledy’s company and the Ministry of Construction and Transport, led at the time by János Lázár. Documents obtained by Telex show that the ministry paid Feledy’s company a total of HUF 84.2 million (EUR 230,000) for foreign policy analyses over several years. According to the report, the working relationship continued until after the 2026 parliamentary election, with a further HUF 19 million paid after the vote.

Feledy responded to his dismissal in a Facebook post, explaining that his company had provided independent analytical work rather than traditional consultancy or political advice.

He said the ministry had approached his three-person company in 2023 because it wanted an independent perspective on international affairs. He argued that this allowed him to provide critical assessments of countries such as Russia and China, which government-aligned think tanks might have been reluctant to publish.

Feledy insisted that his clients had never influenced his professional opinions and said he intended to continue working towards political change in Hungary.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar commented on the post, saying that anyone accepting a senior government appointment should disclose potentially controversial previous contracts.

He specifically criticised Feledy for failing to mention that his company had received HUF 84 million in public money from the previous government, including HUF 19 million after the election.

A key figure in the institute’s attempted renewal

Feledy was appointed director of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs in August, alongside Russia expert András Rácz, who became his deputy. The new leadership was expected to move the institution away from its previous political orientation, which had been associated with Balázs Orbán and the American MAGA movement.

Their priorities included developing a new Hungarian foreign policy strategy, strengthening the professional foundations of foreign policy decisions and rebuilding expertise on European Union affairs.

Feledy had spent around 20 years working in foreign policy as a journalist, analyst, media entrepreneur and university lecturer. He had previously lived in Brussels but moved back to Budapest with his family to take up the position.

At the time of his appointment, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the new leadership would promote thorough, independent and forward-looking research.

If you missed it: Was Viktor Orbán a communist agent? Former PM shared documents of communist recruitment and surveillance

Ministry refuses to provide further details

The Foreign Ministry has offered little additional explanation for the sudden dismissal. Responding to questions from Telex, it said senior appointments require proof of professional qualifications and language skills, as well as a criminal record certificate, a competency test and national security screening.

Velkey later told Telex that Feledy had been asked during the appointment process whether there was anything in his professional background that could make him vulnerable to criticism. According to the state secretary, the new institute chief did not disclose his previous contracts with Lázár’s ministry. Velkey also stressed that the Foreign Ministry had learned about the agreements from another government department, rather than from Telex’s reporting.

The ministry also confirmed that the institute is a separate legal entity owned by the Foreign Ministry, adding that similar employment suitability criteria apply there as within the ministry itself.

However, it declined to provide further details about Feledy’s dismissal or his successor. It also did not clarify whether his deputy, András Rácz, could temporarily or permanently take over the leadership.

World.title: Was Viktor Orbán a communist agent? Former PM shared documents of communist recruitment and surveillance
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed that Hungary’s communist-era state security services attempted to recruit him as an informant during his compulsory military service, a claim that has reignited debate over his past and the country’s unreleased intelligence files.

Viktor Orbán talked about recruitment and surveillance

In a statement published on Tuesday, the former prime minister said he had rejected the recruitment attempt during the early period of his military service. He also claimed that, following the failed effort, he, his wife and fellow opposition figures were subjected to continuous surveillance by the communist authorities. The former prime minister wrote that

“During the first period of my compulsory military service, they tried to recruit me, but I refused, so the attempt ended unsuccessfully.”

According to Orbán, secret surveillance operations against him and his associates included monitoring, the use of informants and the installation of listening devices at their workplaces and homes – allegedly even in their bedrooms. A formerly classified report issued by the Szolnok County Police Headquarters reportedly records that the former prime minister was examined for potential recruitment in 1982, but the authorities ultimately abandoned the effort.

Rumours started spreading very quickly about Orbán’s past

The latest statements have emerged amid renewed media speculation about whether Orbán ever worked for the communist-era state security apparatus. Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi recently said in a podcast that former Hungarian Prime Minister Miklós Németh claimed to have seen three handwritten and signed intelligence reports allegedly authored by Orbán.

According to the account, Németh was shown the documents in 1990 by then Defence Minister Ferenc Kárpáti. The reports reportedly contained observations about the conduct and personal characteristics of conscripts serving in Zalaegerszeg. Németh allegedly recognised Orbán’s handwriting and signature, although he could not independently verify their authenticity, as per Telex.

Historian urges caution over agent allegations

Historian Krisztián Ungváry, who is involved in a committee reviewing classified documents, cautioned against drawing conclusions based on the allegations. He stressed that the presumption of innocence applies to everyone and that the claims require evidence. Ungváry said that after Orbán’s military service, he was himself a target of state surveillance. While he acknowledged that it was possible the politician had carried out intelligence tasks before his discharge, he argued that this had not been proven.

The historian also pointed to references in another person’s file suggesting that authorities attempted to recruit Orbán again in 1988 under the codename “Kurázsi” (Courage). Ungváry said the available indications suggested this attempt had also failed, as Orbán continued to be listed as a surveillance target. In his 2017 book A szembenézés hiánya (The Absence of Confrontation), Ungváry devoted a chapter to the allegations and concluded that there was no evidence of closer cooperation between Orbán and the state security services.

Stay up-to-date: Viktor Orbán reported to police over controversial speech about ‘handing out appropriate tools’

Fidesz rejects the allegations

Orbán’s Fidesz party also responded to the claims, insisting that the available facts, data and documents demonstrate that the politician was not an agent but a person monitored by the communist state. The renewed discussion comes amid broader calls for greater transparency regarding Hungary’s communist-era intelligence archives and the identities of those who collaborated with the secret services.

World.title: Hungarian prison ordered to apologise after father was denied chance to say goodbye to dying son
World.content:
A Hungarian prison has been ordered to apologise and pay compensation to a father who was not informed in time that his son had suffered life-threatening injuries in custody and was denied the chance to speak to him while he was still conscious. The Győr Court of Appeal issued the final ruling on 15 October, finding that the prison had violated the man’s right to private and family life.

His son was brutally beaten in his cell

József Ruckel’s son, René, was seriously injured at Szombathely Prison on 25 January 2023, following a fight with a cellmate. The young man emerged from his cell with a bloodied head before collapsing in the corridor. He suffered a spinal injury that left him paralysed from the neck down and was transferred to hospital, where he later died. One of his cellmates was convicted over the assault that led to his death.

René’s father was not notified directly by the prison. Instead, he learned that his son had been hospitalised through a friend of the young man. When he contacted the prison service, he was told that René had become dizzy, fallen and hit a door. The fight that had preceded his injuries was not disclosed.

Father’s request to visit delayed for three days

József immediately went to the hospital, hoping to see his son while he was still conscious. However, he was not allowed to visit him. According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, René even called out to his father, saying, “Dad, I’m here”, but the meeting was not permitted. The father spent several days making phone calls and attempting to secure an extraordinary hospital visit.

His request was only assessed three days later, as the application had been filed during working hours shortly before the weekend. By the time he was finally allowed to enter, René was in a deep medically induced coma and never regained consciousness. József was able to hold his son’s hand for an hour, but they could no longer speak to each other.

The father initially did not want to take legal action, saying he would have accepted an apology and an admission of wrongdoing. The prison commander expressed condolences but repeatedly refused to apologise or reach an out-of-court settlement, reports 444.hu.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Appeal court finds prison responsible

The Szombathely Court of First Instance had rejected the father’s claim. However, the Győr Court of Appeal overturned that decision, establishing that René had already been in a life-threatening condition on the day he was admitted to hospital.

The appeal court noted that medical records showed René required circulatory support from 12.45 PM on 25 January. It ruled that prison authorities should have obtained adequate information about his condition and that a request for an urgent visit could not be delayed for days simply because of weekend working arrangements.

The prison has now been ordered to issue a formal apology and pay HUF 500,000 (approximately EUR 1,370) in compensation. József intends to donate the compensation to charity. The father said the ruling offered some satisfaction because he felt he had fought for justice. He added that its real value would depend on whether the prison learned from the case and prevented similar tragedies from happening again.

World.title: Hungary makes 24 December a public holiday starting this year
World.content:
Hungary’s National Assembly has voted to make 24 December a public holiday, meaning workers will no longer have to make up the day off as previously required. The new measure will take effect this year, giving Hungarians an additional day of rest ahead of Christmas.

No need to compensate for 24 December anymore

The bill was approved on Tuesday with 193 votes in favour, with no votes against or abstentions. The proposal was submitted by three MPs from the Tisza Party in September. Under the new legislation, Christmas Eve will join 25 and 26 December as official public holidays. Previously, 24 December was designated as a rest day, but employees were required to work on 12 December to compensate for it. The newly approved law removes this obligation.

The measure also introduces restrictions on shop opening hours on Christmas Eve. Most retail outlets will be required to close, allowing a wider range of employees in the sector to spend the holiday with their families. However, exemptions will apply to restaurants, accommodation providers, flower shops, confectionery stores, petrol stations and shops located within railway and bus stations or airports. These businesses will still be permitted to operate, writes Telex.

A long-running campaign for Christmas Eve off

The bill’s justification highlights the importance of 24 December in Hungarian society, describing it as an integral part of the Christmas season, traditionally associated with family gatherings, festive preparations and religious and community traditions. The legislation is also intended to provide a predictable legal framework, ensuring that Christmas Eve is a public holiday every year rather than depending on annual adjustments to the working calendar.

The issue has been debated for years. The Jobbik party launched referendum initiatives in both 2024 and 2025, seeking public support for making 24 December a non-working day. The first was rejected by the Curia, Hungary’s supreme court. The second was approved by both the National Election Committee and the Curia, but failed to secure enough signatures.

Probably the most unanimous vote in the National Assembly since May

The Trade Union of Commercial Employees also repeatedly attempted to gather support for the change, most recently in April this year. The union previously argued that although Christmas Eve was already far from an ordinary working day, hundreds of thousands of people were still required to work. Under the new rules, most employees will be able to stay home, while those required to work may be entitled to double pay.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar welcomed the development, saying the change had finally been achieved after 36 years. Christian Democrat politician Csaba Latorcai, meanwhile, described the decision as a victory for Christian Democrats.

World.title: New Chinese restaurant chain opens in Budapest: How much does a bowl of noodles cost? – PHOTOS
World.content:
Budapest has welcomed another international restaurant chain, bringing a taste of north-western China to the Hungarian capital. Mr. Noodle Chen has opened its doors on Corvin Promenade, offering freshly hand-pulled noodles and traditional Lanzhou-style beef soup. The brand already operates hundreds of restaurants across China and is now expanding its presence in Europe.

From Shanghai to Budapest: A Chinese success story

Mr. Noodle Chen is the European brand name of Chen Xiang Gui, a Chinese restaurant chain specialising in Lanzhou beef noodles, Pénzcentrum reported. Unlike many Asian fast-food restaurants, its concept puts the traditional art of hand-pulled noodle making centre stage.

Visitors can watch skilled noodle makers working behind a glass partition, stretching a ball of dough into long strands of different thicknesses. The technique is based on lamian, a traditional Chinese method of preparing hand-pulled noodles.

The company group was founded in 2014, while the Chen Xiang Gui restaurant brand itself was established in 2020. Its first restaurant opened in Shanghai, and the business expanded rapidly.

According to figures published on the company’s official website, the chain now operates more than 300 restaurants in China, including 230 directly managed locations. It employs over 3,800 people and has 120 restaurants in Shanghai alone.

Interestingly, the business does not follow the traditional operating model of Chinese restaurants. Founder Jiang Jun previously worked for international hospitality companies, while several members of the management team have backgrounds at McDonald’s and KFC.

The company has incorporated some of the operational methods of major international fast-food chains into its business. Ingredients are carefully measured, soup recipes are standardised, and restaurant operations follow a highly organised system.

The first Chen Xiang Gui restaurant opened in Shanghai in March 2020. By the end of that year, the chain already had ten locations. It passed the 200-restaurant milestone by December 2021 and reported more than 260 restaurants in China in 2024.

Braised beef and pickled cabbage soup. Photo: Mr. Noodle Chen

European expansion reaches Berlin, Vienna and Budapest

The brand’s international expansion under the Mr. Noodle Chen name began in Germany. Its first European restaurant opened in Berlin in 2025, followed by another location in Hamburg.

In May 2026, the chain entered the Austrian market with its first restaurant in Vienna, at Kirchengasse 3. According to Austrian lifestyle magazine Falstaff, customers there can also watch the noodle-making process through a glass partition.

Budapest is now the latest addition to the brand’s European expansion, with its new restaurant located on Corvin Promenade.

Mixed noodles with stir-fried beef. Photo: Mr. Noodle Chen

How much does a bowl of noodles cost in Budapest?

The Budapest restaurant focuses primarily on beef noodle soups, alongside stir-fried and mixed noodle dishes. The classic Lanzhou soup is prepared with beef, white radish, coriander, spring onions and a broth made from beef bones.

Customers can also choose tomato-based and pickled cabbage variations.

Based on the prices listed on the restaurant’s Wolt delivery menu, a classic beef noodle soup costs HUF 3,890 (EUR 10.7), while the version with extra meat is available for HUF 5,190 (EUR 14.3). (1 euro = 364 forints)

Other options include:

Tomato beef noodle soup: HUF 5,590

Pickled cabbage noodle soup: HUF 5,990

Braised beef and pickled cabbage soup: HUF 6,390

Beef Biángbiáng stir-fried noodles: from HUF 5,990

Braised beef noodles: HUF 6,490

Vegan noodle dishes: HUF 3,890–5,590

The menu also includes several smaller dishes and snacks. A Chinese beef burger costs HUF 2,990, chicken skewers are priced at HUF 2,290, while beef and lamb skewers cost HUF 2,590. Cucumber salad is available for HUF 1,790.

For more information, visit the restaurant’s official Hungarian website.

World.title: Major upgrade coming to Budapest’s airport express: Brand-new buses hit the road – PHOTOS
World.content:
Budapest’s popular 100E Airport Express is getting a major upgrade, with brand-new articulated buses featuring dedicated luggage storage areas set to make journeys between the city centre and the airport more comfortable. The first six new vehicles entered service on 2 November, with the entire new fleet expected to consist of 24 buses.

More room for suitcases on the 100E

The new MAN Lion’s City 18C articulated buses have been specifically designed to meet the needs of airport passengers. Their most notable feature is a dedicated luggage storage area inside the passenger compartment, located in front of the second set of doors.

Depending on the size of the bags, each bus can comfortably accommodate between 15 and 25 suitcases or larger backpacks. The new arrangement should make travelling with bulky luggage considerably easier, particularly for tourists arriving in Budapest or heading to the airport.

The low-floor vehicles also come with modern passenger information systems and onboard cameras. They comply with the latest transport safety requirements and are equipped with blind-spot monitoring systems to assist drivers.

The first six buses began operating on Monday, 2 November, as part of a new fleet of 24 vehicles dedicated to the airport service.

Record passenger numbers drive improvements

The upgrade comes as the 100E Airport Express continues to attract growing numbers of passengers.

According to Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), an average of around 13,400 people used the service each day in August 2026, compared with approximately 10,800 in August 2025. This represents an increase of more than 20 per cent, or nearly 2,700 additional passengers per day.

Passenger numbers were also higher year on year in July, suggesting that demand for the direct connection between central Budapest and Liszt Ferenc International Airport is continuing to grow.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Cheaper airport transfers for Budapest pass holders

BKK has introduced several measures to improve the service and make it more convenient for travellers.

The 100E was the first public transport route in Budapest to introduce Budapest Pay&GO, a contactless bank card payment system that allows passengers to buy tickets quickly and easily.

Since 1 October 2025, passengers with a valid Budapest Pass, Pest County Pass or Hungary Pass have also been able to purchase a discounted supplementary airport ticket for just HUF 1,000 through the BudapestGO app.

Another development, introduced in spring 2026, uses flight traffic monitoring data to predict passenger demand based on actual aircraft arrivals. This allows transport planners to arrange additional buses more quickly when necessary, helping to prevent overcrowding.

More than 380 new buses coming to Budapest

The arrival of the new airport buses is part of a wider renewal of Budapest’s public transport fleet. Under the programme launched in 2025, more than 380 new diesel and electric buses are expected to enter service by the end of 2027. So far, 289 vehicles have arrived and begun operating.

The modern buses are designed to provide more comfortable and reliable journeys while producing fewer harmful emissions, contributing to better air quality in the Hungarian capital.

Importantly, the existing buses currently serving the 100E will not be taken out of service. Instead, they will be transferred to other routes, including the 97E, 142E and 32, bringing improvements to passengers travelling elsewhere in Budapest as well.

World.title: Seven Arrested in International Investment Fraud Crackdown in Balkans
World.content:
Kosovo police and Europol during the raids against an international investment fraud scheme, November 3, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Police

The European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, Eurojust, announced on Tuesday that seven persons were arrested in an international action against investment fraud in an action conducted with the EU police agency Europol that also involved Germany, Cyprus, Finland, Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Israel.

“Authorities, supported by Eurojust and Europol, have taken action against a criminal network running an investment fraud scheme, leading to the shutdown of over 100 servers and seven arrests,” Eurojust announced. According to Europol, extradition to Germany is being considered for the arrested.

The operation started in 2022 after a German couple reported that they had been victims of a fraud scheme after they invested savings but could not withdraw their profits from the online platform they had used.

Europol explained that, “led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor’s Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.”

Kosovo police announced on Facebook that after raiding five locations, three suspects were arrested in Kosovo. “M.P., I.H., and F.Z., [were arrested] on suspicion of committing the criminal offences of participating in or organising an organised criminal group, fraud, unauthorised computer access and computer fraud”. Police announced that “cars, mobile phones, computers and other electronic devices that may serve as evidence in criminal proceedings” were seized.

This is not the first time the international operation has made arrests in this case.

In May 2025, Eurojust announced that one suspect had been arrested in Cyprus after “an organised criminal group (OCG) operating globally defrauded more than 100 victims of over EUR 3 million through a fake online investment platform”.

In September 2022, Eurojust announced that two suspects had been arrested after raids in 12 locations. “With the support of Eurojust, authorities in Finland, Germany, Belgium and Latvia have succeeded in striking a blow against the operators of various fraudulent online investment platforms that have defrauded victims from 11 different countries out of several million euros,” it said.

World.title: Serbia Detains Police Officials Over Abuse of Position, Torture, Allegations
World.content:
The Higher Court in Belgrade on Tuesday ordered 30 days of detention for the head of the Criminal Police Directorate, Marko Kricak, and the head of the Crime Suppression Service, Bosko Sekulovic.

They are charged with abuse of official position, while Kricak is also charged with mistreatment and torture, both linked to a murder in a Belgrade restaurant in May.

Detention was ordered to prevent them influencing witnesses. However, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it would complain about the court’s decision and demand that detention be ordered both due to the potential to influence witnesses and to prevent any repeat of the criminal offence within a short period of time, as earlier proposed by the prosecution.

Kricak and Sekulovic were arrested on Sunday, a week after parliamentary elections in which the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party lost power after 14 years.

Belgrade’s chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, insisted on Monday that the arrests “have nothing to do with electoral processes or the results of the parliamentary elections”.

Kricak and Sekulovic are suspected of abusing their official positions and of “failing to perform their official duty” during their handling of the case of the murder of A.N. in “27” Belgrade’s restaurant on May 12, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said on Tuesday.

Their actions between May 12 and June 3 allegedly caused damage and also violated the rights of the former head of the Belgrade Police Department, Veselin Milic.

Milic was arrested on May 15 under suspicion that he had assisted an offender in the murder and had failed to report the crime. In June, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office dropped part of the complaint relating to assisting an offender after the commission of a crime.

The prosecution said on Tuesday that Sekulovic had drafted a criminal complaint that also named Milic, even though he knew that Milic had left the restaurant before the murder took place. Kricak allegedly gave verbal approval to Sekulovic to submit the criminal complaint, despite being aware of its contents.

On May 21, police found a dead body in a metal drum buried near the town of Indjija. Five days later, it was confirmed that it belonged to A.N. Media have reported that the victim was a gangland figure.

Kricak was also suspected of having used force against those suspected of being involved in the murder.

“Additionally, there are grounds for suspicion that Marko K. on May 16, 2026 … abused the victim N.L. while performing his official duties, in such a way that he, together with unidentified police officers, first struck him with open hands and closed fists in the head area, and placed a hood over his head, suffocating him,” the prosecution’s press release said.

Furthermore, Kricak is suspected of removing the victim’s socks and of beating him on the soles of his feet and back with a belt.

During the massive anti-government protests in Serbia in the last two years, some protesters have claimed that Kricak used force against them. One female detainee, Nikolina Sindjelic, said in August 2025 that Kricak had threatened her with rape. He has not been prosecuted over these allegations.

World.title: Bosnian Serb Army Ex-Members Jailed for 83 Years for Sokolac Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Six former Second Romanija Brigade members have been sentenced by Bosnia’s state court to 83 years in jail in total for crimes against humanity committed near Sokolac in eastern Bosnia in 1992.

Momcilo Pajic was sentenced to 20 years, Miladin Gasevic to 15 and Branislav Kezunovic, Zeljko Gasevic, Jadranko Suka and Nikola Koprivica to 12 years each.

The first-instance verdict acquitted Dragomir Obradovic and Aleksa Gordic.

By the state court’s decision, Pajic, Kezunovic, Gasevic and Suka were ordered to be detained. Miladin Gasevic and Suka did not appear at the hearing at which the verdict was pronounced.

According to the verdict, the six defendants knew about a widespread and systematic attack on the Bosniak civilian population in the Sokolac area lasting from May to September 1992, when disarmament, arrests, transportation and military operations took place.

“All this could not have gone unnoticed by the defendants,” said presiding judge, Enida Hadziomerovic in the verdict explanation.

The chamber concluded that the aim of the action in Novoseoci village was the ethnic cleansing of the population who had previously surrendered their weapons and were loyal to the Bosnian Serb authorities in Sokolac.

Members of the Second Romanija Brigade reportedly deployed themselves around the village on the night of September 21,22, 1992. “The assignment and deployment were managed by Momcilo Pajic and Miladin Gasevic,” Judge Hadziomerovic stated.

Pajic was found guilty as commander of the Military Police, and Gasevic as deputy commander of the Reconnaissance Company.

According to the verdict, the villagers were ordered to leave their homes in the morning and gather at the Metaljka site. Pajic was summoned to the nearby Buljukovina site by the commander of the Second Romanija Brigade, Radislav Krstic, who ordered him to return to Novoseoci and implement the agreed plan to kill the men and deport the women and children.

Meanwhile, in Novoseoci, an elderly woman, Devla Karic, who had been told to look for her husband, was killed by Reconnaissance Company member Slavisa Cvijetic.

Upon Pajic’s return to the village, the women and children were separated and taken to Sarajevo by bus. “The men were detained with Pajic’s announcement that they would be designated for exchange,” the verdict statede.

Pajic, as noted, selected a group to liquidate the village men, which included former members of the Reconnaissance Company, Miladin and Zeljko Gasevic, Momir and Branislav Kezunovic, Jadranko Suka, and former military policeman Nikola Koprivica, as well as other members who have since died.

“They got into the vehicles, knowing that they were being taken to kill [people],” the chamber stated.

As stated, the men were taken in two trucks to the Ivan Polje location, where the group was led by Miladin Gasevic. There, at the sinkhole, they first brought men from one truck and then from another and killed all 44 of them.

“178 shots were fired from automatic weapons … The remains were found in 2000, covered in garbage and the ruins of the mosque in Novoseoci,” Hadziomerovic stated.

She added that, for the killing at Ivan Polje, the Chamber was primarily guided by the statements from the investigation from protected witnesses N-2 and N-3, as well as other witnesses. According to her, later denials by N-2 and N-3, that they were not at Ivan Polje, were unconvincing.

The chamber said the sentences imposed were in accordance with the actions committed by the accused. “The court did not establish special mitigating circumstances,” Hadziomerovic noted.

The chamber concluded that the prosecution had not proven a joint criminal enterprise. On this basis, the former commander of the Sokolac Police Station, Dragomir Obradovic, was acquitted. Hadziomerovic said it was not proven that Obradovic took any other actions or knowingly assisted them.

The chamber also did not establish that Gordic, indicted as deputy commander of the Military Police, took any specific actions.

The trial began in May 2021. Proceedings against Milan Tupajic and Momir Kezunovic were suspended by their deaths. The former commander of the Second Romanija Motorized Brigade of the Bosnian Serb Army, Radislav Krstic, who is serving a sentence in Estonia imposed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, for aiding and abetting genocide, was later indicted.

An appeal against this verdict is allowed.

World.title: Jailed Albanian Mayor Accuses PM of Sending Threats Via Minister
World.content:
Jailed Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj being accompanied to the Constitutional Court in October 2025. Photo: LSA

Relations between Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and jailed Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj further deteriorated on Monday after the Mayor claimed that Rama used a minister to pressure him to resign and to admit he stands behind the violent protests that have rocked Tirana in recent weeks.

Veliaj’s lawyer, Plarent Ndreca, disclosed that last Friday, the Minister of Justice, Toni Gogu, visited the prison where Veliaj was transferred last week with a list of demands from Rama.

Later, Gogu accepted holding the meeting but denied sending any such messages from Rama to Veliaj.

“I met with Erion Veliaj on Friday. In the exercise of my responsibilities as Minister of Justice, I went to assess the conditions of his treatment and to hear the complaints that had been publicly voiced by his lawyer,” Gogu wrote on Monday.

He added: “Those who know me are aware there is no chance, in this world or the next, that I would ever utter the ‘messages’ attributed to me. I am truly taken aback.”

Hours later, Veliaj himself posted two handwritten notes allegedly taken from the meeting, with Rama’s demands.

“I may indeed have less freedom than the Prime Minister but I possess far more dignity than he does … I challenge the Prime Minister to produce even a single piece of evidence to support his insinuations about the protests,” Veliaj said.

The allegations about threats being made against Veliaj emerged just days after his transfer from the pre-trial detention centre in Durres to one in Fier, a move carried out via a contested procedure. In the absence of a written order, Veliaj denounced the transfer as politically motivated and a “police abduction”.

The General Directorate of Prisons said the transfer was a “standard procedure” but that the transfer order had been classified as a “state secret”.

Veliaj’s claims prompted the Albanian Helsinki Committee to conduct monitoring at Fier prison, which revealed serious issues regarding Veliaj’s rights and legal guarantees, specifically about a lack of transparency over the reasons for his transfer, the classification of the transfer order as restricted information and obstacles to exercising the right to an effective appeal.

“Pre-trial detention does not entail the loss of rights that have not been restricted by law or a judicial decision, and security cannot be used as a blanket justification to circumvent transparency, proportionality, and judicial oversight,” it stated.

Veliaj’s prison transfer and his claims have become a hot topic, as Veliaj was once a close ally of PM and Socialist leader Edi Rama.

Political analyst Lutfi Dervishi said that, “for the first time, Veliaj is publicly challenging Rama using language that leaves little room for misunderstanding.”

“If Socialists begin to question whether they should support the party or defend every decision made by its leader, the debate ceases to be merely personal, and for Rama, a new problem emerges,” Dervishi said.

“Until now, the Prime Minister has had to contend with managing government scandals, street protests and the opposition in parliament; now he also faces public accusations from one of his most prominent associates,” he added.

Former Socialist minister Ermelinda Meksi commented that, “if Veliaj’s claims are substantiated, we are dealing with a highly concerning precedent: the use of state authority and instruments to exert political pressure on an individual in pre-trial detention”.

On a local show, “Opinion”, Veliaj’s lawyer, Plarent Ndreca, said that it all arose “from a message issued by Mr Veliaj regarding the Belgrade issue; ever since that message was sent, there has been a shift in institutional behavior.”

Ndreca referred to a congratulatory message that Veliaj issued about the recent elections in Serbia that toppled the regime of Aleksandar Vucic.

“Congratulations to the students for toppling the Machiavellian and populist from Belgrade! Student movements and protests do not signify the ‘end of the world’ but rather the end of ‘a world’. The sooner we as citizens and policymakers grasp this, the better equipped we will be to respond to the needs and expectations of this generation,” Veliaj wrote on October 26.

Albanians have been similarly protesting for almost five months against the government, with students in October joining the anti-government protests, demanding Rama’s resignation.

Veliaj has been in a jail since February 10, 2025, when he was arrested by the Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, on charges of corruption and money laundering, allegedly carried out through a scheme that also involves his wife, Ajola Xoxa. He has denied the accusations.

World.title: Albanian Journalists Complain of Police Violence, Abuse During Anti-Govt Protests
World.content:
Glidona Daci was reporting live from anti-government protests in Albania when she was pepper-sprayed by police.

In her report for Klan News, Daci is seen telling police officers: “The camera is live, don’t touch the operator, and don’t spray me with pepper spray.”

Pushed by police, Daci said police ignored her protestations.

World.title: Post-Vucic Serbia Will Reengage with Europe, But It Will Not Be a Honeymoon
World.content:
On October 25, 2025, Serbian students and the coalition they formed, the Student List, shocked the world by defeating the ruling Serbian Progressive Party in a landslide electoral victory. This ended 14-years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader Aleksandar Vucic, a period in which the SNS dominated public institutions, the media and national security services.

After the elections, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos declared that “a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.” Not so fast. The end of the old regime does not mean the EU-Serbia honeymoon can begin, nor does it mean EU membership for Serbia is a slam dunk.

What is realistic to expect in the post-election period? The new government will make goodwill gestures towards Brussels and European capitals. Ilija Srdanovic, first on the Student List, said Serbia remains committed to European integration and that the new government will continue normalisation talks between Belgrade and Pristina, mediated by Brussels.

World.title: Waste Crisis Blights Kosovo’s Capital and its Mayor’s Political Ambitions
World.content:
Earlier this month, in a video made by an influencer in New York, Pristina mayor Perparim Rama unveiled his latest ambition - to become prime minister of Kosovo.

The response from many residents of Kosovo’s capital was tongue-in-cheek, to say the least.

They flooded social media with photos and videos depicting the waste crisis afflicting Pristina for the past couple of years, questioning Rama’s readiness to lead the country if he can’t even fix its biggest city.

Uncollected garbage regularly blights Pristina’s streets, as the result of a lack of resources and a row between local authorities and the state government.

Last week, Rama, who is not a member of any party but ran for mayor on behalf of the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, said the crisis was the fault of the central government, and accused Finance Minister Hekuran Murati of failing to sign off on the money needed to pay for new waste trucks and dumpsters.

Rama said the government was blocking municipal efforts to open a new city waste company, while preventing trucks from unloading waste at the landfill overnight.

“The city then gets filled with waste,” he told TV Dukagjini. “Then they photograph it and tell me ‘look how you have filled the city with garbage.’”

World.title: Serbia Bank Owner Arrested Following Licence Revocation
World.content:
Alta Bank HQ in Belgrade. Photo: Wikimedia/Andrei Romanenko

The owner of Serbia’s Alta Bank, Davor Macura, was arrested on Monday, three days after the National Bank revoked the bank’s licence.

Macura was arrested on suspicion of abuse of office for withdrawing money from Alta Bank’s treasury and obtaining a financial gain of 45 billion dinars (nearly 385 million euros).

In addition to Macura, G.M., director of the Bank’s Treasury and Cash Management Department, and I.P., an employee responsible for treasury operations, were also arrested on the orders of the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime. They are suspected of assisting Macura in committing the alleged criminal offence.

The prosecution suspects that Macura exceeded the limits of his authority up until October 31. G.M. and I.P., who were responsible for the direct handling of assets held in Alta Bank’s treasury, allegedly provided Macura with “access cards or used their own cards and were physically present to enable unauthorised entry into the bank’s treasury”.

“During these unauthorised entries, D.M. [Macura] allegedly removed money from the vault, thereby obtaining an illicit financial gain amounting to approximately 45 billion dinars,” the prosecution said.

The National Bank of Serbia, NBS, revoked Alta Bank’s operating licence on October 31 citing a significant deterioration in its finances and concerns over its liquidity.

“The Executive Board noted that the revocation of the licence was preceded by supervisory measures aimed at ensuring that the bank increased its liquidity levels,” the NBS said, adding that the interests of the bank’s depositors had been put at risk.

Alta Bank expanded its operations during the Serbian Progressive Party’s time in power under former President Aleksandar Vucic. In 2025, for example, Serbia’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda Srbije, EPS, changed its payment arrangements, directing Belgrade residents to pay their electricity bills into Alta Bank accounts.

Shortly before calling parliamentary elections, former President Vucic launched a podcast on his YouTube channel with Alta Bank among its main sponsors, featuring s for it displayed in the studio.

Vucic’s list in the October 25 parliamentary elections lost power after 14 years of rule to the Student List, which has won an absolute majority.

North Macedonia Bank takes control of Alta subsidiary

Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Macedonia, the central bank has placed Alta Bank AD Bitola under temporary administration, taking control of its assets following the collapse of its majority shareholder, Alta Bank AD Belgrade, in Serbia.

The measure on Sunday was intended to protect the bank’s assets and depositors amid a sharp withdrawal of funds, North Macedonia’s Central Bank governor, Trajko Slaveski, told a press conference.

Slaveski said around 2 million euros had been withdrawn from the Bitola-based bank within days, prompting the intervention. He stressed that the North Macedonian bank remained liquid and had a sound loan portfolio. The Serbian bank’s exposure to its North Macedonia counterpart was relatively small, he added, at around 1 million euros, and did not threaten its liquidity.

Under the temporary administration, which can last up to three months, central bank-appointed administrators will assume management responsibilities, while the Serbian-majority shareholder will lose its voting rights. Customers will be meanwhile allowed to withdraw no more than 10,000 denars [around 160 euros] per week through payment cards issued by the bank.

The bank said its branches will temporarily stop serving customers from Monday until further notice. Slaveski also said potential buyers may acquire the Serbian shareholder’s stake in the bank as a potential long-term solution.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport Scandal – Wrong Pipes Used, €22 Million Must be Returned
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – The Dubrovnik Airport scandal is being hailed as among the worst ever involving EU cash and an airport, with the wrong piping installed and a massive €22 million now needing to be returned.

Dubrovnik Airport must return €22 euros received of European Union funds after the uncovering of a scandal like few could have imagined. Index reports that the decision was made due to established irregularities in public procurement procedures during the airport reconstruction project, which began a whole thirteen years ago and was one of the largest infrastructure projects co-financed with EU funds.

problematic procurement processes and unusable system…

The total value of the reconstruction amounted to an enormous €230 million, of which almost €160 million was non-refundable The total amount that must now be returned represents around 14 percent of those funds. “It’s an amount of approximately €22 million that must be returned. That’s about 14 percent of the non-refundable funds provided by the European Union. The problem related to public procurement procedures and the signing of the main contracts, mostly in the period from 2013 to 2017,” explained Viktor Šober, director of Dubrovnik Airport.

Among the disputed public procurement procedures, the one for the aircraft fuel supply system stands out in particular. The problem arose because the wrong pipes were installed during construction. “We engaged a serious international company specialised in underground hydrant systems for fuel delivery to the apron. They are not optimistic,” Šober added. Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković confirmed the scale of the problem. “The fact is that ten public procurements were penalised, and instead of adequate pipes for aviation fuel, sewage pipes were installed, which is why the entire system is not operational,” Franković said.

information was received about the case in 2022…

The European Public Prosecutor’s Office also commented on the genuinely somewhat shocking Dubrovnik Airport scandal case. They explained that they received information from national authorities back in 2022, but decided not to take over the case because the reported facts were outside their temporal jurisdiction.

Former airport director Roko Tolić, now executive director of Airports of Montenegro, also reacted to the scandal. He claims that the fuel system was not constructed during his term. “The building permit for that facility was issued on the 3rd of September 2018, seven whole months after my departure, and the works were carried out from September 2018 and completed during 2019. Whether the installed pipes are in accordance with the permit and the project is determined by a technical inspection before the competent authority. I cannot speak about the pipes and the as-built condition from my own knowledge because I did not participate in those works,” Tolić said. The management of Dubrovnik Airport emphasises that this is a serious issue for them, given that they invested significant funds in a system that they ultimately cannot use at all.

World.title: First Snow of Winter Arrives – 20 cm Falls in Highest Croatian Settlement!
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – The very first snow of the winter has arrived, with around 20 cm falling and settling in the highest Croatian settlement.

In the highest parts of Croatia, the very first snow of the winter season has fallen. Approximately 12 centimetres were measured on Zavižan, and a snow cover also formed on Platak near Rijeka and in mountainous Gorski Kotar. Index reports that the highest amount of snow, currently measuring at around 20 centimetres, has been measured in Begovo Razdolje, the highest inhabited settlement in all of Croatia.

Because of the fresh snowfall, the residents of Begovo Razdolje had to take up their shovels a little later than usual and clear the approaches to their houses and driveways. “I’m 82 years old, so this comes as recreation for me. A bit of physical activity and fresh air does me good,” local resident Franjo Štritof told Nova TV. For the twenty or so permanent residents of the settlement, snow at the beginning of November at 1,078 metres above sea level is no surprise. “Everyone chooses whether this is for them or not, but life here is good,” says farm owner Bojan Francišković.

During the day, the air temperature hovered around three degrees Celsius, meaning that eventually, the snow turned into rain. “Now, it’s raining a little and snowing a little, and at night, pure snow falls,” Franjo Štritof explained. According to current forecasts, the first snow of the season won’t stay until the weekend. “This is nothing new. Usually it turns white like this in the middle of October, lasts for about a day or two, and after that the weather improves again and autumn is still alright for a while,” concluded Bojan Francišković.
