World.title: HDZ Candidate and Hospital Commission Member Arrested in Corruption Probe
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – Vladimir Ovčarić, HDZ local candidate and head of the Technical and Service Activities Department of the Zabok General Hospital and Croatian Veterans’ Hospital, has been arrested in a wider corruption probe.

Ovčarić is also particularly active in local politics and holds positions in the Krapina Hunting Society. Index reports that as was shown by the official election results for Krapina, HDZ’s Ovčarić was the lead candidate of the joint HDZ and Zagorje Party list for the Podgora Local Committee in the elections for local committee councils back in May 2025.

politics, hunting and hospital fire brigade president

His list won 291 votes, or 42.61 percent, and three seats on the seven-member local committee council. Alongside Ovčarić, Slavko Vincelj and Marijo Družinec were elected. At the constitutive session held on 9 June 2025, Ovčarić was elected deputy president of the Podgora Local Committee Council, while Tomislav Pernjek from the SDP list was elected president.

Ovčarić is also active in the Krapina Hunting Society. According to publicly available data, he is listed as the society’s secretary and as one of the persons authorised to represent it. On the society’s official website he also appears among the members of the executive board and is listed on the register of full members of the society. Ovčarić was previously president of the Volunteer Fire Brigade of the Zabok General Hospital. His name appears in the data of the Firefighting Association of Krapina-Zagorje County, while publicly available data show that this function ended on the 11th of March 2020. He has worked at the hospital for very many years. Back in 2012, he was mentioned as head of the technical and service department when he took part with the police in a project to place anti-burglary warnings for cars in the hospital car park.

he was on the commission for the hospital kiosk tender

Particularly interesting are also the official minutes of the hospital’s Governing Board. From the minutes of the session held on the 10th of October 2024 it emerges that Ovčarić was appointed to a three-member commission for the implementation of a public tender for the lease of hospital premises and land. The tender concerned space for the installation of machines for hot and cold drinks and land for the installation of a fast-food facility. According to the decision of the Governing Board, the commission was responsible for preparing the tender, opening and reviewing bids, and proposing the selection of the most favourable bidder. Ovčarić was, according to the minutes from March 2025, also appointed to the commission for the implementation of the tender for the lease of parking spaces in the hospital garage. These documents confirm that Ovčarić had a role in conducting hospital tenders. For the time being, however, it has not been officially confirmed whether precisely these procedures are the subject of the current investigation.

what sort of corruption is he suspected of?

As was previously reported, Ovčarić is suspected of having accepted several hundred euros in bribes from convicts in order to enable them to avoid the community service work they were required to perform at the hospital. Investigators also suspect that he favoured companies in obtaining jobs. In one case a company allegedly received a new job with the explanation that it had leftover unused stone from previous works, which enabled it to offer a lower price.

According to information obtained by Index, the award of the contract for the hospital kiosk to the owner of a service craft business with whom Ovčarić was close is also being investigated. It is suspected that Ovčarić himself actually ran the kiosk and earned income from its turnover. Allegations that hospital employees performed work on his private properties are also being checked. According to unofficial information, the USKOK action has involved eight persons. Police are carrying out arrests and urgent investigative measures in the area of Krapina-Zagorje County, Zagreb and Osijek. The Zabok General Hospital and Croatian Veterans’ Hospital confirmed that the police had requested documentation relating to one employee. They said they are cooperating with investigators but that, due to the ongoing investigation, they currently cannot comment on media reports.

World.title: 56,000 People in Croatia Diagnosed With a Disability in One Year
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – There has been a staggering increase of 56,000 people across Croatia diagnosed with some kind of disability in just one year. As things currently stand, every fifth person in Croatia is disabled.

In just one single year, the number of recorded persons with disabilities in Croatia rose by as many as 56,000, according to a new report by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ). Ivana Krnic reports for Jutarnji that according to the report, on 28 September this year there were 730,987 persons with disabilities living in Croatia, compared with 675,213 one year earlier. In other words, almost every fifth resident of Croatia is now officially recorded as a person with a disability.

Such a worrying and high increase is primarily, according to those familiar with the matter, a consequence of the introduction of the inclusive allowance. Namely, the Register of Persons with Disabilities is actually a database of persons who exercise some right on the basis of disability: persons who have not been assessed or do not exercise any right cannot be in that database, regardless of their actual disability.

Since the criteria for obtaining the inclusive allowance are incomparably milder than the criteria for the personal disability benefit or the allowance for another person’s assistance and care — rights that preceded the inclusive allowance — the number of persons receiving the inclusive allowance is significantly higher than the number of persons who previously received cash assistance. Specifically speaking, before the introduction of the inclusive allowance, around 150,000 persons received the personal disability benefit and the allowance for another person’s assistance and care, while the inclusive allowance is now received by around 240,000 persons, with around another hundred thousand applications still pending. The majority of persons receiving the inclusive allowance had the same or very similar difficulties earlier, but did not meet the strict criteria for receiving cash assistance and were therefore not registered as persons with disabilities.

The HZJZ response also confirms that the new rights have significantly increased interest in assessments.

new rights prompted an assessment increase

“It covers a wide range of rights and that has attracted a large number of persons who hadn’t previously been assessed to undergo assessment and try in this way to exercise some of the mentioned rights,” doc. dr. sc. Tomislav Benjak, assistant director of the HZJZ for the quality of healthcare and author of the Report on Persons with Disabilities, told Jutarnji list.

In addition to the inclusive allowance, he also mentions other rights, such as priority in employment, transport privileges, scholarships and tax reliefs, which can be exercised on the basis of an established disability. The method of collecting data also influenced the increase. Today almost all findings and decisions arrive digitally, practically immediately after the assessment, whereas previously they were partly delivered by post. Such a system did not guarantee that all of the data was indeed recorded in the Register. The largest part of the increase relates to persons over the age of 65. Their number rose in one year from 317,164 to 358,806, i.e. by 41,642 persons. That is almost three quarters of the total annual increase.

Today almost half of all persons recorded in the Register are over 65 years old, and disability has been established in approximately 40 percent of the population of that age. Benjak says that the ageing of the population is one of the main reasons for the long-term increase in the number of persons with disabilities. In older age, difficulties with mobility, impairments of sight and hearing, and the consequences of chronic diseases occur more frequently. However, part of the increase also stems from the fact that persons who were already recorded eventually move into the older age group.

“The natural transition from the age group up to 65 years into the age group of 65 years and over affects this distribution by approximately 30 percent,” he explains. Croatia is also not helped by the health habits of the population. Benjak warns of the high frequency of cardiovascular and malignant diseases, smoking, obesity and insufficient physical activity.

how much does croatia actually deviate from global trends?

Despite this, he emphasises that Croatia does not deviate significantly from international trends. When the first Register data was published back in 2007, the share of persons with disabilities was 10.7 percent, and today it is 18.9 percent. According to the data he cites, the World Health Organisation estimates that persons with disabilities make up around 16 percent of the world’s population, while Eurostat for the European Union cites 23.9 percent. These data, however, are not necessarily completely comparable because they are based on different methods of establishing disability. The new HZJZ report for the first time also brings a division according to the severity of disability. According to that classification, 106,724 persons have severe disability and 142,722 persons have more severe disability. Together that is almost 250,000 people. However, for as many as 206,902 persons, or 28.3 percent of all those recorded, the severity of disability has not been classified.

Benjak explains that these are mostly persons who were assessed many years ago, when the findings from the then social welfare centres did not contain the data needed for today’s classification.

Interestingly, a large part of these persons, despite the possibility of exercising these new rights, have not undergone a new assessment. It is also possible that they are not sufficiently informed. “What somehow surprises us as well is that around 200,000 persons assessed at that time with rights from social welfare and elements for entry into the Register have not requested new assessments in order to exercise the right to, for example, the inclusive allowance or rights in transport,” Benjak is also surprised.

He emphasises that this is not a matter of double entries or of deceased persons. Every person is tracked by personal identification number (OIB), and the HZJZ also has data on deaths. He confirms that all 206,902 persons are alive and that there is a legal basis for their entry into the Register. The new division according to the severity of disability serves exclusively for statistical purposes and does not affect the exercise of rights. Nevertheless, the fact that data needed for classification are missing for more than a quarter of the recorded persons shows how difficult it is to obtain a complete picture of the structure of disability in Croatia.

huge differences on a county by county basis

There are also large differences among counties. In Šibenik-Knin County disability is recorded in 24.4 percent of the population, almost twice as much as in Istria County, where that share is 12.3 percent. The range is even greater among those over 65 years of age. In Šibenik-Knin County 49.6 percent of the population of that age have a disability, in Požega-Slavonia County 49.5 percent, and in Istria County 25.1 percent.

Data for children and young people in Sisak-Moslavina County are particularly worrying. There the prevalence of disability in the age group up to 19 years rose from 17.9 to 20.5 percent, while the Croatian average is 12.3 percent. This means that disability is recorded in approximately every fifth child or young person in that county. Asked why the differences are so large, Benjak says that a special study would need to be conducted. Nevertheless, he warns that Sisak-Moslavina is one of the most deprived Croatian counties, with lower wages, weaker employment, higher unemployment and unfavourable demographic trends.

“All of the above certainly also has as a consequence the occurrence of disability and developmental difficulties in children,” Benjak believes. Without additional analysis it is not possible to determine how much health and social conditions, and how much the availability of diagnostics, assessments and the method of recording, influence such a high prevalence.

the case with children across croatia

Another seemingly unusual piece of data appears in the report. Although the total number of children and young people with disabilities is rising, the number of persons for whom decisions on an appropriate form of schooling arrived in the Register has decreased from 57,703 to 49,847. Nevertheless, it seems that the reason is not necessarily a smaller number of children with difficulties, but a change in the records.

According to Benjak’s explanation, the Ministry of Education requested the deactivation of records of persons up to the age of 21 whose only basis for entry into the Register was a decision on an appropriate form of schooling, and who after 2015 weren’t ever reassessed. Among them are persons who during childhood had developmental difficulties such as dyslexia, dysgraphia, behavioural disorders or learning difficulties, which over time may have decreased or disappeared. Changes in the records also explain the decrease in the number of Croatian war military invalids. Their number fell from 54,640 to 46,132, i.e. by 8,508 persons.

According to instructions from the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, only persons who are in its official database remain in the HRVI category. Some previously recorded persons no longer appear in that database, so their HRVI status in the Register has been deactivated. Despite such changes, Benjak claims that the annual reports have been prepared using the same methodology and that it is possible to track trends. In fact, the only novelty in the 2026 report is the additional statistical division according to the severity of disability. However, precisely the changes in the records of children and veterans show how much administrative decisions can influence the statistics.

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.

World.title: 135 Years of the Zagreb Tram – From Horses to Modernity
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – 135 years is the time period during which the now iconic blue Zagreb tram has snaked through the capital city. From being pulled by horses to new vehicles, let’s look back at the history of what we now know as ZET.

Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that frequent trams have been circulating Zagreb’s streets for 135 years now. They have become the blue symbol of the city, living history on the rails, and transport without which Zagreb can hardly function, something Zagreb residents felt most clearly during the recent multi-day ZET workers’ strike, which caused days of traffic problems until a court declared it illegal and banned it.

horse-drawn trams named after vineyard pests…

The first tram circled Zagreb back in 1891. It was pulled by horses and was far from the technical modernity we know today. Zagreb’s trams were once yellow and ran on only a few lines through the very city centre. People affectionately called them “konjka” (horse-tram), but also mockingly “filoksera”, after the notorious wine louse (phylloxera) that was ravaging vineyards in those years, because the workers laying the tracks had dug up and torn apart half the city. Before the trams, passengers were transported around Zagreb by omnibuses that resembled stagecoaches from Western films. They ran from the city centre to the bathing spots on the Sava and from the railway station to a few hotels. As ZET explains, “the city fathers in Zagreb began discussing the need to introduce a horse-drawn tram as a means of transport” in 1885.

French engineer Raoul Pierre Alexandre Gautier proposed a contract for the introduction of tram traffic to the Zagreb City Magistrate on the 20th of June 1887. The city municipality accepted his offer and on the 26th of March 1889 issued him a permit to build a tram line on the ground of the city streets. The Association of Engineers and Technicians allowed the construction of a 76-centimetre-wide track, and the Tramway Company, a special private enterprise, began work. The first tram depot was built on the site of today’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum.

ilica, zagreb’s modern main artery, was dug up

zagreb.hr

The first lines were built from the corner of Ilica and Mandaličina Street to Maksimir, from the corner of Ilica and Frankopanska Street to the Sava Bridge, and from the corner of Ilica and today’s Republic of Austria Street to the Western Railway Station. Construction began in May 1891, and the trams started running a few months later. Historian Lelja Dobronić, in the article “Old Notes on the Zagreb Tram” published in the magazine Kaj, cites a document from the 17th of August 1891: “Since the long-awaited rails from England and the carriages from Graz (in Austria) have finally arrived, Upper Ilica has been being dug up since last Thursday, and from today Frankopanska Street as well, so that the rails can be laid. Certainly by this Sunday the rails will be laid through the whole of Ilica and Jelačić Square. Up to 500 workers are working a day.”

At the time when Zagreb’s trams were pulled by horses, there were ten closed and six open vehicles available, manufactured at the Weitzer factory in Graz. The average speed of the horse-drawn tram cars was 7.5 km/h. Zagreb’s horse-drawn tram also carried passengers in Velika Gorica, where the joint-stock company Horse Railway was founded back in 1907. They had a seven-kilometre line from the railway station, through the centre of Velika Gorica, to Novo Čiče. It was called “konjača.” After 1945 the horses were replaced by a small diesel locomotive.

electrification and expansion

The electric tram started in August 1910, but horse-drawn trams continued to operate for the following year. Zagreb’s trams changed colour in 1923. They became blue instead of yellow, while the vehicles were reconstructed. A new model, the M-24, manufactured in Zagreb and running on the right-hand track, also appeared on the streets. Summer open-air trams soon became available as well. During the time of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), Zagreb’s trams ran with increasing difficulty because of bombing, and services were suspended in 1944. Traffic resumed after liberation, and in the autumn of 1945 tracks were built through Vodnikova and Mihanovićeva streets. From then on, the tram lines had numbers. In the following years lines were built towards Žitnjak as well as the Mihaljevac–Dolje line. A building for ZET workers was constructed in Puljska Street.

bull, czech and katica…

At the beginning of the 1950s, Zagreb’s residents also received the first domestically produced tram, built in the ZET workshop. It was prototype 101 with 95 passenger seats. This was followed by cooperation with the “Đuro Đaković” wagon factory from Slavonski Brod and the purchase of M-201 vehicles.

The last example of the M-201 tram, nicknamed “Đuro” or “Bik” (Bull), ran until June 2024 on line 9. Its predecessor, the M-24, ran from 1924 to 1977. Today it is used as the Christmas tram. In 1977 Czechoslovak trams from the ČKD-Tatra factory in Prague were purchased. The Czech T4 model trams, known as “Čeh” (Czech), ran for years on lines 4, 6 and 14. Years later the Tatra KT4YU trams, better known as “Katice,” also arrived. An important date in the history of the Zagreb tram was the 25th of November 1979, when the line along Držićeva Street, across the Bridge of Youth, to New Zagreb was opened. That was when the tram crossed the Sava. In 1980 a tram-bus terminal was built at Črnomerec on the site of a former brickworks. In November 1985 the tram also started running across the Adriatic Bridge towards New Zagreb. Further development of ZET includes the abolition of the conductor’s job in 1996 (conductors had been cancelling and selling tickets in the vehicles for 105 years) and the extension of tram routes to Dubec and Prečko.

and then came končar…

Over the last thirty years or so the old trams, Bulls, Czechs and Katicas, have been replaced by trams manufactured at Končar, Zagreb’s technological giant.

“In more than 30 years of operation on Zagreb’s tram network, Končar trams have covered more than 140 million kilometres, confirming their quality, reliability and indispensable role in the lives of Zagreb residents,” Končar told Index. The company had already begun manufacturing electric rectifier stations for ZET back in 1954. “After almost three decades of cooperation on energy infrastructure, ZET and Končar began joint development of tram vehicles. Production of the TMK 2100 series trams began in 1993, and the prototype was presented on the 5th of September 1994 and immediately put into regular service,” the company notes, also recalling the TMK 2200 trams. “From June 2010 a total of 140 TMK 2200 series trams and two shorter TMK 2200-K trams (which carry the designation TMK 2300 in ZET’s fleet) have been produced for Zagreb,” Končar says. The company later also manufactured shorter trams for the Latvian city of Liepāja.

zagreb’s blue trams

In order to fill gaps in the timetable until the delivery of new vehicles, ZET bought 11 used GT6M trams from Augsburg, Germany, at the end of 2023 and during 2024. This sparked lively public debate because of their age and the fact that the passenger areas are not air-conditioned. The newest Zagreb trams, the TMK 2300, have been in service since February 2025, and there will be forty of them. Through their rich history Zagreb’s trams have become the city’s blue symbol, a mark of the development of domestic technology, and an indicator of Zagreb’s expansion ever further from its historic centre. Zagreb is, along with Osijek, the only Croatian city with tram traffic. Trams once also ran in Pula (from 1904 to 1934), Dubrovnik (from 1910 to 1970), and Rijeka and Opatija.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Accuses EU of Wanting to be a Superstate
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian President Zoran Milanović has accused the EU of wanting to become a superstate, adding that Montenegro, with which Croatia has multiple open issues, is otherwise welcome to join.

President Zoran Milanović stated that Montenegro is welcome to become a full member of the European Union, while at the same time criticising the direction in which the EU is developing. Index reports that the president believes the EU is increasingly trying to become a superstate, whereas it should focus on free trade, freedom of movement and the harmonisation of rules among member states.

Milanović spoke at the 27th Lučindan Gatherings in Zagreb, a traditional meeting of the Montenegrin community in Croatia. The event was also attended by Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović, who is on a working visit to Croatia. The two presidents discussed relations between the two countries and Montenegro’s European future.

“montenegro is welcome to join”

“Montenegro is a candidate for membership of the European Union, it is moving towards the EU and let it come. As far as I am concerned, it is welcome,” Milanović said. Nevertheless, he repeated his criticisms of the European Union, which he believes is exceeding the powers and possibilities on which it was originally founded. In his view, the EU should stick to economic cooperation, free movement and the alignment of rules, rather than striving to create a superstate.

Milanović told Montenegrins that the greatest value they have is their state. He emphasised that Montenegro has realised its statehood and that its future success does not depend exclusively on membership of the European Union. “The greatest thing you have is your state. Montenegro has realised itself, and everything else consists of greater or lesser advances that do not stand in the way of Montenegro being successful, well-governed and relatively prosperous,” Milanović said. He wished Montenegro to continue on its own path and develop as a successful and well-governed state. He concluded his address with verses by the Montenegrin ruler and poet Petar II Petrović Njegoš.

trust between croatia and montenegro must be strengthened

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović assessed that Croatia and Montenegro are friendly countries and that Montenegro’s membership of the European Union is in the interest of both countries. He stressed that improving relations requires continuing political dialogue and resolving existing open issues.

“It is our shared responsibility to build good-neighbourly relations, foster open dialogue, overcome current challenges and strengthen mutual trust,” Milatović said. He emphasised that a common European future implies political and economic cooperation, mutual respect and a willingness to resolve disagreements. He thanked the Montenegrin community in Croatia for preserving national identity, culture and ties with the home country.

The Lučindan Gatherings are a traditional event dedicated to preserving Montenegrin cultural identity, tradition and ties with Montenegro. They bring together members of the Montenegrin national minority in Croatia as well as representatives of the cultural and public life of the two countries. According to the 2021 census, 3,127 members of the Montenegrin national minority live in Croatia, or 0.08 percent of the total population.

World.title: Before You Apply: The Legal Deadline Blocking Croatian Descendants
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – There is a somewhat unknown legal deadline blocking Croatian descendants from obtaining their Croatian and as such EU passport.

That issue relates to the exact reason your family left the former Yugoslavia, and why exactly this could throw a spanner in the works of your EU future. Let’s turn the clock back to October the 8th, 1991… If you’re exploring your eligibility for Croatian citizenship by descent, you have likely come across a specific date repeatedly, and that date is October the 8th, 1991. In the (often confusing) world of Croatian citizenship law, this is the ultimate historical line in the sand. Under the descent and emigrant pathways of the Croatian Citizenship Act, your ancestor must have left the territory of what is now the recognised territory of Croatia before this exact date to grant you a pathway to a Croatian and therefore EU passport of your own.

For many second- and third-generation descendants of those who left what was then Yugoslavia, this seems straightforward at first glance. They look at their family history, note that their parents or grandparents moved to the United States 1960s, 1970s, or 1980s, and check the box. However, many “DIY applicants” face rejections from the Croatian side of the fence because they fail to realise that the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) enforces strict, hidden caveats regarding why and how your ancestor left when they did. Simply proving your family departed before the clock struck 1991 is not quite enough. To secure your Croatian citizenship, you must prove the exact legal nature of their exit. That is where, quite understandably, many people become unstuck and their citizenship applications get shoved to the back of a shelf somewhere to gather dust.

what exactly does croatia deem to be an emigrant?

The Croatian side evaluates citizenship applications based on a highly specific legal definition of what they deem an emigrant to actually be. Under the law as it stands, an emigrant is someone who left the territory of Croatia with the clear, permanent intention of abandoning their domestic residence and resettling somewhere abroad. Because of this ultra-narrow definition that leaves very little wiggle room, there are two major legal traps that routinely catch DIY applicants by surprise.

the so-called internal migration problem

If your ancestor was born in Croatia but moved to another republic within former Yugoslavia, such as Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Slovenia, and then moved across the pond to North America, Croatia’s authorities may not view them as a legal emigrant from Croatia because of that, regardless of the fact that they still ended up in the USA. If that person’s initial move was treated as an internal migration within the same federal state, the chain of continuity for Croatian descent can be heavily compromised or, as is often the case, simply rejected outright.

the curse of the Croatian gastarbajteri…

A Monument to Croatian Emigrants – Anglogermantranslations

During the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of people left the former Yugoslavia to work abroad as temporary economic migrants, often referred to as gastarbajteri (guest workers). Many of these individuals retained their active residency rights, property registrations, and legal ties to Croatia and as such to Yugoslavia, fully intending to return after a few years. If MUP reviews your ancestor’s file and determines that their departure was legally categorised as a “temporary economic migration” rather than a permanent severance of domestic ties, your application under the emigrant track can be denied.

verifying permanence…

Commons/Bain News Service

When you submit your application to a Croatian consulate, the reviewing officers will thoroughly inspect your paperwork to determine the legal permanence of your ancestor’s departure. A simple plane ticket or family story will not suffice. To build an airtight case, you must present a synchronised paper trail that cross-references multiple things.

The first is what’s known as a foreign naturalisation timeline. This works to document precisely when your Croatian ancestor applied for and received citizenship in their new country, showing a definitive shift in legal allegiance. Then come the international arrival records. These are official historical maritime or flight manifests matching the timeline of their permanent resettlement. Last but not least comes the so-called letter of motivation. This might seem odd, but there should always be an explicit structure built up of your family’s narrative, framing their historical departure to meet the rigid legal thresholds expected by Croatia.

for croatia, the year 1991 represents a minefield in several ways…

Proving the legal nuances of a person’s departure that took place forty or fifty years ago is a massive bureaucratic challenge. It requires a deep understanding of historical (and of course needlessly complicated) Yugoslav exit laws, international naturalisation records, and precise legal phrasing in the Croatian language. This is exactly why the structured service provided by Croatian By Descent is an essential safeguard for diaspora families.

croatian by descent‘s experts understand the complexities of the former state

Rather than treating your citizenship application like a roll of the dice, their team conducts an exhaustive upfront document review. They analyse your family’s specific migration timeline, identify potential vulnerabilities in how your ancestors left Yugoslavia, and help you with your application package. By coordinating the procurement of records and managing the precise drafting of your legal motivation letter, they ensure that the Ministry views your family’s departure as a definitive, permanent emigration. They handle the heavy administrative legal lifting, protecting your application from common 1991 cutoff traps and turning your family history into a submission package. Outsource the endless guesswork and verify your eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent.

World.title: Expert warns against 'Christmas' wish list in Estonia's defense plans
World.content:
Defense expert Meelis Oidsalu warns that Estonia's new defense plans risk becoming a wish list of costly military capabilities the country can't afford to maintain.

In a recent blog post, Oidsalu cautioned that pre-election pressure could lead to costly purchases without enough consideration of the associated long-term maintenance.

Speaking to ERR, he said his biggest concern is Estonia's National Defense Development Plan becoming a patchwork document as it is continually expanded.

"Each branch of the military walks away with some shiny new gift," Oidsalu said, bringing up 90-meter ships for the Navy, missile defense or aircraft for the Air Force and more firepower for the Army. "I've gotten the impression this year that it's Christmas in the defense sector."

The expert warned that adding capabilities Estonia cannot afford to maintain could divert funds from more immediate needs, including ammunition stocks.

"If we start building 'trophy' capabilities that we'll never be able to manage to develop at a meaningful scale, we're wasting resources that could instead go toward increasing the number of days we could sustain combat."

Martin Herem. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Minister of Defense Martin Herem said Tuesday that the threat posed by Russia could grow if the war in Ukraine ends, making it necessary to develop certain capabilities quickly even if they prove difficult to maintain.

He later clarified that he did not expect Estonia to actually acquire capabilities beyond what it could sustain.

'Take a step back'

Oidsalu emphasized that Estonia has little experience estimating the long-term costs of major naval vessels and missile defense systems, which international experience suggests often exceed initial estimates.

"We should take a step back and calculate over the long term whether we can afford to deploy all these capabilities," he added.

While acknowledging that the military's assessment of its needs has changed this year, Oidsalu said planning cannot remain in flux. He warned against adding impressive-sounding capabilities in the run-up to an election without ensuring Estonia can actually afford to put them into service and maintain them.

World.title: Drone imagery reveals likely sites of future Pakri cliff collapses
World.content:
Years of drone surveys by University of Tartu geologists have shown that the Pakri Cliffs often erode from below, with seawater washing away soft sandstone until overlying limestone collapses into the sea. The resulting 3D models can identify dangerous areas before a collapse occurs.

Two winters ago, in mid-January, an observation platform at the Pakri Cliffs collapsed into the sea. A 30-meter section of the cliff edge broke away, and the cliff retreated 12 meters in a single event. About 2,800 cubic meters of rock, equivalent to roughly 160 dump truck loads, fell into the water. Although the collapse appeared sudden from above, it could have been anticipated from the side, writes University of Tartu junior research fellow in geology Tiia-Linda Purge.

Not everything is visible from the top

Near Paldiski, the Baltic Klint rises directly from the sea to heights of up to 25 meters. A historic lighthouse dating to the era of Russian czar Peter I stands at the edge, alongside well-worn visitor trails. Geologists have studied this section of the cliff for more than two centuries, focusing mainly on its rock layers and composition. Until now, however, cliff retreat has largely been measured from above by comparing historical maps and aerial imagery.

The cliff edge tells only part of the story. The Pakri Cliffs resemble a layer cake. The upper seven meters consist of limestone, with harder, fractured rock near the top and more clay-rich, sandy, and fragile layers below. Beneath that lies green glauconitic sandstone, once studied as a source material for potassium fertilizer, followed by black shale, also known as graptolite argillite, and softer sandstones at the base. These rocks were deposited on the floor of an ancient sea nearly 500 million years ago.

If scientists evaluate cliff retreat solely by studying the edge, they miss what is happening beneath it. A significant part of the process occurs midway down the vertical cliff face, an area inaccessible to people without ropes and difficult to observe from conventional aerial surveys. That is why researchers set out to map the cliff from the side and in three dimensions.

Potential zones of cliff failure based on the study authors' expert opinion. Source: Tiia-Linda Purge et al. / Estonian Journal of Earth Sciences

Using drones to reach inaccessible areas

Researchers photographed the cliff using drones in 2015, 2022, and 2024. Software then combined the images into a three-dimensional model, allowing every layer, fracture, and cave to be measured and analyzed on a computer. The team also traced the cliff edge using six aerial photographs covering the period from 1959 to 2024.

The work was far from simple. Drones had to be flown just a few meters from the cliff face and the water's surface while avoiding fallen rock debris and ensuring all key features were captured. Waves and boulder fields prevented researchers from surveying the base of the cliff as closely as they would have liked, and the ceilings of deeper caves remained hidden from view.

The method, known as photogrammetry, more specifically structure-from-motion photogrammetry, involves photographing the same location from multiple angles. Computer vision algorithms identify common points across images and create a three-dimensional model from ordinary photographs. The more sharp, overlapping images available, the more accurate and detailed the result.

To detect change over time, researchers aligned models from different years. Precise drone positioning helped with newer surveys, while older datasets required the use of stable reference points that had remained unchanged.

The secret of cliff collapses lies below

Aerial photographs show the Pakri Cliffs have lost more than a football field's worth of land over the past 65 years. The cliff edge retreated by an average of 18 centimeters per year, and by as much as 30 centimeters annually near the historic lighthouse and the collapsed observation deck.

Those rates are similar to coastal cliffs in northern Germany and northwestern Poland, which retreat at rates of 19 and 14 centimeters per year, respectively. Unlike those cliffs, however, Pakri is capped by hard limestone. The cliffs of Osmussaar, which consist entirely of limestone, retreat on average by only seven centimeters per year.

Average figures can be misleading. The cliff does not retreat at a steady pace. Years may pass with little change before a large section suddenly collapses, as happened in January 2024 when the observation deck fell and the cliff retreated 12 meters. Smaller collapses often go unnoticed by the public, but drone models can detect them.

The underlying cause is the interaction between geology and rock layers. Rainwater seeps through fractured limestone and emerges along weaker sandstone layers beneath it. The water gradually washes away the sandstone grain by grain, leaving limestone suspended overhead. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles widen fractures until a rock block finally breaks away. Both the observation deck collapse and a collapse near the lighthouse in 2021 were preceded by significant sandstone erosion beneath the limestone.

The cliff also breaks along existing joint systems (natural rock fractures). Researchers mapped more than 400 joint surfaces from drone models. Two dominant fracture systems, running northwest-southeast and northeast-southwest, create the Pakri coastline's distinctive zigzag shape. The cliff retreats most rapidly where fractures intersect and where underlying sandstone has already been eroded away.

The sea also plays a key role. Waves carve coastal notches (wave-cut undercuts) into the sandstone at the cliff base. Geologists mapped 18 such notches and 19 shallow indentations representing proto-notches in the early stages of formation. These features develop where the rock is naturally weaker. Poorly cemented sandstone yields to wave action, while the black shale layers above it resist erosion longer. As a result, the cliff erodes unevenly, with each layer wearing away at its own pace.

The cliff also has a natural defense mechanism. Fallen limestone blocks accumulate at the base, forming a rubble slope that absorbs wave energy. After the observation platform collapse, a rock barrier nearly five meters high formed in front of the cliff. The protection lasts only until waves carry the debris away and regain access to the base of the cliff.

Pakri peninsula coastline. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Mapping hazardous areas

The 3D models help scientists identify locations where sandstone has already eroded from beneath limestone, leaving dangerous overhangs. Based on those findings, researchers mapped potential collapse zones along the Pakri Cliffs. Such maps can help redirect hiking trails away from hazardous areas and warn visitors of potential risks.

Researchers caution that not everything can be predicted. The hazard zones are based on expert assessment rather than precise forecasts because the behavior of such a complex system cannot be predicted with complete accuracy. The visible fractures on the rock surface may represent only part of a much denser network hidden within the cliff. Scientists also lack a full understanding of how the underwater cliff base modifies wave energy.

The team plans to produce a new model at least once a year. The longer the dataset becomes, the better researchers will understand the cliff's natural rhythm and identify areas preparing for future collapses or responding to changing environmental conditions.

While coastal scientists around the world already make extensive use of drones and related surveying technologies, the approach remains relatively new in Estonia. Compared with satellites and aircraft, drones offer a flexible and cost-effective tool that can be deployed exactly where and when it is needed. The Pakri Cliffs demonstrate how this new perspective can advance coastal research in Estonia.

The study was published in the journal Estonian Journal of Earth Sciences.

World.title: Estonian-American producer umru to headline Tallinn club on Saturday
World.content:
New York-based producer and DJ umru has worked with the likes of Tommy Cash and Charli XCX. This Saturday, the Estonian-American artist takes the stage at Tallinn's club MOD.

Brooklyn native Umru Rothenberg began producing music as a teenager, uploading his early tracks to SoundCloud. His work caught the attention of A.G. Cook, founder of the influential label PC Music, who invited him to contribute to Charli XCX's 2017 song "I Got It" when he was just 18.

The collaboration helped launch umru's international career, leading to projects with a range of experimental pop artists, including Laura Les of 100 Gecs, Dorian Electra, Empress of and Caroline Polachek, as well as Estonia's own Tommy Cash.

Having made his name in the hyperpop scene, umru has increasingly moved toward club music. Last year, he released the EP "Matter of Time" on Scottish label LuckyMe, featuring producers Jacques Greene and Nikki Nair.

He also released the single "Poplife" together with American musician Underscores.

This Saturday, umru will headline at Tallinn's club MOD, joined by DJs Vaatab Jooksvalt and White Gloss.

Close Estonian ties

In an appearance on the No Tags podcast last year, umru shared that he spent a year living and attending school in Estonia at age seven, but has otherwise lived his entire life in New York.

His mother is Estonian-born artist Jaanika Peerna.

World.title: KOOS party may be allowed to pay 2027 Riigikogu election deposit in cash
World.content:
An exception may be granted for a political party to pay its deposit ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election in cash.

The KOOS party has been unable to open up a bank account in Estonia, which would be the normal means of making payment according to the rule-book.

However the requirement may more be a case of the spirit of the law rather than the letter of the law.

Justice Ministry Deputy Secretary General Heddi Lutterus said the requirement is not enshrined in law however, and an exception may be granted in this case.

"The Political Parties Act, which regulates the establishment of political parties, their activities and the supervision of their financing, does not require a registered political party to have or open an account with a credit institution," Lutterus said in a written response to a request for clarification from party representative Igor Hopp.

"If a party duly fulfills its obligations under the Accounting Act and the Political Parties Act and maintains financial discipline without having an account, then, while this is not standard practice, the mere fact of not having an account cannot in itself be held against the party," Lutterus added in her response.

Lutterus pointed out that the financing reports available on the website of the Political Parties Financing Surveillance Committee (ERJK) show that KOOS has submitted income and expenditure reports, Lutterus noted, though added that in establishing the rules for paying election deposits under another act, the Riigikogu Election Act, the Riigikogu likely had the payment of deposits in cash in mind.

Consequently, a party must submit a copy of the payment order confirming payment of the deposit along with its other candidacy documents.

Another aspect of the law is the fact that a party's deposit need not be made from that party's own account, Lutterus went on, with the most important parameter being payment is made on time – if a credit institution or other financial services company provided cash payment, for instance, this could be a feasible avenue of payment, Lutterus continued, noting that "the service may involve fees or transaction limits."

Polling day is March 7, 2027.

World.title: Raimond Kaljulaid leaving politics, will not run at Riigikogu election
World.content:
Social Democratic Party (SDE) MP Raimond Kaljulaid has announced he will not be running in next spring's Riigikogu election, and is leaving politics.

Kaljulaid, who is a member of the Riigikogu National Defense Committee, said he made his decision in August, and is going back to work in the private sector.

"Returning to the private sector, I can also draw on the knowledge and experience in management and business development that I had before entering politics, when I worked as an entrepreneur in marketing and communications," Kaljulaid said.

"For the past eight years, I have been involved in foreign and security policy. I have worked on the principle that maintaining very good relations with all our allies and partners is vitally important for Estonia. I cannot count how many meetings I have had during this time with politicians, diplomats and entrepreneurs from Europe, the U.S., the Gulf states and Asian countries," he went on.

Kaljulaid added he has not yet made a final decision on exactly what he will do next. "I am considering various options and thinking things through carefully. I will make a decision in the coming months."

While he said he does not rule out ever returning to politics, he is certain that he will not consider doing so in the immediate next years, nor likely beyond that either, adding he is "serious" about working in the private sector again.

Kaljulaid also stated former Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov's decision to join SDE did not play a role in his move either.

"Jonatan Vseviov's decision to join obviously could not have influenced my decision in any way, as it happened long after I had made my decision. However, I welcome this step. Jonatan Vseviov brings very strong knowledge of foreign and security policy to the party. Alongside that, I would also consider it very important that he is coming from the position of secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Kaljulaid on this.

He expressed a hope that the party's current upward trend in the polls will continue and that it will play a highly significant role both in the next Riigikogu composition and in the next administration.

He noted that the example of where " neoliberal right-wing economic policies lead" from some of the Western European countries, adding "what happens to society when inequality grows rapidly and people feel that the state does not need them and that they do not need the state either has had a "destabilixing" effect in those lands, and one which Estonia and its political parties could pay heed to.

He said he would continue to vote for SDE and encouraged all voters to do so too.

Kaljulaid 44, had been a Center Party member for the best part of 20 years before joining SDE in 2019. He won a Riigikogu seat in his own right with Center at the 2019 elections, but quit in protest of the party's coalition talks which involved the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE). He was re-elected at the 2023 elections with SDE. In the current Riigikogu he sat on the Security Authorities Surveillance Select Committee, as well as the defense committee, and chaired the Estonian delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. His 20,643 votes attained at the 2019 European Parliament elections was the seventh best result.

Riigikogu election polling day is March 7, 2027.

World.title: Consumer inspection finds violations in all e-scooters checked
World.content:
Estonia's consumer watchdog found issues with all e-scooters on sale in a sample taken this year, with several models banned from sale as a result.

The Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA) investigated 18 e-scooter models on sale across 10 different retailers, between April and September this year.

The TTJA found violations in all products, with the most common shortcomings relating to product documentation: 11 e-scooters lacked a declaration of conformity, or information that was provided in it was incomplete.

Nine sales listings for high-powered or high-speed electric scooters lacked information stating that the product must not be used in traffic. Several products also lacked an Estonian-language user manual.

During the supervisory proceedings, businesses submitted missing manuals or conformity documents for nine products and, where necessary, clarified the information provided in sales listings, the TTJA said.

As a result of the proceedings, five product models have been withdrawn from sale and sales of two product models have been temporarily suspended. Sales were suspended or products withdrawn from sale in cases where the company was unable to provide the required conformity documents or remedy shortcomings, for example by failing to provide the product with a user manual.

The seller is responsible for the information provided in sales listings: if the technical specifications of a personal mobility device exceed the limits established for its use, consumers must be clearly informed of this and, where necessary, told that the device is not intended for use in traffic.

Misleading consumers is not permitted, the TTJA noted. When purchasing an e-scooter, consumers should in any case check not only the price and technical specifications but also that the product meets the requirements and that the necessary information and documents are available.

World.title: Funding shortfall forces museum of communist crimes to cut Holocaust section and other exhibits
World.content:
A planned museum of communist crimes at Tallinn's Patarei Prison has cut roughly one-third of its exhibition because of budget constraints, raising doubts about whether it will have the funding needed to open and operate in 2027.

In 2018, the government decided to establish an international Museum of Communist Crimes and Research Center in the former Patarei Prison in Tallinn. The plans were ambitious: the 5,000-square-meter museum was intended to become the first large-scale exhibition in the Baltic Sea region dedicated to the crimes and operating mechanisms of communist regimes.

Now, historian Martin Andreller, a board member of the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory, which is curating the museum, said the funding allocated by the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs is insufficient to complete the exhibition as originally planned.

"When the exhibition procurement was launched, about 35 percent of the content had already been cut," Andreller said.

Martin Andreller Autor/allikas: Kirke Ert/ERR

The cuts included the audio guide, the entire Holocaust section, as well as other content blocks and technical solutions needed to stay within the available budget, he explained.

"We are heading toward the opening with a heavily reduced exhibition that does not represent the complete vision developed during the planning process," Andreller said. "At the same time, it remains unclear whether and how next year's budget will be resolved, even though that funding is needed to open the museum, keep it running, and provide services to visitors."

Andreller said an additional €500,000 is needed to complete the exhibition, not including personnel costs.

"The reduced exhibition will be completed by June 14, but we still have no certainty about next year's budget. That makes it impossible to plan pre-opening activities such as marketing, communications, educational programs, staffing, and the museum's day-to-day operations," he added.

2027 budget mostly unclear

"In the worst-case scenario, no funding will be provided, and there will be no way to open the museum on June 14."

"We have never operated a museum before. The doors will somehow open in June, but we do not know how many visitors will come because we also need to market and promote the museum, and for that we need additional staff," he added.

"The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs has not told us we will receive nothing, but we have not received any confirmation about next year's budget, even though we informed them how much funding is needed to open the museum. We requested €2.4 million to complete the exhibition in full," Andreller said.

According to Andreller, the ministry has also not indicated when information about next year's budget will become available or how much funding the museum could expect to receive.

"The relevant regulation has not yet begun moving through the ministry," he said.

In an effort to raise additional funds, the museum has begun collecting donations through its website.

The construction site of the Patarei Museum for the Victims of Communism in Tallinn. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

No extra funding made available

The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs acknowledged that it has no funding available for the museum's operating support and plans to provide resources on a project-by-project basis. The amount available will be determined after the state budget is approved.

"Next year's state budget cuts affect all ministries and government agencies. Unfortunately, foundations that receive sectoral support from the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs are not exempt," said Rein Oidekivi, the ministry's head of strategic communications.

Oidekivi noted that the museum's budget for next year will become clear after the Riigikogu adopts the state budget.

"Under amendments to the State Budget Act that took effect on December 29, 2025, the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory Foundation must apply for project-based funding instead of receiving its previous operating grant," he added.

Patarei Sea Fortress is being rehauled and repurposed into a museum. March 2025. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Oidekivi said it has been clear for some time that the exhibition, originally planned years ago, could not be completed in full by opening day.

"Prices for services and other direct and indirect costs have risen significantly in recent years, and the ministry cannot find additional funding. Parts of the planned exhibition and necessary technical solutions will be completed in the coming years as financial resources become available," he said.

The international design competition for the museum, held in spring 2018, was won by Japanese architect Shuhei Endo with the proposal "Red Erosion." Before the extensive renovation began, the east wing of Patarei opened in 2019 with the popular temporary exhibition "Communism Is Prison."

In September 2024, the future museum's cornerstone was ceremonially laid. The opening was originally planned for June 14 this year, the 85th anniversary of the June deportations, but was postponed by one year.

World.title: Expert on US midterms: Trump's low approval rating hard to recover from
World.content:
Speaking to "Välisilm;" Arras, an election and political communication expert, noted the Democrats' chances of securing a majority in the House of Representatives at least are high.

President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen into negative territory, making his political future difficult, but much depends on voter turnout, she wen ton.

How likely is it that the Democrats will get a majority in both chambers?

Various prediction models and analysts have put this possibility at rather high. If we are talking about both chambers, that estimate is perhaps a little lower, but when it comes to the House of Representatives, estimates range between 80 and 90 percent that it is achievable. Whether it will also happen in the Senate – there the probability is 50–60 percent, and in some assessments a little higher. But it seems that change is coming.

But couldn't these opinion polls also be wrong in some way? If, for example, the Democrats for some reason do not turn out to vote, the result could still be that the Republicans retain their majority.

Predictions are always just that, predictions, while actual voter behavior will only become clear on election day, as has always been the case. I would say that the main thing to watch out for is which will prevail: money or voter turnout, since the Republicans have considerably more money invested in the campaign – that figure has already exceeded the $1 billion-mark. At the same time, studies indicate that Democrats have much greater motivation to go out there and vote. Dissatisfaction with Trump is running very high, and dissatisfaction, as we know, is a very strong motivating factor for voter mobilization.

We know how Donald Trump reacted when he didn't get the Nobel Peace Prize, or when he doesn't get all the medals and trophies. So how will he take it if he loses this?

He has already been asked that question, and I think he said, with his usual arrogance, that 'I can still veto', meaning that he can continue to veto everything that is decided against him. He certainly won't simply accept defeat.

Another thing worth watching for is whether, and to what extent, Republicans will begin challenging the election results. The first situation of this kind is already unfolding in some states, and there will certainly be more. I believe we may see this kind of deep-state narrative and questioning of the legitimacy of the elections, though of course only if he does not get a result favorable to him.

Are the Democrats prepared for the possible outcome that they might win? Do they have any outstanding leaders in sight, are they ready to start torpedoing everything the Republicans do? We could say that this might lead American life down a path of turmoil, but on the other hand, at least we would see some change.

The Democrats have been part of U.S. politics for just as long as the Republicans, so there is surely some readiness among them, and at the moment there is certainly also a greater desire to do something. At the same time, we cannot really state that there is one clearly established leader today. The Democrats are still in a period of testing the waters to understand who could potentially become their next presidential candidate, and the next elections are in 2028. I believe the results of these midterm elections will also reveal quite a lot about how the balance of power within the Democratic Party will develop.

How can it be that in a country like America, where so many people live, where democracy prevails, where it is basically possible to scramble your way into any position, they cannot find a single outstanding candidate everyone can agree on?

I think the key word is interests. Interests exist both between parties and within parties, and there are surely quite a few people within the Democratic Party who want to be number one themselves. That is why they are testing the waters. It has also been said of Kamala Harris that she could potentially give it another try. But within certain groups in the Democratic Party, there is considerable strong sentiment among those who, after she failed once already, no longer believe in her. On that basis, one would not expect her to run again, although there is talk about her doing so.

So what, ultimately, is it about Donald Trump that has disappointed the voters, including Republican voters, the most? Here we imagine it is the Strait of Hormuz crisis, perhaps we also think about Ukraine, but what is it that has now disappointed Americans?

The biggest concerns are actually domestic ones, but these domestic concerns largely stem from those same issues. Inflation is one of the main concerns. On the subject of inflation, I looked at a recent survey – nearly 75 percent of people say they are highly dissatisfied with how Trump has handled this issue.

The same applies to immigration, where he has made rather abrupt decisions that have affected certain voter groups. In light of this, it is certainly worth watching constituencies with Latin American backgrounds and Latino voters. That is another major source of dissatisfaction, and certainly the war in Iran and everything related to it in the energy sector are under very strong criticism. This may also be one of the reasons why – although there was talk at one point that he might take some more active steps toward Iran again before the elections – I do not believe that will happen. But at the same time, there can always be surprises. Simply looking at the dissatisfaction in this area, it is very unlikely that they would do anything immediately before people go to the polls.

Donald Trump is in his second term, and essentially the president no longer has to worry about anything. He can do whatever he wants as he doesn't have to think about not being elected next time. Is losing even a substantial issue for him?

Looking at how he has operated so far, we cannot be certain that he himself believes this is his final term in office. I say this half-ironically, but given his conviction that he can still accomplish great things, and that he is also pursuing the Nobel Prize, in light of all this... I believe he may still see that he has something to lose, so he certainly does not regard this fight as an easy one.

Even if things now turn out such that the majority in the Senate or the House of Representatives shifts to the Democrats, things will not be easy for them. Even if you have a small majority, in the Senate, for example, they would need at least enough additional votes to be able to end obstruction in the first place. They need at least 60 seats.

If we look at these election results now, it is said that they need only five or six votes to achieve a majority, but those five or six votes or seats will not actually change the bigger picture much for the Democrats. So what is more likely to happen is that Trump will continue operating as he has so far. There will be an even greater deadlock and trench warfare, but no results will actually be achieved, which in turn will probably lead to the American people being even more dissatisfied than they already are today.

How might Donald Trump, if he loses, take it out on the rest of the world? We know he has a habit of doing that.

He has made various attempts regarding Ukraine, as we have seen. That is certainly one area where he can continue along that path. Another is something he has been somewhat threatening to do, where he has become friendlier with various autocratic countries than the democratic world considers reasonable or thinks he should be at all – that is certainly another direction.

Iran also cannot be overlooked in any way, because energy is one of his strategic objectives. If we look, for example, at the decision he signed a year ago launching a major artificial intelligence development program, one of its cornerstones, alongside technological dominance, was also securing energy and its supply.

Where might we now expect the biggest surprises in this spectacle?

Certain states should be watched: Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Michigan and Maine. These are said to be the six main states where the numbers currently indicate that the Democrats are very likely to be able to achieve some kind of breakthrough. These will become decisive, but it is certainly also worth watching voters in large cities and suburbs, who are usually unpredictable in their behavior. Whether and how actively will they turn out at all? They are also among those most strongly affected by inflation, and the same applies to rural areas. There could be surprises in turnout there – specifically, which side sees an increase in turnout.

A Democratic victory in Texas... He will certainly comment on that somehow, he will have something to say to the people of Texas about it.

If that should happen, then that is certainly one state where I would predict that the election results will be called into question. Presumably someone will have had their fingers in the till there.

If there is a defeat, could we also expect something similar to the Capitol riot?

I would like to hope not. So far, I have not really seen analyses from American analysts suggesting that this is considered likely. But Trump has surprised me before as well. At present, I would not really expect it to happen again.

It has also been said that there are fears he will start weakening NATO as well.

NATO is certainly one of the critical issues to watch. If he really takes offense to the depths of his soul, then Ukraine, NATO and liberal democratic principles are also things that will certainly come under attack.

If the election results turn out so that the Republicans win in both chambers, will we, along with the rest of the world, view it as though the elections were rigged?

I do not believe we will, because certain processes in that country are still functioning, and I think going along with the same kind of dubious theory does democracy no good whatsoever.

But we will certainly be seeing a very confident Trump, who will thump his chest and say that everything he has done so far has been right and that he must continue in the same way. However, he still has a problem, because according to the latest surveys, his rating today is minus 20, minus 30, meaning that the net figure is negative. When politicians' approval ratings fall into negative territory, it is generally very difficult to recover from that. Regardless of Trump, the Republicans would still like the next president to come from their own party, so what may happen instead is that a problem eventually emerges within the Republican Party itself.

Background:

The midterms are today, November 3. All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs, prompting speculation of Trump and the Republicans losing their majorities in both the house and the senate.

World.title: Italy holds security talks after European freezer cyberattacks
World.content:
Rome – Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence chiefs on Tuesday following cyberattacks on supermarket freezer systems in at least 11 European countries.

The attacks in recent days, for which no one has claimed responsibility, have prompted the EU to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt its food supply chain.

EU spokesman Thomas Regnier said EU agencies were also holding meetings on Tuesday with national authorities on “how to best respond to this collectively”.

“The investigations are currently being carried out by the national authorities, and we are in close contact with them,” he said.

“These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents.”

Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania and Sweden reported refrigeration problems that forced several retailers to discard food after temperatures rose.

The incident came three weeks after a cyberattack disrupted French grocery stores and led hundreds of outlets to throw away spoiled stock.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said on Monday the bloc was taking the incidents “very seriously”.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it — a warning that we must take seriously,” Hansen said.

In Italy, government ministers had a meeting with intelligence chiefs and the National Cyber Security Agency, which also issued technical advice for retailers to protect their systems.

“Initial investigations show that, in Italy, the impact of the attacks is currently highly limited. Only a small number of commercial units have been affected,” the government said in a statement.

It said affected outlets had “outdated security systems, with interfaces exposed directly to the internet and weaknesses in authentication mechanisms”.

– ‘Semi-amateurish’ –

There were reports of around 20 outlets affected nationwide in Italy.

Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that manages the Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of the company’s 300 stores were hit.

“We estimate the damage at several thousands of euros. We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty. We are waiting for suppliers today to replenish the stock,” he was quoted as saying by the Corriere della Sera daily.

“To be honest, we did not think that as supermarkets we would be targeted by a cyberattack. This shows that any connected device can become a target. So we will invest more — that is essential,” he said.

Four supermarket outlets were affected in Germany and six in Romania, officials and company representatives said on Tuesday.

“No other infrastructure was compromised,” Dan Cimpean, director of Romania’s National Cyber Security Directorate (DNSC), told AFP.

“It seems semi-amateurish. We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor,” he said.

Carlos Cancinos, spokesperson for the Coop chain in Sweden, said that the group’s seven affected shops had resumed “normal functioning”.

Refrigeration equipment and freezers affected overnight from Monday to Tuesday were connected to “old 4G networks”, he said.

“We have launched a major programme to modernise a large part of our store network, equipping connected refrigerators and ensuring that they operate via 5G networks. This helps to solve a large share of problems of this kind,” he said.

Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries, with dozens of stores across several grocery chains reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation.

World.title: Lufthansa latest airline to flag ticket price hikes amid Iran war energy shock
World.content:
Frankfurt – Lufthansa on Tuesday became the latest airline to warn that ticket prices will rise further, as it forecast a two-billion-euro ($2.2 billion) jump in annual fuel costs due to the Middle East conflict.

It came a day after Irish no-frills carrier Ryanair said it would raise prices and launch a cost-cutting drive, as the US-Israeli war on Iran keeps global energy costs elevated.

The conflict, which started in February, has led to the near total closure of key oil and gas trade route the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up airline fuel costs as well as fares.

The German firm, Europe’s biggest airline group by sales, said the outlook for fuel costs had worsened from just a few months ago, predicting a bill of 9.3 billion euros for 2026, two billion higher than last year.

Price hikes would be necessary “to pass on the increase in kerosene costs,” finance chief Till Streichert told journalists, after the group released forecast-beating quarterly results.

“Ticket prices will increase by double digits next year.”

He also warned fuel costs would increase in 2027, but added: “That can still change — and hopefully for the better — if the geopolitical situation eases.”

Streichert stressed that Lufthansa had hedged over 80 percent its fuel costs for 2026, meaning they had it largely locked in prices and was less exposed to market volatility.

For 2027 over 60 percent of fuel costs were already hedged, he said.

– AI boom lifts cargo division –

The higher fuel costs prompted Lufthansa, which also operates carriers including Swiss, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines and Eurowings, to adjust its earnings forecast for the year.

It now expects core profit in a range of between 1.7 and 2.0 billion euros for 2026. Previously it predicted a range of between 1.7 and 2.2 billion euros.

Despite the slightly bleaker outlook, the group reported a 30-percent jump in profits for the July-September period, beating forecasts.

Net profit came in at 1.26 billion euros, boosted by strong demand for premium tickets to Asia and North America.

Revenues increased nine percent from a year earlier to 12.2 billion euros.

The group’s cargo division tripled its core profit, boosted by deliveries of equipment for data centres that are being rapidly built to power the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, according to CEO Carsten Spohr.

German companies manufacturing equipment such as industrial lasers in data centres are enjoying strond demand.

But the group’s flagship airline Lufthansa saw its operating profit fall in part due to cabin crew and pilot strikes.

Spohr nevertheless said it was the strongest quarter “in terms of revenue in the history of the Lufthansa Group.

“With rising revenues amid consistently high demand and strict cost discipline, we were able to more than offset the increase in fuel costs of approximately half a billion euros,” he said.

Lufthansa’s shares rose over three percent on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange after the results were released.
