World.title: Talking braille blocks allow people with visual impairments to walk around freely
World.content:
This is a sponsored story, created and edited exclusively by Tokyo Metropolitan Government’s Tokyo Updates website.

“Straight ahead are the elevator and information desk. To your left is the north exit.” Hold your smartphone over the braille blocks at your feet, and get an audio explanation of your surroundings. This “coded braille block” system is being introduced at 21 locations across Japan, including the Setagaya City Hall in Tokyo. Here, we take a look at this initiative by W&M systems LLC, a company that aims to create a society where everyone, including those with visual impairments, can enjoy getting around and exploring freely.

Braille blocks are a form of barrier-free infrastructure that originated in Okayama Prefecture, located in western Japan, in 1967. The system combines guided braille blocks, with their four raised lines, and alert braille blocks, with their raised dots, to help people with visual impairments get around safely on foot. It was Hiroyasu Takayama, CEO of W&M systems, who saw the new potential in this familiar piece of infrastructure.

The inspiration came from a pen-shaped sensor developed by lead engineer Kazuya Chiba while he was searching for ways to communicate with his mother, who was living with a rare disease. When the pen was touched to paper printed with special codes, it would play recorded messages such as “I’m hot” or “I’d like some water.” This mechanism proved to be a key source of inspiration.

Looking back, Takayama recalls: “I thought maybe we could apply the same mechanism — playing audio when a sensor touches something — to help those with visual impairments get around on foot. From there, we began a long process of trial and error.”

A smarter path forward

The initial idea was to turn the white canes used by those with visual impairments into touch pens themselves. A sensor would be attached to the tip of the cane, and audio guidance would be played when the user touched it to the braille blocks. While they succeeded in using the sensor to read information, the dust and dirt that accumulated on outdoor braille blocks rendered it unusable within a day. The sensors attached to the tips of the canes were also prone to breaking or flying off, making the system impractical for everyday use.

CEO Takayama Hiroyasu of W&M systems explaining the role of the white cane. | Katsuya Inoue

“For those with visual impairments, the white cane is an extension of the body. No matter how convenient or groundbreaking a system may be, it won’t work if it’s not easy to use.”

They next turned their attention to the raised bumps on the braille blocks themselves. By adding markings to the 25 bumps (arranged in a 5x5 grid) on the alert braille blocks, they created a code that could be read in the same way as a QR code. By varying which bumps were marked in black, the system could generate over 30 million unique codes.

The prototype developed to bring the concept to life was a cumbersome setup that required users to attach a microcamera to their white cane, connect it by cable to a computer and battery worn on the body, and wear earphones. While the idea and the technology were innovative, participants in the trial noted that the many cords made it tedious to put on, and that it would prevent them from going out spontaneously.

A major breakthrough came when Takayama consulted his friend, Professor Kunio Matsui of the Kanazawa Institute of Technology in Ishikawa Prefecture, on Japan’s west coast. Acting on Matsui’s advice that the issue could be solved by using a smartphone — which already combines a camera, computer and telecommunication capabilities — they began joint development. And in 2019, their coded braille block recognition system was released as the smartphone app, Walk and Mobile.

The Walk and Mobile interface; when users scan coded braille block with their camera, audio guidance provides information about their location and surroundings. | Katsuya Inoue

The freedom to wander

The defining feature of this coded braille block system is that it provides different audio guidance depending on which of the four directions the user is traveling. Map apps that rely on GPS often do not function indoors or underground, and even outdoors can be off by several meters, making it easy to lose one’s sense of direction while navigating. By using the braille blocks as a fixed physical reference point, users are able to confirm their location at a centimeter-level accuracy without losing their orientation.

“The greatest challenge for people with visual impairments is when they lose their orientation,” Takayama explains. “Close your eyes and spin around a bit, and you lose track of where you’re facing. This is something that people with visual impairments experience on a daily basis.”

To help users maintain their orientation, the system provides different audio guidance depending on which of the four directions the user is traveling. | Katsuya Inoue

The coded braille blocks also fundamentally differ from route-guidance systems in their design philosophy. While many barrier-free systems are designed to guide users to a specific destination, W&M systems envisions “a society where all people can enjoy the freedom to wander about freely.”

“There’s a bench over there.” “There’s a vending machine.” “There’s a new wagashi (traditional Japanese confectionery) shop.” The audio guidance incorporates the kinds of information that sighted people naturally pick up on as they walk, as well as things that can be awkward to ask others about, such as the location of nearby restrooms. The company has received many enthusiastic responses from users, including comments like, “It’s like having a map appear in my head” and “It makes me comfortable walking around on my own.” Enabling this kind of wandering about in a city like Tokyo, where every walk can bring a new discovery, is likely to help further spread the vision across Japan.

As of June 2026, coded braille blocks have been installed at 21 locations across Japan, mainly in facilities in Tokyo such as the Setagaya City Office and Shinagawa City Office in Tokyo, as well as sites in Kanazawa City, Ishikawa Prefecture; Shiojiri City, Nagano Prefecture; Tottori City; and Hiroshima City. Because the system provides seamless coverage across indoor and outdoor environments and includes an evacuation mode that functions even when offline, it can deliver audio guidance that helps users navigate to nearby evacuation shelters during disasters.

The company is also exploring applications in tourism through multilingual support. In Kanazawa, there is a pilot project planned for this year to test a “Tourism Mode” that provides information about local sightseeing destinations. This mode is also expected to help address labor shortages among tour guides by offering multilingual audio guidance on nearby machiya (traditional Japanese townhouses), wagashi shops, and other points of interest around Kanazawa Castle Park.

Toward a barrier-free society

The Tokyo Metropolitan Government is advancing barrier-free measures not only in buildings but also on roads and in public transportation facilities, through the Welfare-Friendly Town Development Ordinance, Barrier-Free Building Ordinance, and more.

Takayama, however, points out that improving infrastructure alone is not enough. It is equally important to incorporate the perspectives of the users themselves.

“When people think of visual impairments, they tend to imagine someone who is completely blind. But in reality, only about 10% are totally blind. Around 90% have what’s called low vision, meaning they may be able to perceive light but see only blurred images, or have a hard time seeing in the center of their field of vision. The way they see varies greatly from person to person.”

With braille blocks, it is important not only to provide physical raised bumps, but also to ensure sufficient contrast with the surrounding pavement by using highly visible colors like yellow. According to Takayama, prioritizing aesthetics and installing blocks in colors similar to the surrounding pavement, or creating overly complex branching routes of braille blocks, can actually cause confusion for those with visual impairments.

“The dividing line between what’s truly barrier-free and what’s not lies in whether the infrastructure is created with the users themselves, rather than from the perspective of those who can see,” Takayama says.

Takayama shares his vision of a society where all people—regardless of whether they can see or have difficulty seeing—are able to explore the city in the same way. | Katsuya Inoue

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism publishes numerical data on the adoption of barrier-free infrastructure in buildings and public transportation. However, W&M systems, in collaboration with the Kanazawa Institute of Technology, is working to develop a Barrier-Free Achievement Index that would measure not only the physical infrastructure, but also the usability of it — factors such as ease of use and public understanding.

“People who have difficulty seeing or hearing, people who use wheelchairs... There are many different kinds of people in our cities. I think that taking small actions, such as paying attention to those around us and offering help when someone appears to be struggling, will be the first steps toward changing our society.”

As Tokyo continues to enhance its urban infrastructure, it must also continue to address the question of whether that infrastructure is equally accessible to all. The act of giving braille blocks a “voice” has slowly begun to change the assumptions that have long supported everyday life. As braille blocks, originally developed in Japan, continue to evolve, the hope is that they will spread from Tokyo to the rest of the world as a form of social infrastructure and an embodiment of a new standard for barrier-free accessibility — a society where everyone can enjoy walking around as they please.

Translation by Seira Tanaka

World.title: Private sector steps in to revitalize Japan’s rural communities
World.content:
A growing number of companies are launching local projects and working directly with residents to tackle the problems confronting farming, fishing and mountainous communities hit by depopulation and aging.

Such efforts are expected to help secure agricultural labor and broaden the ranks of people with continuing ties to the regions. They also offer benefits to the companies themselves, by showcasing their social contributions and opening the door to new business opportunities.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, for its part, is stepping up efforts to draw in corporate participants and to support the communities that host their activities.

World.title: For many Russians, higher utility bills are latest inflation shock
World.content:
In the Russian capital Moscow, history teacher Polina Ibragimova was shocked when a utility bill arrived that amounted to more than half her monthly pay.

At first, the 34-year-old mother of two thought her children must have spent too long splashing around in a steaming bath. Then she read the bill line by line and discovered the real culprit: a sharp increase in utility tariffs.

The rise in utility bills comes as Russia grapples with inflation fueled by a wartime economy, with a tight labor market and higher military spending adding to price pressures. For households such as Ibragimova’s, those strains are increasingly visible in monthly bills and day-to-day expenses.

World.title: Japan’s newest female astronaut wants to speak Japanese on the moon
World.content:
Ever since Neil Armstrong first set foot on the moon in 1969, every word broadcast from the lunar surface has been spoken in English.

Ayu Yoneda, the Japanese space agency’s youngest astronaut at 31, envisions a different future.

“If I’m able to go to the moon, I want to share my thoughts in Japanese,” she said in an interview with The Japan Times. “I believe English is the only language that’s ever been spoken there, but I want to speak in Japanese, too — to connect with people at home and anyone around the world who speaks or is learning our language.”

World.title: Asia for China? Tokyo’s answer to Beijing’s coercive strategy
World.content:
As the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference approaches in Shenzhen, China, this month, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi faces mounting pressure to choose between diplomatic optics and strategic principle.

A high-profile encounter with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Nov. 18-19 gathering may offer the appearance of improved relations, but it should not come at the expense of Japan’s right to speak candidly about Taiwan and cross-strait peace.

When Xi froze high-level communication with Takaichi following remarks last November, Beijing followed a familiar authoritarian playbook. Addressing the strategic realities facing Tokyo, Takaichi stated that a Chinese military assault on Taiwan would directly threaten Japan’s security, potentially creating an “existential” crisis that could require deploying Japan’s Self-Defense Forces to defend the country and protect its citizens.

World.title: India faces prolonged food inflation as weak monsoon threatens winter crops
World.content:
Indian farmer Amarsingh Gushinge wants to sow wheat and chickpeas in coming weeks to capitalize on attractive prices, but dwindling water supplies after below-average monsoon rains are preventing him from planting either crop.

Like Gushinge, millions of farmers, especially in southern and western India, are facing water shortages as they prepare to plant winter crops.

“There’s not enough moisture in the soil to sow the next crop, and no money left to do so either,” said Gushinge, 78, in the village of Rajewadi, about 400 kilometers east of Mumbai. The Jalna district around his village has received about 48% less rain than average this year, the local weather office has said.

World.title: Japan and Vietnam consider new pact to prevent crimes
World.content:
The Japanese and Vietnamese governments are considering concluding a new pact allowing them to mutually provide information on each other’s nationals arrested or detained in their own countries, sources have said.

The planned pact is aimed at strengthening deterrence amid an increase in the number of crimes committed by Vietnamese nationals in Japan.

During their meeting on Monday next week, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Communist Party of Vietnam General Secretary To Lam, also president of the Southeast Asian nation, are expected to confirm the plan to conclude the new pact, Japanese government sources said. The Vietnamese leader is slated to visit Japan for four days from Sunday.

When they met in Hanoi in May, the two leaders agreed to strengthen cooperation over consular affairs.

Under the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, reporting the arrest or detention of a foreigner to his or her home country requires the consent of the individual in principle.

Japan and Vietnam are considering allowing such reporting without the consent of arrested or detained individuals under the envisaged pact, according to the sources.

“As Vietnam has strong public security authorities, reporting the arrest or detention swiftly will be a major deterrent,” a Japanese official said.

While details, such as the types of incidents subject to such reporting, will be discussed in the future, it will take at least two or three years before the pact takes effects because it concerns human rights.

According to the National Police Agency, police took action against 10,773 cases involving Vietnamese nationals, excluding permanent residents in Japan, in 2025, up about 11% from the preceding year. The figure accounted for more than 40% all such cases involving foreigners.

Japan has so far signed a similar reporting pact or treaty with the United States, Britain China and the former Soviet Union.

The Japan-Soviet consular affairs treaty and related protocols stipulate the right to seek reporting within three days of arrest or detention and meetings between arrested or detained individuals and consuls within four days.

Based on the treaty and protocols, the Japanese government requested an early consular meeting for a Japanese reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, a daily newspaper in the northernmost Japan prefecture of Hokkaido, who was detained by Russian authorities on Oct. 13 on suspicion of espionage.

World.title: Japan and South Korea agree to cooperate over remains from undersea mine
World.content:
Senior Japanese and South Korean diplomats have agreed to work closely together for the return to South Korea of human remains recovered from an undersea coal mine in western Japan, where fatal flooding occurred during World War II.

The two countries will continue cooperation on DNA analysis.

The agreement was reached at a strategic dialogue held between the two countries’ vice foreign ministers in the town of Karuizawa, Nagano Prefecture, on Monday. This was the first such dialogue in about a year.

Workers from the Korean Peninsula were among victims of the 1942 flooding at the Chosei coal mine in the city of Ube in Yamaguchi Prefecture.

At the dialogue, Vice Foreign Minister Takehiro Funakoshi and South Korean First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoonjoo also exchanged views on North Korea’s movements, including its relations with China and Russia.

They reaffirmed continued cooperation for resolving North Korea’s nuclear program and its abductions of foreign nationals, including Japanese citizens.

Funakoshi and Park also confirmed that diplomatic authorities of Japan and South Korea will communicate closely for the stable development of the two countries’ relations.

World.title: Hong Kong BN(O) visa holders exempt from UK’s proposed 10-year settlement wait
World.content:
Hongkongers moving to the United Kingdom under the British National (Overseas) visa scheme will be exempt from plans to double the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years, according to an official announcement.

But they will still face stricter English-language requirements and tighter rules on criminal records, alongside existing conditions such as completing five years of continuous residence and passing the Life in the UK test.

British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood on Monday outlined plans to overhaul immigration rules, under which migrants would no longer gain the right to live permanently in the UK almost automatically after five years.

World.title: Hong Kong set for first taste of autumn as a strong northeast monsoon approaches
World.content:
Hong Kong could be in store for its first real taste of autumn early next week, with temperatures forecast to dip below 20 degrees Celsius (50 Fahrenheit) as a strong northeast monsoon approaches the Guangdong coast.

The Hong Kong Observatory said the monsoon would bring windy conditions to the region over the weekend, with offshore areas and high ground expected to experience strong winds at times on Saturday.

Temperatures across southern China were expected to fall between early and midweek next week under the influence of the dry replenishment of the monsoon.

World.title: 5 Hong Kong universities in Asia’s top 10, with 3 in top 5 after more than a decade
World.content:
Five Hong Kong universities have been ranked among Asia’s top 10, with three of them in the top five for the first time in more than a decade and the University of Hong Kong (HKU) retaining its No 1 spot, according to an annual UK survey.

Meanwhile, three universities in mainland China were ranked in the top 10. Peking University held on to second place, Tsinghua University leapt from ninth to third and Fudan University dropped from fifth to sixth, giving the mainland two universities in the top three for the first time since 2023.

World.title: Mind-controlled drone-flying at Hong Kong’s Being Human Festival among varied programme
World.content:
Think you can steer a drone using nothing more than your own concentrated thoughts?

It may sound like science fiction, but mind-controlled drone-flying is one of the free activities the public can take part in at the upcoming Being Human Festival in Hong Kong.

Running from November 5 to 15, the festival is the first Hong Kong edition of the UK’s national festival of the humanities, which was founded in 2014. Organised by the University of Hong Kong (HKU)’s Faculty of Arts under the theme “Crossroads”, the event stages talks, performances and workshops across the city.

World.title: Journalists may need judicial review to access land records under new rules
World.content:
Hong Kong journalists may have to rely on judicial reviews if the government refuses to provide land records under a proposed new system, although authorities have vowed to simplify applications and deliver records in as little as one to two working days.

Officials made the pledge on Tuesday as lawmakers raised concerns over possible restrictions on media access during the first meeting of a Legislative Council subcommittee examining eight pieces of subsidiary legislation for the proposed land record search arrangement and other operations under a new title registration system.

Legal advisers to the Legislative Council also asked whether the government would consult the public on the criteria for assessing applications made on public-interest grounds.

World.title: Chinese University of Hong Kong to offer free AI dementia screening to 2,700 seniors
World.content:
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) will launch its first free, district-based dementia screening programme next year, using artificial intelligence (AI)-powered retinal imaging to detect early signs of cognitive decline in 2,700 older residents within two years.

The programme will be implemented in Wong Tai Sin, which has one of the highest proportion of elderly residents among Hong Kong’s 18 districts.

Participants identified as being at risk will be paired with volunteers to receive tailored advice to help delay the onset of dementia.

World.title: Hong Kong homeowners prompt government rethink on proxy vote proposals
World.content:
Hong Kong homeowners’ pushback against proposals to limit proxy votes and restrict meeting attendance to relatives has prompted authorities to study alternatives to resolve estate management issues behind the deadly Tai Po fire.

In a paper submitted to the Legislative Council on Tuesday, the Home and Youth Affairs Bureau revealed the findings of its month-long public consultation on amendments to the Building Management Ordinance, part of proposed reforms after the Wang Fuk Court fire that killed 168 people.

The independent inquiry into the inferno found that “numerous features” of the HK$336 million (US$43 million) renovation project under way at the estate at the time of the tragedy “bore the hallmarks of bid-rigging and anti-competitive conduct”. They included an aggressively low consultancy bid and concentrated proxy votes over critical appointments for the project.

World.title: Hong Kong records 15th straight quarter of growth as GDP rises 5.2%
World.content:
Hong Kong’s economy grew by 5.2 per cent year on year in the third quarter, marking its 15th consecutive quarter of expansion, while retail sales rose by 6.4 per cent in September.

For the first three quarters combined, the economy expanded by 5.1 per cent, its fastest growth for the period in five years, advance estimates released by the Census and Statistics Department on Tuesday showed.

This compared with increases of 4.2 per cent in the second quarter and 5.9 per cent in the first.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.content:
China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.

PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.

Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.

The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.

China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

Development of the new formula began in 2024 and received regulatory approval in September 2026. The research team has also worked with companies to develop everyday foods for PKU patients, including noodles, steamed buns, cookies, and mochi.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: From the Shanghai Morning Post)

World.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.content:
At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.

“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).

But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.

Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.

Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.

As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.

“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.

(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.content:
China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.

Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.

As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.

Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

Fu, a 21-year-old viewer from the southern Guangdong province, told Sixth Tone that she found the show’s focus on friendship “refreshing” given how rarely such relationships take center stage on screen.

“We’re so used to understanding intimate relationships through the lens of romance, but rarely give serious thought to the love, possessiveness, jealousy, dependence, disappointment, and reconciliation that exist in friendships,” she said.

Another 21-year-old viewer based in Shanghai, surnamed You, added that the show’s appeal lies in friendship’s lack of definition.

“Friendship can be as intense and possessive as romance, full of love and resentment, or it can be something much more casual,” You said. “People can have very different ideas of what friendship means, and that alone can create tension.”

Contributions: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “I Miss You.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.content:
Many assume the writing is on the wall for human typographers. For decades, the industry has been slowly decimated by the advance of digital publishing software. Now, artificial intelligence is here to finish off the job.

That view has only strengthened since the launch of OpenAI’s Image 2.0 earlier this year. Until then, type designers and typographers had clung to the hope that AI would never be able to replace them: AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent, error-ridden, or somehow just a bit off.

But Image 2.0’s capabilities took many by surprise: it was able to produce beautifully designed documents featuring long passages of text in multiple languages, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that produced by professional type designers, but for a layperson looking to make a poster or a brochure, it was just fine.

Suddenly, typography — perhaps the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers — looked at risk of falling as well. If everyone can generate typefaces and layouts with a simple prompt, or even ask a frontier AI model to operate design software on its own — just as non-programmers can now “write code” through vibe coding — how many designers will lose their jobs?

In the English-speaking world, the AI revolution may indeed prove to be a hammer blow for the typography community. But things are likely to play out a little differently in China: the relationship between text and technology has always been more complex due to the nature of its writing system.

Most contemporary typographic practice derives from movable-type printing technology. Developed in medieval Germany, typography is closely tied to the inherent characteristics of the Latin alphabet: there are only a few dozen letters, and the same letters recur constantly throughout a printed text.

With these characteristics in mind, Johannes Gutenberg developed an entire technological process of carving, reproducing, retrieving, and repeatedly reusing individual letter forms. Once a complete set of letters had been produced, it could be used to print texts containing vast numbers of repetitions of exactly the same glyphs.

Gutenberg would later be credited as a pioneer of movable type printing, a technology whose logic has been carried intact from books to the screen you are now looking at. But applying this technique to Chinese characters is a huge challenge, as there is such a vast number of them. While function words such as de may appear repeatedly on a single page, most characters may occur only once or twice in a given text — or not at all.

Statistically, 3,500 characters is enough to cover most everyday text — studies have shown they account for 99.5% of character usage. But to avoid the awkward situation where a character outside the “common 3,500” can’t be rendered properly, the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface. Some larger projects cover 27,000, or even 87,000 characters.

This means that Chinese typeface design has always been extremely labor-intensive. Designers have to invest huge resources in reproducing thousands of rare characters that are only used about 1% of the time. It’s one reason why Chinese printers — who actually invented movable type even earlier than Gutenberg — largely stuck with carving entire texts onto woodblocks to mass-print books for centuries. It saved producing and organizing thousands of characters that might never be used. Only gigantic projects, such as state-backed archives, would use movable-type printing.

But in the modern era, movable type-inspired workflows have come to dominate Chinese typeface design. As a result, advertisers who need to print a 20-character slogan may have to purchase the license for a typeface containing 7,000 characters. Understandably, many users are reluctant to pay type foundries, who also feel it’s an enormous burden to cover as many characters as possible.

This cost-efficiency problem is where AI can help. In fact, Chinese type foundries have been using internal AI tools to assist in typeface production for years.

Traditionally, when developing a new typeface, the lead designer will often create several hundred characters to establish the design direction, with the remaining thousands produced by a team along those lines. An AI model can also do this work with a little training: extracting patterns from those hundreds of directional characters, learning the typeface’s stylistic characteristics, and then applying them according to the structural features of different characters. The model doesn’t have to be advanced, and with human adjustment, it can deliver products with considerably increased productivity.

Since the early 2020s, open-source AI tools have also enabled independent designers to produce usable typefaces on their own. For example, designer Wang Tingrui has been using AI tools to develop typefaces reminiscent of classic lead-type printing. With the emergence of stronger models capable of generating high-quality glyph outlines, such work has become even easier.

These developments mark a new chapter for Chinese typeface design. Once a typeface’s design concept is established, whether by a lead designer or an independent practitioner, AI could be used to expand it across thousands of additional characters, making that long tail of less common characters far less of a burden.

AI may also unlock new possibilities for Chinese characters once incompatible with movable type or typefaces. The overwhelming majority of Chinese characters are created by flexibly combining different components. In theory, anyone can combine components to create a new Chinese character.

This happened in the 19th century, when Chinese chemists — tasked with translating the names of newly discovered elements into Chinese — created compound characters by combining a semantic component indicating the element type and a phonetic component based on the initial sound of its Western name. This system continues to this day, when scientists occasionally need to name new synthetic elements.

While inventing a new character is relatively simple, it used to be difficult to introduce them into everyday language because of the inherent barriers created by digital typefaces. Traditional typeface design is built around recording whole characters, not their components, so any new character would not appear in previously existing typefaces.

With AI, however, that could all change. The technology should allow users to render new characters in the style of an existing typeface, making it easier for them to gain traction.

Beyond this, AI is ushering in a fundamental shift in the nature of typography. While the modern typeface system uses the single character or letter as its basic unit, this is just one way to recreate text. In woodblock printing, for example, Chinese printers produced entire pages all at once.

Today’s leading AI models — including Qwen, Seedream, ChatGPT, and DALL-E — are moving towards a system that bypasses typefaces entirely. Text is generated directly onto posters, videos, and the cover images for posts on China’s version of TikTok, Douyin, in a particular visual style, according to a user’s preferences. Users specify the style they want using a prompt — or a handwritten demonstration — and the AI model simply creates a font, rather than using a commercial one.

This approach still has problems. One issue often raised is the inconsistency of AI-crafted characters, but this should be solvable as models become more advanced. There is also a debate over copyright, especially when generated text resembles existing typefaces. Yet these issues are unlikely to stop ordinary users from using AI to speed up their design work.

It is easy to imagine a not-so-distant future in which everyone can generate high-quality typefaces and typography through instructions, whether they are designing for an illustration, an , a poster, or even an entire book. For type foundries, AI is likely to be incorporated into their workflows, just like what has been happening in the “hybrid” mode of production in the film industry.

Then, what is left for professional type designers to do?

One thing is clear: they will no longer monopolize the creation of stylistic Chinese characters. Similar upheavals have happened in the past, when typewriters, computers, and smartphones granted more people the power to produce texts.

But professionals have a more important job: pushing the boundaries of design. In a world where the production of text becomes effortless and inexhaustible, designers’ role as the gatekeepers of taste and judgment only becomes more prominent.

We should keep experimenting to deliver high-quality work with novel and sophisticated aesthetics. The decades of training we have received won’t be wasted. Rather, it will continue to shape a philosophy that pioneers future designs, regardless of what technology is involved.

(Header image: Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.content:
Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

The researchers also found that microRNA in milk vesicles from depressed mothers blocks a “brake” receptor called mGluR8 in pups’ brains. Without this brake, brain regions can become overstimulated, impairing the development of neural connections. As a result, new brain cells are more active overall but respond more weakly to memory tasks, helping explain the cognitive problems seen in pups nursed by depressed mothers.

The study offers the key findings of both a new communication pathway and a microRNA-based mechanism of inheritance between mothers and babies, according to the researchers.

Breastfeeding is widely seen as good for babies’ brain development, but this study also suggests that breastfeeding by mothers with postpartum depression may have a “double-edged effect on offspring health,” the researchers wrote.

“Elucidating the molecular mechanisms linking maternal postnatal depression to offspring neurological outcomes therefore holds considerable public health value and underscores the urgent need for targeted maternal mental health interventions during lactation,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.content:
Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.

To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.

The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

Li Huaisheng recommended that market regulatory authorities establish early-warning models to flag suspicious company registrations, and tax authorities improve big-data checks on invoices, capital, contracts, and goods.

In an interview with CCTV, Zhou Xianbao, a lawyer at BZW Law Firm in Beijing, also recommended establishing a system requiring real-name authorization for invoice issuance and formal tax-compliance commitments.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.title: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.content:
When most Chinese people think of World War I, they think of it as a “European war.” This is not simply an oversight. It is the result of a century of forgetting.

Few people are aware that between 1916 and 1918, Britain and France recruited around 140,000 Chinese laborers from Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong, Hong Kong, and other regions to work on the Western Front. They dug trenches, built defenses, and transported ammunition. After the fighting ended, they stayed on to help with reconstruction, clearing battlefields and filling in shell craters. Some did not return home until 1922.

Sending laborers overseas was not simply a matter of supplying manpower. It was also part of a carefully considered political strategy. Politicians such as Liang Shiyi — an influential adviser to then-President Yuan Shikai — believed that Germany and Austria-Hungary were unlikely to defeat Britain and France, and advocated a “laborers-as-soldiers” strategy that would allow China to participate indirectly in the war and break its diplomatic isolation. Meanwhile, figures associated with the New Culture Movement, an early 20th-century intellectual and cultural reform movement, saw sending laborers overseas as an opportunity to develop China’s working class. They included Li Shizeng, a French-educated anarchist and organizer of the Diligent Work-Frugal Study Movement, and Cai Yuanpei, a leading educator and president of Peking University.

Yet China’s participation in the Allied war effort did not bring the diplomatic gains its leaders had hoped for. At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, the victorious powers agreed to transfer Germany’s former rights in Shandong province to Japan rather than return them to China, a decision that helped spark the May Fourth Movement, a wave of student-led protests that became a turning point in modern Chinese history.

The contributions of the Chinese laborers themselves also received little recognition. When they returned home in the 1920s, they found a country gripped by political upheaval and were often met with indifference or even suspicion.

The result was a double erasure. The West forgot their contributions, while China forgot their sacrifices.

In July 2019, a delegation from Belgium’s In Flanders Fields Museum visited Shanghai University. The two institutions agreed to jointly investigate, excavate, study, and exhibit the remains of Chinese labor camps on the Western Front during World War I. By then, scholars from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Germany, Canada, and other countries, led by Professor Nicholas J. Saunders of the University of Bristol, had spent nearly a decade systematically surveying the physical remains and landscapes of the Western Front. Yet the Chinese labor camps remained a missing piece of the puzzle. Although frequently mentioned in historical records, they had never been systematically investigated or excavated by archaeologists.

In May 2023, Shanghai University officially launched the Chinese Labour Corps (CLC) Camp Project, in collaboration with the In Flanders Fields Museum, Ghent University, and Howest University of Applied Sciences. A non-invasive geophysical survey was completed in April 2024, and excavation began in February 2025. The project concluded in March 2026.

Before we began digging, information about the Chinese labor camps could be found in historical documents, but it was fragmented. Official military archives paid little attention to these noncombatants from China, while local records offered a more vivid picture. One example is the diary of Belgian priest Achiel Van Walleghem. In August 1917, he recorded the presence of two Chinese labor camps in the village of Reningelst, near the Belgian town of Ypres, a major battleground during World War I. In January 1918, he noted that some shop owners had begun learning Chinese to attract the laborers. And on the night of April 13, 1918, when one of the camps came under German artillery fire, he recorded 10 deaths and more than 30 injuries. In fact, the threat of shelling had already prompted strikes and protests among Chinese laborers in late 1917. British military records provided another crucial detail: the 75th Company of the Chinese Labour Corps was stationed there from August 1917 to April 1918. Gu Xingqing, an interpreter for the Chinese laborers, also described the night of the bombardment in his memoirs.

Historical records also reveal differences in how the British and French treated Chinese laborers. Those recruited by the French worked alongside locals under relatively loose supervision, making the remains of their camps difficult to identify. By contrast, British-recruited laborers — organized into the Chinese Labour Corps — were subject to military-style discipline and housed in enclosed camps surrounded by barbed wire. The camps followed a military organizational structure. Initially, each battalion consisted of 1,031 men, with 10 to 12 sharing a tent. Each camp had just one iron gate, which was locked at night. To leave, the men had to obtain permission and travel in groups, and they were forbidden from venturing more than 3 miles away.

Documents even record how the laborers died and were commemorated. The leading causes of death were tuberculosis and the 1918 influenza pandemic, rather than artillery fire. However, the death tolls vary considerably: British records put the figure at around 2,000, French records at approximately 1,500, while Chinese figures suggest that at least 20,000 did not come back to China. Chinese laborers recruited by the British were buried in military cemeteries. Their headstones followed the same style as those of British soldiers, but bore inscriptions in both languages, including the laborers’ names and places of origin in Chinese, alongside English epitaphs such as “Though Dead, He Still Liveth” and “A Noble Duty Bravely Done.”

After the war, returning French and Belgian residents sometimes blamed the surviving Chinese laborers for social unrest. Yet the laborers were still bound by their contracts and remained to clear the battlefields. Some stayed in France to work in mines until 1929, while others married and settled there permanently.

In June 1921, the British military issued a total of 93,357 commemorative medals at its Chinese labor base in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao. Some were presented in person, while others were mailed to the laborers’ homes. Even today, these medals can occasionally be found in remote villages across Shandong and Hebei.

If historical records tell us so much, why was archaeological excavation necessary? Because documents can tell us where the camps were and what happened there, but they cannot fully reveal what the camps looked like. Their layouts were never systematically recorded, and the sites had long since been cleared and leveled after the war. This is where archaeology comes in.

The non-invasive geophysical surveys of the site we commenced in spring 2024 used high-resolution electromagnetic induction and magnetic survey techniques. The data revealed numerous anomalies at depths of 1 to 1.5 meters, including fragments of artillery shells of various calibers. This was consistent with local farmers’ accounts of still unearthing shrapnel when plowing their fields.

The two intersecting trenches excavated in February 2025 covered 512 square meters. We uncovered two ash pits with traces of burning at their bases, eight shell craters ranging from 1 to 5 meters in diameter, foundation stones from barracks, tent pole bases, and clusters of communication cables. For the first time, we were able to reconstruct the layout of a camp whose physical arrangement had never been documented, identifying its barracks, tent area, and main road.

We also unearthed more than 520 artifacts that offered glimpses of everyday life: belt buckles, Royal Engineers and Royal Artillery cap badges, surgical forceps from a field hospital, piles of bullet and shell casings, and nearly intact British army-issued rum jars and lemonade bottles. If historical documents help us understand the Chinese labor camps, archaeology brings us closer to the people who lived in them.

The significance of the project extends beyond the discoveries themselves. For a long time, World War I archaeology was mainly the preserve of metal detectorists, while professional archaeologists generally avoided the subject. This began to change with archaeological investigations conducted ahead of construction of Belgium’s A19 highway in 2002, which helped establish the field as a serious area of academic research.

Our excavation of the Chinese labor camp was the first of its kind to be led by a Chinese academic institution.

The project also opened up new avenues for Chinese archaeological research in two fields. The first is conflict archaeology, which looks beyond weapons and battlefields to examine entire societies caught up in war. The second is industrial archaeology, which can shift attention away from industrial achievements alone and toward the people and human efforts behind them. At its heart, this approach is about focusing on people rather than objects.

The Chinese laborers were not merely supporting characters in World War I. They found themselves caught up in a conflict involving Eastern and Western societies, working and dying amid misunderstanding and hostility. Yet even in the face of constant danger, they found ways to express themselves, creating trench art engraved with dragon motifs and landscape scenes.

Even the idyllic scenery of Flanders today was partly shaped by Chinese laborers, who filled in many of the trenches and craters left by the war. The experiences of these 140,000 ordinary Chinese men lie at the intersection of 20th-century Chinese and world history, reflecting the interactions and tensions between different societies.

“In Flanders fields the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row,” wrote John McCrae in his poem “In Flanders Fields.” Today, the poppies still bloom every year. But among those fields and crosses, Chinese laborers once lived and worked. Archaeology cannot bring them back to life, but it can give the soil a voice and remind the world that they were here.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A British soldier and a Chinese laborer examine written identification ribbons during a roll call at a Chinese Labour Corps camp in Samer, France, May 26, 1918. From the collection of the Imperial War Museums)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.title: China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.content:
China’s popular chili sauce brand Lao Gan Ma has drawn public scrutiny for adopting AI-driven production, allegedly at the expense of hundreds of jobs.

The controversy began after multiple domestic media outlets reported that Li Xin, Lao Gan Ma’s executive vice general manager and chief quality officer, touted the company’s use of AI at a provincial business conference last month in China’s southwestern Guizhou province, where the sauce originates.

Li reportedly said the number of workers on one production line fell from over 600 to just 48 after the company introduced an AI-powered pepper inspection system last year. He added that the company’s 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan ($810 million), crediting AI with reducing production errors to almost 0%. Li’s full remarks are not publicly available online.

The company’s history of touting its dedication to working people has drawn particular criticism over the potential layoffs, according to a commentary by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper. Lao Gan Ma’s founder, Tao Huabi, whose portrait adorns the brand’s jars and is known across China, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997.

As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal has garnered more than 120 million views on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users said automation is a standard part of industrial upgrading that can help improve efficiency and ensure consistent product quality. Others argued that the company should consider its responsibilities to workers.

“If everything is done by AI and robots, and people have no jobs or income, they won’t be able to afford to consume. What’s the point of producing so much, then?” one highly upvoted Weibo comment read.

Many also called for a boycott of the brand, reposting one user’s comment: “If you lay off workers, we’ll get your products pulled from the shelves.”

Responding to the controversy, Lao Gan Ma human resources representatives stated in an interview with domestic media on Oct. 26 that Li had not referenced staffing figures in his remarks.

In response to the company’s denial, users scrutinized its social insurance enrollment figures, which often reflect a company’s workforce size. Corporate filings disclosed by business data platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha show that the number of employees insured by the company fell from nearly 3,000 in 2022 to 740 in 2025 — a roughly 75% decline.

However, changes in social insurance enrollment do not prove AI use drove the layoffs, as other factors such as retirement and employee turnover also affect employment figures.

The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative impacts on employment. On Oct. 23, the State Council issued guidelines calling for “maximizing AI’s potential to create jobs, empower workers in traditional occupations, improve job quality, and stimulate innovation” while “slowing down the impact of AI-related job replacement.”

The guidelines also urge companies to deploy AI with caution in labor-intensive industries. They encourage employers to provide transition periods for displaced workers, give advance notice before large-scale AI rollouts, and offer retraining and support for locating new jobs.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: World No. 17 Alex Eala downs Emerson Jones to start Hong Kong Open bid
World.content:
FOCUSED. The Philippines' Alexandra Eala in action during her quarterfinal match against Russia's Diana Shnaider at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, Japan.

A day after climbing to a career-high world No. 17 ranking, Alex Eala holds off replacement foe Emerson Jones of Australia to kick off her Hong Kong Open campaign

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala kicked off her Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open campaign on a high.

Apart from entering the tournament at a career-high world No. 17 in the latest WTA rankings, the Filipina tennis star also cruised past Australia’s Emerson Jones, 6-4, 6-3, on Tuesday, November 3.

Eala rose to world No. 17 just a few months after her previous career-high ranking of No. 18 in August.

The 21-year-old Filipina, the second seed in the WTA 250 tournament, was originally supposed to go head to head with Alycia Parks. The American player, however, was forced to withdraw from the competition at the last minute due to a shoulder injury.

“It was a really good match. Emerson is such a sweetheart off the court and such a great player on the court, so I’m looking forward to many more matches together,” Eala said of world No. 132 Jones.

She will face Czechia’s Tereza Valentová on Thursday, November 5, in the round of 16.

The Hong Kong Open is Eala’s last tournament for the year.

Eala will then mark her homecoming with “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate” on December 8 at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan, where she is set to face Indonesia’s Janice Tjen. – Rappler.com

World.title: Amazon UK offers November 26 deal for Maria Ressa’s ‘The Fight Back’
World.content:
Ressa's new book, 'The Fight Back: A Citizen's Guide to Standing Up to Dictators,' lays out practical strategies for citizens to resist authoritarianism and reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives

MANILA, Philippines – The Kindle edition of Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa’s latest book will be available at 99p (£0.99)* for one day only on November 26, Amazon UK has announced.

Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, lays out practical strategies for citizens to resist authoritarianism and reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives.

Drawing from Rappler’s experience under former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, Ressa argued that the Philippines offers important lessons for the United States and other democracies now confronting similar threats, emphasizing how the fight can start at the individual level and that it will take a global effort to reverse the world’s current course.

From Amazon UK’s page: “This is a frontline guide to understanding, defending, and rebuilding democracy in the age of AI, with 10 strategic goals broken down into 100 concrete actions citizens can take right now.”

Get the e-book edition of The Fight Back on November 26 for only 99p at Amazon UK’s website here. – Rappler.com

*£1 = P85.11

World.title: Brazil wraps up COP30 with fossil fuel, forest roadmaps, urging shift from talks to action
World.content:
DEADLOCK. COP30 President Andre Correa Do Lago speaks to the media during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), in Belem, Brazil, on November 21, 2025.

'We don't need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,' says COP30 president Correa do Lago, who led last November's UN climate summit in Belem

BRASILIA, Brazil – Brazil is ending its year-long presidency of the UN climate process with roadmaps aimed at curbing deforestation and accelerating a shift away from fossil fuels to help governments deliver on past climate agreements.

COP30 president Andre Correa do Lago, who led last November’s UN climate summit in Belem, said governments must integrate climate goals into policymaking.

“We don’t need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,” Correa do Lago told Reuters. “We need to completely change the way governments deal with climate change. To implement this, we need finance, infrastructure and transportation ministers at the table.”

Shifting away from fossil fuels and reducing deforestation are considered essential to limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, a goal set at the Paris climate talks in 2015.

But oil-producing nations have been reluctant to embrace measures that could undermine a key source of revenue while efforts to curb deforestation face a chronic lack of funding. A UN report last month showed 1.5ºC was increasingly out of reach.

This year’s climate summit, COP31, is due to get underway in Antalya in southern Turkey on November 9. Murat Kurum, the summit president and Turkish environment, urbanisation and climate ​change minister, told the UN in September the agenda would also focus on implementation rather than new ⁠pledges and was based on “dialogue, consensus and action.”

Replacing fossil fuels

In Belem, Brazil sought to formalise an energy transition roadmap, after more than 100 countries agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. But while the plan had European support, it failed to secure a consensus after opposition from major oil-producing countries.

Under the roadmap, countries would spend the period to 2028 assessing their energy systems, strengthening regulations and institutions, and developing national transition plans ahead of the second Global Stocktake, an evaluation of whether the world is heading in the right direction to contain global warming.

By 2030, infrastructure upgrades and renewable energy investments should be underway. A final phase between 2031 and 2033 would focus on accelerating renewable energy deployment, replacing fossil fuels and consolidating cleaner energy systems.

Global renewable energy capacity reached a record 5,149 gigawatts at the end of 2025, up 692 GW from the previous year, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency.

Brazil’s roadmap notes that most recent growth in renewable energy has gone toward meeting new demand rather than replacing fossil fuel use.

“My opinion is that it doesn’t need to be negotiated again because that negotiation has already taken place,” said Correa do Lago. “It needs to be implemented.”

Protecting forests

A lack of consensus also kept Brazil’s proposed deforestation roadmap out of the final COP30 agreement, reflecting persistent disagreements over how to finance forest protection.

According to the United Nations Environment Programme, annual funding for forests must rise from $84.5 billion in 2023 to more than $300 billion by 2030.

Most current funding comes from national governments, which account for 88.3% of forest finance, with international public funding at only 3.4%, placing much of the burden on the developing countries where most of the world’s tropical forests are located.

Brazil has proposed a Tropical Forests Forever Facility that would use returns from a sovereign fund to provide ongoing payments to countries that preserve their forests.

The initiative had secured $7.6 billion by the end of COP30, against a target of $10 billion, according to Corrêa do Lago.

The roadmap also calls for expanding other funding initiatives, including strengthening carbon markets, improving direct access to finance for Indigenous peoples and local communities, and using debt-relief instruments.

“Public financing from developed countries is absolutely essential,” Corrêa do Lago said. “But we have a much more sophisticated and diversified way of financing the various activities that would reduce deforestation.”

He said the roadmap’s main value was in highlighting the complexity of tackling forest loss.

“It is not an easy task, and it is not just about financing. But financing is a central part of this process.” – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: PLDT’s longtime auditor SGV resigns, withdraws opinion amid accounting issues
World.content:
PwC takes over the telco giant’s audits after SGV earlier identified a material weakness in financial reporting controls and withdrew its 2024 and 2025 audit opinions

MANILA, Philippines – After nearly 24 years of serving as PLDT’s auditor, SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (SGV) has resigned and withdrawn its audit opinions on the company’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements prepared for international reporting.

SGV, the country’s largest professional services firm and a member of Ernst & Young, informed PLDT on October 31 that it was resigning after determining that it was no longer independent under US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and auditing oversight rules.

“SGV has now concluded that its independence was impaired as of the issuance of its Fiscal 2025 Audit Opinions, and this impairment continues through today. Accordingly, SGV has submitted its resignation as the Company’s independent registered public accounting firm,” PLDT said in a disclosure.

An external auditor is supposed to independently examine a company’s financial statements and assure investors that these fairly present its finances. SGV concluded that its independence had already been impaired when it issued its 2025 audit opinions in April. While PLDT’s disclosure discussed the accounting errors and weaknesses in its financial controls, it did not specify what caused SGV’s independence to be impaired.

SGV’s resignation comes after accounting errors were earlier uncovered at PLDT. In August, PLDT acknowledged these errors arising from “deficiencies in controls over the accounting for certain structured hedge arrangements.” These hedge arrangements often protect companies from financial risks, such as fluctations in currency exchange rates. The errors involved how gains and losses from these contracts were recorded in its financial statements.

More seriously, SGV concluded that “a material weakness existed in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2025.”

SGV had initially issued unqualified, or clean, audit opinions on PLDT’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements before now withdrawing them following the discovery of accounting issues.

The auditor has since withdrawn its 2025 audit opinions, saying they “could no longer be relied upon.” On October 31, it also withdrew its 2024 opinion because it could not complete its assessment of additional accounting information before resigning.

PLDT said there had been no disagreements with SGV over accounting practices or audit procedures, apart from the unfinished assessment. The telco giant also stressed the revisions identified so far were not expected to materially affect its net income, EBITDA, earnings per share, cash flows, or key operating metrics.

Still, the August disclosure was serious enough for the Philippine Stock Exchange to halt trading in PLDT shares for one hour on August 14 as investors digested the news. PLDT shares later fell 4.49% to P1,170 by the end of that day.

It was not PLDT’s first controversy involving financial controls. In December 2022, the company disclosed capital expenditure budget overruns estimated at P48 billion covering 2019 to 2022. A later review found no evidence of fraud, but PLDT still introduced changes to its spending controls. (READ: PLDT cleans up, moves on from capex overrun mess)

Meanwhile, PLDT appointed Isla Lipana & Co., the Philippine member firm of PwC, as its new external auditor effective Monday, November 2.

PwC will handle its Philippine financial statements, but PLDT is still searching for an auditor to handle its international financial statements and internal control reporting required by US regulators. PLDT’s US reporting obligations arise from its listing on the New York Stock Exchange, where its American depositary shares trade.

PwC Philippines’ chairman emeritus, Alexander Cabrera, recently grabbed the spotlight as the forensic accounting expert who testified for the prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial in October. – Rappler.com

World.title: Defense’s list of witnesses in Sara Duterte trial expected this week
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
