“Since the beginning of his second term, attacks on the press have increasingly gone beyond rhetoric and general government policy, escalating into physical restrictions on journalists,” the organisation’s report said.

The list is divided into five categories according to the type of persecution faced by media outlets in each country: political pressure, threats to safety, legal pressure, economic pressure and social pressure.

Bidzina Ivanishvili is included in the economic category, while Ilham Aliyev is listed in the political category.

In the economic category — which includes those who “financially strangle media outlets” — Ivanishvili is joined by technology giants Alphabet and Meta, French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, head of a pro-Kremlin propaganda organisation Vladimir Tabak, and Kenyan President William Ruto.

RSF on Bidzina Ivanishvili

The RSF report describes Ivanishvili as a billionaire oligarch, former prime minister and founder of the Georgian Dream party.

“He remains the real power behind Georgia’s government. His business empire and network of influence allow him to exercise tight control over the country’s media landscape, particularly through the pro-government television channels Imedi and Rustavi 2,” RSF said in its profile of Ivanishvili.

According to the profile, under his influence, the country’s economic resources and state institutions are used to restrict independent media through financial pressure, repressive laws, censorship and legal prosecution.

Independent journalists are stigmatised, intimidated and silenced.

The following incidents of pressure on the press were documented in Georgia during 2026:

Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent figure in independent journalism, remained in custody after the Supreme Court rejected an application for her early release.

New repressive laws were adopted, introducing criminal liability for receiving certain forms of foreign funding, thereby threatening the existence of independent media outlets and the NGOs supporting them.

The Communications Commission was allegedly manipulated to punish television channels seeking to hold the authorities accountable, particularly Formula TV and TV Pirveli. The restrictions went as far as prohibiting them from using certain critical expressions about the authorities.

There was a growing trend of legal proceedings and sanctions against journalists, alongside restrictions on their parliamentary accreditation.

Ivanishvili’s profile also quotes remarks he made in 2024:

“…Human rights and freedom of thought and expression are protected; we have a sound judiciary, the media are independent, and businesses are inviolable — a country where people live freely and no longer fear political persecution.”

The following year, in 2025, Ivanishvili was included in the “Press Freedom Predators” list for the first time.

Georgian Dream’s reaction

The Georgian Dream party attributed Bidzina Ivanishvili’s inclusion in the “Press Freedom Predators” list to the machinations of the “global war party” — a mysterious, supposedly all-powerful organisation that the Georgian government blames for all its troubles.

Georgian Dream’s official position is that Ivanishvili’s inclusion in the list is “nothing more than the price that the honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, the figure with the greatest political — and not only political — authority in Georgia, is paying at great personal risk for refusing to sacrifice our country’s peace, national interests and sovereignty to serve the interests of the global war party”

Background

Over the past two years, the work of independent media in Georgia has been restricted in several ways. The authorities have tightened legislation, physical and legal pressure on journalists has intensified, and financial difficulties have threatened the survival of several independent and regional media outlets.

The main restrictions include:

Restrictions on foreign funding: The Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, adopted in 2024, required media outlets and organisations receiving foreign funding to undergo special registration. An additional law adopted in 2025 made government approval mandatory for receiving foreign grants.

Expanded powers for the regulator: Amendments to the Law on Broadcasting gave the Communications Commission greater powers to interfere in the operations and content of media outlets. The commission has repeatedly used these powers to fine broadcasters critical of the government.

Persecution and intimidation of journalists: Physical attacks, threats, detentions and legal proceedings against journalists have become more frequent. Four journalists are currently in prison, three convicted on criminal charges and one on administrative charges.

Restrictions on court reporting: Legislative amendments have restricted the right to film and report on court hearings. Over the past year, filming has been banned not only in courtrooms but also in courthouse corridors and courtyards.

Obstacles to journalists working in parliament: Georgian Dream has sought to prevent correspondents from media outlets it considers unfavourable from entering parliament wherever possible. It uses the accreditation system as a means of imposing restrictions. Following a complaint from an MP, parliament can suspend a journalist’s accreditation for a specified period. The rules for issuing single-use accreditations have become increasingly bureaucratic, with more and more journalists being denied them.

Financial pressure: Repressive laws adopted over the past two years have reduced funding sources for independent media outlets. Georgia’s advertising market was already limited, and it has now become highly polarised, with most advertising revenue going to pro-government television companies. As a result of the financial crisis, one opposition television channel and several small regional media outlets have closed over the past two years. Some outlets have switched to remote working with reduced resources. Many journalists have been forced to change professions, while many others have emigrated.

As a result, independent media outlets in Georgia now face legal, financial and physical pressure simultaneously.

Georgia ranked 135th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index, down from 114th place in 2025.

World.title: Where do you see your children’s future – in Georgia or abroad? JAMnews street poll. Video
World.content:
Where do parents see their children’s future in ten years’ time – in Georgia or abroad? What influences their choices, and how confident are they that their children can have a better life in Georgia? This time, we put these questions to passers-by on the streets of Tbilisi.

Context

Over the past few years, increasing numbers of people have been leaving Georgia. Emigration has long been one of the country’s main challenges, but its nature and scale have now changed.

In the past, those who left were mostly middle-aged people, often just one member of a family, seeking work abroad. Now, however, young people and families with children are leaving. Most have no plans to return.

According to the National Statistics Office of Georgia, 114,374 people left the country in 2025, most of them young people, official data show.

Some leave to study, others to find better jobs. Others have lost everything they had in Georgia because of the country’s ongoing political and economic crisis. People who have experienced political repression are also choosing to emigrate.

Most respondents said they would all like to live in Georgia. They enjoy life there and believe that living in one’s homeland is always better. However, they feel that opportunities to do so are becoming increasingly scarce.

Some said their children had been living abroad for a long time. They had settled there and started families of their own. “Sadly, my grandchildren do not even speak Georgian,” one respondent lamented.

Many respondents admitted that they would like their children to stay in their homeland, close to their parents. However, they do not want to deprive them of opportunities to build a better future.

Here are some of the most telling responses we received:

“My children live abroad. Not because life there is better, but because life here was bad. They want to return to Georgia. But I am a mother, and I want to make sure they do not face discrimination or disadvantage here”;

“Life in Georgia is still better. But given the current situation and the atmosphere in the country, I would not be entirely happy for my child to grow up here”;

“I will support my child whatever they want and decide. If they want to stay in Georgia, they can stay. If not, they can go abroad. Personally, I think going abroad is better because I don’t see much opportunity for development here. I cannot create the future I want for my child,” said a young woman pushing a pram with her newborn baby.

One respondent said that she had lived in Spain with her three children for several years, but the family had recently decided to return to Georgia so that the children would not forget their mother tongue.

“When they grow up, they can choose for themselves where they want to live. But I want conditions here to be good enough for them not even to think about leaving.”

Street poll in Tbilisi

World.title: Karabakh: Why have only 40,000 of planned 140,000 Azerbaijanis returned?
World.content:
Return of Azerbaijanis to Karabakh

Azerbaijan will mark Victory Day on 8 November. The first state programme, known as the “Great Return”, is due to conclude at the end of this year. According to data from the State Statistical Committee, 40,520 former internally displaced persons (IDPs) had returned to Karabakh and East Zangezur as of 1 October.

However, under the programme, 140,000 people were expected to return by the end of 2026. With just three months remaining before the programme’s conclusion, only around 29% of the target had been met.

In 2025, JAMnews reported on the social problems associated with the return of displaced people. This time, we examine a different question:

Why has less than a third of the target been achieved as the first programme nears its end, and what could the second programme change?

What do the figures show?

Indicator Target

Latest figures

Number of former internally displaced persons (IDPs) who have returned

Around 140,000 people

40,520 people (as of 1 October)

Number of settlements 100 47 (as of September)

Area cleared of landmines 280 000 hectares

Around 300,000 hectares (as of September)

Funding

More than 32bn manats (approx. $18.8bn)

More than 25bn manats (approx. $14.7bn) (2020–2026)

Sources: Official government portal, State Statistical Committee, Prime Minister Ali Asadov and Azerbaijan National Agency for Mine Action (ANAMA).

The pace of returns is increasing. At the beginning of the year, the number of returnees stood at 26,014. This means that a further 14,506 people returned to the region over nine months. If the current pace continues, it will take another five years for the remaining roughly 100,000 people to return.

The frequently cited figure of 96,068 refers to the total number of people living, working and studying in the region. In January, President Ilham Aliyev said that “120,000, 130,000 or 140,000 people” could be living and working there by the end of the year. However, he also acknowledged that implementation of the programme could take longer than expected:

“I have told everyone, and I can tell the public now, that I have never set any deadlines.”

Nevertheless, the programme itself sets the end of 2026 as the deadline for achieving its target.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, told Meydan TV that around 20 of the 47 settlements had been rebuilt, while the remainder were villages that came under Azerbaijani control in 2023.

That same year, around 100,000–120,000 ethnic Armenian residents of the region were forced to flee to Armenia. Yerevan describes the events as ethnic cleansing, while Baku maintains that Armenians can return if they accept Azerbaijani citizenship.

What has the money been spent on?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that more than 25bn manats (approximately $14.7bn) had been allocated from the state budget for the reconstruction of the region since 2020.

This year’s budget earmarked 3.5bn manats (approximately $2.06bn) for reconstruction. According to Finance Ministry figures, 1.76bn manats (approximately $1.035bn) was spent over the first nine months of the year. Of this amount, 891.8m manats (approximately $524.6m) went towards infrastructure development, while a further 692.5m manats (approximately $407.35m) was allocated to projects in education, healthcare and culture.

Ilham Aliyev explained the distribution of funds, saying: “As infrastructure projects are implemented, more funds will naturally be allocated to housing construction.”

However, critics argue that the main problem is a lack of transparency. According to Meydan TV, annual progress reports on the programme’s implementation are not publicly available, while the website of the centre responsible for monitoring the programme does not publish its findings.

How serious an obstacle do landmines remain?

According to Azerbaijan’s Mine Action Agency (ANAMA), 979 landmines and 3,070 unexploded ordnance items were discovered in October alone. The agency had previously reported that 421 people had been injured or killed by landmines and other explosive devices between November 2020 and April 2026, including 72 fatalities. In September, ANAMA chairman Vugar Suleymanov said there had also been cases of previously cleared areas becoming contaminated with landmines again as a result of flooding.

Journalist Tapdig Farhadoglu told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that much of the territory could become habitable within 10–15 years, while the full restoration of mountainous areas could take 20–30 years.

Economist Natig Jafarli, meanwhile, considers the current pace of returns justified. Speaking to the same outlet, he expressed confidence in the official statistics and noted that a phased return of displaced people made it easier to ensure their safety. He argued that too much emphasis should not be placed on deadlines and numerical targets, saying that “these are not Soviet five-year plans”.

Housing is available, but what about jobs?

Analyst Togrul Juvarli told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that the 1,200-square-metre plots of land provided with houses were insufficient for viable farming. Meanwhile, large agricultural enterprises offer local residents low-paid jobs. Economist Natig Jafarli also pointed out that internally displaced persons had not received land plots during the agricultural reforms of the late 1990s. He believes they should now be granted private ownership of land.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, described the situation in an interview with Meydan TV:

“If a village has housing but no jobs, opportunities to use land are limited, starting a business is difficult, and people have to leave again to find work in other cities, it is hard to call this a genuine Great Return.”

Aytaj Amirjanli, who relocated to the village of Vangli in Aghdara district, told Radio Liberty that she had been registered with the employment service for ten months. According to her, the village has neither a pharmacy nor public transport. She claimed that “most residents are already locking up their homes and leaving for Baku”.

Meanwhile, presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev advised residents to submit complaints directly to government officials rather than record and circulate videos expressing their grievances.

On 30 October, MP Agil Abbas told parliament that around 10,000 people originally from Aghdam were not registered in the city and did not have internally displaced person status. Parliamentary Speaker Sahiba Gafarova objected, saying: “So much work has been done. Why are you trying to discredit it?”

What could the second programme change?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that the draft of the second programme had been submitted to the president. He also described the implementation of the first programme as successful. The targets of the new programme have yet to be made public. According to Finance Ministry projections, 13.2bn manats (approximately $7.765bn) is expected to be allocated to the region’s reconstruction between 2027 and 2030.

Under amendments approved in July, anyone who refuses housing offered by the state loses their status as an internally displaced person. Human rights defenders argue that this violates the principle of voluntary return, while pro-government media portray the changes as a restoration of property rights.

Razim Amiraslanli has called for a comprehensive audit of the first programme. He believes the new programme should focus not on the number of buildings constructed, but on the number of people who have found employment and families who have received land plots.

Новости в Азербайджане

World.title: Garibashvili case 2.0: Trial begins over second charge against Georgia’s ex-PM
World.content:
Second charge against Georgia’s ex-PM

On 2 November, Tbilisi City Court began hearing the bribery case against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili.

This time, Garibashvili himself was present in the courtroom, marking his first appearance at a hearing in the case. He had previously described the court proceedings as a “masquerade” and maintained in letters from prison that he would not take part in them.

“It is very important that the proceedings are conducted transparently,” Irakli Garibashvili said at the start of the hearing, explaining his decision to attend.

However, the hearing was closed to the public at the prosecution’s request. Prosecutors argued that the case involved the Defence Ministry, required testimony from other senior officials and concerned personal data.

Garibashvili and his defence team strongly opposed the decision. His lawyer argued that such proceedings had never previously been held behind closed doors. He maintained that the case involved no classified information and that the decision had been made solely because Garibashvili was attending the hearing.

This is the second criminal case against Garibashvili. He was charged with accepting a bribe on 24 August 2026, an offence punishable by 11 to 15 years in prison. According to investigators, former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze handed Garibashvili, who was prime minister at the time, 750,000 lari (approximately $292,000) from a 1.5m-lari (approximately $584,590) bribe allegedly received from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who had won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital. In effect, prosecutors allege that Burchuladze shared the bribe with Garibashvili. Burchuladze himself testified against the former prime minister. The first criminal case against Garibashvili concerned money laundering. On 12 January 2026, he pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors, receiving a five-year prison sentence instead of the nine to 12 years prescribed by the Criminal Code.

“Long live the layman!”

Despite being held behind closed doors, the hearing was well attended. Those present included Irakli Garibashvili’s wife, eldest son, brother-in-law and uncle. However, only two of his allies from the ruling Georgian Dream party attended: former Justice Minister Rati Bregadze and former MP Luka Kurtanidze.

“Long live the layman!” Luka Kurtanidze cheerfully exclaimed as Garibashvili entered the courtroom, apparently seeking to emphasise that the former prime minister was now an ordinary citizen. The remark earned him a stern warning from Judge Tamar Mchedlishvili.

Garibashvili sat in a glass-enclosed dock reserved for defendants, surrounded by security guards. Dressed entirely in black, he appeared to have lost weight. He occasionally glanced towards the courtroom from behind a guard’s shoulder and smiled at his wife.

The hearing began with the standard procedure of establishing the defendant’s identity.

“First name, surname?“

“Irakli Garibashvili, son of Tariel.”

“Do you speak the state language?“

“I’m trying,” Garibashvili replied, attempting to make a joke.

“I can make jokes too, but this is a courtroom. Let’s keep things appropriate,” the judge responded sternly.

Shortly afterwards, journalists were asked to leave, and the hearing continued behind closed doors.

“Ivanishvili has been misled”

Following the hearing, Garibashvili’s family members declined to comment to the media. The former prime minister’s son, Nikoloz, tried to push reporters aside to escort his mother out of the courtroom.

Garibashvili’s lawyer and two fellow party members who had come to support him spoke to journalists.

“I came to see a friend whom I have missed very much. I want to wish him strength and hope that he will return to his family very soon,” former Justice Minister Rati Bregadze said.

Asked whether he believed his friend had committed a corruption offence, Bregadze said it was for the court to decide.

“I am truly proud to have had the opportunity to work alongside Irakli Garibashvili. The court will determine everything else. This is all very emotional for me,” he said.

The former minister declined to answer when asked whether the new charge was linked to the appointment of Mamuka Mdinaradze as head of the State Security Service.

However, Luka Kurtanidze, a former freestyle wrestler turned politician known for his fiery temperament, was more forthcoming. He called Mdinaradze a “rat” and claimed that Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili had been “misled”.

“I am happy to have seen the layman, Irakli Garibashvili. He is healthy and strong. Only fools and rats like Mdinaradze would believe this nonsense [about accepting a bribe],” he said.

“Garibashvili was subjected to psychological pressure”

Details of what Garibashvili said after journalists were ordered to leave the courtroom emerged from his lawyer, Soso Baratashvili.

According to Baratashvili, the former prime minister told the court that he had been subjected to psychological and moral pressure before the investigation began in an attempt to force him to admit to accepting a bribe.

The lawyer called on investigators to launch an inquiry, claiming that Garibashvili could provide information confirming that he had been subjected to pressure.

“He did not name anyone today. But during the investigation, he will, of course, identify who made the proposal. He will explain all the details to investigators. This allegation is not unfounded,” the lawyer said.

Baratashvili argued that the decision to hold the trial behind closed doors was unjustified and intended to conceal details of the case.

“The prosecution is using this as a tool. It wants to cover up the case and hide the details from the public, the media and human rights defenders. This is a very serious violation,” he said.

According to Baratashvili, the defence intends to appeal the judge’s decision.

Background

Irakli Garibashvili is more than just a former prime minister. For nearly two decades, he was one of the closest and most trusted associates of Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is widely regarded as Georgia’s de facto ruler.

Before entering politics, Garibashvili served as director-general of Ivanishvili’s Cartu Foundation and represented his business group. When Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister in 2013, he effectively handed the position to Garibashvili, who was just 31 at the time.

Garibashvili served as prime minister from 2013 to 2015. He later became defence minister before Ivanishvili backed his return to the premiership in 2021.

In April 2025, Garibashvili announced his retirement from politics. Later that year, he was imprisoned on money-laundering charges.

World.title: ‘Certain circles in Russia and Eurasian Economic Union back secret plan by Armenian opposition’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on secret plan by Russia and Armenian opposition

Armenia has reached a very important historic turning point, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the 2027 state budget. He described it as a moment that would have a decisive impact on the country’s political, economic and social development.

However, he said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were seeking to prevent this historic moment from arriving. According to Pashinyan, similar forces had opposed Armenian statehood in the past, dating back to 2018. That was the year of Armenia’s “Velvet Revolution”, which brought him and his team to power. “But this year, their cards have been laid bare,” Pashinyan stressed.

He singled out the so-called “secret plan”, which opposition circles have been discussing recently.

“The aim of this plan is to prevent Armenia from continuing on its path of economic development. There are not enough resources inside Armenia to implement this secret plan, so its authors must do everything possible to secure resources from abroad,” he said.

The prime minister spoke about this “secret plan” a couple of weeks ago, but did not specify which countries he meant. This time, however, he openly named them:

“I do not want to hide the fact that certain circles within the Eurasian Economic Union, led by Russia, and in the Russian Federation itself support this plan. And there are reasons for this, because people have been sent to Armenia with specific promises and guarantees.”

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition Strong Armenia party, has repeatedly spoken about a “secret plan” to change the government in Armenia. He made these remarks in response to a question about the steps the opposition intended to take to oust the current authorities. At his weekly briefing on 22 October, Nikol Pashinyan said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were taking steps to effectively eliminate the country: “The aim is to provoke political instability inside Armenia. As a result, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to strip Armenia of its independence – first de facto, and then de jure.” The prime minister also said that several similar attempts had taken place over the past three years. He cited, in particular, the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023 and hybrid attacks on Armenia during the parliamentary elections, which took place in June this year. He believes a third attempt is now under way. In particular, he was referring to an expert forecast by the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, which warned of an allegedly catastrophic economic downturn in Armenia if the country left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU. “This is part of the ‘secret plan’ that people are actively discussing now,” Pashinyan said.

“Armenia’s political forces must understand that the people are their only guarantee”

The prime minister said that certain opposition figures had “received specific guarantees and been sent to Armenia”. He then asked: “So why are these guarantees not being honoured?” He went on to answer his own question, urging the opposition to look back at the history of the Armenian people. He said that whenever such “guarantors” had emerged, the outcome had invariably been another catastrophe.

“I am essentially doing our opposition colleagues a favour by pointing out that they still have time to avoid a similar catastrophe. I am talking about the political catastrophe facing opposition parties, which you all know about. I hope they will seize this opportunity to avoid it.”

He recalled that he had previously urged the opposition to stop relying on these “guarantors” and instead focus its efforts on strengthening Armenia’s independence and sovereignty. However, his proposal went unanswered.

“In effect, it was rejected through silence. I believe the window of opportunity has not yet closed. Ultimately, our political forces must understand that there is only one guarantee – the people of Armenia,” he stressed.

World.title: GYLA challenges conviction of defendant in case over storming of Georgia’s presidential palace
World.content:
According to the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the case against Paata Manjgaladze, one of the leaders of the opposition Strategy Aghmashenebeli party, who was convicted in the so-called “4 October case”, lacks sufficient evidence that he planned, organised or led group violence.

In a detailed assessment, the association says the prosecution has failed to distinguish Manjgaladze’s political activities from any alleged involvement in violent acts.

In particular, it has presented no evidence linking him to the violence outside the presidential palace in Tbilisi.

On 4 October 2025, Georgia held local government elections. Much of the opposition boycotted the vote and staged a large-scale protest in Tbilisi that day. The demonstration ended with an attempt to storm the presidential palace.

GYLA argues that these claims are not substantiated by Manjgaladze’s previous political statements either, as some of them are undated and the circumstances in which they were made remain unclear.

“A political or organisational connection to a protest cannot in itself constitute grounds for liability for organising violence unless the defendant’s specific contribution is established,” GYLA writes.

Paata Manjgaladze

Paata Manjgaladze is the secretary-general of the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party and a former member of the Georgian parliament. On 4 October 2025, he took part in a protest in Tbilisi. Prosecutors accused him of organising group violence and leading it. On 7 May 2026, a court found him guilty and sentenced him to seven years in prison. His case is now before the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.

What Manjgaladze is accused of

Prosecutors charged Paata Manjgaladze on 6 October 2025. According to their account, he and other opposition figures arrested in connection with the case had urged citizens to overthrow the government by force. On 4 October, they then decided to organise group violence.

Opera singer Paata Burchuladze, who organised the rally and was later arrested in the same case, announced the plan at the protest. Murtaz Zodelava, a member of the United National Movement party, then called on the crowd to march towards the presidential palace and seize it.

To support the charges, prosecutors cite witness testimony, media reports, written documents, expert assessments, audio and video recordings from the scene, as well as objects found there and damaged equipment. The investigation also relied on search and seizure records and other materials gathered during the inquiry.

The prosecution maintains that this evidence is sufficient to establish the defendants’ involvement in the crime.

However, it remains unclear which specific pieces of evidence relate directly to Manjgaladze. In GYLA’s assessment, the indictment does not adequately explain what specific actions Manjgaladze himself took or what evidence demonstrates his involvement in the crime.

GYLA argues that political activity, attendance at a protest, a photograph with other organisers or a particular sequence of events cannot, in themselves, justify charging someone with organising group violence. This is especially important when the defendant is a politician. The charges must leave no doubt that the prosecution is not politically motivated.

What GYLA wants the Court of Appeal to do

GYLA is calling on the Court of Appeal to examine what specific actions prosecutors attribute to Manjgaladze, what evidence supports the allegations and how the court assessed the defence’s arguments.

The organisation also notes that Georgia’s Public Defender (ombudsman) has submitted an opinion in the case. The Public Defender likewise found no clear evidence of Manjgaladze’s specific role in organising group violence, arguing that merely describing him as one of the protest organisers is not sufficient grounds for criminal prosecution.

GYLA believes that if the Court of Appeal agrees with its position and that of the Public Defender, and the legal grounds exist, it should acquit Manjgaladze.

Criminal proceedings have been launched against 64 people in connection with the events of 4 October. Prosecutors charged those detained with organising group violence, leading it or taking part in it, attempting to seize a strategic facility, and calling for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order. The case was divided into several separate proceedings.

The first-instance trials have now concluded. Of the 64 defendants:

One person was fined;

was fined; 29 people were sentenced to prison terms, three of them in absentia;

were sentenced to prison terms, three of them in absentia; 12 defendants had their sentences reduced under plea agreements;

had their sentences reduced under plea agreements; 22 people received suspended sentences under plea agreements and avoided prison.

World.title: Horrific discovery at cemetery renews debate over fate of stray dogs in Georgia
World.content:
Journalists and animal rights activists have discovered burial pits in Georgia’s capital Tbilisi, containing dozens of dead dogs dumped and covered with soil. Activists suspect the animals were healthy strays taken from the city streets. Judging by the condition of the bodies, veterinarians believe the dogs suffered greatly before they died.

The disturbing footage sparked widespread outrage on social media. Animal rights activists have called for an immediate investigation. A large protest took place in Tbilisi on the evening of 1 November. The city authorities deny accusations that they killed healthy dogs, dismiss them as a deliberate disinformation campaign and threaten criminal charges against activists who opened the burial pits without permission.

Nevertheless, Georgia’s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which concerns animal cruelty.

What do we know so far about the dog burial pits discovered in Tbilisi? Why do animal rights activists distrust the city authorities and municipal services? And why has Georgia been unable to solve its stray animal problem for years?

Night-time trips to Veli Cemetery

Blurred photograph of one of the burial sites at Veli Cemetery in Tbilisi. As the footage filmed by activists is extremely distressing, JAMnews has deliberately chosen not to use it in this article.

Under cover of darkness, a white minibus leaves Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter. Someone has removed the shelter’s logo from the vehicle. The minibus soon stops at Veli Cemetery on the outskirts of the Georgian capital. The engine keeps running, but the driver switches off the headlights.

Two people get out. They wear the shelter’s uniform and latex gloves. In complete darkness, lit only by the moon, they take the bodies of dogs out of the vehicle and dump them into pits that someone has dug in advance.

This continues over several nights. On one occasion, the workers dump seven dogs into a pit, while an eighth falls beside the vehicle. Despite the darkness, the footage clearly shows a man wearing gloves dragging the animal towards the burial site.

On the third night, the makeshift grave is already full of dogs’ bodies, and the workers begin covering it with soil. They do this in darkness too, switching on the vehicle’s headlights only occasionally to check their progress.

These images come from a report that TV Pirveli broadcast on 31 October. It documents alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Tbilisi. Someone filmed the footage with a hidden camera over several nights.

According to the programme’s journalists, people regularly remove dozens of dead dogs from Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter without permission and bury them in specially dug deep pits at the cemetery. Citing their sources, the journalists also report that the shelter has a quarantine area where staff euthanise healthy animals picked up from the streets.

Even before the report aired, shortly after the channel announced it, animal rights activists discovered additional burial sites near Veli Cemetery. They filmed and circulated even more disturbing footage. It shows graves filled with dogs whose eyes bulge and bodies appear twisted (JAMnews warning: the footage at this link is extremely distressing.)

The activists called the police to the site. Police representatives told TV Pirveli that they would investigate the matter step by step and report their findings.

Animal rights activists’ demands

After the story came to light, animal rights activists drew up a petition, calling on the prosecutor’s office to launch an immediate investigation. The petition’s authors point to an increasing number of suspicious cases in which dogs have disappeared across Georgia. They want investigators to examine the burial site at Veli Cemetery, exhume the remains and commission an independent veterinary and forensic examination to establish when and how the animals died.

The activists also urge prosecutors to check the microchips and other identification marks on stray animals, compare reports from members of the public about missing dogs with the remains found at the cemetery, and examine the shelter’s veterinary records on euthanasia and its accounts of drugs used for the procedure.

In their view, investigators must establish who ordered the animals’ burial, the legal grounds for removing their bodies and whether the burial process complied with the law. The petition’s authors stress that the public has the right to know how many animals died, under what circumstances and whether official statistics reflect the true scale of the situation.

Some people recognised among the dead dogs found at the burial site in Veli Cemetery strays they had been caring for. The image illustrates one such case: a Tbilisi resident writes on social media that a dog he looked after is lying in the pit (right-hand photo).

Tbilisi City Hall denies killing animals

The Animal Monitoring Agency, which operates under Tbilisi City Hall, denies the allegations. In an official statement, the agency says that “the footage broadcast by TV Pirveli shows a procedure permitted by law”.

The agency claims that the burial site at Veli Cemetery holds the remains of dogs that died in Tbilisi for various reasons, including illness, road accidents and other incidents, as well as natural causes.

“Across the capital, hundreds of animals die through euthanasia every year, while thousands die of natural causes,” the agency says in its statement.

It categorically denies allegations of mass, deliberate killings, insisting that the information circulated by journalists and activists amounts to disinformation intended to discredit the Animal Monitoring Agency and damage its reputation.

Tbilisi City Hall also says that unauthorised exhumations and the removal of remains violate the law, risk biological contamination and pose a threat to public health. On these grounds, the city authorities have threatened activists with criminal liability.

“We have already asked law enforcement agencies to investigate acts of vandalism committed by a particular group and take appropriate legal action,” City Hall said.

Signs of torture on the animals’ bodies

Animal rights activists question the agency’s claims that the dogs found at Veli Cemetery died of natural causes or were humanely euthanised. Activist Keso Baramidze, who has had dozens of animals euthanised when it was genuinely necessary, says dogs usually retain a peaceful expression after euthanasia.

“Sadly, dozens of animals have fallen asleep in my arms. Not one of them had an expression like the dogs found in the burial pits. They all simply looked as though they were sleeping. That is why the procedure is called ‘putting to sleep’,” she says in a social media post.

Baramidze outlines several possible causes of muscle tension and facial distortion in animals after death. These include:

Mechanical asphyxiation (strangulation) with a rope or wire, as well as burying an animal alive or while it still shows signs of life. This can deprive it of oxygen and cause severe agony;

with a rope or wire, as well as burying an animal alive or while it still shows signs of life. This can deprive it of oxygen and cause severe agony; Improperly administered chemical euthanasia – using drugs that cause muscle paralysis or other toxic substances without adequate anaesthesia. In such cases, the animal may die while still conscious;

– using drugs that cause muscle paralysis or other toxic substances without adequate anaesthesia. In such cases, the animal may die while still conscious; Severe physical trauma or electric shock – a powerful blow to the head or neck, or exposure to an electric current, which can cause severe muscle spasms and body tension.

“With any of these methods, when a dog dies amid extreme stress, fear, struggle and muscle exhaustion, its reserves of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) are depleted almost immediately. This causes rigor mortis to set in very early, almost instantly, within the first 10–20 minutes.

“Since rigor mortis always begins in the facial and jaw muscles, any grimace caused during the animal’s death throes becomes ‘frozen’. Even while the body remains warm, the face stays contorted,” Baramidze writes, citing scientific sources from abroad.

Protests and investigation

On Sunday, 1 November, the day after the report aired, animal rights activists staged a protest outside the government chancellery in Tbilisi. “We demand answers. Punish the officials responsible,” they called.

“Dogs tortured to death”, “Where have you taken the dogs?”, “I speak for those without a voice” read the banners held by protesters, including both activists and ordinary animal lovers. Many brought their pets to the demonstration.

“What we have been saying for several months has now been confirmed. They are continuing to exterminate stray dogs instead of sterilising and vaccinating them in an effort to reduce their numbers. I hope society will now become more active. Because if there aren’t enough of us, they will obviously not stop,” said Lasha Chkhartishvili, one of the protest organisers.

Protest outside the Government Chancellery on 1 November 2026. Photo: Rusudan Jakeli.

“A dog tortured to death” – reads the banner at the 1 November protest.

That same evening, Georgia’s Interior Ministry announced that it had opened an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which covers torture, cruel treatment and other forms of violence against animals.

Not an isolated incident, but a pattern

This is not the first case, nor the first footage to emerge showing alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Georgia.

In mid-October, a video filmed on a mobile phone at the municipal animal shelter in the town of Gori spread across social media. It showed a filthy enclosure measuring just five to seven square metres, with a damp floor and crammed with dozens of puppies. Many of the animals looked extremely thin and malnourished.

The following day, volunteers rescued the puppies from the enclosures, set up temporary shelters for them and began treating them. Social media users also launched a fundraising campaign to help the puppies and the people who had taken them in.

Earlier, in April 2026, disturbing footage from Gori also emerged, apparently showing animals being burned at a crematorium. However, the Gori shelter insisted that it had cremated dead dogs or amputated body parts.

Stray animals on the streets have long been a serious problem in Georgia. The streets are full of stray dogs, some of which are aggressive and pose a danger to passers-by. Yet no one knows exactly how many homeless animals live in the country. Georgia has never maintained comprehensive statistics on their numbers. Animal rights activists estimate that the population could reach hundreds of thousands.

Georgia has been running a new stray animal population management programme for the past two years. In theory, it should reduce the number of stray dogs through humane methods. However, animal rights activists suspect that the authorities are trying to solve the problem through straightforward extermination. They say dogs have been disappearing from the streets in large numbers since the programme began.

JAMnews reported on the situation in May 2026, when activists across Georgia raised the alarm over dogs taken from the streets and then reported missing. Some of the animals had been cared for by specific individuals, vaccinated, sterilised and identified.

The World Organisation for Animal Health recommends the CNVR method – Collect, Neuter, Vaccinate and Return – in its guidelines for managing stray dog populations. When properly implemented, this approach can gradually reduce the number of animals without resorting to mass killing.

Activists in Georgia also regard this as the best approach. None of them wants packs of stray dogs roaming the streets. But they insist that the authorities must tackle the problem humanely. The footage that has emerged in recent weeks has raised growing questions about the conduct of government agencies and strengthened suspicions that the authorities intend to reduce the stray animal population by killing the dogs.

World.title: Azerbaijan gets just $65 of every $120 barrel of oil – where does rest go?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s oil revenues

The price of Azerbaijani oil on the global market fluctuated between $120 and $130 a barrel in October, reaching $133 on 9 October. However, the state budget was drawn up on the basis of a forecast price of $65 a barrel.

The government is now using the same benchmark price for the 2027 budget.

Yet rising oil prices have not translated into the expected increase in either the State Oil Fund’s assets or state budget revenues.

According to a report published by the State Oil Fund on 20 October, its assets have increased by just $462 million since the beginning of the year. Meanwhile, transfers from the fund to the state budget have fallen by 11.4% compared with the same period last year.

JAMnews previously reported that the government plans to reduce transfers from the Oil Fund and increase income tax deductions from salaries in the 2027 budget. Now another question arises:

If oil is selling for significantly more than the price assumed in the budget, where is the additional revenue going?

Why is the budget based on a price of $65 a barrel?

Every year, when preparing the state budget, the government forecasts the average oil price for the coming year. It uses this estimate to calculate tax receipts and other revenues.

In November 2025, Finance Minister Sahil Babayev told parliament that the government had set its 2026 oil price forecast at $65 a barrel based on average estimates from 22 organisations. At the time, Brent crude traded at $64–65 a barrel.

However, the situation changed in early 2026.

In its July report, the State Oil Fund noted that the conflict between the US and Iran had triggered “high volatility” in energy markets. According to figures that Samir Nasirov, head of the Central Bank’s Statistics Department, presented in September, Azerbaijani oil averaged $94.5 a barrel in the first half of the year.

That was 33% higher than in the same period last year and approximately 45% above the price assumed in the budget.

According to the Finance Ministry’s preliminary figures, the 2027 budget also assumes an oil price of $65 a barrel. However, in its medium-term expenditure framework for 2027–2030, the ministry describes the likelihood of oil prices falling below $65 next year as “low”.

In other words, the budget relies on a price close to what the ministry itself considers one of the less favourable scenarios.

Using a lower forecast price means that additional oil revenues go to the State Oil Fund rather than directly into the state budget.

Economist Natig Jafarli made this point back in March, when oil prices began to rise.

He said higher prices would affect “not the state budget directly”, but the consolidated budget, which also includes the State Oil Fund’s resources.

According to Jafarli’s calculations, every $1 increase in the oil price brings the fund approximately $450,000 in additional revenue each day.

Supporters of the government’s policy see this additional revenue as a reserve that could help finance security spending.

In March, Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, told OC Media that the additional revenue would allow the government to fund “priority areas such as national security”.

Why are higher oil prices not bringing additional revenue into the state budget?

The government determines how much money the State Oil Fund must transfer to the state budget each year before the financial year begins. It sets the amount out in the fund’s budget.

According to the Finance Ministry, the fund transferred 9.628 billion manats (approximately $5.663 billion) to the state budget between January and September, exactly as planned.

However, this was 1.23 billion manats (approximately $723 million) less than in the same period last year.

Total state budget revenue from the oil and gas sector reached 12.93 billion manats (approximately $7.6 billion). This was 625.5 million manats (approximately $368 million), or 5.1%, above the forecast.

Since the State Oil Fund made transfers as planned, tax payments from oil companies accounted for the additional revenue.

According to the ministry, the Shah Deniz project paid 1.54 billion manats in taxes (approximately $906 million), SOCAR paid 1.3 billion manats (approximately $765 million), and the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli project contributed 461 million manats (approximately $271.2 million).

Overall, state budget revenues in the first nine months exceeded the forecast by 2.8%.

In other words:

In the first half of the year, oil prices were approximately 45% above the level assumed in the budget.

Yet total state budget revenues exceeded the forecast by just 2.8% in the first nine months.

Если деньги остаются в фонде, почему его активы не растут?

Согласно отчету Нефтяного фонда, значительная часть дополнительных доходов либо не поступила в фонд, либо была поглощена другими расходами и убытками.

Нефтяной фонд, январь–сентябрь 2026 года (млн манатов):

Indicator Amount Revenues from the sale of profitable oil and gas 7 343,9 Proceeds from the sale of the state’s stake in the Southern Gas Corridor 1 390,9 Other oil and gas revenues 5,8 Income from asset management 3 600,7 Total revenues 12 341,3 Transfers to the state budget -9 628,0 Expenditure on project implementation and management -53,2 Losses due to changes in gold prices and foreign exchange rates -1 874,0 Increase in the Fund’s assets 786.1 (approximately $462 million)

Source: State Oil Fund. JAMnews calculated the figure in the final row using the fund’s published data on asset growth.

The figures point to three conclusions.

First, the fund’s revenue from oil and gas sales (7.34 billion manats) fell 2.3 billion manats short of the amount it transferred to the state budget (9.63 billion manats). Revenue from the fund’s overseas investments and proceeds from the sale of the state’s stake in the Southern Gas Corridor helped cover the gap.

Second, changes in gold prices and exchange rates caused losses of 1.87 billion manats (approximately $1.01 billion). At the end of the first half of the year, losses stood at 3.69 billion manats (approximately $2.17 billion), but they narrowed in the third quarter. Gold has become one of the fund’s key assets in recent years. In its assessment of the fund’s 2026 budget, the Chamber of Accounts noted that rising gold prices had generated a significant share of the fund’s non-budget revenues in the first nine months of 2025. The same assessment warned that, as oil revenues and production volumes decline, the fund’s assets could “be rapidly depleted”.

Third, despite higher oil prices, the fund’s oil revenues did not grow at a comparable rate. According to the fund’s report, receipts from the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli field averaged 729 million manats (approximately $428.8 million) a month in the first half of the year, compared with 732 million manats (approximately $430.6 million) in the third quarter. JAMnews calculated these figures using data from the State Oil Fund.

Oil production is declining

According to preliminary figures from the Energy Ministry, Azerbaijan produced 19.9 million tonnes of oil, including gas condensate, between January and September. This was 3.9% less than in the same period last year.

Exports show a similar trend. According to State Customs Committee data for January–August, the physical volume of crude oil exports fell by 7.8% compared with the same period last year, while their value increased by just 10.5%.

In other words, although Azerbaijan sells each barrel of oil at a higher price, it exports less oil. Falling production partly offsets the additional revenue from higher prices.

In September, economist Elchin Mammadov highlighted this contradiction in an interview with Sfera.az:

“Although the average oil price has risen by around 30% this year compared with 2025, the latest published statistics point to a continued decline in the oil and gas sector.”

He said the sector’s gross domestic product had fallen by 0.8%.

In the assessment mentioned above, the Chamber of Accounts also forecast that oil production at the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli fields would fall to 120.1 million barrels in 2026, down 3 million barrels from the previous year.

What will change for citizens?

According to the preliminary 2027 budget figures presented by the government, transfers from the State Oil Fund will fall by 935 million manats to 11.9 billion manats (approximately $550 million).

The income tax rate on the portion of salaries up to 2,500 manats (approximately $1,470) in the private non-oil and gas sector will rise from 3% to 5%. It will increase further to 7% in 2028. Meanwhile, the government plans to cover 2.75 billion manats (approximately $1.617 billion) of the projected budget deficit of 3.17 billion manats (approximately $1.867 billion) through borrowing.

News that the country’s foreign exchange reserves had exceeded $90 billion had already sparked public debate. Critics called on the government to use some of these funds to improve living standards.

The government, meanwhile, sees reducing the budget’s dependence on oil revenues as a positive trend. Commenting on the preliminary 2027 budget figures, Vugar Bayramov welcomed the increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60%, saying this would make the budget more resilient.

Under this approach, the less the budget depends on oil revenues, the less vulnerable it becomes to falling oil prices.

What happens next?

Oil prices through the end of this year and into next year will depend largely on developments in the Middle East.

However, the Finance Ministry’s forecast suggests that even if oil prices remain high, the State Oil Fund’s assets will not grow. According to the ministry’s medium-term expenditure framework, the fund’s assets are expected to stand at $73.9 billion by 2030. That is below their current level of $74 billion.

An analysis by Meydan TV, based on the document, forecasts a 25.5% decline in oil and gas revenues to the budget between 2026 and 2030. Meanwhile, debt servicing costs are expected to rise to around 3 billion manats (approximately $1.765 billion).

The government’s draft budget for 2027 once again assumes an oil price of $65 a barrel. It also provides for lower transfers from the State Oil Fund and higher income tax deductions from salaries.

Azerbaijan’s oil revenues

World.title: EDB outlines conditions for Central Asian electricity exports to China (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. Electricity exports from Central Asia to China could become a long-term strategic option for the region, but their implementation would require confirmed demand, clear commercial terms, and an assessment of technical feasibility.

This is stated in the report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), "Energy Without Borders: Architecture of Energy Connectivity in Central Asia," provided exclusively to Trend.

According to the report, China has extensive experience in high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission technologies, renewable energy, grid construction and battery energy storage systems. This could give Central Asian countries potential access to capital, technology and new markets.

However, the eastward route should currently be viewed as a strategic project option rather than an established export corridor. The publicly available materials used in the report do not confirm a potential buyer, supply volumes, a route, a technical configuration, a commercial model, or the allocation of risks.

"The Chinese market is not homogeneous. The Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region is geographically close to Central Asia, but proximity does not automatically translate into demand for imported electricity. China is actively developing its own generation capacity, ultra-high-voltage grids, renewable energy and interregional transmission lines. The practical question, therefore, is whether there is a specific creditworthy buyer, a connection point, a pricing formula and a long-term contractual model," the report states.

From a technical perspective, electricity transmission eastward would likely require HVDC technology or another controllable grid interconnection scheme. Such solutions allow power flows to be managed and help reduce risks to grid stability without requiring the power systems to operate in strict synchronization.

However, the necessary infrastructure would require substantial capital investment and large, guaranteed electricity supply volumes, the report notes.

Another key consideration is how an export project would be integrated into Central Asia’s regional power system. According to the EDB, a model focused exclusively on exporting electricity from individual large power plants could have limited benefits for the region’s interconnected grid.

By contrast, integrating the eastward route into the broader regional energy system could increase the economic value of renewable energy, create additional external demand, build expertise in HVDC technologies and attract investment.

Realizing this potential would require a separate preliminary feasibility study, confirmation of buyer interest, an assessment of technical standards and an analysis of the potential impact of exports on the reliability of electricity supplies within Central Asia.

The EDB emphasizes that developing the region’s interconnected power system remains a necessary foundation for export projects. Coordinated efforts by Central Asian countries could strengthen the region’s negotiating position and reduce the dependence of potential electricity exports on a single external buyer.

World.title: Türkiye refutes claims about removal of Heydar Aliyev bust in Istanbul
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. Reports claiming that the bust in Heydar Aliyev Park in Istanbul, Türkiye, would be removed and that a cultural center would be built on the site of the park have been refuted.

This was stated in a post published on the social media account of the Center for Combating Disinformation under the Turkish Presidential Communications Directorate on X.

"Claims circulating on some social media accounts that the bust located in Heydar Aliyev Park in the Şişli district would be removed and that the area would be demolished to make way for a cultural center are unfounded.

The Şişli Municipality is not carrying out any work on the area in question, and no such project is on the agenda.

The public is urged not to believe provocative and disinformation-based claims aimed at misleading the public and targeting relations between the two friendly and brotherly countries," the post said.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s oil reserve life falls to 18 years from 47 in 2015 – Eni
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. Kyrgyzstan’s oil reserves-to-production (R/P) ratio stood at 18 years in 2025, down from 47 years in 2015, according to the latest report by the Italian Eni energy company.

The ratio shows how long proved oil reserves would last at the current rate of production. It fell sharply over the decade, standing at 21 years in both 2019 and 2020 before dropping to 19 years in 2021, 17 years in 2022, and 16 years in 2023. It then recovered slightly, to 17 years in 2024 and 18 years in 2025.

For comparison, the R/P ratio for Russia and Central Asia as a region stood at 29 years in 2025, compared with 27 years in 2015. The regional indicator reached 30 years in 2020 and 2024 and was 29 years in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2025.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan’s population reached 7.3 million in 2025, up from 7.2 million in 2024, an annual increase of 1.4%.

The population has grown steadily over the past decade, from 6 million in 2015 to 6.6 million in 2019 and 6.7 million in 2020. It then rose to 6.9 million in 2021, 7 million in 2022, 7.1 million in 2023, and 7.2 million in 2024.

The compound annual growth rate of Kyrgyzstan’s population between 2015 and 2025 was 2%.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Victory Day marked with official reception in Uzbekistan (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. An official reception was held in Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, to mark November 8, Victory Day of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The official reception, held at the Hyatt Regency Tashkent hotel with joint organizational support from the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Republic of Uzbekistan and the Heydar Aliyev Azerbaijan Cultural Center at the Embassy, was attended by representatives of the state and government, members of the diplomatic corps, representatives of international organizations, figures from the fields of science, culture, and the arts, members of the diaspora, as well as representatives of local and foreign media.

As part of the event, a photo exhibition titled “44 Days of Our Glorious History” was organized, reflecting the glorious chronicle of Azerbaijan’s Victory. On display were photographs depicting the heroism shown by the Azerbaijani Army during the 44-day Patriotic War, the liberation of Azerbaijani lands from occupation, and unforgettable moments of our historic Victory. The photographs were met with great interest by government officials and members of the public in attendance at the event.

Speaking at an official reception, Rashad Mammadov, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Azerbaijan to the Republic of Uzbekistan, spoke about the exceptional significance of November 8, Victory Day, in the history of the Azerbaijani people. The ambassador stated that the Patriotic War, which began on September 27, 2020, under the leadership of Ilham Aliyev, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, and lasted 44 days, became a triumph of the unity, resilience, and determination of the Azerbaijani people. As a result of the heroism, courage, and self-sacrifice demonstrated by the Azerbaijani Army, our lands, which had remained under occupation for many years, were liberated, and on November 8, 2020, with the liberation of the ancient city of Shusha, the cultural capital of Azerbaijan and the Turkic world, a historic victory was achieved.

The diplomat emphasized that the Victory of November 8 is forever enshrined in the national memory of the Azerbaijani people and laid the foundation for a new stage in the history of our country’s modern statehood.

Following the official proceedings, a festive artistic program dedicated to Victory Day was presented. The concert program featured performances by the Azerbaijani State Ensemble “Gaya,” the “Karabakh Zaferi” (“Victory of Karabakh”) Dance Ensemble of the Heydar Aliyev Azerbaijan Cultural Center at the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Republic of Uzbekistan, soloists from the “Kharibulbul” Theater Troupe, as well as the People’s Artist of Uzbekistan and Karakalpakstan, Honored Artist of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan Yulduz Usmanova. The musical and dance performances presented by the artists added a special flair to the concert program and were received with great interest by the guests.

One of the highlights of the concert program was the presentation of the “Zangezur Yallisi” dance by the “Karabakh Zaferi” dance ensemble of the Heydar Aliyev Azerbaijani Cultural Center. The dance preserves the rich folk traditions of Zangezur, an ancient Azerbaijani region. Reflecting ancient national dance traditions, as well as the spirit of unity and solidarity of the Azerbaijani people, the performance was warmly received by the audience, who showed great interest in its distinctive rhythm and dynamic execution.

The creative evening was significant in terms of further strengthening cultural ties between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, promoting examples of national art, and expanding cultural exchange between the two peoples.
