World.title: Can anything break politics out of its inflation doom loop?
World.content:
Jim Chalmers is a man stuck in an endless loop. Time and again in his four and a half years as treasurer, he has had to front up after bad news and spin the unspinnable.

His scorecard, across 41 post-rates press conferences: 17 hikes, 21 holds, three cuts.

That's an awful lot of times to reach for the same, gloomy script. And the talking points are becoming gratingly familiar. We know you're doing it tough. We're trying to help in a responsible way. Oh, and this isn't our fault.

Not that there's anything wrong with repetition. Politics works on the "vomit principle": to make sure your message is heard, you need to say it over and over again until it makes you want to vomit.

But after nearly five years of high inflation and high interest rates, the treasurer and his colleagues are at risk of triggering the wrong kind of nausea. Their challenge now is to find something fresh to stay.

The squeeze

That is difficult when the economic story hasn't changed much. The entire tenure of the Albanese government has taken place in a state of suspended animation, as it grapples with both the dual pain of the inflation disease and the harsh medicine of interest rates.

There is little room to manoeuvre. The billions spent on short-term cost-of-living help have done little to ease the anger of struggling voters, while opening the government up to opposition accusations that it is making the problem worse.

Chalmers rejects rate hike blame Treasurer Jim Chalmers seizes on weak public demand figures to argue his government is not to blame after a widely expected interest rate hike.

Ministers do not believe they could have done things any other way and are struggling to see what else they may cut from a federal budget heaving under the weight of long-term pressures in health, defence and social programs.

Meanwhile, the shocks keep coming. In the first wave four years ago, the Ukraine war and a global supply crunch arrived at precisely the worst time for Australia and other countries who were still in economy-stimulating mode after the pandemic.

This time, the Middle East war has combined with a spectacularly ill-timed artificial intelligence investment boom, which may yield fruit in years to come if the optimists are to be believed, but which for now is mostly a capital-heavy cash splash.

On both occasions, one great big hammer blow from the universe has pushed up the level of demand in our economy just as another big hammer blow from the opposite direction has pushed down what we are able to supply.

None of these can reasonably be seen as the government's fault. Yes, it's true the list of new spending decisions made under Chalmers's watch includes some expensive items we could have done without. A little less cash could have meant a little less pain.

But no set of government decisions, however courageous, could have spared us from all pain. Inflation, as Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock puts it, makes us poorer. Our dollars don't go as far. Excising it from our system hurts, whichever way you slice it.

Courage to change the things I can

All of which is to say that there's nothing wrong, as such, with the government's talking points. It's not wrong to say that the root causes lie elsewhere. It's not wrong to say that it's a fine balance between helping and hindering. And it's not wrong to say it sucks.

But the missing ingredient, of which the government is in desperate need, is hope.

In its first term, when they endured a similar cost-of-living slump, ministers could reasonably hold out hope that the clouds would part before the election. And they did. Three rate cuts created a well-timed sense that the worst was over.

This time, hoping for the cycle to turn will not be enough, not least because the curveballs from a volatile world won't stop coming.

Around the world, the mainstream politicians faring best are those who have been able to bend the volatility to their advantage. As the saying goes: don't waste a crisis.

Loading

Losing paint

There are signs the government has grasped this. Both Chalmers and Albanese have framed the budget's changes to the capital gains tax, negative gearing and trusts as their answer to voter anger at the "broken status quo".

The policy has been contentious, and Chalmers has taken to remarking in the past week that he believes he has "lost some paint" over the political risk.

No easy way out of inflation Another bad inflation result causes pain for households, business and the government. They also show that a tougher approach may well be needed to curb the problem.

"I think any treasurer taking on difficult reforms, which have been neglected for too long, in our tax system, in our housing market and elsewhere — no reforming treasurer expects there to be some kind of unanimously positive reaction," he said on Tuesday.

Whether Chalmers is actually relaxed about the backlash, and whether his colleagues feel the same, is unclear. But if the lesson from the tax decision, by far Labor's riskiest decision, is to take fewer risks, the outcome will likely be a hiding to nothing.

The same is true for the Coalition, which has adopted a bold proposal to index tax brackets but has baulked at suggestions from prominent former politicians to raise GST. None of these ideas are universally popular, and all of them create losers.

But the Coalition needs a fresh script every bit as much as Labor; its lines about the government's "spending addiction" are just as worn out from overuse.

With the federal budget under sustained pressure, and inflation likely to constrain the choices of governments for some time to come, a big risk grounded in political conviction might be the only way for either party to break their doom loop.

World.title: 'Like they don't care': RBA's fifth rate hike a huge blow to mortgage borrowers
World.content:
As a renter Laura Mayer is worried she won't be able to cope with Tuesday's Reserve Bank interest rate hike.

"For me, the fact of the matter is that my rent has gone up 32 per cent in a one-off increase this year," she said.

Ms Mayer blames rising interest rates.

Share your experience with the housing market ABC News wants to hear your housing journey to better understand how the changing market is affecting your decisions.

The Reserve Bank raised the cash rate by a quarter of a percentage point for the fifth time this year on Tuesday, taking the cash rate to 4.85 per cent.

"If the landlords pass on the cost of any interest rate rise, I won't be able to absorb it and will have to move," Laura Mayer said.

"The cost of housing is a constant state of stress for me, and it currently affects every aspect of my life.

"I continually worry that I will be a lifelong renter, and I cannot see how it gets better without genuine government intervention."

Bullock concedes the economy’s stressful

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock expressed some sympathy for those on the wrong side of interest rate hikes at Tuesday's press conference.

"The fact that we've had this massive shock has meant that we're poorer and that's what people are feeling," she said.

New research from Canstar has found one in 10 mortgage customers will have trouble meeting their soon-to-be higher repayments, following the RBA's decision.

The interest rate comparison website surveyed borrowers, renters and those who own their own home outright.

As many as 10 per cent of borrowers surveyed said they would be unable to meet the higher repayments if today's cash rate hike materialised, while a further 28 per cent said meeting the increase would not be easy.

The financial pain isn't limited to borrowers, with the majority (68 per cent) of renters saying they were concerned about the impact of today's rate hike on their rent or living costs.

'Almost like they don't care'

Sixty-year-old-mortgage borrower Lina Pugliese's job was recently made redundant, making her budget squeeze extra tight.

Lina Pugliese is among those feeling the pressure from successive interest rate rises. (Supplied)

She told the ABC finding work was getting "really tough".

"The buck stops with me," she said.

" I can't get work. I'm afraid to open my bank account because I don't want to see it going down. "

She also expressed concern the Reserve Bank did not care about her financial position and was more intent on reducing inflation.

"There seems to be an indifference coming from the RBA — almost like they don't care," Ms Pugliese said.

RBA wrestled with rate hike

Tuesday's RBA interest rates decision was a split one: six members voted to increase the cash rate target; three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent.

The reason for this, Michele Bullock said, was that board members were conscious of economic stress emerging.

"Those looking for a [rates on] hold [decision] were thinking that housing has reacted, the unemployment rate is drifting up … they felt that there were potential downside risks in these circumstances," she said.

Tracking how prices have changed with inflation If everything feels more expensive, that's because it is. With inflation rising again this week, we've tracked how prices of everyday items have increased.

But most board members saw fit to hike interest rates, and there may be more to come.

"As a result, given the elevated near-term inflation outlook and the likely ongoing global sources of inflationary pressure, my base case is that the RBA has at least one more shot in the locker," Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said.

In fact, two further rate hikes in the first half of next year can't be ruled out to ensure a decent slowing in domestic demand and containment of inflation expectations."

IT professional Stephen Macchia does not know what else he can cut back on to absorb higher mortgage repayments.

Stephen Macchia and his family have already cut back on spending to absorb the rate rises. (Supplied: Stephen Macchia)

"Our family has cut back as much as we can, stopped swimming and music lessons, purchase the cheapest variety of our regular food choices, we don't eat out or go on holidays — these increases are hurting," he said.

"What does the RBA expect us to do as costs are out of our control — we are all price takers for fuel, insurance, and food.

"There is no choice here — maybe there needs to be another instrument, like a variable portion of the GST or super to take money out of the economy."

Signs of growing financial stress

The Reserve Bank's interest rate rise is tipping more Australians into financial distress, with calls about people missing mortgage repayments now making up a greater portion of calls to the National Debt Helpline.

Calls and chats to the National Debt Helpline reached 187,905 in the 12 months to the end of August 2026, up 11.76 per cent from 168,133 over the same period the year before, with a greater portion coming from people unable to make mortgage repayments or at risk of arrears.

What's impacted by RBA rate hike Mortgage borrowers are likely to feel the sting of the RBA's latest cash rate rise, but savers and overseas travellers will also see the effects.

More than 1.82 million borrowers could be in mortgage stress due to the Melbourne Cup Day rate rise, according to Roy Morgan data.

On Monday Westpac reported that it offered 42,000 financial hardship assistance and disaster relief packages during the year.

Commonwealth Bank recently revealed in its financial results that the lender had "provided more than 147,000 tailored payment arrangements for customers in need of support".

Vicki Staff works with Financial Counselling Australia (FCA) as the coordinator for the National Debt Helpline.

Vicki Staff is coordinator of the National Debt Helpline for Financial Counselling Australia. (ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering )

Ms Staff said the latest data showed more than four in 10 callers were in paid employment demonstrating that having a job was no guarantee of financial security.

Further, mortgage stress was making up a bigger proportion of people who were contacting the helpline.

"We're hearing from people who've never had to ask for help before," she said.

"In the past where we've seen mortgage stress represent maybe 10 to 11 per cent of callers, we're now seeing it creep up to 14, 15 per cent of callers."

The Uniting Church has also seen a rise in people in need of financial assistance.

Spokeswoman Aileen Muldoon said most clients accessing Uniting's financial counselling services have household incomes below $50,000, but that "we are seeing more people in paid work whose income is no longer sufficient".

"This leads to debt hardship and housing insecurity with many people choosing to pay their bills so they can keep a roof over their heads and the lights on and go without essentials like groceries," she said.

World.title: Shake-up of specialist healthcare proposed to cut prohibitive costs
World.content:
Patients could make fewer visits to specialists and instead rely on their GP to treat some medical conditions, under a possible shake-up of specialist care in Australia.

A parliamentary inquiry is considering a sweeping overhaul of the system to help patients who struggle to afford private specialists or languish on public waitlists for years.

"I think we are at a tipping point … we knew this was going to happen, it was predictable," committee chair and Labor MP Mike Freelander said.

"I'm not interested in this being a blame game, I'm interested in this inquiry being one that looks at solutions and that all governments take responsibility."

Suzanne Luder has suffered from severe and unexplained abdomen pain. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Each year, almost 2 million people delay seeing a specialist or skip it altogether, according to the Grattan Institute.

Pensioner and former librarian Suzanne Luder has been on a public waitlist to see a gastroenterologist for the past two years, while suffering from severe and unexplained abdomen pain.

"Sitting in the darkness and wondering what the hell is wrong with you — I think that's the worst part," she said.

Eventually she was diagnosed with gastritis and oesophagitis after paying more than $1,000 to be treated in the private system.

"The doctor said it was one of the most dramatic examples of [those conditions] he had seen in his practice," she said.

"I'm not the poorest pensioner on the block … but if I'm going to live till I'm 95 I'm going to need the money I've got."

Some patients could avoid seeing a specialist

One of the potential solutions being canvassed by the inquiry is government funding for what are known as "secondary consultations", where GPs can ask specialists for advice on a diagnosis, management of a patient or whether a referral is needed.

Existing Medicare items cover some similar consults, but they are not broadly available.

Dr Freelander said an example could be a GP calling a dermatologist for advice about whether a mole on their patient required urgent attention, with both the GP and specialist paid for their time.

"At the moment it's a bit of an ad hoc arrangement. Many GPs will ring specialists they know and ask them for advice about a particular patient," Dr Freelander said.

"But we think we could formalise that … and it would help people in rural and remote areas."

Mike Freelander says GPs and specialists can work together. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

A 2022 evaluation of a Queensland pilot program found patients avoided a face-to-face specialist appointment in 86 per cent of cases after their GP obtained specialist advice.

Grattan Institute health program director Peter Breadon said evaluations of similar "secondary consultation" systems had also found a large proportion of cases could be managed without a specialist appointment, reducing demand and helping patients avoid long waits for care.

"Not only do you free up the specialist time, that patient saves money as well and we found that it would not diminish the quality of care at all," Mr Breadon said.

The proposal could also reduce pressure on public outpatient clinics.

While clinics provide one-third of specialist care, in some parts of Australia patients are languishing on waitlists for years.

The inquiry has written to the states and territories, which run the clinics, to discuss how to improve access.

"We've heard that some people go blind with the retinal deterioration in older age because they can't access ophthalmologists … I think we need to change that on an urgent basis," Dr Freelander said.

Julian Rait says action should have been taken sooner. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Ophthalmologist and outgoing vice-president of the Australian Medical Association Julian Rait said he had seen outpatient capacity collapse over his 35-year-career.

"I'm a little despondent about how late this discussion has occurred," Dr Rait said.

"Now we're in a situation where we've reached a high-inflation environment where we haven't prepared the system adequately."

Should doctors be penalised for charging exorbitant fees?

Demand for specialists is partly being driven by an aging population and the increasing prevalence of chronic illnesses.

But training places for the next generation of doctors are limited, tied to funding and teaching capacity, with the health department predicting a shortage of almost 7,000 specialists by 2033.

Shortages are particularly prevalent in regional and rural areas of Australia, where people report travelling hours for basic care.

Peter Breadon said rules were needed to "target the bad apples". (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Mr Breadon said the projections of how many specialists were needed should be turned into targets for training.

"In the absence of those targets, it's very hard to hold the medical colleges to account and to make sure the hospitals are funding and supporting the training places that are needed."

The lack of specialists has driven up fees, according to the Grattan Institute, which argues some private specialists are charging too much because they know their patients cannot easily go elsewhere for care.

A recent health department consultation paper found Australians spent more than $4 billion on out-of-hospital specialist services in 2025, an increase of more than 75 per cent since 2019.

"Surely it's within our power … to set some rules to target the bad apples that are charging too much and protect patients," Mr Breadon said.

Average out-of-pocket costs of an initial consultation with a specialist (three times the Medicare schedule fee): $670 for a psychiatrist

$370 for an endocrinologist

$369 for a cardiologist

$363 for a paediatrician Source: Grattan Institute

Dr Freelander said the inquiry would examine a range of drivers behind rising out-of-pocket specialist costs, such as patients presenting with more complex conditions and increasing practice overheads.

"It's easy to label doctors as greedy and sometimes it does seem that the fees are large, but there are reasons why large gap fees are being charged," he said.

The inquiry will also examine whether Medicare rebates need to be lifted, with doctors describing them as "almost meaningless".

"Over time, because of the erosion of the Medicare rebate relative to the costs of providing the care, the out-of-pocket expenses we've had to levy on patients have been increasing," Dr Rait said.

With submissions due to close this month, Suzanne Luder said she hoped the inquiry would prompt change.

"Life's too precious to be hanging around waiting on a list."

World.title: Gas policy consultants worked for industry and government at same time
World.content:
A consulting firm hired by the federal government to help develop its Future Gas Strategy was simultaneously doing paid work for the gas industry and did not disclose that conflict of interest to the energy department.

An investigation by advocacy group Climate Integrity found ACIL Allen did not disclose that while it was working on two reports for the government, it was also undertaking work for Gas Energy Australia, the Australian Pipelines and Gas Association and the Business Council of Australia, which represents several gas giants as members.

Consultancy ACIL Allen was commissioned to assess proposed reforms to the east coast gas market in late 2023, at the same time it was working for three gas industry groups to produce reports about the benefit of gas to the economy and its role in Australia's transition to net zero emissions by 2050.

Months later, ACIL Allen was hired by the government again to provide advice on Australia's gas needs, to be fed into the government's landmark Future Gas Strategy — the policy plan for how Australia will transition away from gas towards net zero emissions.

"This will inform an understanding of energy security, whether other sources of firming can perform this role and whether government action is needed," a department official wrote about the ACIL Allen contract, in emails released under freedom of information (FOI) laws.

Tender records and documents obtained under FOI show ACIL Allen's work for government and industry over 2023 and 2024 directly overlapped.

Madeleine King delivered the Future Gas Strategy in 2024. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The ABC attempted to reach ACIL Allen, including in questions sent by email. When the ABC spoke to an unidentified ACIL Allen representative by phone, he responded, "Yeah, no, I don't want to talk to you, thank you," before hanging up.

ACIL Allen also did not respond to questions put by Climate Integrity several months ago.

Future Gas Strategy promised plan for gas beyond 2050

The Future Gas Strategy delivered by Resources Minister Madeleine King in 2024 concluded that "the analytical findings are clear … natural gas is needed through to 2050 and beyond", with the policy committing to expand Australia's gas investment.

Labor backbench 'blindsided' by Albanese gas strategy Labor backbenchers say they were caught off guard by the government's new gas policy, which the resources minister says will keep the fossil fuel in Australia's energy mix until 2050 "and beyond".

It prompted a revolt on Labor's back bench, with several MPs at the time telling the ABC they had been blindsided by the policy, and its focus on expanding gas and continuing it beyond 2050.

Climate Integrity executive director Claire Snyder said the gas industry had obvious financial interests in shaping the Future Gas Strategy, and ACIL Allen should have been clear it was also doing work for them.

"The gas industry clients of ACIL Allen have a direct financial interest in the outcomes of the Future Gas Strategy and of the gas policies that ACIL Allen is working on for the government. So to us that is a clear conflict of interest," executive director Claire Snyder said.

"What we have is a consultancy with undeclared ties to the gas industry advising the government on consequential gas policy.

"Our analysis has also shown that the body of work produced by ACIL Allen over that period of time consistently overstated the cost of zero emissions alternatives to gas, and it entirely omitted the climate cost of developing new gas supplies. The result of this is it advantaged the case for gas."

As an example, Climate Integrity pointed to modelling based on up-front capital costs of energy projects, rather than system costs comparing expense over a project's lifetime, as a methodology that advantaged gas.

Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the non-disclosure called into question the government's Future Gas Strategy.

"It has no integrity. You cannot develop a gas strategy that is flavoured by … consultancy firms who are simultaneously working for the gas industry," Senator Hodgins-May said.

"It looks like, simply, a closed shop between government, between gas companies and their consultants, and this is exactly why the government won't act on a gas tax for Australians."

Steph Hodgins-May says the government is running a "closed shop" on its gas policy. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Questions to answer' on how disclosure was missed

Commonwealth procurement guidelines state that a conflict of interest exists where a contractor or consultancy has a competing duty that could affect the way they perform their work.

The government's supplier code of conduct, which was introduced four days before ACIL Allen's first report related to the Future Gas Strategy, requires suppliers to declare and manage conflicts of interest.

Where conflicts of interest are disclosed, companies can take steps to manage them by isolating teams on each project. The ABC asked ACIL Allen what steps it took to manage any conflicts of interest, and did not receive a response.

The combined value of ACIL Allen's work for the government over the two reports was more than $350,000.

The company employs about 60 consultants, and regularly consults on energy, resources, transport, infrastructure and public policy for government and industry clients.

Ms Snyder said the onus was on ACIL Allen to declare any conflicts of interest, but the department had also failed to make sure the rules had been followed.

"One of the most important safeguards we have to make sure that public policymaking is free from industry influence is declaring conflicts of interest," Ms Snyder said.

"The conflict of interest rules show [ACIL Allen] should have declared that, they should have made that clear to government."

The energy department confirmed to the ABC that ACIL Allen "did not declare any conflicts of interest in the procurement process".

Senator Hodgins-May said the government and department must explain why perceived conflicts of interest were missed.

"There is this closed shop that is deeply disturbing and means that decisions aren't being made that are best for our climate, for our planet, for getting wealth back that Australians deserve," Senator Hodgins-May said.

"I would say government probably knew exactly what they were getting [ACIL Allen] to do when they contracted them, but there certainly are questions to answer about why government didn't do that level of due diligence, and why ACIL Allen didn't disclose really important public interest information."

World.title: 'No need to sack the governor' and other reasons for the RBA's inflation target
World.content:
The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, delivering another blow to indebted households in its efforts to squash inflation.

RBA governor Michele Bullock says inflation is too high and it has to be dragged back down into the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target range.

Headline inflation in Australia is rising at an annual pace of 4.3 per cent at the moment.

RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years, in majority decision by RBA board.

"We are not looking to tip the economy into recession if we can avoid it, but we do need to get inflation down, and we do have excess demand at the moment, so that is the key," Ms Bullock said on Tuesday.

But why does the RBA think annual inflation of 2 to 3 per cent is optimal?

Why does it target that particular range for inflation?

Why not inflation of less than 2 per cent? Or slightly higher at 3–4 per cent?

For a number that's so consequential, its origins are surprisingly imprecise.

Copy New Zealand's idea, but with an Australian twist

The RBA adopted its inflation target in the early 1990s.

It copied the idea from New Zealand, which pioneered the concept and became the first country in the world to formally adopt inflation targeting as we know it in 1990.

But the RBA didn't copy New Zealand's model completely.

The RBA and the inflation myth The Reserve Bank doesn't want consumer prices to come down, but to rise more slowly. It's a common misunderstanding that the ABS is partly responsible for.

New Zealand originally picked an inflation target of 0–2 per cent, and senior officials at the RBA thought that was misguided, and wanted a different target.

Stephen Grenville, a former RBA deputy governor, recalled the history in 2023 as part of the RBA's oral history collection of interviews.

Dr Grenville worked at the RBA between 1982 and 2001 (his last five years as deputy governor).

"Any inflation target that contemplates getting to zero — or would think that being at, or near, zero is a good thing — just misunderstands the nature of inflation," he said.

"Economies work much better with a little bit of inflation so that relative prices can change, and in any case, quality improvements and a whole lot of those technical issues mean that zero makes no sense.

"So that [lower] end of the New Zealand target was wrong.

"They were also, we thought, 'inflation nutters' in that they thought inflation was the only thing that mattered," he said.

Miss the target and the governor gets sacked?

Dr Grenville said there were other reasons why the RBA didn't like New Zealand's 0–2 per cent target.

One reason was that New Zealand's original target was going to have "electric fences" on it — the edges, zero and two, were "very clear penalty areas" — which didn't make sense to RBA officials.

Who's to blame for interest rate hikes? The Coalition has been blaming federal government spending for rising inflation and another impending rate rise for Melbourne Cup Day, but the figures tell a different story.

"You could have 1.9 per cent [inflation] and that was OK, but if you slipped over to 2.1 [per cent], various bad things happened, and at least initially there was talk that the governor would be sacked," Dr Grenville recalled.

In the end, New Zealand didn't go ahead with that harsh plan, but they still saw it as a very bad thing if they ever recorded an inflation number bigger than 2 per cent.

"[W]hereas we thought the proper way to think about an inflation target was like an archer's target: that an archer always aims for the centre [and] doesn't expect to hit the centre of the bullseye all the time, but consistently aims for the bullseye," Dr Grenville said.

"[We] thought the right answer was to just mention a single number — which would be the centre of the target — and there wouldn't be any electric fences.

"The presumption, of course, would be the further away you were from the bullseye, the more you needed to do as the more you were off target.

"So it was a much more graduated thing that you could be off the bullseye, and no need to sack the governor," he said.

Inflation under 2pc is too low, above 3pc is too high

That's how the RBA stumbled upon its "2–3 per cent" target.

Dr Grenville said in the early 1990s, after more than a decade of high inflation and economic disruption, RBA officials didn't think they could get Australia's annual inflation down to 2 per cent sustainably, but they still wanted to be ambitious.

"We knew we'd had 'the recession we had to have' and we were going to make a lot of progress on inflation, but we didn't think we'd get much below 3 [per cent]," he said.

Are inflation-targeting central banks ready for the 'new inflation'? IMF economists say inflation-targeting central banks did not achieve better outcomes than others following the 2022 surge.

"We thought to mention 2 [per cent], which by then some other central bankers were talking about, and of course was the top of the New Zealand target.

"[So] 2 would be too ambitious, but 3 would sound like we weren't trying hard enough, so we suggested 2 to 3 [per cent, but] not as a range, and this was something we had a lot of trouble explaining.

"We didn't think we would stay within 2 to 3 [per cent], because we really thought of it as — I think Glenn [Stevens] invented the term — a 'thick point'.

"We just wanted people to be saying: well, if we had a number starting with 2, most of the time we would regard that as a satisfactory outcome.

"So that's one advance, as we saw it, over the New Zealand inflation targeting," he said.

Add a time dimension and you're sweet

Dr Grenville said the RBA also included a time dimension in its inflation target to allow for the fact that economies moved in cycles over many years.

"We somehow had to make sense of a single objective, so if people said to us 'don't you care about unemployment?', we would say 'this is where unemployment fits into our single objective'," he said.

The RBA's post-COVID rate hikes caused Australians to work more The International Monetary Fund found that thousands of Australians took on a second or third job when the RBA hiked rates rapidly in 2022 and 2023. It expected the opposite.

"The critical thing was the time dimension, and I think we were clearly the first to grapple with that idea that you had to get a time dimension into the inflation target.

"The time dimension we introduced was we wanted to get the 2 to 3 [per cent] over the course of the cycle, and that fitted with the idea that, yes, monetary policy does have some influence on the shape of the cycle.

"[And] over time, over the first four or five years of inflation targeting as it spread through more and more countries, everyone adopted our formula of 'over the course of the cycle', or gave themselves some time to get inflation back where it had to be," he said.

An eventual return to lower inflation

So there you have it.

Those are the fascinating origins of Australia's 2–3 per cent inflation target, a concept that is highly consequential in Australia's economy.

Yesterday, after the RBA lifted interest rates for the fifth time in 2026, governor Michele Bullock acknowledged that home loan borrowers would feel more pain from the higher rates.

But she said if inflation didn't come down, the pain of prolonged high inflation would be worse.

And she said the RBA now expected headline inflation to peak at 4.5 per cent at the end of this year [up from 4.3 per cent currently] and to not return to the RBA's 2–3 per cent inflation target band until late 2027.

World.title: Democrats forecast to make gains as US voters go to polls in midterms
World.content:
Democrats have firmed up as narrow favourites to win control of both houses of the US Congress in today's midterm elections, according to the US's top political forecasters.

The result would open new pathways for the party to frustrate Donald Trump's agenda in his final two years in office.

Voting is underway across the US, with polls finding many Americans intend to punish Mr Trump's Republican Party over cost-of-living pressures, including higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war.

"I think the results are going to be better than you think," the president told national breakfast television show Fox and Friends in a phone interview, shortly after polls opened.

Many polls say otherwise, with predictions some states that have not elected Democratic senators for decades could flip.

A dog watches people casting their ballots in Brooklyn on Tuesday. (Reuters: David Dee Delgado)

Growing concerns about corruption have also featured heavily in some surveys.

But many Democrats are wary of putting stock in the forecasts after polls overestimated their fortunes in several recent elections.

Forecasters say the Senate remains a very close contest that cannot be predicted with much confidence.

In Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost four decades, some polls show the party's candidate James Talarico ahead of his GOP rival.

"Let's show the world why you should always bet on the underdog," Mr Talarico, who like other Democrats has made pocketbook issues and cleaning up politics central to his campaign, wrote in a social media post on Tuesday.

In a taco restaurant in San Antonio, patrons were split on whether to vote red or blue.

"James Talarico seems to do a lot more for the people," one woman said. "And so just the stuff that he's talked about, I feel a lot better about voting for him than anybody else."

But not everyone was convinced.

"I'll vote Ken Paxton [the Republican Senate candidate]. It's not even a lesser-of-two-evils thing," a local man told the ABC. "I can tell you what he stands for."

America's political microscope has been on Texas ahead of the midterms. (ABC News: Cameron Schwarz)

To win the Senate, Democrats must win four seats currently held by Republicans without losing any of their own.

The respected Cook Political Report rates six Senate seats, which are all currently held by Republicans, as toss-up contests: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas.

But the Republican-held seat in North Carolina is forecast to fall into Democratic hands.

And the Democrat-held Michigan was moved from the "toss-up" category to "leans Democrat" on election eve, despite an eleventh-hour controversy caused by party infighting in that state.

"While Senate control could still swing either way, Democrats have the momentum in the final stretch," Cook analyst Jessica Taylor wrote.

Analysts at Sabato's Crystal Ball, at the University of Virginia, favour Democrats to end up with a 53-47 majority in the chamber. But they note "it wouldn't take much" for the numbers to shift in Republicans' favour.

Democrats have been tipped to win a majority in the House of Representatives for months, but their position appears to have improved in recent days.

The Cook report is projecting Democrats should win 230 to 240 House seats, well above the 218 needed to form majority.

Sabato's Crystal Ball predicts a similar outcome.

Donald Trump makes his final pitch to voters in Washington DC. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Americans are casting ballots for all 435 seats in the House of Representatives. They are also voting for 35 members in the 100-seat Senate, where senators serve six-year terms. Thirty-six states are also electing governors.

Mr Trump is not on the ballot, but has repeatedly urged voters to "pretend" he is, including at a series of rallies in the days leading up to the midterms.

The strategy is not appreciated by everyone in his party, given his approval ratings have been at record-low levels and continue to decline.

Loading

About 50 million ballots have already been cast, with early turnout outpacing the last midterm cycle in each of the major Senate battlegrounds.

Mr Trump is not on the ballot, but has repeatedly urged voters to "pretend" he is, including at a series of rallies in the days leading up to the midterms.

The strategy is not appreciated by everyone in his party, given his approval ratings have been at record-low levels and continue to decline.

"He started out good, but then he messed up getting involved in that war," Debra Simmons said after casting her ballot in Rocky Mount, North Carolina.

She still voted Republican because "they have more common sense", but said she hoped Mr Trump changed his attitude about rising prices.

Loading...

"It's unfair," said Wallace Cherry, who was handing out Democrat voting material for North Carolina's First Congressional District in Rocky Mount.

The district's boundaries were redrawn last year, reducing the proportion of Black voters and giving the Republican candidate an advantage.

"They're trying to make sure that their vote is counted more than ours," he said.

Overall, Republicans had hoped to win at least 13 redrawn seats, but analysts say that now looks unlikely.

"We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats," the Republicans' House Whip, Tom Emmer, told Axios last month.

California is the only state where Democrats have enacted a new map, which could help them pick up five extra seats.

World.title: Ticketek, Virgin and 'protein chips' win big at annual Shonky Awards
World.content:
Two ticketing companies, an airline, and a washer-dryer that takes 25 hours are among the recipients of the one award no business wants.

Consumer group Choice has released the winners of its 21st annual Shonky Awards, handed to the worst products and services of 2026.

Tricky ticket tactics

Ticketek and Ticketmaster have been awarded their second Shonky. (Supplied: Choice)

Ticketek and Ticketmaster have won their second Shonky, this time for "fleecing fans with tricky ticket tactics", called out for using dynamic pricing and "in demand" tickets.

Tickets sold by Ticketek this year for a John Farnham Tribute concert had prices up to $1,650.

NRL fans purchasing through Ticketmaster were asked to pay $50 more for "in demand" seats just one row or bay apart from regular seats.

A Ticketek spokesperson said variable pricing was used on less than 7 per cent of the John Farnham Tribute and this did not apply to the $1,650 tickets.

"Where it is used, fans are notified about potential price changes before they enter the on-sale," they said.

Ticketmaster has been called out for the use of "in-demand" tickets. (AP: Phelan M Ebenhack)

Changes to Australian Consumer Law from July 2027 ban dynamic pricing under certain circumstances where it unreasonably manipulates customers or distorts their decision-making.

Choice editorial director Mark Serrels said there was heightened awareness around ticket prices.

"I think it was really exacerbated by these big events like the Oasis reunion," he said.

A Ticketmaster spokesperson said it did not use surge pricing and "for in-demand tickets" and that "event organisers set the prices of sought-after seats closer to market value and may review these over the sales period."

Expired flight credits pocketed

This year, Choice gave Qantas a break and awarded Virgin Australia its first Shonky, for pocketing $75 million worth of expired flight credits.

The airline cancelled several flights between April 2020 and July 2022, at the height of the COVID pandemic, holding about $93 million in unused flight credits as of February this year.

Virgin Australia has earned its first Shonky Award. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Customers were forced to book trips by June 30 this year, with a deadline to fly by May 27, 2027.

"At best, these [credits] should be around until I want to use them … and at worst, you should just give me my money back," Mr Serrels said.

Virgin notes in its 2025/26 annual report that $75 million worth of expired COVID-19 credits "impacted" its underlying net profit of $404 million.

A Virgin Australia spokesperson said more than 93 per cent of COVID credits were redeemed.

"We regularly communicated the expiry date and later extended the fly-by date to 27 May 2027, giving guests almost another year to travel," they said.

25 hours of laundry, protein tax

Hisense earned its first Shonky for releasing an 8-star energy-rated "super energy efficient" washer-dryer. The catch? That rating is tied to the machine's eco settings that take 12 hours to wash and 13 hours to dry — 25 hours for a load of laundry.

Mark Serrels says Hisense's 25-hour washer-dryer cycle could be a form of "greenwashing" — pun intended. (Supplied: Choice)

Mr Serrels said the energy rating system was due for an overhaul, with almost all white goods manufacturers exploiting it.

"These [ratings] aren't really that accurate to your everyday use," he said.

Also claiming a Shonky are Quest Nacho Cheese Protein Chips priced at more than $20 per 100g — 886 per cent more than a pack of Doritos without the protein label.

Quest Protein Chips will help get you ripped (off). (Supplied: Choice)

Mr Serrels said this was a difficult decision with an influx of added-protein goods hitting store shelves, noting some of these goods were ultra-processed with very little additional protein and a much higher ticket price.

While the entire pet insurance industry has won a Shonky, with insurers not covering pre-existing conditions the main issue, this year Petcover has earned its own for taking things further.

One of its policies requires customers to enter a new policy every 12 months, which classifies all conditions the pet has previously experienced as pre-existing, therefore excluding them from the cover.

And its definition of pre-existing conditions is broad, including any condition with the same clinical signs as another injury or illness.

Play but don't own

Mark Serrels says Sony once mocked X-Box's plans to go digital, but now it has taken things to the extreme. (Supplied: Choice)

Rounding out the 2026 list is Sony for announcing that all new PlayStation games would be digital only from January 2028, under a model where customers did not actually own the games but instead licence them from the storefront.

"Sony, at any time, can remove these games from the store. In some cases, they can close the store entirely," Mr Serrels said.

Loading...

Sony said earlier this year the move was a natural direction for the company as, "The general preference for digital media significantly outpaces physical discs."

This year Sony removed more than 500 StudioCanal movies and TV show titles from users' libraries after a licensing deal expired.

Mr Serrels added the move would remove price competition, stop game sharing, and negatively affect the second-hand market as well as game preservation.

"This might be a canary in the coal mine situation with all video games; we'll start to see them all moving fully digital."

World.title: We want to gift our daughter $200k. Will that get us on the age pension?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAsk an expert Opinion We want to gift our daughter $200k. Will that get us on the age pension? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 4, 2026 — 5:01am

November 4, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We are considering giving our daughter, a single mother of two girls, a $200,000 advance on her inheritance to help her buy her first home. I intend to have proper documentation prepared to record the advance, including an agreement similar to a prenuptial agreement to protect her in the event of a future relationship. I am 69 and my wife is 63. We are both retired. I have $980,000 in superannuation and my wife has $220,000. We also have $320,000 in a term deposit and $137,000 in a bank account. We own our home, worth approximately $1 million. How long would Centrelink continue to assess the $200,000 advance as a gift? I estimate it could take another ten years before we qualify for a meaningful part age pension, assuming annual spending of $75,000 and investment returns of 7 per cent. Does that sound reasonable? Finally, would the gift or our financial position affect our eligibility for the Commonwealth Seniors Health Card? Gifting kids an early inheritance can be a good move, but don’t expect it to magically move you into age pension range. Simon Letch Provided the $200,000 is a genuine gift rather than a loan, Centrelink will cease to assess the amount above the allowable gifting limit five years after the gift is made. You’ll need to be particularly careful with the legal documentation to ensure that arrangements intended to protect your daughter don’t inadvertently turn the gift into a repayable loan. After the gift, you’ll have approximately $1.457 million in financial assets. Although the $220,000 your wife holds in superannuation will not count under the Centrelink assets test until she reaches 67, provided she leaves it in accumulation phase, your remaining assessable assets are still well above the couple’s age pension assets test cut-off point.



If you enter $1.457 million into the Retirement Drawdown Calculator on my website, assuming annual returns of 7 per cent and initial withdrawals of $75,000 indexed to inflation, you’ll find that the money could still be worth around $1.7 million in ten years. On those assumptions, I doubt you’ll qualify for an age pension unless your financial circumstances change significantly. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64 with just $93,000 in super. Should I add to it before retiring? Paul Benson Money contributor The Commonwealth Seniors Health Card is not assets tested, so having substantial investments doesn’t automatically disqualify you. Eligibility depends on your taxable income plus deemed income from account-based pensions. Based on the figures you’ve supplied, you may well qualify, but you should check your assessable income against the current limits. You have said that once a person has used their maximum transfer balance cap, they cannot transfer any more money into pension mode during their lifetime. I transferred $2 million into pension mode in August 2025 and have since made lump sum withdrawals totalling $500,000, which were paid into my bank account. My understanding is that these withdrawals allow me to transfer another $500,000 from my accumulation account into a new pension account. My myGov account shows available cap space of $550,000 and a personal transfer balance cap of $2 million. Does this mean I can make further transfers into pension mode?



Yes, provided your withdrawals were processed as lump-sum commutations rather than pension payments. Commutations free up transfer balance cap space to enable further transfers into pension mode, while pension payments do not. Before proceeding, ask your super fund to reconcile the $550,000 shown in myGov with your stated $500,000 of withdrawals. If the available cap space is confirmed as correct and all transactions are up-to-date, you can transfer up to $550,000 into pension mode. My wife and I are both members of AustralianSuper, and we have each nominated the other as the 100 per cent beneficiary of our superannuation through a non-lapsing death benefit nomination. I would like to clarify what happens in the following scenario. Imagine that 25 years from now we are both old and forgetful. My wife passes away, and her superannuation benefits are paid to me in accordance with her nomination. Six months later, I also pass away. By that time, my original non-lapsing death benefit nomination, which names my wife as my sole beneficiary, is still in place and has not been updated. What happens to the money remaining in my AustralianSuper account when I die? We have two children, and our wills state that our estate is to be distributed to them when the surviving parent passes away. However, I understand that superannuation does not automatically form part of a person’s estate and that a will may not determine who receives the superannuation benefits. As the non-lapsing nomination form does not appear to provide an option to nominate alternative beneficiaries if both my wife and I have passed away, I would like to understand what happens if my nominated beneficiary has already died. Would my remaining superannuation benefits be paid to my estate, distributed in full to our two children, or handled in another way? Would the provisions in our wills have any effect on the distribution? And what arrangements does AustralianSuper offer to ensure that, when the surviving parent dies, any remaining superannuation benefits are distributed to our two children in accordance with our wishes? Leigh Mansell of Heffron tells me that although your nomination is described as non-lapsing, it cannot operate if the nominated beneficiary has already died. If your wife dies before you and you don’t update your nomination, it will no longer be valid when you die.



AustralianSuper’s trustee would then decide how to distribute your death benefit under superannuation law and the fund’s rules. It could pay the benefit directly to one or both children, to the legal personal representative of your estate, or divide it between them. Neither your children nor your estate would have an automatic entitlement. Your will would apply only to the amount paid to your estate, after taxes and debts are settled, and not to any benefits paid directly to your children. For greater certainty, you could update your nomination after your wife’s death, naming your children in specified proportions or your legal personal representative so the benefit passes through your estate under your will. However, you would need to check the nomination requirements and tax consequences at that time, as superannuation law and AustralianSuper’s rules may change over the next 25 years. A shoddily drafted will can cause plenty of issues in the long run. iStock We are an age pension couple who have gifted $10,000 to our grandchildren in November 2022, October 2024 and January 2027. We understand Centrelink allows gifts of $10,000 a financial year, up to $30,000 over five years, without affecting our pension. Does the first gift cease to count on July 1, 2027 or must we wait until its fifth anniversary on November 10, 2027? We would like to make another $10,000 gift in August 2027, but Centrelink has given us conflicting advice.



You can make the further $10,000 gift from July 1, 2027 without the deprivation rules applying. The $30,000 gifting limit applies over five financial years, not five years from each gift’s anniversary. From July 1, 2027, your November 2022 gift falls outside the relevant period. The separate five-year period measured from the actual gift date applies only to excess gifts assessed under the deprivation rules. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: How home owners are beating the latest rate hike
World.content:
PropertyNewsInterest rates How home owners are beating the latest rate hike Melissa Heagney-Bayliss November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Home owners grappling with higher interest rates could be free of their mortgage sooner and save hundreds of thousands of dollars in interest by making extra payments, but the higher cost of living has made that almost impossible to afford. An analysis by Canstar shows an owner who borrowed $810,000 in January last year and paid an extra $400 a month would save more than $200,000 in interest over the life of their loan. They could pay off their 30-year mortgage five years and five months earlier. In the short term, someone who started paying $400 extra a month in January 2025 would have already saved $578 in interest. The analysis assumes the average size mortgage in NSW and that interest rate cuts predicted for next year are passed on in full.



But after another 0.25 per cent cash rate hike by the Reserve Bank on Tuesday, the fifth this year, combined with higher petrol and grocery prices, home owners’ plans to make extra repayments are under pressure. Canstar’s director of data insights Sally Tindall said owners hoping to pay off their loan sooner needed to structure their mortgages so extra payments would shorten the length of the loan, rather than being used to lower the monthly repayment amount on a 30-year term. “Most banks do it the best practice way,” Tindall said. “But if your minimum repayment drops after you pay extra then the bank is not doing you a service.” Tindall said having extra repayments in the bank not only help to pay off a loan sooner, allowing more savings for retirement, but they could also be used as a buffer if interest rates rise so high that borrowers struggle to meet minimum payments.





That figure was higher in Sydney, where 0.91 per cent of people with a home loan were late, and Melbourne, where 1 per cent were behind. Many borrowers have planned for higher rates. Calum Howe, 35, who recently bought an apartment in Sydney’s Potts Point, assumed there would be three extra rate rises when he applied for a loan. “I’m already two-thirds of the way there,” Howe said, as interest rates have risen twice since he got his mortgage.



After the rate rise announcement, Howe said he was confident he would still be able to meet his higher payments. Calum Howe was prepared for more interest rate rises when he bought recently. Sitthixay Ditthavong “It’s a bit daunting, especially when you’ve just bought something and it’s the highest debt ratio you’ll ever have,” he said. Working as a property valuer in the Potts Point area, Howe has had to tighten the belt to make mortgage repayments on his new home and an investment property he owns. “The social life has definitely taken a bit of a hit,” he said. “When I move I’m being a bit savvy and will be shopping in the Black Friday sales and Christmas sales.



“On a day-to-day basis I’m driving a little bit less and on the weekends I’m having cheaper meals out, and I’ve given up on Uber Eats and conveniences like that.” Related Article Home loans The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage Renee Cross, from Ray White Touma Taylor Potts Point and Elizabeth Bay, helped Howe purchase. She said both buyers and vendors were preparing for higher rates. “Vendors need to adjust their expectations – there are buyers in the market, but they need to be realistic – there are no inflated prices now,” Cross said. In Melbourne, Cody Preston, 25, and partner Alicia Harris, 22, are also facing higher mortgage repayments, having bought their first home in Hoppers Crossing in October.



But the rate rises, and subsequent house price falls, have been a silver lining, allowing them to buy for a better price than they would have otherwise been able to. The couple will move into their new house in just a few weeks. Cody Preston and partner Alicia Harris are nervous about interest rate rises, but happy to have bought their first home. Simon Schluter On Tuesday, Preston said the couple weren’t too concerned about the interest rate hike, having already taken it into consideration. “We’d already predicted that rates would go up and estimated what we’ll have to pay,” Preston said. “It’s only going to be an extra $30 or $40 which is OK for us, but for other couples it could be absolutely ball-breaking.” He said he was blessed to have a job that pays well, being a FIFO worker in the Northern Territory, while Harris is a teacher.



Even though the couple have not had to cut back on much so far, they are nervous about any future interest rate rises. Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne set to drop out of the $1 million club as house prices fall “If anyone says to you that they don’t care about the interest rates, they’re lying to your face,” Preston said. Ray White Hoppers Crossing’s Shahid Khan said properties in the outer west, known as one of Melbourne’s mortgage belts, had fallen further since the last rate rise in September. “Buyers are making a couple of offers on different properties – on one that’s cheaper and one that’s more expensive – and if the cheaper one is accepted they’ll negotiate a lowball offer to get a better deal on the more expensive home,” Khan said. World.title: Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby? Kirstin Ferguson November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: job-hunting while trying for a baby, the out-of-reach job interview and a divided workplace. Trying for a baby does not mean putting your career on pause. Dionne Gain Is it unethical to apply for and accept a leadership position while going through IVF? I am dissatisfied in my current role and have been doing IVF for two years. If it continues to be unsuccessful, I’m stuck in a job I don’t enjoy, going nowhere. Is it OK to take something new, even if it means I may end up pregnant in three months? It is entirely ethical for you to apply and accept the leadership role. One hundred per cent. Apply for this job or any other job you might want. You are not expected to suspend your professional life because you are trying to fall pregnant. You are also not a unit of labour that needs to be permanently available. When people become pregnant – and I sincerely hope you do – employers adjust.



Related Article Got a Minute? I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work? You are not required to disclose your IVF treatment or a possible future pregnancy at any stage during the recruitment process. If you fall pregnant, you can tell your current employer or a new one when you are ready. The only thing I would suggest you think about is any impact changing employers might have on any possible employer-funded parental leave, since minimum service periods sometimes apply. Accepting a leadership role does not mean promising uninterrupted availability. Leaders build teams, delegate and plan for absences, including their own. If your IVF treatment requires appointments, manage them professionally as you would any medical commitment. You owe an employer honesty about your availability, not access to your reproductive plans. Please don't spend a moment more worrying about this. Focus on your health and applying for the job and career you want. All the very best.



While working full-time, I completed a finance degree with distinction after not qualifying for university directly from school. Since graduating six years ago, I have applied repeatedly for finance-related roles similar to my current work but have not received a single interview. I even paid for a professionally written resume. I am too experienced – and financially committed – to accept a significant pay cut for an entry-level role, yet employers apparently don’t consider me experienced enough to change fields. I feel trapped and increasingly like a failure. How can I break through? Six years without an interview definitely suggests something is not working in your approach. You are not a failure and you have not wasted your life. You have shown drive, commitment and resilience. But it is time to think differently. I know you paid for a professional resume, but I suspect it may not be doing you any favours. It may not position you as well as you might hope, or it may not be persuasive to financial employers. Do you have any contacts in the industry you could ask to look at your resume you give you any feedback? Could anyone in your network let you know about roles you could be suited to that are not necessarily being loaded onto a job website? You may need to find a role, initially at least, that bridges your current work experiences with the ideal finance role you want. At this stage, I would be applying for any finance-related projects, secondments or vacancies inside your own organisation where your capabilities are already known and respected. I know it feels like an uphill battle, but please don’t give up. It is simply time for a new approach. Why are operational employees sometimes looked down upon or treated as a threat by office-based staff? I work for a large corporation where the office employees are polite and friendly when our work intersects, but they seem determined to prevent those relationships becoming any more familiar. There is a definite divide between the two groups, and operational staff often feel regarded as somehow less important. Am I misreading professional boundaries, or does this reflect a broader cultural problem?



Related Article Got a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Large organisations can sometimes feel like an episode of Utopia, with operational employees trying to get the actual work done, while office staff seem only to hold meetings about the strategic framework and corporate values. Neither stereotype is always true. However, the divide can create what feels like two different tribes. Office employees often have greater access to executives, corporate language and decision-making, which can be mistaken for greater importance. Operational staff possess something just as valuable: first-hand knowledge of what actually works on the ground. Whether office-based staff are feeling threatened by operational staff in your case is simply an interpretation, not a fact. Office colleagues are entitled to be polite and friendly without becoming friends. The real concern is whether operational employees are being excluded from information, development opportunities or decisions affecting their work. If that is happening, the workplace culture is failing. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. World.content:
Travel newsAustralia One of Australia’s most spectacular wilderness stays just went next level Julietta Jameson November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. It’s hard to believe that Tasmania was ever anything other than appealing to travellers, but the state’s metamorphosis from homely Apple Isle to high-end international holiday destination over the past few decades has been nothing short of extraordinary. It’s a journey that can be mapped out alongside the opening of boutique hotels such as Hobart’s Henry Jones Art Hotel in 2004, which transformed Hobart’s industrial heritage into sophisticated accommodation and earnt a place on the prestigious Conde Nast Traveller Gold List in 2009 and 2010. Other properties, including Cradle Mountain Lodge, have done their bit to establish a market for high-end stays. In addition to lodgings, there was the arrival of MONA and the blossoming of the state’s food and wine industry. An artist’s impression of the Jewel Private Villa at Saffire Freycinet. In 2010, Saffire Freycinet, which overlooks remote Great Oyster Bay on the east coast, made its dazzling debut. When the luxury wilderness lodge opened, it changed the game again and introduced a new level of sophistication to Tasmania’s tourism landscape. Its nightly suite rates of $1000 to $3000 a night reflected an ambition to establish a new level of luxury in Tasmania.



And with the Jewel Private Villa, a three-bedroom accommodation option that leans into international ultra-luxury, Saffire goes next level. Its first $25,000-a-night villa welcomes guests from December 1. 



Super luxe isn’t really a space the country has laid claim to, except for the exclusive four-bedroom Baillie Pavilion at Kangaroo Island’s Southern Ocean Lodge, Longitude 131° at Uluru, and the three-bedroom private villa at Queensland’s Lizard Island. There are other contenders, particularly private islands and exclusive-use estates, but it remains a relatively small field. Like Lizard Island’s villa, Jewel Private Villa is separated but connected to the original property, where 20 suites, including the 140-square-metre Private Pavilions, have largely appealed to couples seeking an intimate escape. It gives Saffire a new option for families and groups of up to eight people wanting to travel together without sacrificing privacy, service or a high standard of amenity. Occupying 800 square metres of indoor and outdoor space adjacent to Saffire’s main lodge, the villa overlooks Great Oyster Bay and the pink granite peaks of The Hazards.



Its three master suites each have a private lounge and en suite, while shared spaces include a generous living room with fireplace, dining room, fully equipped kitchen, butler’s pantry and curated wine cellar. Related Article Australia The pristine Australian island that just eight guests can stay on Outside, there’s an 18-metre infinity pool, accompanied by a jacuzzi, barbecue terrace and fire pit. Designed by Sydney-based architect Andrew O’Connell of Altis Architecture, Jewel makes extensive use of natural materials, including charred timber, local stone, smoked gum veneer, aged bronze and Verde Alpi marble. Bespoke Tasmanian artworks reinforce the connection to place. Guests have access to a dedicated villa host, concierge and private guide, with experiences tailored to individual interests.



Private dining, including breakfasts prepared by a chef, is part of the offering, alongside access to Saffire’s existing facilities and experiences. See saffire-freycinet.com.au

World.title: Why the Powerhouse chose shopping centres for its first western Sydney show
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Why the Powerhouse chose shopping centres for its first western Sydney show Anthony Segaert and Mostafa Rachwani November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Herald charts the ups and downs of the creation of Sydney’s newest cultural institution. See all stories .

When considering what western Sydney has contributed to the world, the Powerhouse Parramatta team landed on a surprising choice: shopping centres. Is it offensive or revelatory? Cringe or smart? Authentic or fake? It all depends on who you ask. The original Parramall Shopping Centre light fixture will be on display at The Mall exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong The first western Sydney-focused exhibition at the Powerhouse will explore the history and development of shopping centres. The Mall is an immense, immersive two-storey exhibition that winds its way through the different eras of shopping through both curated items on display and the architecture of the show itself.



Attendees will be able to walk through some of the reconstructed history, complete with neon signs and fountains. Loading The exhibition is organised like a shopping centre. Visitors enter a space designed to resemble a car park, and are greeted by an electric neon sign for Parramall, the shopping strip that opened in the 1980s. The museum obtained the sign from Sydney Metro; Parramall existed on the site of the Parramatta metro station, to open in 2032. Visitors then progress through the uncanny exhibit that can at times feel like a theme park, charting everything from window displays to payment systems, via fashion and familiar brands. It is one of five exhibitions that form part of the Parramatta campus launch, with the $1 billion museum due to open to the public on Saturday.



Gemma Savio, head of exhibitions curatorial, said it focused on the architecture and the cultural phenomenon of the shopping mall. Staff inspect The Mall exhibition at the Powerhouse Museum, Parramatta. Sitthixay Ditthavong Western Sydney faces will be prominent in Moroccan-British artist Hassan Hajjaj’s work in The Mall exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong Youth brand Sportsgirl is featured in the Powerhouse exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong “The premise for this exhibition came out of the fact that Frank Lowy was really responsible for the generation of the shopping mall and the transformation of retail spaces,” she said.



Lowy started Westfield in Blacktown in 1959, with that first centre hosting 13 stores and a car park capacity of 90. From there it expanded across Sydney and the rest of the country, revolutionising how people shopped and reshaping many suburbs in western Sydney. “And that model has really changed the way that we spend time buying things, receiving things, and transacting with one another.” The exhibition will feature more than 1350 objects, ranging from old signs and cash registers to eftpos machines and old Myer gift cards. It will also feature shopfronts from brands that have partnered with the Powerhouse on the program, including Oroton, David Jones, R.M. Williams and Sportsgirl. A spokesperson for the Powerhouse said any exhibition on “Australian retail culture would be incomplete without presenting some of the brands and retail experiences that have shaped them”.



“ ‘Arcade’ in The Mall highlights [the] skilled practice of window dressing and visual merchandising,” they said. “Powerhouse curators worked with the brands to curate and design the window displays. As a museum of applied arts and sciences, Powerhouse has a longstanding history of collecting and interpreting Australian design, manufacturing, fashion and retail culture.” The Mall, a new exhibition at the Powerhouse Museum in Parramatta, has an advertising campaign drawn from Sydney’s western suburbs. Sitthixay Ditthavong Powerhouse Parramatta staff put The Mall exhibition together. Sitthixay Ditthavong The other opening shows include The Dark, an immersive exhibition created for children aged four to 12 years old, and Es Devlin: The Turning, where visitors can explore five immersive installations, as well as the First Nations-led Overflow and Task Eternal, which is focused on aerospace history and development.



As part of the opening, the Powerhouse will feature a range of unique objects pulled from its collection, including drawings from Leonardo da Vinci, a boilerplate from an Apollo command module made by NASA, and an amethyst that is more than 100 million years old.

World.title: The Fiji resort one traveller has visited more than 50 times
World.content:
InspirationOceania The Fiji resort one traveller has visited more than 50 times Shaney Hudson November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
