Many travellers are driven by curiosity, forever looking towards the next destination, the next experience, the next place to tick off the list. But there is another, quieter breed of traveller who knows what fills their cup; who, like migrating birds, return instinctively to the same place year after year. For these people, travel feels like coming home. And for many Australians travelling to Fiji that place is Castaway Island. Located in the Mamanuca Islands, the much-loved Fijian resort celebrates its 60th anniversary this year. Today, you can reach it in about 90 minutes on South Sea Cruise’s catamaran service from Port Denarau. However, a few decades ago, getting to the island was a far more adventurous affair. Home away from home: Castaway Island has a loyal Australian clientele. “Back then, you used to get to the island on a sailing boat from Lautoka, and it used to take four hours,” says Ian Branddock, who first visited in 1970. “And when the boat came around the point and was in view of the beach, 80 per cent of the guests would just dive over the side to get there.” Branddock is one of Castaway’s extended family: he has been more than 50 times since his first visit, with his next trip booked for later this year. “People say, why do you keep going there? Why don’t you go somewhere else?” he laughs. “The staff greet you like you’re part of the family. We are part of the family.”



I’ve planned a visit to Castaway on my 14th trip to the South Pacific island group. For years, I’ve understood the quiet lure of Fiji: the genuine hospitality, the pristine waters, the way time slows down every time I visit, and stress melts away. But the devotion some people have to Castaway Island has always left me slightly puzzled. What makes people want to return year in, year out? 



It’s just the right fit for our family of four. Our bure is on the south side of the island, a much quieter refuge away from North Beach, the main swimming and snorkelling spot. A large timber seawall wraps around this side of the beach, with steps to the water below. At low tide, there’s a small beach where the kids play; at high tide, we wade in. The quality of snorkelling directly in front of our bure is genuinely surprising. One small bommie features a giant clam, the seagrass meadow is scattered with blue starfish, and in a small rocky outcrop, two bossy clownfish protect a clutch of eggs. Just as I begin to back off, I spy a tiny version of Nemo – no bigger than my fingernail – hiding below. One genuine part of the Castaway experience is that it’s incredibly family-oriented. Food is a cosmopolitan affair: there’s the Water’s Edge main restaurant and buffet, Nuku Marau Bar & Grill serving sushi by the kids’ pool by day, and an adults-only Fijian-Asian restaurant on the beach by night. But with two kids who can’t sit still, we opt for takeaway wood-fired pizza from the Sundowner Bar early each evening, watching the sun go down. We sit in the sand making a meal out of their discarded pizza crusts, while the kids sit in their cossies in just a few inches of water, snacking away. It’s an easy way to dine out. Back in the day, however, the resort had a strict dress code: No sulu, no dinner, referring to the traditional Fijian wrap skirt worn by both men and women.



But on Castaway the trick is to do as little as possible, for as long as you can. Graeme Field, who has visited Castaway more than 40 times since 1980, recalls showing up to dinner on the island in jeans on his first day, only to be unceremoniously told to strip behind the bar by one of the island’s long-time staff members, Mere Kasaqa. “She said, ‘No! Jeans have to come off’,” he recalls. “And we went behind the bar, and she taught me to tie a sulu.” One genuine part of the Castaway experience is that it’s incredibly family oriented. Over the years, many of the staff working at Castaway have been second and third-generation staff members, forming tight bonds with guests. Field became best friends with Kasaqa’s brother, Nemani. Over the years, Nemani welcomed him into his village north of Suva; Field invited Nemani to be the guest of honour at his Australian wedding, and years later, attended Nemani’s funeral in Fiji. To this day, Field and Mere are in contact. I plan to ask Castaway’s General Manager, Steven Roberts, about the dynamic between staff and guests. However, our first meeting happens in the middle of a huge celebration: the Castaway Rugby team has won the inter-island rugby cup, and the entire island is celebrating on the beach. The next day we meet to chat, but an Australian jogs up from behind and throws his arm around the GM’s shoulders in a bear hug, and they embrace. A visitor for decades, he quickly asks me if he can steal him away: his dad has dementia, he explains cheerfully, and has been asking to see Roberts since they arrived that morning.



“Dad’s always happy when he’s here,” the son beams. Of course, it’s a yes, and I slip away on my morning excursion to the resort’s newest attraction: the coral gene bank. Related Article Opinion

Family holidays The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids Ben Groundwater Travel writer Installed in partnership with non-profit Counting Coral, each offshore sculpture has been engineered using marine-grade steel, with 500 individual “parent” corals attached. The look is steampunk tropical: the five, truck-sized, domed metal sculptures sit in a few metres of water and are adorned with vivid corals: some thriving, others striking a lonely figure, while small schools of fish have begun to cluster around the artificial reef. There’s plenty to do in the water and around the island: bounce on the inflatables anchored just offshore, take out a paddleboard, or hike to the top of the island. But I work out quickly that on Castaway, the trick is to do as little as possible, for as long as you possibly can. And that’s more than enough to keep our family happy for days.



When we gather our things to check out, we’re simply not ready to go. This place has gotten under our skin. Castaway is proof that a holiday isn’t just about a destination, and a place can be part of who you are. And now, having experienced this little slice of Fijian paradise myself, I have to agree with the long-timers: being here really does feel like coming home. DETAILS For 2027, Castaway Island rates start from $F1159 ($737) a night, plus tax (17.5 per cent). Depending on travel dates, all meals may be included. See outrigger.com; South Sea Cruises offers multiple daily transfers to Castaway Island Resort from Port Denarau. See southseacruisesfiji.com The writer travelled as a guest of Tourism Fiji, Castaway Island Resort and South Sea Cruises

World.title: Why a ‘blue wave’ today is not necessarily a rejection of Trumpism
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Why a ‘blue wave’ today is not necessarily a rejection of Trumpism Michael Koziol November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow our live coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections here. Washington: The temptation after a Democratic victory at today’s midterm elections – if that is indeed what transpires – will be to parse the results as Americans turning the page on Donald Trump and his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. But that could be a dangerous mistake. At the 2018 midterms, during Trump’s first term, Democrats gained 40 seats and took control of the House of Representatives. Americans removed Trump from office two years later, and, amid an onslaught of criminal charges, he seemed destined for the dustbin of political history. Donald Trump faces a blue wave at Tuesday’s midterm elections. Marija Ercegovac As we know, voters felt otherwise. Trump achieved a bigger victory in 2024 than 2016 – despite, and possibly because of, everything Americans knew about him and his policies.



Their vote was not necessarily a wholesale embrace of Trump the man, but a rejection of the Democrats after four years of Joe Biden. The Trump agenda at the time – lower prices, no new foreign wars, tariffs, closing the border and dismantling the “woke” agenda – carried the day because it appealed. Related Article Foreign relations ‘Crazy’ Coalition making huge mistake by opposing EU trade deal: Turnbull Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull notes Trump won a genuine majority for “his ‘America first’ views, his protectionist views, his view that America should use its power to extract the best deal for itself, and his views that America should not be overly concerned about its allies”. Trump himself may be historically unpopular – and that will impact today’s results – but the factors that led Americans to support him twice are still there. Arguably, it is not so much that voters have moved away from Trumpism, but that he let them down. “In a sense, you could say Trump’s political problems today are caused by him abandoning key elements of MAGA,” Turnbull told this masthead last week in New York.



“One of the key parts of the MAGA agenda was no new foreign wars. This is a guy who was seeking the Nobel Peace Prize. This is a guy who railed against George W. Bush’s war in Iraq and Afghanistan. He talked to me and Lucy [Turnbull’s wife] about it once. He was obsessed about this.” Trump played the populist card in 2024, and Democrats have played it in 2026. The party’s key election message has been about affordability: that Trump’s tariffs, trade disputes and war with Iran mean you are paying more for petrol and groceries. Trump likes to boast about winning in Iran. However, the longer the war drags on, the more obvious it becomes that there is no winning exit for the US. Bloomberg That is true – petrol prices are higher than usual, though not as high as their all-time peak in 2022. Australians, who depend on imports, also pay much more for petrol than Americans. If it is the case that affordability is the big issue at this election, then, as with foreign policy, it is not so much that voters are abandoning their populist positions as judging that the president and his Republicans have not fulfilled them.



Most US states beat nearly all European countries on median income. So it is striking that the cost of living has become the perennial cudgel for an opposition to bash an incumbent, before becoming the albatross around the neck of the next incumbent. But such is the nature of populism. And Trump has remade the GOP into much more of a populist party. Even with the Iran war and all the other baggage of the second Trump administration, the candidates he endorsed performed very well in Republican primaries, regularly beating incumbents – such as Texas senator John Cornyn, who lost to Ken Paxton. ‘I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.’ US President Donald Trump, at a rally in Iowa How much power Trump retains within his own party will shape the endurance of Trumpism and MAGA. As political strategist Douglas Heye says, Republicans may feel liberated after the midterms to be “a bit more outspoken about what they really think about Trump”, and say publicly what they only admit privately now. The size of Republican losses will help determine Trump’s ongoing influence: a bloodbath would weaken him, while losses in line with a standard midterm election could be dismissed as inevitable.



Vice President JD Vance is positioning himself as a viable candidate for the MAGA true believers. Bloomberg At any rate, the immense power Republicans have invested in Trump does not dissipate overnight. And Trump himself is aware of this. In a little-noticed aside during a recent rally in Iowa, he made a prediction. “I’ll always have that little extra power,” he said, while talking about his eventual exit from the White House. “I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.” Trump’s assumed successor, Vice President J.D. Vance, has positioned himself to capture those voters who feel betrayed by Trump. He never fully signed on to the Iran war, and does not echo the president’s rhetoric that – current petrol prices notwithstanding – Americans have never had it so good. At Trump rallies around the country, supporters consistently say Vance is the guy they like for 2028. He represents the MAGA constituency more so than Secretary of State Marco Rubio, another likely contender. If Trumpism is to continue post-Trump, it probably runs through Vance. But the president has been non-committal so far in terms of an endorsement, and appears to enjoy fostering a competitive rivalry between the two men – or perhaps someone else.



“I can’t see him staying out of this,” says Bob Shapiro, political scientist at Columbia University. “To the extent that he’s in this, that’s going to tell us whether Trumpism has legs or not, and whether there is a candidate he picks or a candidate who steps forward and ascends and basically carries the mantle of Trumpism.” Related Article US midterms Are these the worst US midterm attack ads of all time? Beyond policy, perhaps the hallmark of Trumpism is the jettisoning of the normal rules of engagement. It is a skill in which he is uniquely gifted, once boasting – correctly, it seems – that he could shoot someone on Fifth Avenue and not lose any votes. Others may be less adept and less brazen, but they’re happy to try. Vance dishes it out, and saw no problem with the Vivek Ramaswamy ad in Ohio that enlisted a Democratic candidate’s estranged and reportedly mentally ill mother to tar her own daughter. Most Republicans are comfortable attacking Muslim Democrats as jihadist communists. Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, regularly mocks “trannies” and “fatties”. When it comes to political discourse, we’re through the looking glass – and all else aside, that may be the lasting legacy of Trumpism.

World.title: The $1b idea for early intervention as rate rise looms over struggling families
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament The $1b idea for early intervention as rate rise looms over struggling families Jessica McSweeney November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Frontline domestic violence, homelessness and mental health service providers are demanding a $1 billion pre-election funding commitment from the state government as they anticipate the interest rate hike will further strain community groups already overrun with calls for help. More than 11 charities, unions and church groups have written an open letter to the Minns government urging an overhaul of state funding, which they say focuses on crisis support but leads to ballooning wait lists for early intervention services. Salote Moso accessed support services after leaving a relationship she says included coercive control and financial abuse. Wolter Peeters Uniting director of advocacy and external relations Emma Maiden said: “We’re parking the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, and we’re not putting that fence at the top of the cliff.” The group is on Wednesday calling for the state government to introduce a “preventing harm framework”, under which funding would be targeted to reach at-risk people at earlier stages, before they are in crisis.



Maiden said Tuesday’s rate rise would put further pressure on Uniting’s support services, where an increase in working families experiencing poverty is driving a surge in demand for help. Related Article Graphic content

Domestic violence She tried to leave her abusive partner. It cost Sophia her children “We’re already exceeding the number of people that we’re funded to service in our family support services by about 30 per cent due to increasing demand. So we just try and make those dollars stretch further,” she said. “Community organisations are already turning people away, and every rate rise adds more pressure on households and adds to that queue.” Reducing wait times for help is one of the core goals of the campaign. Domestic Violence NSW reports waitlists regularly exceed three months, while the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare found an average of 31 requests for emergency accommodation were going unassisted every day in NSW.



Minto single mother Salote Moso, 27, was financially dependent on her ex-partner, who she said would take control of her money to the point of denying her $20 for her Opal card. Moso said when she questioned his spending, he would become aggressive. When she decided to leave the controlling relationship, Moso couch surfed with her infant son while she waited a month to secure financial support. Since Moso was at risk of homelessness, she was connected with a social worker with a two-week wait time, but those two weeks weighed heavily as she was forced to skip meals to put food on the table for her son. “I was mostly on survival mode the whole time … I’m not really proud of it, but there came a point where I started thinking dark thoughts,” Moso said. “With a long waiting time, it can also be isolating because then you’re starting to think or feel like, oh, what if they’ve forgotten about me?”



NSW Council of Social Service policy and advocacy director Ben McAlpine said when people reached out for help but got stuck on lengthy wait lists, it could erode their trust in the system and in government. NCOSS was one of the signatories of the open letter, which argues a $1 billion investment over four years will unlock savings by reducing the strain on crisis services and getting people back on their feet earlier. “The NSW government cannot set interest rates, but it can decide to fund early intervention instead of paying for crisis later, and that’s at the core of this conversation,” McAlpine said. The campaign, dubbed Right Help, Right Time, faces an uphill battle to secure its $1 billion demand as the state government faces pressure to rein in spending ahead of the March election. In the June budget, the government committed an additional $184.1 million to six specialist domestic violence services.

World.title: We want to gift our daughter $200k. Will that get us on the age pension?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAsk an expert Opinion We want to gift our daughter $200k. Will that get us on the age pension? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 4, 2026 — 5:01am

November 4, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We are considering giving our daughter, a single mother of two girls, a $200,000 advance on her inheritance to help her buy her first home. I intend to have proper documentation prepared to record the advance, including an agreement similar to a prenuptial agreement to protect her in the event of a future relationship. I am 69 and my wife is 63. We are both retired. I have $980,000 in superannuation and my wife has $220,000. We also have $320,000 in a term deposit and $137,000 in a bank account. We own our home, worth approximately $1 million. How long would Centrelink continue to assess the $200,000 advance as a gift? I estimate it could take another ten years before we qualify for a meaningful part age pension, assuming annual spending of $75,000 and investment returns of 7 per cent. Does that sound reasonable? Finally, would the gift or our financial position affect our eligibility for the Commonwealth Seniors Health Card? Gifting kids an early inheritance can be a good move, but don’t expect it to magically move you into age pension range. Simon Letch Provided the $200,000 is a genuine gift rather than a loan, Centrelink will cease to assess the amount above the allowable gifting limit five years after the gift is made. You’ll need to be particularly careful with the legal documentation to ensure that arrangements intended to protect your daughter don’t inadvertently turn the gift into a repayable loan. After the gift, you’ll have approximately $1.457 million in financial assets. Although the $220,000 your wife holds in superannuation will not count under the Centrelink assets test until she reaches 67, provided she leaves it in accumulation phase, your remaining assessable assets are still well above the couple’s age pension assets test cut-off point.



If you enter $1.457 million into the Retirement Drawdown Calculator on my website, assuming annual returns of 7 per cent and initial withdrawals of $75,000 indexed to inflation, you’ll find that the money could still be worth around $1.7 million in ten years. On those assumptions, I doubt you’ll qualify for an age pension unless your financial circumstances change significantly. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64 with just $93,000 in super. Should I add to it before retiring? Paul Benson Money contributor The Commonwealth Seniors Health Card is not assets tested, so having substantial investments doesn’t automatically disqualify you. Eligibility depends on your taxable income plus deemed income from account-based pensions. Based on the figures you’ve supplied, you may well qualify, but you should check your assessable income against the current limits. You have said that once a person has used their maximum transfer balance cap, they cannot transfer any more money into pension mode during their lifetime. I transferred $2 million into pension mode in August 2025 and have since made lump sum withdrawals totalling $500,000, which were paid into my bank account. My understanding is that these withdrawals allow me to transfer another $500,000 from my accumulation account into a new pension account. My myGov account shows available cap space of $550,000 and a personal transfer balance cap of $2 million. Does this mean I can make further transfers into pension mode?



Yes, provided your withdrawals were processed as lump-sum commutations rather than pension payments. Commutations free up transfer balance cap space to enable further transfers into pension mode, while pension payments do not. Before proceeding, ask your super fund to reconcile the $550,000 shown in myGov with your stated $500,000 of withdrawals. If the available cap space is confirmed as correct and all transactions are up-to-date, you can transfer up to $550,000 into pension mode. My wife and I are both members of AustralianSuper, and we have each nominated the other as the 100 per cent beneficiary of our superannuation through a non-lapsing death benefit nomination. I would like to clarify what happens in the following scenario. Imagine that 25 years from now we are both old and forgetful. My wife passes away, and her superannuation benefits are paid to me in accordance with her nomination. Six months later, I also pass away. By that time, my original non-lapsing death benefit nomination, which names my wife as my sole beneficiary, is still in place and has not been updated. What happens to the money remaining in my AustralianSuper account when I die? We have two children, and our wills state that our estate is to be distributed to them when the surviving parent passes away. However, I understand that superannuation does not automatically form part of a person’s estate and that a will may not determine who receives the superannuation benefits. As the non-lapsing nomination form does not appear to provide an option to nominate alternative beneficiaries if both my wife and I have passed away, I would like to understand what happens if my nominated beneficiary has already died. Would my remaining superannuation benefits be paid to my estate, distributed in full to our two children, or handled in another way? Would the provisions in our wills have any effect on the distribution? And what arrangements does AustralianSuper offer to ensure that, when the surviving parent dies, any remaining superannuation benefits are distributed to our two children in accordance with our wishes? Leigh Mansell of Heffron tells me that although your nomination is described as non-lapsing, it cannot operate if the nominated beneficiary has already died. If your wife dies before you and you don’t update your nomination, it will no longer be valid when you die.



AustralianSuper’s trustee would then decide how to distribute your death benefit under superannuation law and the fund’s rules. It could pay the benefit directly to one or both children, to the legal personal representative of your estate, or divide it between them. Neither your children nor your estate would have an automatic entitlement. Your will would apply only to the amount paid to your estate, after taxes and debts are settled, and not to any benefits paid directly to your children. For greater certainty, you could update your nomination after your wife’s death, naming your children in specified proportions or your legal personal representative so the benefit passes through your estate under your will. However, you would need to check the nomination requirements and tax consequences at that time, as superannuation law and AustralianSuper’s rules may change over the next 25 years. A shoddily drafted will can cause plenty of issues in the long run. iStock We are an age pension couple who have gifted $10,000 to our grandchildren in November 2022, October 2024 and January 2027. We understand Centrelink allows gifts of $10,000 a financial year, up to $30,000 over five years, without affecting our pension. Does the first gift cease to count on July 1, 2027 or must we wait until its fifth anniversary on November 10, 2027? We would like to make another $10,000 gift in August 2027, but Centrelink has given us conflicting advice.



You can make the further $10,000 gift from July 1, 2027 without the deprivation rules applying. The $30,000 gifting limit applies over five financial years, not five years from each gift’s anniversary. From July 1, 2027, your November 2022 gift falls outside the relevant period. The separate five-year period measured from the actual gift date applies only to excess gifts assessed under the deprivation rules. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. World.title: How home owners are beating the latest rate hike
World.content:
PropertyNewsInterest rates How home owners are beating the latest rate hike Melissa Heagney-Bayliss November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. Home owners grappling with higher interest rates could be free of their mortgage sooner and save hundreds of thousands of dollars in interest by making extra payments, but the higher cost of living has made that almost impossible to afford. An analysis by Canstar shows an owner who borrowed $810,000 in January last year and paid an extra $400 a month would save more than $200,000 in interest over the life of their loan. They could pay off their 30-year mortgage five years and five months earlier. In the short term, someone who started paying $400 extra a month in January 2025 would have already saved $578 in interest. The analysis assumes the average size mortgage in NSW and that interest rate cuts predicted for next year are passed on in full.



But after another 0.25 per cent cash rate hike by the Reserve Bank on Tuesday, the fifth this year, combined with higher petrol and grocery prices, home owners’ plans to make extra repayments are under pressure. Canstar’s director of data insights Sally Tindall said owners hoping to pay off their loan sooner needed to structure their mortgages so extra payments would shorten the length of the loan, rather than being used to lower the monthly repayment amount on a 30-year term. “Most banks do it the best practice way,” Tindall said. “But if your minimum repayment drops after you pay extra then the bank is not doing you a service.” Tindall said having extra repayments in the bank not only help to pay off a loan sooner, allowing more savings for retirement, but they could also be used as a buffer if interest rates rise so high that borrowers struggle to meet minimum payments.





That figure was higher in Sydney, where 0.91 per cent of people with a home loan were late, and Melbourne, where 1 per cent were behind. Many borrowers have planned for higher rates. Calum Howe, 35, who recently bought an apartment in Sydney’s Potts Point, assumed there would be three extra rate rises when he applied for a loan. “I’m already two-thirds of the way there,” Howe said, as interest rates have risen twice since he got his mortgage.



After the rate rise announcement, Howe said he was confident he would still be able to meet his higher payments. Calum Howe was prepared for more interest rate rises when he bought recently. Sitthixay Ditthavong “It’s a bit daunting, especially when you’ve just bought something and it’s the highest debt ratio you’ll ever have,” he said. Working as a property valuer in the Potts Point area, Howe has had to tighten the belt to make mortgage repayments on his new home and an investment property he owns. “The social life has definitely taken a bit of a hit,” he said. “When I move I’m being a bit savvy and will be shopping in the Black Friday sales and Christmas sales.



“On a day-to-day basis I’m driving a little bit less and on the weekends I’m having cheaper meals out, and I’ve given up on Uber Eats and conveniences like that.” Related Article Home loans The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage Renee Cross, from Ray White Touma Taylor Potts Point and Elizabeth Bay, helped Howe purchase. She said both buyers and vendors were preparing for higher rates. “Vendors need to adjust their expectations – there are buyers in the market, but they need to be realistic – there are no inflated prices now,” Cross said. In Melbourne, Cody Preston, 25, and partner Alicia Harris, 22, are also facing higher mortgage repayments, having bought their first home in Hoppers Crossing in October.



But the rate rises, and subsequent house price falls, have been a silver lining, allowing them to buy for a better price than they would have otherwise been able to. The couple will move into their new house in just a few weeks. Cody Preston and partner Alicia Harris are nervous about interest rate rises, but happy to have bought their first home. Simon Schluter On Tuesday, Preston said the couple weren’t too concerned about the interest rate hike, having already taken it into consideration. “We’d already predicted that rates would go up and estimated what we’ll have to pay,” Preston said. “It’s only going to be an extra $30 or $40 which is OK for us, but for other couples it could be absolutely ball-breaking.” He said he was blessed to have a job that pays well, being a FIFO worker in the Northern Territory, while Harris is a teacher.



Even though the couple have not had to cut back on much so far, they are nervous about any future interest rate rises. Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne set to drop out of the $1 million club as house prices fall “If anyone says to you that they don’t care about the interest rates, they’re lying to your face,” Preston said. Ray White Hoppers Crossing’s Shahid Khan said properties in the outer west, known as one of Melbourne’s mortgage belts, had fallen further since the last rate rise in September. “Buyers are making a couple of offers on different properties – on one that’s cheaper and one that’s more expensive – and if the cheaper one is accepted they’ll negotiate a lowball offer to get a better deal on the more expensive home,” Khan said. World.title: Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby? Kirstin Ferguson November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: job-hunting while trying for a baby, the out-of-reach job interview and a divided workplace. Trying for a baby does not mean putting your career on pause. Dionne Gain Is it unethical to apply for and accept a leadership position while going through IVF? I am dissatisfied in my current role and have been doing IVF for two years. If it continues to be unsuccessful, I’m stuck in a job I don’t enjoy, going nowhere. Is it OK to take something new, even if it means I may end up pregnant in three months? It is entirely ethical for you to apply and accept the leadership role. One hundred per cent. Apply for this job or any other job you might want. You are not expected to suspend your professional life because you are trying to fall pregnant. You are also not a unit of labour that needs to be permanently available. When people become pregnant – and I sincerely hope you do – employers adjust.



Related Article Got a Minute? I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work? You are not required to disclose your IVF treatment or a possible future pregnancy at any stage during the recruitment process. If you fall pregnant, you can tell your current employer or a new one when you are ready. The only thing I would suggest you think about is any impact changing employers might have on any possible employer-funded parental leave, since minimum service periods sometimes apply. Accepting a leadership role does not mean promising uninterrupted availability. Leaders build teams, delegate and plan for absences, including their own. If your IVF treatment requires appointments, manage them professionally as you would any medical commitment. You owe an employer honesty about your availability, not access to your reproductive plans. Please don't spend a moment more worrying about this. Focus on your health and applying for the job and career you want. All the very best.



While working full-time, I completed a finance degree with distinction after not qualifying for university directly from school. Since graduating six years ago, I have applied repeatedly for finance-related roles similar to my current work but have not received a single interview. I even paid for a professionally written resume. I am too experienced – and financially committed – to accept a significant pay cut for an entry-level role, yet employers apparently don’t consider me experienced enough to change fields. I feel trapped and increasingly like a failure. How can I break through? Six years without an interview definitely suggests something is not working in your approach. You are not a failure and you have not wasted your life. You have shown drive, commitment and resilience. But it is time to think differently. I know you paid for a professional resume, but I suspect it may not be doing you any favours. It may not position you as well as you might hope, or it may not be persuasive to financial employers. Do you have any contacts in the industry you could ask to look at your resume you give you any feedback? Could anyone in your network let you know about roles you could be suited to that are not necessarily being loaded onto a job website? You may need to find a role, initially at least, that bridges your current work experiences with the ideal finance role you want. At this stage, I would be applying for any finance-related projects, secondments or vacancies inside your own organisation where your capabilities are already known and respected. I know it feels like an uphill battle, but please don’t give up. It is simply time for a new approach. Why are operational employees sometimes looked down upon or treated as a threat by office-based staff? I work for a large corporation where the office employees are polite and friendly when our work intersects, but they seem determined to prevent those relationships becoming any more familiar. There is a definite divide between the two groups, and operational staff often feel regarded as somehow less important. Am I misreading professional boundaries, or does this reflect a broader cultural problem?



Related Article Got a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Large organisations can sometimes feel like an episode of Utopia, with operational employees trying to get the actual work done, while office staff seem only to hold meetings about the strategic framework and corporate values. Neither stereotype is always true. However, the divide can create what feels like two different tribes. Office employees often have greater access to executives, corporate language and decision-making, which can be mistaken for greater importance. Operational staff possess something just as valuable: first-hand knowledge of what actually works on the ground. Whether office-based staff are feeling threatened by operational staff in your case is simply an interpretation, not a fact. Office colleagues are entitled to be polite and friendly without becoming friends. The real concern is whether operational employees are being excluded from information, development opportunities or decisions affecting their work. If that is happening, the workplace culture is failing. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited.

World.content:

It’s hard to believe that Tasmania was ever anything other than appealing to travellers, but the state’s metamorphosis from homely Apple Isle to high-end international holiday destination over the past few decades has been nothing short of extraordinary. It’s a journey that can be mapped out alongside the opening of boutique hotels such as Hobart’s Henry Jones Art Hotel in 2004, which transformed Hobart’s industrial heritage into sophisticated accommodation and earnt a place on the prestigious Conde Nast Traveller Gold List in 2009 and 2010. Other properties, including Cradle Mountain Lodge, have done their bit to establish a market for high-end stays. In addition to lodgings, there was the arrival of MONA and the blossoming of the state’s food and wine industry. An artist’s impression of the Jewel Private Villa at Saffire Freycinet. In 2010, Saffire Freycinet, which overlooks remote Great Oyster Bay on the east coast, made its dazzling debut. When the luxury wilderness lodge opened, it changed the game again and introduced a new level of sophistication to Tasmania’s tourism landscape. Its nightly suite rates of $1000 to $3000 a night reflected an ambition to establish a new level of luxury in Tasmania.



And with the Jewel Private Villa, a three-bedroom accommodation option that leans into international ultra-luxury, Saffire goes next level. Its first $25,000-a-night villa welcomes guests from December 1. 



Super luxe isn’t really a space the country has laid claim to, except for the exclusive four-bedroom Baillie Pavilion at Kangaroo Island’s Southern Ocean Lodge, Longitude 131° at Uluru, and the three-bedroom private villa at Queensland’s Lizard Island. There are other contenders, particularly private islands and exclusive-use estates, but it remains a relatively small field. Like Lizard Island’s villa, Jewel Private Villa is separated but connected to the original property, where 20 suites, including the 140-square-metre Private Pavilions, have largely appealed to couples seeking an intimate escape. It gives Saffire a new option for families and groups of up to eight people wanting to travel together without sacrificing privacy, service or a high standard of amenity. Occupying 800 square metres of indoor and outdoor space adjacent to Saffire’s main lodge, the villa overlooks Great Oyster Bay and the pink granite peaks of The Hazards.



Its three master suites each have a private lounge and en suite, while shared spaces include a generous living room with fireplace, dining room, fully equipped kitchen, butler’s pantry and curated wine cellar. Related Article Australia The pristine Australian island that just eight guests can stay on Outside, there’s an 18-metre infinity pool, accompanied by a jacuzzi, barbecue terrace and fire pit. Designed by Sydney-based architect Andrew O’Connell of Altis Architecture, Jewel makes extensive use of natural materials, including charred timber, local stone, smoked gum veneer, aged bronze and Verde Alpi marble. Bespoke Tasmanian artworks reinforce the connection to place. Guests have access to a dedicated villa host, concierge and private guide, with experiences tailored to individual interests.



Private dining, including breakfasts prepared by a chef, is part of the offering, alongside access to Saffire’s existing facilities and experiences. See saffire-freycinet.com.au

World.title: Why the Powerhouse chose shopping centres for its first western Sydney show
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Why the Powerhouse chose shopping centres for its first western Sydney show Anthony Segaert and Mostafa Rachwani November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Herald charts the ups and downs of the creation of Sydney’s newest cultural institution. See all stories .

When considering what western Sydney has contributed to the world, the Powerhouse Parramatta team landed on a surprising choice: shopping centres. Is it offensive or revelatory? Cringe or smart? Authentic or fake? It all depends on who you ask. The original Parramall Shopping Centre light fixture will be on display at The Mall exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong The first western Sydney-focused exhibition at the Powerhouse will explore the history and development of shopping centres. The Mall is an immense, immersive two-storey exhibition that winds its way through the different eras of shopping through both curated items on display and the architecture of the show itself.



Attendees will be able to walk through some of the reconstructed history, complete with neon signs and fountains. Loading The exhibition is organised like a shopping centre. Visitors enter a space designed to resemble a car park, and are greeted by an electric neon sign for Parramall, the shopping strip that opened in the 1980s. The museum obtained the sign from Sydney Metro; Parramall existed on the site of the Parramatta metro station, to open in 2032. Visitors then progress through the uncanny exhibit that can at times feel like a theme park, charting everything from window displays to payment systems, via fashion and familiar brands. It is one of five exhibitions that form part of the Parramatta campus launch, with the $1 billion museum due to open to the public on Saturday.



Gemma Savio, head of exhibitions curatorial, said it focused on the architecture and the cultural phenomenon of the shopping mall. Staff inspect The Mall exhibition at the Powerhouse Museum, Parramatta. Sitthixay Ditthavong Western Sydney faces will be prominent in Moroccan-British artist Hassan Hajjaj’s work in The Mall exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong Youth brand Sportsgirl is featured in the Powerhouse exhibition. Sitthixay Ditthavong “The premise for this exhibition came out of the fact that Frank Lowy was really responsible for the generation of the shopping mall and the transformation of retail spaces,” she said.



Lowy started Westfield in Blacktown in 1959, with that first centre hosting 13 stores and a car park capacity of 90. From there it expanded across Sydney and the rest of the country, revolutionising how people shopped and reshaping many suburbs in western Sydney. “And that model has really changed the way that we spend time buying things, receiving things, and transacting with one another.” The exhibition will feature more than 1350 objects, ranging from old signs and cash registers to eftpos machines and old Myer gift cards. It will also feature shopfronts from brands that have partnered with the Powerhouse on the program, including Oroton, David Jones, R.M. Williams and Sportsgirl. A spokesperson for the Powerhouse said any exhibition on “Australian retail culture would be incomplete without presenting some of the brands and retail experiences that have shaped them”.



“ ‘Arcade’ in The Mall highlights [the] skilled practice of window dressing and visual merchandising,” they said. “Powerhouse curators worked with the brands to curate and design the window displays. As a museum of applied arts and sciences, Powerhouse has a longstanding history of collecting and interpreting Australian design, manufacturing, fashion and retail culture.” The Mall, a new exhibition at the Powerhouse Museum in Parramatta, has an advertising campaign drawn from Sydney’s western suburbs. Sitthixay Ditthavong Powerhouse Parramatta staff put The Mall exhibition together. Sitthixay Ditthavong The other opening shows include The Dark, an immersive exhibition created for children aged four to 12 years old, and Es Devlin: The Turning, where visitors can explore five immersive installations, as well as the First Nations-led Overflow and Task Eternal, which is focused on aerospace history and development.



As part of the opening, the Powerhouse will feature a range of unique objects pulled from its collection, including drawings from Leonardo da Vinci, a boilerplate from an Apollo command module made by NASA, and an amethyst that is more than 100 million years old.

World.title: The Fiji resort one traveller has visited more than 50 times
World.content:
InspirationOceania The Fiji resort one traveller has visited more than 50 times Shaney Hudson November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Many travellers are driven by curiosity, forever looking towards the next destination, the next experience, the next place to tick off the list. But there is another, quieter breed of traveller who knows what fills their cup; who, like migrating birds, return instinctively to the same place year after year. For these people, travel feels like coming home. And for many Australians travelling to Fiji that place is Castaway Island. Located in the Mamanuca Islands, the much-loved Fijian resort celebrates its 60th anniversary this year. Today, you can reach it in about 90 minutes on South Sea Cruise’s catamaran service from Port Denarau. However, a few decades ago, getting to the island was a far more adventurous affair. Home away from home: Castaway Island has a loyal Australian clientele. “Back then, you used to get to the island on a sailing boat from Lautoka, and it used to take four hours,” says Ian Branddock, who first visited in 1970. “And when the boat came around the point and was in view of the beach, 80 per cent of the guests would just dive over the side to get there.” Branddock is one of Castaway’s extended family: he has been more than 50 times since his first visit, with his next trip booked for later this year. “People say, why do you keep going there? Why don’t you go somewhere else?” he laughs. “The staff greet you like you’re part of the family. We are part of the family.”



I’ve planned a visit to Castaway on my 14th trip to the South Pacific island group. For years, I’ve understood the quiet lure of Fiji: the genuine hospitality, the pristine waters, the way time slows down every time I visit, and stress melts away. But the devotion some people have to Castaway Island has always left me slightly puzzled. What makes people want to return year in, year out? 



It’s just the right fit for our family of four. Our bure is on the south side of the island, a much quieter refuge away from North Beach, the main swimming and snorkelling spot. A large timber seawall wraps around this side of the beach, with steps to the water below. At low tide, there’s a small beach where the kids play; at high tide, we wade in. The quality of snorkelling directly in front of our bure is genuinely surprising. One small bommie features a giant clam, the seagrass meadow is scattered with blue starfish, and in a small rocky outcrop, two bossy clownfish protect a clutch of eggs. Just as I begin to back off, I spy a tiny version of Nemo – no bigger than my fingernail – hiding below. One genuine part of the Castaway experience is that it’s incredibly family-oriented. Food is a cosmopolitan affair: there’s the Water’s Edge main restaurant and buffet, Nuku Marau Bar & Grill serving sushi by the kids’ pool by day, and an adults-only Fijian-Asian restaurant on the beach by night. But with two kids who can’t sit still, we opt for takeaway wood-fired pizza from the Sundowner Bar early each evening, watching the sun go down. We sit in the sand making a meal out of their discarded pizza crusts, while the kids sit in their cossies in just a few inches of water, snacking away. It’s an easy way to dine out. Back in the day, however, the resort had a strict dress code: No sulu, no dinner, referring to the traditional Fijian wrap skirt worn by both men and women.



But on Castaway the trick is to do as little as possible, for as long as you can. Graeme Field, who has visited Castaway more than 40 times since 1980, recalls showing up to dinner on the island in jeans on his first day, only to be unceremoniously told to strip behind the bar by one of the island’s long-time staff members, Mere Kasaqa. “She said, ‘No! Jeans have to come off’,” he recalls. “And we went behind the bar, and she taught me to tie a sulu.” One genuine part of the Castaway experience is that it’s incredibly family oriented. Over the years, many of the staff working at Castaway have been second and third-generation staff members, forming tight bonds with guests. Field became best friends with Kasaqa’s brother, Nemani. Over the years, Nemani welcomed him into his village north of Suva; Field invited Nemani to be the guest of honour at his Australian wedding, and years later, attended Nemani’s funeral in Fiji. To this day, Field and Mere are in contact. I plan to ask Castaway’s General Manager, Steven Roberts, about the dynamic between staff and guests. However, our first meeting happens in the middle of a huge celebration: the Castaway Rugby team has won the inter-island rugby cup, and the entire island is celebrating on the beach. The next day we meet to chat, but an Australian jogs up from behind and throws his arm around the GM’s shoulders in a bear hug, and they embrace. A visitor for decades, he quickly asks me if he can steal him away: his dad has dementia, he explains cheerfully, and has been asking to see Roberts since they arrived that morning.



“Dad’s always happy when he’s here,” the son beams. Of course, it’s a yes, and I slip away on my morning excursion to the resort’s newest attraction: the coral gene bank. Related Article Opinion

Family holidays The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids Ben Groundwater Travel writer Installed in partnership with non-profit Counting Coral, each offshore sculpture has been engineered using marine-grade steel, with 500 individual “parent” corals attached. The look is steampunk tropical: the five, truck-sized, domed metal sculptures sit in a few metres of water and are adorned with vivid corals: some thriving, others striking a lonely figure, while small schools of fish have begun to cluster around the artificial reef. There’s plenty to do in the water and around the island: bounce on the inflatables anchored just offshore, take out a paddleboard, or hike to the top of the island. But I work out quickly that on Castaway, the trick is to do as little as possible, for as long as you possibly can. And that’s more than enough to keep our family happy for days.



When we gather our things to check out, we’re simply not ready to go. This place has gotten under our skin. Castaway is proof that a holiday isn’t just about a destination, and a place can be part of who you are. And now, having experienced this little slice of Fijian paradise myself, I have to agree with the long-timers: being here really does feel like coming home. DETAILS For 2027, Castaway Island rates start from $F1159 ($737) a night, plus tax (17.5 per cent). Depending on travel dates, all meals may be included. World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Why a ‘blue wave’ today is not necessarily a rejection of Trumpism Michael Koziol November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow our live coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections here. Washington: The temptation after a Democratic victory at today’s midterm elections – if that is indeed what transpires – will be to parse the results as Americans turning the page on Donald Trump and his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. But that could be a dangerous mistake. At the 2018 midterms, during Trump’s first term, Democrats gained 40 seats and took control of the House of Representatives. Americans removed Trump from office two years later, and, amid an onslaught of criminal charges, he seemed destined for the dustbin of political history. Donald Trump faces a blue wave at Tuesday’s midterm elections. Marija Ercegovac As we know, voters felt otherwise. Trump achieved a bigger victory in 2024 than 2016 – despite, and possibly because of, everything Americans knew about him and his policies.



Their vote was not necessarily a wholesale embrace of Trump the man, but a rejection of the Democrats after four years of Joe Biden. The Trump agenda at the time – lower prices, no new foreign wars, tariffs, closing the border and dismantling the “woke” agenda – carried the day because it appealed. Related Article Foreign relations ‘Crazy’ Coalition making huge mistake by opposing EU trade deal: Turnbull Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull notes Trump won a genuine majority for “his ‘America first’ views, his protectionist views, his view that America should use its power to extract the best deal for itself, and his views that America should not be overly concerned about its allies”. Trump himself may be historically unpopular – and that will impact today’s results – but the factors that led Americans to support him twice are still there. Arguably, it is not so much that voters have moved away from Trumpism, but that he let them down. “In a sense, you could say Trump’s political problems today are caused by him abandoning key elements of MAGA,” Turnbull told this masthead last week in New York.



“One of the key parts of the MAGA agenda was no new foreign wars. This is a guy who was seeking the Nobel Peace Prize. This is a guy who railed against George W. Bush’s war in Iraq and Afghanistan. He talked to me and Lucy [Turnbull’s wife] about it once. He was obsessed about this.” Trump played the populist card in 2024, and Democrats have played it in 2026. The party’s key election message has been about affordability: that Trump’s tariffs, trade disputes and war with Iran mean you are paying more for petrol and groceries. Trump likes to boast about winning in Iran. However, the longer the war drags on, the more obvious it becomes that there is no winning exit for the US. Bloomberg That is true – petrol prices are higher than usual, though not as high as their all-time peak in 2022. Australians, who depend on imports, also pay much more for petrol than Americans. If it is the case that affordability is the big issue at this election, then, as with foreign policy, it is not so much that voters are abandoning their populist positions as judging that the president and his Republicans have not fulfilled them.



Most US states beat nearly all European countries on median income. So it is striking that the cost of living has become the perennial cudgel for an opposition to bash an incumbent, before becoming the albatross around the neck of the next incumbent. But such is the nature of populism. And Trump has remade the GOP into much more of a populist party. Even with the Iran war and all the other baggage of the second Trump administration, the candidates he endorsed performed very well in Republican primaries, regularly beating incumbents – such as Texas senator John Cornyn, who lost to Ken Paxton. ‘I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.’ US President Donald Trump, at a rally in Iowa How much power Trump retains within his own party will shape the endurance of Trumpism and MAGA. As political strategist Douglas Heye says, Republicans may feel liberated after the midterms to be “a bit more outspoken about what they really think about Trump”, and say publicly what they only admit privately now. The size of Republican losses will help determine Trump’s ongoing influence: a bloodbath would weaken him, while losses in line with a standard midterm election could be dismissed as inevitable.



Vice President JD Vance is positioning himself as a viable candidate for the MAGA true believers. Bloomberg At any rate, the immense power Republicans have invested in Trump does not dissipate overnight. And Trump himself is aware of this. In a little-noticed aside during a recent rally in Iowa, he made a prediction. “I’ll always have that little extra power,” he said, while talking about his eventual exit from the White House. “I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.” Trump’s assumed successor, Vice President J.D. Vance, has positioned himself to capture those voters who feel betrayed by Trump. He never fully signed on to the Iran war, and does not echo the president’s rhetoric that – current petrol prices notwithstanding – Americans have never had it so good. At Trump rallies around the country, supporters consistently say Vance is the guy they like for 2028. He represents the MAGA constituency more so than Secretary of State Marco Rubio, another likely contender. If Trumpism is to continue post-Trump, it probably runs through Vance. But the president has been non-committal so far in terms of an endorsement, and appears to enjoy fostering a competitive rivalry between the two men – or perhaps someone else.



“I can’t see him staying out of this,” says Bob Shapiro, political scientist at Columbia University. “To the extent that he’s in this, that’s going to tell us whether Trumpism has legs or not, and whether there is a candidate he picks or a candidate who steps forward and ascends and basically carries the mantle of Trumpism.” Related Article US midterms Are these the worst US midterm attack ads of all time? Beyond policy, perhaps the hallmark of Trumpism is the jettisoning of the normal rules of engagement. It is a skill in which he is uniquely gifted, once boasting – correctly, it seems – that he could shoot someone on Fifth Avenue and not lose any votes. Others may be less adept and less brazen, but they’re happy to try. Vance dishes it out, and saw no problem with the Vivek Ramaswamy ad in Ohio that enlisted a Democratic candidate’s estranged and reportedly mentally ill mother to tar her own daughter. Most Republicans are comfortable attacking Muslim Democrats as jihadist communists. Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, regularly mocks “trannies” and “fatties”. When it comes to political discourse, we’re through the looking glass – and all else aside, that may be the lasting legacy of Trumpism.

World.title: The $1b idea for early intervention as rate rise looms over struggling families
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament The $1b idea for early intervention as rate rise looms over struggling families Jessica McSweeney November 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Frontline domestic violence, homelessness and mental health service providers are demanding a $1 billion pre-election funding commitment from the state government as they anticipate the interest rate hike will further strain community groups already overrun with calls for help. More than 11 charities, unions and church groups have written an open letter to the Minns government urging an overhaul of state funding, which they say focuses on crisis support but leads to ballooning wait lists for early intervention services. Salote Moso accessed support services after leaving a relationship she says included coercive control and financial abuse. Wolter Peeters Uniting director of advocacy and external relations Emma Maiden said: “We’re parking the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, and we’re not putting that fence at the top of the cliff.” The group is on Wednesday calling for the state government to introduce a “preventing harm framework”, under which funding would be targeted to reach at-risk people at earlier stages, before they are in crisis.



Maiden said Tuesday’s rate rise would put further pressure on Uniting’s support services, where an increase in working families experiencing poverty is driving a surge in demand for help. Related Article Graphic content

Domestic violence She tried to leave her abusive partner. It cost Sophia her children “We’re already exceeding the number of people that we’re funded to service in our family support services by about 30 per cent due to increasing demand. So we just try and make those dollars stretch further,” she said. “Community organisations are already turning people away, and every rate rise adds more pressure on households and adds to that queue.” Reducing wait times for help is one of the core goals of the campaign. Domestic Violence NSW reports waitlists regularly exceed three months, while the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare found an average of 31 requests for emergency accommodation were going unassisted every day in NSW.



Minto single mother Salote Moso, 27, was financially dependent on her ex-partner, who she said would take control of her money to the point of denying her $20 for her Opal card. Moso said when she questioned his spending, he would become aggressive. When she decided to leave the controlling relationship, Moso couch surfed with her infant son while she waited a month to secure financial support. Since Moso was at risk of homelessness, she was connected with a social worker with a two-week wait time, but those two weeks weighed heavily as she was forced to skip meals to put food on the table for her son. “I was mostly on survival mode the whole time … I’m not really proud of it, but there came a point where I started thinking dark thoughts,” Moso said. “With a long waiting time, it can also be isolating because then you’re starting to think or feel like, oh, what if they’ve forgotten about me?”



NSW Council of Social Service policy and advocacy director Ben McAlpine said when people reached out for help but got stuck on lengthy wait lists, it could erode their trust in the system and in government. NCOSS was one of the signatories of the open letter, which argues a $1 billion investment over four years will unlock savings by reducing the strain on crisis services and getting people back on their feet earlier. “The NSW government cannot set interest rates, but it can decide to fund early intervention instead of paying for crisis later, and that’s at the core of this conversation,” McAlpine said. The campaign, dubbed Right Help, Right Time, faces an uphill battle to secure its $1 billion demand as the state government faces pressure to rein in spending ahead of the March election. In the June budget, the government committed an additional $184.1 million to six specialist domestic violence services.

World.title: Police won't say which makes of Subaru are being targeted by Otago car thieves
World.content:
Police are refusing to say which models of Subaru vehicles are being targeted in a spate of car thefts in Otago.

On Monday, Inspector Sam Ramsay from Otago Coastal Police said there had been a "noticeable" spike in thefts across the wider Dunedin area in recent months, with offenders "targeting Subaru vehicles".

"In many cases there is little or no sign of forced entry, with offenders exploiting known vulnerabilities in some vehicle models," he said.

In response to further questions from RNZ, police said they would not be revealing any information about which models were being targeted, or about the vulnerabilities mentioned.

"We won't be going into specific detail about the methods used, as doing so could inadvertently assist offenders, but investigations indicate offenders are exploiting vulnerabilities in some vehicles," Ramsay said.

"For the same reason, we are not identifying specific makes or models that may be vulnerable. Vehicle owners should ensure their vehicles are locked when unattended and consider additional security measures where appropriate and possible."

Meanwhile, Inchcape New Zealand - which handles distribution, marketing, and retail for Subaru here - said it was unaware of any vulnerabilites in its vehicles.

"Subaru New Zealand has not been contacted by the police in regards to stolen vehicles, or any vulnerabilities," general manager Paul Mallard said.

"Subaru New Zealand is not aware of any known security vulnerabilities on New Zealand-new Subaru vehicles."

World.title: How much does government affect the economy?
World.content:
Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2325404%2Fhow-much-does-government-affect-the-economy

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Over the course of the next few weeks - or months - New Zealand will know what form its next government will it take, but does any of it have an impact on the economy?

Economists say perhaps not as much as you think.

Massey University economist Matt Roskruge said governments had less control over the economy than their election campaigns might suggest.

"Aotearoa is exposed to global shocks and no government can insulate us completely," he said. "Where governments make a real difference is in how they respond and who carries the costs.

"Choices about tax, public services, benefits and investment affect employment, household incomes and how well people weather a downturn.

Matt Roskruge says governments can't insulate New Zealand completely from global shocks. David Wiltshire

"There are trade-offs. Greater spending or tax cuts can support jobs and incomes, but can also add to inflation pressure, depending on how they're funded and how much spare capacity the economy has.

"Cutting spending can ease that pressure, but risks weakening employment and services."

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said, while people might be affected on an individual level, the overall impact was small, because the difference in approach between the two main factions wasn't significant.

"There are probably some differences at the margin. A right-leaning coalition is more quite likely to be more fiscally austere than a left one, probably less borrowing coming through.

"Our pre-election preview noted that ACT is possibly a bit harder-core in terms of fiscal consolidation. Some of those things will matter at the margin."

Businesses might be slightly more confident under a right-leaning government.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub agreed that some specific groups, such as workers in the public service or those who relied on welfare, would be affected by policy changes, but overall, the impact was limited.

"There is just this extraordinary focus on what government does and people think about it as if they've got their fingers in every aspect of your life, but that's not quite how it works. Government is more at the periphery, in some ways.

"You think about the rules and regulations. We don't interact with rules and regulations every day, unless you're a fairly risky kind of person.

"The government provides public services, we consume quite a lot of that. We drive, we send our kids to school, we go to doctors, that kind of stuff.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub supplied

"Those are personal interactions, but do these things change materially, whenever there's a change of government? My GP didn't change much just because of the colour of the government in Wellington."

ASB economists said the next government, whether it was National-led or Labour-led, would inherit significant fiscal and infrastructural challenges.

Crown debt has risen from below 6 percent of GDP in 2007 to more than 40 percent.

ASB estimates New Zealand faces an infrastructure deficit of about $200 billion and about $1 trillion of infrastructure investment requirements over the next 30 years.

"We need to invest in infrastructure that can support productivity and resilience, but we also need to be realistic about how much the economy can absorb at once," senior economist Mark Smith said.

"Trying to do everything immediately risks running into capacity constraints and putting more pressure on inflation."

Roskruge said a drawn-out negotiation period to form a coalition could be more of a concern.

"Normal government business continues under caretaker arrangements. A prolonged period of uncertainty could, however, cause businesses to delay investment and hiring, particularly where decisions depend on government policy.

"I think the bigger question is which government has the most credible plan to lift productivity and build resilience, so we're better placed to withstand the next shock."

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said New Zealanders were generally used to the uncertainty of elections and coalition negotiations.

"Although the closeness of this election campaign, and broader challenges created by the overhang and potential influence of Opportunity have meant that the uncertainty has been elevated this time," he said. "Depending on how the seats come out, there's potential for the post-election uncertainty to be more elevated than at any time since 1996.

"Normally, that could be an issue for businesses and the economy, but given we've been operating in a highly variable - and often challenging - environment for the last two years, I suspect that an extra layer of uncertainty is not going to make a great deal of difference to most people's decision making.

"The exception to that statement might be key policy areas, where there are significant differences between Labour and National, such as Labour's capital gains tax, but across a lot of economic policy, the difference between the two major parties is not particularly stark."

World.title: Political donations tracker: The wealthy donors dominating large donations
World.content:
More than $8 million dollars in large donations has been given this election year, with almost 40 percent coming from just 10 donors.

Throughout the campaign, RNZ has been tracking the money flowing to the parties and where it has come from.

Some of the country's wealthiest individuals are linked to the biggest donation totals.



Nick Mowbray donated $475,000 and Rank Group, owned by Graeme Hart, donated $700,000, according to Electoral Commission disclosures.

Their donations went to parties in the current coalition government, taking the total given to coalition parties to more than $6m, roughly three quarters of the large donation total. Parties not in the coalition received $2.2m.



Tech entrepreneur Brian Cartmell was the only big donor who gave to parties both in the coalition and outside of it, supporting ACT, NZ First and Opportunity.

But Opportunity’s biggest donor was board member Alan Wilderland, who has given around $221,000 to the party, both individually and through a company.



Despite being a large donor he says he supports Opportunity’s policy of a $30,000 cap on donations. The party says this would be among its “bottom lines” in any talks to form a government.

“To change the game, you have to play the game first,” Wilderland told RNZ.

The Green party also has a policy calling for a $30,000 cap.



The cap was a recommendation made in an independent review of the electoral system. A survey found 43 percent of people think big donors have undue influence on politics.

The review's recommendation was not implemented by the current government.



Academic Max Rashbrooke, who is also in favour of capping donations to improve trust in the political system, told RNZ there’s no incentive to change the status quo.

"That's why it stays as it is - not because the public likes it, but because politicians don't really want to change."

Here’s where things stand, as of 3 November, across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

To date $8,254,331 has been donated. Large donations made anonymously, classed as “protected from disclosure” add a further $629,322 to the total.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.

Each line represents a donor with wider lines indicating larger amounts.

How the money grew

If someone makes numerous donations under $20,000, once the cumulative total tops $20,000 it must be declared.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

The below chart shows the 2023 annual total of donations over $20,000, compared to the current 2026 total.

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. If Joan Smith had the same address as John Smith and had donated individually, as well as made a joint donation with John Smith, the name is updated to John and / or Joan Smith.

Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: Kick Back report exposes extent, causes of youth homelessness
World.content:
Warning: This story discusses suicide.

"We're all still young, but going on the streets right now, it's like the government's trying to make us grow up faster and we're still kids at the end of the day."

Frankie has lived on the streets since he was just 11 years old, one of many clients of youth charity Kick Back, which is reporting a 95 percent increase in those desperate for help.

On Wednesday morning, Kick Back released its second 'State of the Street' report, which finds 73 percent of the young people accessing its services are either sleeping rough or couch surfing.

That's up from 44 percent in its previous report.

The latest result finds family breakdown is a leading cause of youth homelessness, and 31 percent say they've suffered from violence or abuse, or left home because they feel unsafe.

At 10.50am, outside Kick Back's Karangahape Rd youth hub, a young man, maybe 16 or 17, is slumped on the sidewalk, staring into the middle distance and waiting for it to open at 11am.

He clearly hasn't slept for some time. One of his boots doesn't have laces, his only luggage is a reusable New World shopping bag.

Sitting and lying down on the footpath across the road, a group of older people are already on the Lion Reds, their duvets and other belongings stuffed into rubbish bags.

One of the volunteers comes down to let the young man in, and gives him a towel and some soap for the shower. He picks out something clean to wear from a rack of donated clothes.

He has been helped into emergency motel accommodation, but he's spent the past few days roughing it on the streets.

Kick Back general manager Aaron Hendrey says young people increasingly rely on charities like his just to get the basics.

"We've seen a real huge increase in young people reaching out for support over the last year," he says. "We've got about 90, over 90 percent, 95 percent increase in referrals coming through to us, which I think is a real sign of the scale of the crisis and how much it's getting worse."

According to the Kick Back report, the homelessness crisis has even reaching primary school-aged children.

Now in his early 20s, Frankie first became homeless when he was 11 years old.

"I lost my dad at a young age, at 11 years old, and OT [Oranga Tamariki] was trying to put me into different houses.

"I was getting picked on. It was to that point that I was going to commit suicide, so I ran away from the foster homes to the streets."

He says he roughed it, living in places like cemeteries, until he was 21, when he came into contact with Kick Back.

Now a firm part of the Kick Back whanau, Frankie is passionate about helping other young people who fall through the cracks.

"I just really want to yell at the prime minister, to be honest," he said. "Make more houses for the youth and people that's on the streets right now."

When he sees young people on the streets who are as young as he was, he says he feels "heartbroken".

"We're all still young, but like going on the streets right now, it's like the government's trying to make us grow up faster and we're still kids at the end of the day."

It's Anita's 23rd birthday, and she's come to the youth hub with her niece to get some kai and celebrate with her friends.

She moved to the streets because she felt she couldn't stay at home. She feels fortunate to have at last found secure accommodation.

"We were in and out of lodges and stuff and, kind of, that situation. City is really bad for young kids to live around homeless, because you can be in danger or anything that can happen to you.

"I'd rather house youth, because we don't want them to die young."

Kick Back's 'State of the Streets' report contains 12 recommendations for ending youth homelessness, including introducing duty-to-assist legislation, returning access to benefits for 18-19 year olds and developing a national strategy to end youth homelessness.
