World.title: Hawke's Bay vegetable growers on the hunt for higher value crops after McCain closure
World.content:
A group of Hawke's Bay vegetable farmers are trying to work out what to grow after a feasibility study found they should avoid a McCain-style large scale model again.

McCain's closure of its frozen vegetable processing factory in Hastings impacted 100 farmers across the region and a group of growers looked at taking the factory over, but the company sold its processing equipment.

The group embarked on a feasibility study, with $50,000 of government funding, which confirmed there were still domestic and international market opportunities for processed vegetables grown in Hawke's Bay.

But it said further work was needed to determine whether they could become viable commercial propositions.

"However, recreating the previous large-scale processing model is unlikely to be commercially competitive, given lower-cost imports and New Zealand's higher energy, labour and freight costs.

"The strongest opportunities appear to be in higher-value and speciality products, where New Zealand-grown vegetables can compete on quality, provenance and other points of difference rather than price alone," said the report.

It stated that "potential export opportunities have been identified", particularly where New Zealand's quality and counter-seasonal production offered an advantage.

Many farmers in the region who were supplying McCain are now growing forage crops while they look for longer term options. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Central Hawke's Bay farmer Sam Reynolds was part of the group, as he used to grow peas for McCain. Since McCain closed he's growing forage crops for the sheep, beef and dairy sectors.

"Luckily the industries in a pretty good place because of the alternatives there, but that's not always going to be the case," said Reynolds.

The feasibility study found a key threat to growing and processing cheaper foods in New Zealand, such as frozen vegetables, was the ability for companies to import them at a fraction of the price.

"It is hard to compete with countries like China and India where they get government support to build factories.

"India in particular has spent a lot of money on cold store infrastructure and cold chain infrastructure so those imports are possibly only going to get cheaper," said Reynolds.

The group of growers wanted to proceed to Stage 2 of the study - which would test three potential opportunities: higher value processed vegetables for domestic food service and specialty markets, export opportunities for frozen peas and value added processed vegetable products for export.

This second phase would cost about $130,000.

"A bit of government support for another study on different opportunites for us would be helpful because it does look increasingly likely we are not competitive in the frozen vege market anymore.

"We've got good land, we've got good water and a lot of sunshine but we just need to think of different things to grow with it," said Reynolds.

Central Hawke's Bay farmer Sam Reynolds. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Arable sector at a 'crisis point' says farming leader

Central Hawke's Bay grower Hugh Ritchie was also on board. He's farming 2000 hectares near Otane and half of it was growing a big variety of crops - from rocket and carrot seed to soya beans and ryegrass.

Ritchie had been farming for decades and seen many of the sectors ups and downs.

"Not only Hawke's Bay but if you look at the arable industry in general in New Zealand it is at a crisis point," he said.

About a quarter of his business was in growing peas, corn and carrots for McCain, and he told RNZ the study was clear in its findings that growers must seek out higher value crops.

"It's more intensive and it's more complex farming, but if the value is right then it works.

"You know we aren't the prairies of Canada or Western Australia and growing cereal crops ... we are smaller areas and we have to play to our strengths," he said.

But just what these future crops were for Hawke's Bay farmers remained a mystery - although the study found there's a bit of pressure to find a solution before Hawke's Bay lost more of its vegetable growing and processing capability.

Ritchie said if growers were serious about establishing a commercially viable business opportunity, then they needed to be willing to invest.

"If we're not prepared to help ourselves then you can't expect someone else to help ... so growers - if we want to try and have an alternate and come up with alternative strategies then we need to be prepared to go and help ourselves."

Farmer Hugh Ritchie says growers are looking for higher value crops that can 'play to the strengths' of being grown locally. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The report stated that growers were not asking for a commitment to build a new processing facility, but support to establish whether a commercially viable business could be developed.

"Beyond the regional economic benefits, retaining domestic processing capability would support New Zealand's food security and reduce reliance on imported vegetables," it said.

Minister Todd McClay told RNZ the government was open to supporting the next stage of the feasibility work and would make a decision about additional funding before the end of the year.

"This has been a difficult period for Hawke's Bay growers, and I understand the uncertainty many are facing.

"The report is a useful piece of work. It sets out clearly both the challenges and the opportunities for vegetable processing in the region," he said.

McClay said New Zealand did not apply tariffs to imported frozen peas, beans or carrots before its agreements with China or India.

"Trade agreements are vital to Hawke's Bay. The region's total exports are around $3 billion a year, and they are a direct result of our many trade agreements. Nearly one in three jobs in the region depends on exports.

Hawke's Bay exported up to $1b of goods to China each year, and the India agreement was expected to add as much as $300 million."China is also one of the largest buyers of New Zealand frozen vegetables. Last year it took around $32 million, almost all of it peas."

Hugh Ritchie's crop of carrot seed that will be exported overseas. RNZ / Alexa Cook

New seed procesing facility for Central Hawke's Bay

The region was set to benefit from a $3m government investment in a new grower-led seed cleaning, processing and storage facility in Central Hawke's Bay.

Associate Regional Development Minister Mark Patterson said this positioned Hawke's Bay as a key hub for high-value seed production and would help support future growth in the sector.

"Currently, much of the seed grown in Hawke's Bay that requires specialist cleaning and processing is sent outside the region, including to as far away as Canterbury, before it can be sold domestically or exported. This adds cost, creates inefficiencies, and reduces returns for local growers," he said.

Patterson said the new hub would bring the full seed value chain together in one location, from drying and cleaning through to processing and storage.

World.title: Banks Peninsula: Christchurch's biggest electorate is a swing seat
World.content:
It's all on in Christchurch's biggest electorate, the swing seat of Banks Peninsula.

Covering a vast and diverse area, the peninsula switched from red to blue for the first time in more than 20 years at the last election, by a slim margin.

The electorate covers tourist hotspots like Akaroa, the bohemian enclave of Lyttelton, the industrial city-fringe suburb of Woolston and Halswell's swiftly growing subdivisions, as well as some of the city's most exclusive neighbourhoods, such as the coastal communities of Sumner and Redcliffs and hilltop Cashmere.

It's also one of the country's most engaged electorates - boasting the highest percentage of eligible enrolled voters, and at the last election, the highest voter turn-out.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407824323112

When National's Vanessa Weenink beat Labour's Tracey McLellan in 2023 by just under 400 votes, it was the first time the electorate had swung blue in 24 years.

Weenink and McLellan are back to contest the seat again, alongside four other candidates - the Green Party's Craig Pauling, Alliance candidate Kyle Turnbull, ACT's Zachary Wellman and Amy Turner of the New Conservatives.

The electorate skewed older than the national median - 53 years for Banks Peninsula compared to 38 years nationwide, had a high percentage of home ownership (83 percent to the national rate of 66 percent) and had an enrolment rate of 98 percent compared to 91 percent nationally.

Eighty-four percent of Banks Peninsula's enrolled voters turned to vote in the last election compared to 78 percent nationwide.

Jemma Hooykass recently returned to New Zealand from 20 years overseas and was taken aback at how much election chatter there was.

"I feel like it's the conversation everywhere, and in places I wouldn't expect like the gym, drop-offs with the kids, dinner parties, even just now I'm here on a play centre visit and we were just having our morning hui and everyone was talking about it and who they're voting for."

She had researched parties' policy positions and took her civic duty seriously.

"I wouldn't want to just show up and tick a box without knowing what I'm doing.

"It's special being able to vote, and I've lived in many countries where you can't, or you can't take that for granted."

Jemma Hooykass. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Halswell voters were united on the need for better infrastructure in the city's largest and fastest-growing suburb.

Peter moved down from the North Island three years ago.

"Infrastructure is going to be a problem. We've got all these houses coming in over here. Yeah, well, it's not just here. I mean, it's all over Canterbury and yeah, probably the countrywide, isn't it?"

He's not convinced the electorate was more engaged than any other, and was most concerned about minor parties delaying the formation of a new government.

He wanted to see a tweak on the current arrangements rather than a wholesale change

"Well, a slight change, not a major change. I mean, the Labour Party's certainly not done us any favours in the last term they had.

"Some of the minor parties would be good - not too much change, but they've certainly got some good ideas."

Halswell resident Neil said he was a little nervous about the outcome.

"I'm feeling ... a little bit apprehensive about what coalition party might be scraped together, either National and their cohorts or Labour and their cohorts."

Banks Peninsula is Christchurch's biggest electorate. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Education and health were the key issues from his perspective.

"Being a teacher and a wife who's a nurse, that's what we're keeping a close eye on, and obviously the cost of living which affects everybody."

He planned to hit the golf course on election day, and "not give it a second thought until night time".

Joseph Quested had lived in the electorate for more than 15 years, and loved the sense of community he'd found in Lyttelton, which he said leant strongly to the left.

"There's one National Party sign up in Lyttelton, just on the corner of the street down there, and it's been vandalised every single night since the moment that it got put up."

The environment, Palestine and the cost of living were among the most important issues for young people, he said.

He felt polling often got the outcome wrong, and was basing his predictions more on vibes.

"I think that the person who is going to win an election is ultimately going to be the person who has the most swag, the most ris [charisma].

"Obviously, if it's going to come down to like Labour or National, I definitely want Labour to win, but I think Chris Hipkins is a deeply swagless individual, you know, I don't think he has much charisma.

"I would be voting for the Green Party either way, but I wish the Labour Party would put up somebody with a little bit more juice in the tank."

Joseph Quested. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Janine Clarke said the strong and engaged community in Diamond Harbour was one of the things that attracted her to the area.

People were definitely interested in the election, with a well attended meet-the-candidates evening and a solid showing by the candidates at various events.

"I think a lot of people are looking for something that isn't sort of same old, same old, bouncing back and forth."

Many Diamond Harbour residents had an interest in conservation and the environment, she said.

"We live in a beautiful place, we want to keep it beautiful."

She could sense some cyncism at the process seeping in, but that made voting more important than ever, Clarke said.

"I guess sometimes that people get a bit disengaged when it becomes like that and that's actually the time we need to get engaged because if we just do the same thing we get the same results."

Clarke said she planned to take a broader view of her vote.

"I'm personally probably not as affected by cost of living issues, but I know there are a lot of people that are, and it's not just about me.

"It's about making New Zealand a better place for everybody. And that way, if everybody's kind of at least a bit happier, then we've done a good job."

Janine Clarke. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Peter Langlands lived in Woolston, and was a frequent visitor to his favourite Lyttelton cafe.

He said his Green Party vote was "pretty hardwired", with conservation and the health system among his chief concerns.

He was against commitments from some parties to cut taxes.

"It's a real false economy in the long term. When people have got a good health system, their well-being is better, their productivity is better, and ultimately we just have a far better system moving forward."

Like much of the electorate, he'd be watching closely on Saturday.

World.title: Only 14% of GP owners support Labour's three free appointments policy - survey
World.content:
A survey of 132 general practice owners shows only 14 percent support Labour's policy promising three free appointments.

GenPro, which says it represents more than 500 GP owners across Aotearoa, has published its results ahead of the election on Saturday.

Read more about party promises here and what the health sector thinks of them here.

According to GenPro chair Dr Angus Chambers, GPs anticipated it would increase demand, and were concerned about their ability to meet it, considering the existing workforce shortages.

"We think it's a good idea to improve access [...] but feel that there's some significant risks that we'll be even more over-burdened than we are."

Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall said in response Labour's plan also included measures to free up time for 4.5 million appointments, "including better telehealth and a digital innovation fund".

Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall. RNZ / Baz MacDonald

She noted GenPro itself supported a number of the measures Labour had proposed, and pointed to two other policies - low-interest loans to set up owner-operated, independent GPs, and an independent authority to determine funding - which were in-line with calls for better funding.

"Our policy is about making primary care more affordable while ensuring GP practices are properly funded. Independent pricing is central to that. It means funding will be based on the actual costs of running a practice, providing certainty for the long term and ensuring GP services are financially sustainable."

GPs weigh in on who they would vote for based on health policy alone. Supplied / GenPro

When asked which party they would vote for based solely on health policy, 42 percent of respondents to the GenPro survey chose the Opportunity Party, 19 percent said National, and 13 percent said ACT.

Labour and the Green Party each received eight percent, New Zealand First 0.8 percent, and 9.1 percent of respondents were undecided or didn't pick one.

"This isn't a prediction of the election result," said Chambers. "What it does provide is a useful indication of which health policies resonate with people running general practices."

GP funding front-of-mind for many

The strongest feedback in the poll was for the Opportunity Party proposal to increase the proportion of Health NZ funding spent on primary care, which was supported by 93 percent of respondents.

ACT's proposed $100 million annual increase in general practice funding was supported by 86 percent, while 71 percent backed streamlining registration processes for overseas-trained doctors.

Chambers said the results reflected the experience of a sector that had "endured several years of severe financial and workforce pressure but is now showing signs of stabilising".

Support for prevention, screening and primary care funding

GPs on Labour's policy for three free GP appointments. Supplied / GenPro

Prevention remained important to GPs, following similar calls from around the sector for investment in primary care ahead of the Budget earlier this year.

National's proposal to lower the bowel screening age, free cervical screening, completing the extension of free breast screening to age 74 by 2029, and new lung and prostate cancer screening pilots were all well supported by GPs.

The Green Party's proposal for greater emphasis on prevention and community-based healthcare drew 80 percent support, while the same proportion backed New Zealand First's proposal to reduce administrative and compliance burdens on general practice.

Telehealth and innovation

Labour's proposed review of telehealth funding was supported by 77 percent, its digital innovation fund for primary care clinics by 71 percent, and low-interest loans to help younger doctors buy into general practices by 66 percent.

"Accessibility and affordability matter enormously, but they need to go hand in hand with investment in the capacity of general practice," Chambers said.

"Ultimately, patients need to be able to get an appointment. That requires a sustainable network of practices, enough doctors and nurses, and funding that reflects the cost of providing care."

Meanwhile, rural New Zealand is short 151 doctors, according to a new survey by the Rural Health Network Hauora Taiwhenua.

Rural Health Network Hauora Taiwhenua chief executive Dr Grant Davidson. Supplied / Rural Health Network

Responses from 141 rural practices showed increasing workloads, persistent staff shortages, ageing facilities and increasingly relying on short-term locums.

Almost half reported at least one GP vacancy.

However, the number of nurse practitioners had more than tripled since 2024.

Network chief executive Dr Grant Davidson said he had been struck by how little attention political parties were paying to rural health.

"This survey shows a sector working incredibly hard to hold things together, but it also shows the cracks," he said.

"Rural practices are expected to provide primary care, urgent care, emergency response, after-hours services, palliative care and workforce training, often with fewer staff and less infrastructure than their urban counterparts."

48 percent of responding practices have a GP vacancy

Workforce shortages have shown little improvement since 2024

46 percent say their facilities are no longer fit for purpose

90 percent are affected by major seasonal population surges

Clinical director Dr Rebekah Doran said the survey demonstrated that rural general practices were "far more than a standard GP clinic".

World.title: Quick hits: A-listers, mistakes and the king's Melbourne Cup connection
World.content:
The 2026 Melbourne Cup race day has provided on-course action and off-track celebrities.

With a generous A-lister shouting fans dinner, a heartfelt message from MND sufferer Nathan Charles and the royal connection to race winner Point of Law, there was a little bit of everything at Flemington.

Here's the quick hits from the race that stops a nation.

1. Waller fined $50,000 for 'honest mistake'

Chris Waller was fined heavily for an error. (AAP: James Ross)

Some mistakes are more costly than others on Melbourne Cup Day, and it's fair to say that Chris Waller paid dearly for an error made by a member of his team on race day morning.

The New Zealand horse Asterix was found to have had Penetrene administered to both forelegs in its stable just hours before the race.

"Unfortunately, there was a topical treatment applied to the horse this morning which is allowed during the week but not on race day," Racing Victoria chief steward Rob Montgomery told Nine.

"It just is an honest mistake but unfortunately has big consequences."

Penetrene is used to relieve muscle soreness and inflammation and is permitted for use, but not on race days.

Waller was fined $50,000 for the error, but said there was no blame for the incident.

"It's a very basic liniment most stables use and I guess the pressure of race day, the person that looks after the horse, put it on his legs right in front of the security guard," Waller said.

"Nothing was hidden … as soon as it happened we knew there was a problem.

"It's not [the stablehand's] fault, I've got to wear the responsibility, it's my team."

2. The Generous Mr Foxx

Jamie Foxx has been particularly generous in Melbourne of late. (Getty Images: Sam Tabone)

The Melbourne Cup is known for attracting everyone and anyone who wants to be seen in high society and this year is no exception.

Hollywood A-lister Jamie Foxx has been in Melbourne shooting his latest film, Deadlocked.

Between takes though, he has been mixing it with the Melbourne public, including at the evocatively named Maison Bâtard where, according to The Age, he paid for several people's dinner by surprise.

He was at Flemington and told the Daily Mail Australia that he was taking his girlfriend, Alyce Huckstepp, and her family to the races as a surprise.

What a generous guy.

3. Nathan Charles flipping the script

On a more serious note, former Wallaby Nathan Charles was also at Flemington today.

The 37-year-old has recently been diagnosed with motor neurone disease and, despite the shock of such a devastating diagnosis, is intent on raising the profile of the disease and living his life to the full at the same time.

"In life, everyone has adversity. I've always been a believer in you should be judged not by how you fall over, but instead how you stand back up. And it's a really unfortunate circumstance," he told Nine.

"But it is my journey and I've just got to keep on moving forward.

"I sort of took the week to get my emotions together.

"And then I just thought, you know what, I gotta flip the script.

"Instead of doing things for the last time I want to start doing things for the first time.

"And I want to provide inspiration and hope to young Australians that they can achieve in the face of adversity."

4. Robbie Williams still entertains us

Robbie Williams wowed onlookers with his pre-race performance. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Racegoers were given a real musical treat ahead of the race, with 52-year-old British legend Robbie Williams performing both pre and post-race at Flemington.

Ahead of his latest Australian tour, which starts at Adelaide Oval on Saturday, Williams performed singalong favourites Feel, Rock DJ, Angels and then Let Me Entertain You.

The crowd at Flemington were up on their feet.

And they'll have another opportunity to enjoy the British legend later on too, when he performs another set at the course.

5. From King Charles to Coaster

Point Of Law claimed the Melbourne Cup, having previously been owned by King Charles III. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Racing Photos)

Cup winner Point of Law has had quite the colourful past.

The four-year-old, who was sired by unbeaten British legend Frankel, formerly belonged to King Charles III, who sold the colt earlier this year.

King Charles's mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, was a noted horse racing fan, with her gleeful celebration of Estimate's victory in the 2013 Ascot Gold Cup a particular highlight.

She even finished sixth in the 1997 Melbourne Cup with Frankie Dettori on Arabian Story.

One can only guess how she'd have felt about her son selling a horse that would go on to win the race later that same year…

A consortium of Australians bought Point of Law, among them legendary West Coast and Carlton superstar, Chris Judd.

6. The Cinderella Horse

The Melbourne Cup offers something for everyone each year.

Sure, there are plenty of punters who study the form guide intently, listen to all the shows, read all the previous and make an educated selection based on all those factors and more.

And then there's the rest of us, who pick the horse with the name they like best or whose colours remind you of your favourite flag.

For tangential sports fans, there may have been one name that stuck out: James J Braddock.

James J Braddock, boxing's Cinderella Man. (Getty Images: Keystone France/Gamma-Rapho)

Film buffs may well recognise this name better than sporties, because James J Braddock was the subject of the 2005 biographical film, Cinderella Man, starring Russell Crowe.

Braddock was an American boxer in the 1930s who, due to persistent hand injuries, jacked in his ring career to work in the docks during the Great Depression.

He came back to the ring though and, after a couple of impressive victories, managed to land a fight against the heavyweight champion of the world, Max Baer, at Madison Square Garden in 1935.

So monumental was the upset and the way he had come back from near retirement, that the press christened him the Cinderella Man.

Braddock's next fight was against Joe Louis, who knocked him out in the eighth round of their bout in Chigaco in 1937.

As for his equine namesake, he finished a credible seventh in the Cup.

World.title: Saudi Arabia Asian Cup postponed due to conflict in Middle East
World.content:
The Socceroos will have to wait another year for the chance to win a second Asian Cup, with the 2027 tournament postponed by nearly a year.

Scheduled to be played in Saudi Arabia in January and February of 2027, the tournament will now be played from December 23, 2027 to January 21, 2028.

The new dates are pending approval from FIFA.

The decision has been forced by conflict in the Middle East, with Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis claiming responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.

A strike on Riyadh's international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.

"The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," an AFC statement read.

The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through its Public Investment Fund in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the World Cup in 2034.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, with golf's Asian Tour postponing the Saudi International indefinitely, while cycling's Urban World Championships were also cancelled.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December and FIFA postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in Jeddah until an unspecified future date.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: This Samoan superman is the World Cup's greatest comeback story
World.content:
As he prepares to lead his nation into a World Cup semifinal against Australia, sometimes Ronald Volkman still can't believe this is happening.

He'd have settled for one NRL game this year with Parramatta and after what he's been through, that really would have been enough.

But instead the best season of his budding career will continue when he lines up for Samoa against the Kangaroos with a World Cup final berth up for grabs, standing on the shoulders of giants with the whole rugby league world watching.

It still feels more like a fantasy than a reality for the 24-year-old, even as he's living it.

"I didn't see myself playing NRL and I didn't see myself playing for my country, in a World Cup, on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"I grew up watching this, I'm still pinching myself that I got to get on these fields.

Ronald Volkman will start in the halves for Samoa against Australia this weekend. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"The players in this team, you look left, you look right, you see guns. It gives you so much confidence in what you can do and that you can take it to the next level."

It has been a long journey. It was only a few years back that Volkman thought his football career was over.

Bad shoulder and hip injuries in 2023 scuppered a move from the Warriors to St George Illawarra the following season, sending Volkman to rock bottom in a full year out of the sport.

The physical pain was such that Volkman could barely move and without the game he loved he lost his way.

He stopped training and put on weight. He didn't know himself and when he was out and about, he'd pull his hood up so nobody would know him.

Mates would reached out to support him, but Volkman often ignored them, trapped in a downward spiral with a heart set on suffering, haunted by football dreams he could barely remember.

At his lowest depths, he leant on the things that mattered most to him.

Ronald Volkman's career and life fell apart after he left the Warriors. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"A big one for me was my faith. I fell down to that faith, my God, my loved ones, my family and my partner family," Volkman said.

"They were there for me during those tough times and it'd be slack for me not to take the opportunity I've had this year and showcase my talent, not for myself but for my loved ones.

"They've been through it as much as I have."

There's a lot of loved ones to repay.

Volkman is one of eight siblings and Samoan on both sides of the family. Growing up they'd go back to the islands every second year.

His father, Tas, wept tears of joy when his son debuted for the Warriors in 2022 and did so again when Volkman made his rugby league return in a pre-season trial for Parramatta last year.

Volkman did the same during the Samoan anthem on Sunday night but Emeline, Tas's mother, doesn't give as much away.

She still lives in Samoa, in a village called Vaitele Tai in the western outskirts of Apia, where she watched her grandson come on against Tonga and score a key try.

Loading Instagram content

Volkman played the final 27 minutes after Chanel Harris-Tavita strained his hamstring while kicking for goal, sparking a Samoan revival that just fell short despite the Toa outscoring Tonga four tries to three.

"I got rattled in the ribs early and struggled to breathe for about five minutes, but it's so good to be out there with my usos (brothers)," Volkman said.

"The first thing I thought was about Chanel. You never want to see a teammate go down like that and to me the way to honour him, to show respect, was to get on and do a job.

"He did a pretty good job for the majority of the game and it made my job easy."

Ronald Volkman has rebuilt his NRL career with Parramatta this year. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Volkman's play — the sharp feet, quick hands, a nose for the tryline and a big shot on Tongan backrower Siua Wong — would have been familiar to any Parramatta fans in the record-breaking crowd.

He made his NRL return for the Eels last year and just getting back at all and having his shoulder hold up was a blessing, even if they lost the two games by a combined total of 88-24.

This season, with the highly-rated Jonah Pezet arriving for one year, Volkman didn't expect to play any first grade.

But instead he relieved the injured Pezet in Round 6 and never looked back, playing every game for the rest of the season and signing a new two-year deal with the Eels in September.

He finished the year a blue and gold fan favourite, with Volkamania running wild among the Parramatta faithful.

In 2027 he'll act as a back-up to Mitchell Moses and Jarome Luai, but the latter has already had an impact on Volkman through Samoa camp.

"He's given me confidence to do what I do," Volkman said.

"The way he trains and prepares himself during the week is relentless.

"He's such a competitor but that's all I can say, because if he hears this he'll think I love him."

Tonga and Samoa can be Origin for the new century The scale and spectacle of Tonga's Rugby League World Cup win over Samoa was not just an instant classic, it proved a demand for this clash that rugby league must find a way to supply.

But before Volkman and Luai are club teammates they will be brothers in arms against Australia, starting in the halves together as the masters of Samoa's chaos.

A win over the Kangaroos would be a glittering prize at any time but with a World Cup final berth on the line the stakes are even higher it shapes as the biggest night of Volkman's career.

It would be Samoa's second and Volkman remembers watching the first four years ago and dreaming of being a part of it. Now, against all odds, that dream is real and the best could still be yet to come.

"I'd just started my first pre-season with the Warriors and it was mind-blowing, to see Samoa on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"We have the chance to do it again next week, so let's do it. I can't wait."

World.title: Opals veteran opens door to Australian return after WNBA retirement
World.content:
Opals Star Bec Allen has kept the door ajar for a return to Australia's domestic women's basketball competition after ending a glittering 11-year tenure in the WNBA.

The 33-year-old's decision to leave the top women's basketball competition in the world has raised questions about whether she is preparing to finish her career back home in the WNBL.

"It's something that I'm not saying a hard no on. Right now the answer is no, purely because my body just needs rest," Allen told AAP.

Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven Australia's Izzy Borlase falls just short of a title as her Atlanta Dream are beaten by Golden State Valkyries in game seven of the WNBA Finals.

"After a year, maybe I'll get a call from Cheryl [Chambers] or a good friend like that, and I'll jump back in and play in Geelong or something like that.

"I just know that I want to be in Melbourne.

"I want to be in Australia and you can't say a hard no to anything."

Allen has a sparkling history in Australia's top domestic league, debuting with the Dandenong Rangers in the 2010-2011 campaign and playing in the competition until 2016.

She claimed the league's Defensive Player of the Year award in 2014, before signing her first WNBA contract with the New York Liberty in 2015.

The WNBL's chief operations officer, Justin Nelson, said he had no doubt some clubs had inquired about securing her signature.

"Bec is an incredible role model, an incredible athlete. She's done so much for girls and women in basketball," he told AAP.

Bec Allen was a member of the Opals squad at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

"All of the fans around Australia would love nothing better than to see her playing in the WNBL, and if the league or I can do anything to help make that happen, we'd love to see Bec playing."

Allen has plans to become a player agent and pursue commentary, but the Tokyo Olympian is currently relishing in some much-deserved rest, having represented the Connecticut Sun, Phoenix Mercury and Chicago Sky before coming back to New York for one final season in 2026.

Reuniting with her past team proved the right move as Allen won the WNBA Commissioner's Cup in June and reached the semi-finals last month.

"My first [WNBA season] was in 2015, and I had impostor syndrome at the beginning, and then I got to realise after years that, hey, I belong here," Allen said.

"I never thought that when I started, I'd play 11 years in the league.

"Body, mind, heart … I've given the game all of myself in those capacities, and so now it's time for the next chapter."

AAP

World.title: Maxwell retires from international cricket but continues franchise T20 career
World.content:
Australian short-form cricket star Glenn Maxwell has retired from the international game.

The 38-year-old retired from one-day international cricket in 2025, but has now hung up his bat and gloves for Australia's Twenty20 team and his state team.

"Post the last one-day game for Victoria, speaking to my teammates and letting them know that was gonna be my last game for the state was probably harder than I thought it was going to be; got a little choked up," Maxwell said on The Final Word.

Maxwell represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka earlier this year and, across his career, played 130 T20 internationals, scoring 2,897 runs at 28.97 and with a strike rate of 154.42.

He also took 51 wickets and claimed 62 catches, with a career-high score of 145 not out against Sri Lanka in 2016.

"I'm grateful for the time I was able to play for my country," he said.

"If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Vic change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.

"I'm extremely grateful to have played that much for my country and to hopefully inspire some kids who want to take the game up, to want to play differently and to be open and vulnerable and to not shy away and be themselves.

"It was pretty incredible when even getting my first Test cap, well and truly before I was probably ready.

"It was pretty exciting, and I'm glad they took a gamble on me, and I'm glad I could, at different stages, repay the faith and be afforded the chance to play as much, for as far, as I did."

Maxwell also played seven Tests for Australia and 149 ODIs, and enjoyed an expansive and productive First Class and List A career with Victoria, too.

He will continue to play Twenty20 franchise cricket, including for the Melbourne Stars in the upcoming Big Bash League.

AAP

World.title: Ciaron Maher becomes first trainer to sweep Melbourne Cup placings
World.content:
Point of Law, a horse sold by King Charles III in July, has won the Melbourne Cup in just its sixth start.

The three-year-old colt trained by Ciaron Maher firmed as the favourite just before the jump, taking the tag away from Hopewell Rock, which began the day as the most fancied to win the famous 3,200m race.

Ridden by Alice Springs native Ethan Brown, Point of Law stormed home late, chasing down long-time leader Royal Supremacy with 150 metres to go, to win ahead of Zahrann and Juja Kibo.

Mahar became the first trainer in Melbourne Cup history to train the trifecta.

Point of Law, the son of famous champion Frankle, was bred in England and owned by King Charles III before being sold in August to an Australian consortium following his Group 3 Bahrain Trophy win at Newmarket.

Its two runs in Australia have both been victorious after winning October's Geelong Cup, becoming just the fourth horse to claim the Geelong-Melbourne Cup double after Media Puzzle (2002), Americain (2010) and Dunaden (2011).

Earlier, Chris Waller-trained Asterix was scratched from the Cup after stewards deemed medication had been used on the horse today. Waller explained it was a simple mistake in the heat of the moment.

Look back at all the action of Melbourne Cup Day at Flemington in our live blog below.

World.title: Addo-Carr's future in Parramatta's hands as B-sample returns negative
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr's immediate playing future is in the hands of the Parramatta hierarchy after police advised the winger his second result from a roadside drugs test had come back negative.

Addo-Carr met Eels officials at a board meeting on Monday afternoon to respond to a breach notice after it was widely presumed the former Test and State of Origin star would be sacked.

The Eels released a statement afterwards.

Eels star Addo-Carr allegedly returns positive test for cocaine NRL player Josh Addo-Carr is being investigated by police after allegedly returning a positive test for cocaine.

"Josh and his legal team were given the opportunity to respond to the notice," the Eels said.

"The club will consider their submission and make a decision in due course."

The 31-year-old allegedly tested positive to cocaine at a random roadside test in September.

But police have confirmed to AAP that no further action will be taken, leaving Addo-Carr to potentially earn a stay of execution.

"About 11.10pm on Friday [11 September 2026], officers attached to Inner West Police Area Command were patrolling Enmore Road, Newtown, when they stopped the driver of a vehicle for random testing," a NSW Police spokeswoman said on Monday: "The driver — a 31-year-old man — was subjected to a roadside breath test, which returned a negative result. "The driver underwent a preliminary drug wipe, which allegedly returned a positive indication for cocaine. An oral fluid sample was obtained and sent away for forensic testing. Following the testing the result has returned a negative result. No further police action is expected."

Addo-Carr has scored 27 tries in two seasons with the Parramatta Eels. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Addo-Carr was sacked by Canterbury almost two years ago to the day for testing positive to cocaine.

He declined to talk to media after leaving the club's headquarters at Belmore about 6pm.

But his lawyer, Elias Tabchouri, thanked the club for being "generous with their time".

"The club were able to allow us to express our thoughts in relation to this situation," Tabchouri said.

"We remain positive in relation to the negative finding for the B test, and we remain committed to the club."

Pressed on whether Addo-Carr would remain with the Eels in 2027, after bagging 27 tries in his first two seasons in blue and gold, Tabchouri said: "That's a matter for the club right now. We're waiting for the outcome".

"Josh has always maintained — and still maintains — a commitment to the Parramatta club."

AAP

Tech.title: Moft’s new origami case adds a kickstand and grip to the iPhone Duo
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Originally released in early 2025 as an accessory for the iPad, Moft has redesigned its Dynamic Folio as a case for the iPhone Duo that does more than just protect Apple’s folding phone. You can use it to prop the Duo up at several different angles for hands-free use, or reconfigure the Dynamic Folio’s origami-like screen cover and use it as a finger grip while you’re holding the phone.

The new Dynamic Folio Case for iPhone Duo is now available for preorder through Moft’s online store for $89.99 in navy blue or misty cove plus sapphire color options, with shipping expected to start in mid December. That’s a small bump in price over Moft’s $69.99 Dynamic Folio, but while that accessory attaches magnetically to the back of the Duo for easier removal, the new case version is designed to clip securely to the phone while providing additional protection for the back and the front and rear edges of Apple’s foldable.

Image: Moft

Both versions of the Dynamic Folio help protect the iPhone Duo’s outer display from scratches while it’s in your bag or pocket, but that cover also folds multiple ways to function as a kickstand that supports the Duo in landscape or portrait orientations. It can even hold the Duo at an angle in “Lounge Mode” so you can more comfortably use the phone hands-free while lying in bed, or it can function as a PopSockets alternative, although it doesn’t look quite as comfortable to hold as those popular grips.

Tech.title: The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is about to launch its new Xbox Nano controller tomorrow, and the tiny device has a little secret. The Nano can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi to improve latency. It’s a feature Microsoft hasn’t officially announced yet, but one I’ve been anticipating since the Xbox Nano leaked earlier this year.

The Nano will be able to connect directly to Microsoft’s cloud servers to reduce latency, much like how Google’s Stadia controllers used to work. This new cloud connect feature for the Nano is being privately tested on the new Xbox Cloud Gaming website, and it will require you to pair the controller over Wi-Fi to Microsoft’s Xbox Cloud Gaming servers using the Xbox mobile app.

The new Xbox Cloud Gaming website will let you connect a Nano controller to the cloud. Screenshot: Microsoft

I’m expecting Microsoft to announce this as a preview for the new Xbox Nano controller soon, before it’s fully supported across Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and on smart TVs. I first started reporting that Microsoft was planning a new controller with Wi-Fi connectivity to reduce Xbox Cloud Gaming latency earlier this year. I’d expect the upcoming Xbox Elite 3 controller will also have the same functionality.

Microsoft had also planned to introduce a direct-to-cloud feature on a new Xbox controller, codenamed Sebile, as part of an Xbox Series X refresh console in 2024. The refresh console was canceled, and it’s not clear when we’ll eventually see a new Xbox wireless controller with direct cloud functionality.

Tech.title: Google is entirely disabling Search in schools that don’t want AI
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is completely turning off Search in schools that reject its AI features, the company told The New York Times. The decision was also shared in a broader education-related update from Google on Tuesday, saying that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search “will be entirely off” for K-12 student accounts unless “administrators explicitly turn them on.”

Administrators will not be given the option to toggle Gemini-powered features off without disabling Search, however. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the NYT, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” adding that schools that disable Google’s AI features “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

The announcement comes just months after Google turned its Gemini AI assistant on by default inside the Google Classroom app, which is used by more than 150 million teachers and students globally. The move added to skepticism surrounding Google’s introduction of AI in schools amid reports of declining test scores and other impacts on students’ learning abilities. Last month, lawmakers pressed Google on the “potential harms” of putting its AI products in schools. Though Google is no longer turning on AI features in schools by default, this choice comes at a cost.

The company is also attempting to address concerns about students using its AI features to find “shortcuts” instead of solving problems themselves. Google is embedding its Guided Learning feature, which is supposed to help students work through problems, into its AI Overviews in Search. Google will begin testing this feature in select US schools this month.

Tech.title: Xbox’s smallest-ever controller is surprisingly comfortable
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Even though I knew Microsoft’s new Xbox Nano controller was tiny, I still gasped when I unboxed it a few days ago. The compact controller is small enough to slip into a pocket unnoticed, and it has been designed specifically for younger people, or for anyone with smaller hands.

I’m not young, but I do have small hands, and I’ve been surprised at how comfortable the Nano is during gaming sessions. At just over 5 inches long, almost everything on this controller has been shrunk down somehow. The ABXY buttons are ever so slightly smaller than a regular Xbox controller, and the thumbsticks feel like miniature versions. Microsoft hasn’t changed the D-pad, though, or the size of the glowing Xbox button at the center of the controller.

The big difference I noticed with the Nano over a regular Xbox controller was the size of the triggers. While they are fully analog and pressure sensitive, they have more of a click when you bottom them out compared with the thud on a bigger Xbox controller. They’re noticeably smaller, as you’d expect, and the bumper buttons above the triggers feel less clicky than the regular ones.

I thought the Nano controller would feel awkward after a few hours of gaming, but the grips really help with comfort levels — a lot of smaller controllers sacrifice grips to keep the controller thin and lightweight. It does mean the Nano doesn’t sit flush on a table, but at 101 grams (0.22 pounds) it’s still really lightweight.

Previous Next

















1 / 10 The Nano controller is ideal for young people.

I can’t speak for those with bigger hands, but I’d expect the Nano controller won’t be well-suited to everyone. The size makes it ideal for young children, though. I tried to get my 1-year-old son to try the Nano, and he responded with a smile, so I guess he likes it.

I haven’t had enough time to get a full idea of battery life yet, but it seems to drain around 10 percent in around 30 to 40 minutes. That suggests a lot less battery life than the 30 hours you’d get on a rechargeable pack for the larger Xbox wireless controller. Thankfully, the Nano charges quickly, and I found I could get from 30 percent to 60 percent charge in less than 10 minutes. You can plug in a USB-C charger to top up the battery and carry on playing while you charge.

The only thing missing on the Nano controller that I would have loved is vibration support. I assume it’s not there because of an impact on battery life, because even the smaller Nintendo Joy-Con controllers have rumble support.

The Xbox Nano controller will be available on November 4th, priced at $49.99.

Tech.title: Windows 11 is now ‘up to 40 percent faster’ on PCs with 8GB of RAM
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft has been doing a lot of work to improve memory usage and increase performance on Windows 11 PCs over the past year. Last month the company revealed Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on PCs with 8GB of RAM, and now the company is releasing a new update today that includes further memory improvements.

“On 8 GB PCs, Windows is now up to 20 percent more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40 percent faster in our lab test,” says Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. One of the key ways Microsoft has achieved better performance on PCs with 8GB of RAM is through compression.

“As a result, Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return,” says Davuluri. This compression helps Windows avoid writing data to a virtual memory paging file on a disk, slowing down apps and performance.

Microsoft is also making improvements across Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365 apps that reduce “committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB.” Memory improvements in Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook alone add up to 360MB of RAM savings. Windows 11 no longer loads widgets on a PC with 8GB of RAM until you open the widgets panel, saving around 200MB of RAM. Inactive tabs in Edge now sleep after 15 minutes, reducing memory consumption further.

While Microsoft is shipping an update to Windows 11 with these memory improvements, the company is still working on improving RAM usage in Windows in the coming months. Memory compression will get “smarter and more efficient” over the next few months, and Windows features and apps will share more common parts like widgets and search sharing a single web engine. Microsoft is also working with PC makers and chipmakers to optimize how much memory a PC needs to reserve for its hardware, enabling more for Windows.

Tech.title: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
Tech.content:
The 2026 midterm elections will determine the scope of President Donald Trump’s power in his final two years in office, and signal what voters care about going into the 2028 presidential election. While this year’s races are expected to be most broadly defined by affordability issues, there are several topics impacting the tech industry that appear to be on voters’ minds.

Among them are concerns about data centers, and whether voters will have to bear the burden of higher energy costs, AI safety, and the rapid expansion of surveillance technology through Flock. There’s also the question of how to tax billionaires’ wealth in California, a topic that has driven heavy tech spending and creative stock class structures meant to keep tech executives from fleeing the state should a ballot measure pass.

Tech.title: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
Tech.content:
is a journalist with 15 years of experience covering how Big Tech companies are reshaping society.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s latest earnings show how it’s continuing to capitalize on the AI boom without busting its budget on the infrastructure spending consuming its competitors.

Overall, Apple posted its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone and Mac sales continued to grow strongly in the fourth quarter. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares nevertheless fell in premarket trading Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze its profit margins in the holiday quarter.

Apple hasn’t disclosed how much of its revenue growth reflects AI demand or higher prices, but its executives clearly see the technology as a way to drive further sales.

During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh cited a “wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time.”

“On the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities,” he said. “And we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Apple can sell its giant user base the devices they use for AI, even if the AI itself comes from someone else. It can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. And it can charge customers who want more access to its own AI features.

“We see tremendous opportunity in AI,” John Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.

AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the earnings call, according to financial research platform AlphaSense — even more than on the call following Apple’s unveiling of the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.

Mentions of AI or “Apple Intelligence” on earnings calls

On the call, Apple continued to position itself as the interface through which consumers use AI — including competitors’ technology. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, it already has an enormous audience for whatever AI services emerge.

Apple, unlike its Big Tech peers, isn’t pouring comparable sums into infrastructure. Its approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology. Siri AI uses models developed with Google’s Gemini technology while Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation.

Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon’s $77.3 billion and Alphabet’s $51.4 billion. Those totals cover companywide CapEx, not just AI, and exclude some AI expenses. Apple’s operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased R&D spending, including on AI. Siri AI’s cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales. Those costs could grow with usage: Parekh said it’s too early to predict how many requests will require servers rather than on-device processing. Still, Apple’s capital spending remains just a fraction of its peers’.

More AI usage also gives Apple something to sell.

Siri AI is only beginning to reach customers. Apple launched the revamped assistant in beta for US English users in September and expanded it to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.

Apple plans to turn some of that usage into subscription revenue. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits. Customers who need more capacity “will be able to purchase expanded access in the future,” he said. “In the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we’ve been adding more capabilities and features to it.”

Apple also benefits when customers buy its hardware to run AI locally, including models developed by other companies. Mac, Ternus said, is “having an AI moment all its own.”

“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities.”

Apple offered specific examples of companies putting its computers to work on AI. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, avoiding cloud token costs for those tasks. Christie’s is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates.

For those customers, buying Apple hardware provides a way to use AI without paying a cloud provider for every request.

Mac Mini and Mac Studio, Ternus said, “are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible.”

The Mac Mini’s emergence as an AI machine has given the small, screenless desktop a new constituency among developers and hobbyists looking for a relatively affordable way to run models locally. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio’s capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.

Apple also makes money when customers subscribe to someone else’s AI. Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to analytics firm AppMagic.

That revenue, of course, depends on customers paying through Apple’s system. OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead of the App Store, bypassing Apple’s commissions, The Wall Street Journal reported. Apple’s position gives it a way to profit from competitors’ AI, but those competitors have an incentive to find a route around its fees.

Still, Apple already has multiple ways to benefit from people using AI. It can sell the computer, collect a subscription commission, and eventually charge for more of its own services. It doesn’t have to build every model — or fund infrastructure on its competitors’ scale — to get paid.
